They get video back, with clips joined and data laid over frames. That last step, rendering, is the slow part. It is slower than the query work itself, and today it runs through slow scripts.

Vidformer adds fast, drop-in rendering to that flow. Users state what they want in a plain, declarative way. The system then speeds up how result videos are made. For teams that search large video sets, this cuts wait time. It makes hands-on video search feel quick and direct.
arxiv-2601-17521:
Dean Kraizberg studies two-player games on infinite trees and their link to prefix codes. Players move in turns along the tree's branches. The trees here are full and regular. The winning set is open in the product topology. Open games have known ties to code design. Prefix codes are codes where no codeword starts another. They run all data compression.

Kraizberg seeks sharp winning criteria for such games. Clear criteria tell who wins from a given start. They also expose how game shape mirrors code shape. That mirror can move results between fields. Game theory and information theory both gain. The work is pure, but its roots touch daily tech.
arxiv-2601-17621:
Tim Ritmeester proposes a new kind of statistical interval. It sits between Bayesian credible intervals and frequentist ones. A standard credible interval claims a set level of belief from full data. Ritmeester weakens that claim in a set way. Having seen only the interval, not the full data, we should still hold at least the stated belief in it.

The design uses one-dimensional priors. It aims for finite-sample claims that stay honest. A middle ground could serve fields split by the old debate. Health and policy work need intervals users can trust. Finite-sample care matters most when data is scarce. The proposal gives statisticians a fresh option to test.
arxiv-2601-17721:
Huy Trinh, Elliot Creager, and George Shaker detect quiet human presence with radar. Radar sensing guards privacy better than cameras or wearables. Long-term care is a prime use case. The hard case is semi-static presence. A person lying, sitting, or standing still gives only subtle micro-motions. Low-resolution SIMO FMCW radar buries near-zero Doppler energy under static clutter.

Their method amplifies respiration in the Doppler domain. Breathing is a steady sign of life even at rest. Lifting that signal above clutter makes presence reads reliable. Care staff gain a quiet monitor that respects dignity. The work pairs signal craft with a real care need.
arxiv-2601-17821:
Jose Segovia-Martin studies how cooperation can get stuck in games played on a grid. His 2026 preprint returns to a classic setup, the spatial Prisoner's Dilemma of Nowak and May. In that setup, players copy the best neighbor they see. Past runs show cooperation falling off a cliff near a key temptation value. The author looks at the shapes that form on the lattice at that point.

Those shapes act as traps set by the layout of the game. Once play falls into a trap, cooperation has a hard time coming back. Naming the trap helps explain why a smooth change in payoffs can cause a sudden drop. The work speaks to the wider study of how norms hold or break.
arxiv-2601-17921:
Yi Zhao, Qinghua Yao, Xinyuan Song, and Wei Zhu refine a cheap way to tune large language models. Their 2026 preprint is about LoRA, which adapts a model by adding small low-rank parts. The standard form gives each part the same rank. Later work showed that picking ranks with care boosts scores. The question is how to split a fixed rank budget across the model.

The team's method, ShapLoRA, borrows the Shapley value from game theory. That value scores how much each part adds to the whole. Ranks then flow to the parts that earn them. Smarter ranks mean better tuning for the same cost. The idea helps groups that cannot afford full fine-tuning.
arxiv-2601-18621:
Fernando Belchior and Roberto Maluf study when two maths forms of the same field world are in truth the same. The world at hand is a pared-down form of light and field maths that keeps just one line of space. On top of it sits a cross term that joins two kinds of field. One form of the world has strict rules for what counts as the same state. The next form drops those rules.

The pair show the two forms match when no fields are at play. They prove the match in two ways: by a straight check of how each form moves, and by a master form that holds both. Such proofs of match let staff pick the form that is less hard to use. They also guard against the same world being counted twice as two finds.
arxiv-2601-19121:
Guilin Zhang and three co-authors put language models in charge of a team of recommendation agents. A recommender must serve many goals at once while obeying hard business rules. A shop, for instance, may demand that each list span several sellers and meet fairness and coverage floors.

The models act as orchestrators, steering sub agents while keeping every rule in force. Letting a model juggle goals is easy; keeping it inside hard limits is the hard part. Systems that do both could tune feeds in real time without breaking the rules firms must keep.
arxiv-2601-19221:
Liu Xiao rethinks the inner state of recurrent language models as something that can be edited. Modern recurrent nets like RWKV model nearby text well and keep a fixed size state, a core edge over transformers. Yet few studies treat that state as a store of knowledge that can be read or changed.

The work, DREAMSTATE, diffuses both states and parameters, borrowing the gradual noise and cleanup of image diffusion. If a recurrent model's state can be edited like a file, builders gain a new lever for fixing facts and behavior. The study opens that lever to its first close look.
arxiv-2601-19421:
Josh Susak, Yifu Liu, Pascal Jansen, and Mark Colley design car assistants that speak first, at the right moments. In-vehicle conversational assistants mostly wait for the driver to ask. The next step is proactive help: the car offers or starts an action before being asked, without nagging or distracting.

The team tunes that proactive behavior with multi objective Bayesian optimization, balancing gains in driver experience against costs. A car that speaks up must earn each interruption. Their method seeks settings where the help lands as timely rather than pushy, a design question every smart car will face.
arxiv-2601-19621:
Nagula Venkata Anirudh, Sachidananda Behera, and Kirti Chandra Sahu simulate what happens when a drop hits a liquid surface. Real drops are rarely perfect spheres. Their shape as they fall changes how they splash. The team runs three-dimensional computer simulations of non-spherical drops striking a still liquid film.

They vary the drop's shape and its impact speed across a wide range. The simulations reveal several distinct behaviours, from smooth spreading to two kinds of splashing. In some cases the drop throws up a canopy, and finger-like jets at the crown can turn unstable. The authors map which behaviour occurs for each mix of shape and speed. Such maps help engineers predict splashes in printing, spraying, and fuel systems.
arxiv-2601-19821:
Kun Li, Michael Ying Yang, and Sami Sebastian Brandt build systems that answer questions about music videos. Audio-visual question answering demands joint reasoning over sound, image, and text. For music, the audio track is not background; it carries the melody, rhythm, and instruments the question may target. Many existing systems lean heavily on the visual stream and underuse the sound.

Their method is guided by the query itself. It models interactions across space, time, and frequency in the audio-visual features. Frequency matters for music in a way it does not for speech scenes. Letting the question steer the fusion should focus the model on the right moments. The work pushes multimodal systems to treat music as a first-class signal.
arxiv-2601-19921:
Xiaochen Zhu and five colleagues dissect multi-agent debate, a popular trick for improving language model answers. Several model instances argue, then settle on an answer. The method costs more compute than a simple majority vote. Recent work shows plain debate often underperforms that cheaper baseline.

The authors ask what role confidence and diversity play in the outcome. Under uniform agents with uniform belief updates, debate preserves expected correctness, so it cannot reliably help. Variety among agents and well-used confidence signals are the candidate fixes. The analysis explains many disappointing results in the literature. It also tells builders when debate is worth its price and when voting suffices.
arxiv-2601-20121:
Jiaming Wang and five colleagues study a long-noted pattern in the solar wind, the stream of charged particles flowing from the Sun. The magnetic field carried by the wind shows a one-over-f pattern of power across low frequencies. That band runs from near the period of the Sun's spin down to much shorter times.

The authors compare synthetic data with real solar wind records to test ideas about how the pattern arises. Their focus is on superposition, the adding of many signals into one. Knowing the source of this pattern helps physicists read spacecraft data and model the space weather that reaches Earth.
arxiv-2601-20321:
A team from Beihang University, ShanghaiTech University, and partner institutes studies how to give robot vision-language-action models a sense of touch. These models are strong generalists for manipulation, but they rely almost wholly on vision. Contact-rich tasks need precise force control and physical reasoning that sight alone cannot supply.

The authors align tactile and force signals with the model's vision and language inputs. Their aim is force-aware manipulation, where the robot adjusts its grip and pressure as contact changes. Robots that can feel what they hold would be safer around fragile objects and people.
arxiv-2601-20521:
Jose Antonio Moreno and seven colleagues measure the superconducting density of states in nitridized aluminum thin films. Nitride-based superconductors often outperform the bare metal in devices, such as sensors for cosmic radiation. Niobium and titanium nitrides have already improved devices for quantum technology.

The authors turn to aluminum treated with nitrogen and probe how its states are distributed in energy. That distribution governs how the film behaves in circuits and detectors. Aluminum is the workhorse of superconducting quantum devices, so a nitride route to better films could raise the quality of qubits and sensors alike.
arxiv-2601-20621:
Agnieszka Bodzenta, Tomasz Pełka, and Dario Weißmann study the saturation of algebraic surfaces. The saturation of a surface is its maximal open embedding whose complement has dimension zero, so only isolated points are added. For schemes, the notion was introduced by Bodzenta with A. Bondal.

They showed that a surface's saturation can be recovered from the category of reflexive sheaves on it. That is a striking bridge: a geometric completion read off from a category of sheaves. The present work develops this theory of saturation for algebraic surfaces. That is a strong claim, and the proof is the heart of the work. It gives the field a new way to build a whole from a part.
arxiv-2601-20821:
Katherine Paulson, Taylor Okonek, and Jon Wakefield build a better way to estimate how many young children die. Their 2026 paper presents a survival framework for child mortality rates. Child mortality is a key sign of population health. Yet many countries lack strong vital registration to measure it well. Rates must then be pieced together from surveys and other partial sources.

Large efforts already model these rates. The United Nations group for child mortality estimation and the Global Burden of Disease study both do so. The authors' framework uses multiple data types at once. It targets the standard summaries: neonatal, infant, and under-five mortality. Better estimates guide health spending where records are thin. The work helps ensure that scarce data still yields rates that leaders can trust.
arxiv-2601-20921:
Faruk Alpay and Levent Sarioglu propose a new index tool for data stored in DNA. Their 2026 paper adds a stochastic primitive for molecular archives. Random access is a central bottleneck in DNA-based data storage. Current systems fetch records by PCR or other multi-step lab work. Those steps do not support fast, parallel, content-based queries. The authors aim to close that gap.

They introduce the Holographic Bloom Filter, or HBF. It encodes key-pointer links as a single high-dimensional vector. A query can probe that vector at once, with no lab work per lookup. The design promises database-like search over DNA stores. The paper lays out the primitive and its promise. It sketches a future where DNA stores answer questions at electronic speed.
arxiv-2601-21621:
Matéo Mahaut and Marco Baroni ask whether vision models not only end at similar inner representations but also get there the same way. A growing body of work says bigger models converge to shared, almost universal representations. That holds despite different training goals, data, and input types.

The authors study the intermediate steps that lead to those shared endpoints. Do models pass through the same stages, or only meet at the finish? The answer bears on whether there is one natural way to process images. It also affects how safely parts can be swapped between models.
arxiv-2601-21921:
Zhouyou Gu and co-authors plan the backbone of future satellite internet. Laser links between low Earth orbit satellites can carry huge capacity, but managing them is hard. Terminals are few, they must aim mechanically, and the network's shape changes rapidly as satellites move.

The team studies the joint problem of establishing connections and routing traffic in real time across mega-constellations. Their 2026 preprint uses duality-guided graph learning, letting optimization theory steer a learning system. Good joint decisions mean fewer dropped links and better use of scarce laser terminals. As constellations grow to thousands of satellites, planning methods that keep up in real time become a condition for the whole service to work.
arxiv-2601-22021:
Yu Chen, Genjiu Xu, Sinan Feng, and Chaoqian Wang model what happens after a disaster, when resources are scarce and infrastructure is paralyzed. Recovery depends on coordination between shelters that hold supplies and the victims who need them. The two groups influence each other as aid moves and needs change.

The authors build a two-layer network model of that feedback. One layer represents shelters, the other victims, and cooperative behavior evolves on the coupled network as resources are redistributed. Their 2026 preprint studies how cooperation emerges or collapses under different conditions. Insights like these could help planners design aid systems that encourage trust and sharing when both are hardest to sustain.
arxiv-2601-22321:
Dominic Payne and a large team track bends in the solar wind near a key border called the Alfvén surface. Inside that border, the Sun's field rules the flow; outside, the flow breaks free. Their 2026 preprint studies sharp magnetic bends, known as switchbacks, on both sides.

They sort the bends by a shared angle measure. A thin shift layer near the border seems to steer how the bends grow and change. That clue helps explain where switchbacks are born. It also guides reads of data from probes that dive near the Sun.
arxiv-2601-22421:
AlexKen Lee and Keyun Wu ask if supersymmetry could leave a hum in the background of gravitational waves. That background hum may have been born in the reheating era, just after the cosmos' first burst of growth. Their 2026 preprint builds a sample contact point for the idea.

The contact links one inflaton field to the D-term parts of a pair of chiral superfields. From it they work out how strong the hum might be. Future detectors could then look for that shape. A match would be a rare clue to physics past the standard model.
arxiv-2601-22821:
Alex Elliott, Scott Parkins, and Takao Aoki propose a way to make linked light, steadily, from a single atom. The light sits in the telecom band, the range used by fiber networks. Two lasers, tuned with care, drive the atom up a two-photon path to a state that emits the wanted light.

A steady source of linked photons would fit well with existing fiber lines. It could serve quantum networks that send secure keys or link distant quantum machines. Single-atom sources are prized because they are clean, small, and well understood.
arxiv-2602-02421:
Florentin Daniel and 5 co-authors model how magnetic fields, flows, and waves interact inside stars, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Deep radiative layers of stars are stably stratified, and their magnetic fields are hard to observe directly. Recent simulations suggest a dynamo, where motion sustains a magnetic field, can operate even in those quiet layers.

Internal gravity waves travel inward from neighboring convective zones and dissipate, driving an oscillating shear layer that can feed the dynamo. Magnetic forces then push back on the mean flow through the Lorentz force. To capture this loop cheaply, the authors build a one-dimensional mean-field model using coefficients taken from three-dimensional spherical simulations. Adding magnetism creates new dynamical regimes. The fast shear oscillation near the wave source is perturbed, which can filter the wave energy sent deeper and alter how the star's core rotation evolves.
arxiv-2602-02621:
Faizuddin Ahmed and 2 co-authors probe a charged black hole sitting in dark matter and a cloud of strings through its shadow and ringing, in a 2026 arXiv paper. It combines magnetic charge from nonlinear electrodynamics with a logarithmic dark matter fix and a string-cloud setting that leaves spacetime not quite flat.

Horizons are mapped first, sorting ordinary black holes from extremal cases and naked singularities. Light bending yields the photon sphere and shadow, and both extra additions enlarge the shadow's size. Neutral particle orbits give energies, angular momenta, and the innermost stable orbit. Oscillation frequencies from those orbits are derived, and scalar perturbations produce an effective potential that sets the quasinormal spectrum, the characteristic ringing tones of the hole. Transmission and reflection probabilities answer the two environmental settings in opposite ways. Separate fingerprints could let future observations pin down dark matter and string effects one by one.
arxiv-2602-03121:
Haoze Guo, together with 1 co-author, catalogs the small on-screen cues that hint how social media feeds are ranked. Those cues differ across platforms and often sit in hard-to-find places. Without a shared scheme, comparing platforms or judging whether transparency creates accountability rather than mere understanding stays difficult for researchers and users alike.

Guo's team proposes a taxonomy organized around design form, information content, and user agency. They apply it across six major platforms, building a reference set of common feature archetypes. The taxonomy can test whether a transparency feature works as intended. It also points toward designs that make algorithms easier to inspect, act on, and contest.
arxiv-2602-03421:
Oblivious transfer is a cryptographic building block where a receiver picks one message without the sender learning the choice. Hadi Aghaee and 2 co-authors ask whether it can run over noisy network channels when the parties also share general non-signaling correlations. Their 2026 paper models what the parties share as an arbitrary three-party non-signaling box.

The main result is negative: perfect oblivious transfer cannot be achieved in this setting. Even in the long-run limit, leakage cannot be made negligible. Repeated use of the resource sharpens the receivers' ability to distinguish messages never meant for them. Interestingly, the receivers' own privacy faces no such universal barrier, so the impossibility cuts in only one direction.
arxiv-2602-03521:
The last stretch of the power grid, where homes connect, is where solar panels, heat pumps, and car chargers are reshaping demand. Manuel Treutlein and 6 co-authors release FeederBW in a 2026 paper. The dataset holds real measurements from 200 low-voltage feeders in Germany, recorded over two years by the operator Netze BW.

Each feeder comes with weather data and rich metadata, including housing units and the installed power of low-carbon technology as it changed over time. One-minute resolution and strong solar feed-in make the set unusual. It supports load forecasting, non-intrusive load monitoring, and synthetic data generation. The records already show the growing fingerprint of low-carbon technology on neighborhood grids.
arxiv-2602-03721:
Growing a perfect germanium crystal for a physics detector is a craft held by very few companies worldwide. Athul Prem and 4 co-authors bring machine learning to that craft in a 2026 paper. Detector-grade high-purity germanium underpins the most sensitive radiation detectors, but yield in Czochralski growth is limited by coupled, nonlinear process physics.

A bidirectional LSTM network with multi-head attention learns from time-resolved growth data across 48 independent crystal runs. The data include heater power, pull rate, and impurity indicators. It predicts each run's final detector-grade fraction before the crystal is even cut. SHAP analysis names impurity concentration and growth rate as the dominant factors, matching empirical wisdom. The framework promises less trial-and-error tuning and a path to scaling production.
arxiv-2602-03921:
Duc Hoang and 3 co-authors benchmark how mixture-of-experts models should cache their specialists. These models activate only a few expert subnetworks per input, so keeping the right experts in memory decides speed. Their 2026 framework, SpecMD, compares caching policies across hardware setups under realistic limits.

Experiments showed expert access ignores the recency patterns classic caches assume. Their new Least-Stale policy exploits predictable access instead, cutting collision misses dramatically against the standard rule. Hit rates above eighty-eight percent came with much faster first-token times while using only a small slice of video memory.
arxiv-2602-04821:
Joydeep Chandra and 3 co-authors unify traffic forecasting, anomaly spotting, and safe control in a 2026 scheme called STREAM-RL. City traffic systems must predict conditions, spot problems, and act safely, ideally with firm promises at each step.

Three parts carry the design. A conformal forecaster uses its own doubt to reweight graph attention while keeping distribution-free coverage. A residual flow network models scaled errors with false-discovery control under dependence. A world-model agent adds stability proofs and carries doubt into its imagined rollouts. On real traffic data, the system improved coverage and safety rates over a standard baseline. It also gained higher reward with fast end-to-end response.
arxiv-2602-04921:
John Zhuoyang Ye and Jens Palsberg wrote this 2026 paper on testing quantum error correction. Such correction keeps fragile quantum computations on track, and the standard test injects random faults to see how often the system still fails logically. The leading tool handles small codes well but slows down badly for larger ones at low error rates.

Their approach samples the easy parts of the fault space directly, then extrapolates to cover the rest. With a two-hour budget on a desktop machine, the tool reached code distance 17 at a very low physical error rate, a regime the standard tool cannot reach. For that case it estimated a logical error rate near one in a hundred billion, with high confidence. The work gives quantum engineers a practical way to check bigger designs.
arxiv-2602-05021:
The Magellanic Clouds, the two largest satellite galaxies of the Milky Way, have been pulling on each other for billions of years. Bethany Garver and 3 co-authors reconstruct that history in this 2026 astronomy paper, submitted to MNRAS. Their goal is to explain the warped disc of the Large Cloud and the streamers of stars and gas around both galaxies.

Simple orbit math cannot handle such strong interactions, so the team paired N-body simulations with a genetic algorithm that searches for starting positions 2.5 billion years ago matching today's observations. After about 8,000 simulations, the best model has the two Clouds passing close twice, most recently about 140 million years ago. That encounter warped the Large Cloud's disc and raised ripples about 1.3 kiloparsecs tall, and the model also reproduces a ring feature and the Small Cloud's stretched shape.
arxiv-2602-05221:
Long-baseline neutrino experiments chase three numbers: a CP-violating phase, a mixing angle, and a mass splitting. Bhavna Yadav and 2 co-authors ask how much information the neutrino state itself could ever deliver about each one, in this 2026 particle physics paper. Their tool is quantum Fisher information, the ceiling on precision for any measurement of a quantum state.

Computing that ceiling as a function of baseline over energy, with current best-fit parameters, reveals a sharp hierarchy. The CP phase and the mixing angle show twin-peaked sensitivity profiles, while sensitivity to the mass splitting grows steeply and ends up orders of magnitude larger. Comparing with classical Fisher information from actual flavor measurements shows the standard measurement does not always extract everything the state holds. For the planned DUNE experiment, matter effects notably boost the quantum information about the CP phase at a few giga-electronvolts.
arxiv-2602-05321:
Wide-angle and 360-degree cameras break the assumptions of most 3D reconstruction software, which expects tidy pinhole images. Dongki Jung and 5 co-authors present Wid3R in this 2026 computer vision paper, a feed-forward network that reconstructs multi-view geometry directly from wide field-of-view imagery. No explicit calibration or undistortion step is needed before the network sees the pictures.

The design represents viewing rays with spherical harmonics and adds a camera model token, so the network knows which distortion family it is dealing with and can correct for it internally. The authors describe Wid3R as the first multi-frame feed-forward method supporting full 360 imagery. Training across diverse camera types also improved generalization and eased data scarcity for 360 scenes. On a fisheye benchmark the accuracy score rose by up to about 34 points, and on a 360 indoor dataset by up to about 77 points, over the comparison methods.
arxiv-2602-06021:
When a diffusion model does not just memorise its training set, where do its new samples land? Ye He and two co-authors answer with geometry, building a time-varying family of ridge manifolds from the smoothed data distribution, tracing log-density ridges. Their main result follows generated samples through a reach-align-slide motion, first entering a ridge neighbourhood, then closing in, then sliding along the ridge.

How far a sample sits from the ridge tracks the normal part of training error, while motion along the ridge tracks the tangential part. The authors tie that picture to training dynamics and spell it out for random feature models, where architecture bias and optimisation error split cleanly. Synthetic multimodal tests and MNIST latent-diffusion trials back the geometry in low and high dimensions. The work gives diffusion generalisation a map, not just a mystery.
arxiv-2602-06121:
Ghostly particles called neutrinos may reveal dark matter by bumping into it on their way to Earth. Khushboo Dixit and 2 co-authors search IceCube telescope data for that effect near four active galaxies. Dark matter is expected to pile up in spikes around the huge black holes at those galaxies' centers.

If neutrinos scatter off dark matter, their pattern should shift in a telling way. The team studied each galaxy alone and then stacked all four together. The stacked search gave the tightest limits yet on how strongly dark matter and neutrinos can interact, for both steady and energy-growing interaction strengths. The bounds hold at a high confidence level.
arxiv-2602-06221:
Multiple-choice tests are the standard yardstick for language models, yet many test items are flawed. Nishant Balepur and 9 co-authors built BenchMarker, a toolkit borrowed from education research that uses language model judges to flag bad items. It hunts three flaws: items copied from the open web, cue patterns that allow guessing, and writing errors.

Checked against human labels, the tool then audited a dozen well-known benchmarks. Flaws were common, especially in machine-made and crowdsourced sets. Copied items inflated scores, while writing errors deflated them and shuffled rankings. Earlier repair attempts fixed their target flaws but added new ones. The authors release the toolkit to help benchmark builders do better.
arxiv-2602-06321:
Fast X-ray flashes from deep space, spotted by the Einstein Probe satellite, need visible-light partners to reveal what they are. Run-Duo Liang and a large international collaboration searched public survey archives and transient databases for those partners. Many flashes still lack any firm classification for want of quick follow-up.

The team reports early results from that archival hunt. One flash was matched to a glowing transient already in the records. Spectra of its host galaxy from a large telescope fixed its distance, and its brightness history fits a core-collapse supernova, the death blast of a massive star. Simulations of detectability round out the study, guiding how future flashes can be pinned down faster.
arxiv-2602-06521:
Self-driving systems increasingly combine vision-language-action planning with world models that imagine future scenes, but the two parts often barely share information. Feiyang jia and 6 co-authors present DriveWorld-VLA, which unifies them in a shared latent space. The world model's latent states become the planner's decision states, so imagined scene evolution feeds planning directly.

Because world modeling stays in latent space rather than pixels, the system imagines action-conditioned futures cheaply, without dense annotations. The planner can weigh how candidate actions reshape the future scene before choosing. Open-loop and closed-loop evaluations showed the unified design works, with the world model's foresight improving the planner's decisions across driving scenarios.
arxiv-2602-06621:
Thorben Pieper-Sethmacher and Daniel Paulin give a careful mathematical treatment of generative diffusion models, the tools behind much modern AI data creation. Most such models are built by reversing a process that adds noise. The authors instead start from a reference process and steer it toward the target data by reweighting its paths.

This steering trick, based on a classic change of measure, extends cleanly to infinite-dimensional settings where the usual reversal approach is hard to define. The paper proves the construction works under checkable conditions and bounds how close the result sits to the target. It also shows the steered process can be learned through a score-matching objective, and tests the idea on both synthetic and real data.
arxiv-2602-06721:
Wenxuan Xia, Mingyu Yang, Wentao Li, and Wei Wang speed up filtered nearest-neighbor search, the workhorse of vector databases. Queries often come with attribute limits, such as a label or a price range, and most systems search the whole index to satisfy them. That wastes effort, because easy queries could stop early while hard ones deserve a longer hunt.

The authors build a light model that predicts a query's search cost from clues gathered in a short probing phase, including attribute distributions and early distance statistics. The search then ends when the predicted cost says enough, adapting per query. On six real-world datasets the method ran between 1.1 and 3.7 times faster than strong baselines at 95 percent recall, with accuracy held steady.
arxiv-2602-07321:
Edge devices cannot simply run bigger models: latency, energy, and memory all cap what is possible, even as wireless networks demand more intelligence.  Changyuan Zhao and five co-authors extend context engineering from language models to wireless systems, as a thorough way to boost edge AI without enlarging the model.

The idea is to filter redundant observations and inject task-relevant information selectively at inference time, illustrated by cases such as beam prediction in dynamic environments.  The method treats limited inference-time input as a resource to manage, not a constraint to suffer.  Wireless and edge AI teams get a design discipline for squeezing more intelligence from fixed hardware.
arxiv-2602-07521:
Game AI for Honor of Kings beats top professionals, but those agents are far too heavy for phones.  Xionghui Yang and ten co-authors build a Pareto-guided pipeline for distilling featherweight agents for mobile multiplayer battle arena games.

A high-efficiency student architecture search space tailored to mobile execution, guided by Pareto optimality across results and cost, produces agents that run at high frequency under strict energy and latency limits.  The work systematically bridges large-scale game AI and on-device deployment for the first time.  Mobile game AI builders get a distillation pipeline that treats phone constraints as design inputs, not afterthoughts.
arxiv-2602-07621:
Checking scientific claims against evidence is hard when the evidence lives in figures and tables, and current data sets rarely include genuinely refuted claims.  Xanh Ho and six co-authors present SciClaimEval, a dataset of authentic claims extracted from published papers, including refuted ones created by modifying supporting evidence rather than fabricating contradictions.

The dataset holds 1,664 annotated samples from 180 papers across machine learning, natural language processing. Medicine, with figures as images and tables in image, LaTeX, HTML, and JSON forms, validated by expert annotation.  Benchmarks of eleven multi-modal foundation models show figure-based checking remains challenging.  Claim checking teams get a cross-modal benchmark built from real papers and real refutations.
arxiv-2602-07721:
Long-context language models slow to a crawl because they must sift through huge stored attention data on every step. Yanlin Qi and five co-authors introduce ParisKV, a system for fetching only the most relevant stored key-value entries when generating text.

ParisKV picks candidates by a collision-based method, then re-ranks them with a quantized scoring step, and can offload stored data to the CPU for million-token contexts. It matches full attention quality on long-input and long-generation tests while running up to 2.8 times faster in full attention's range, and it keeps going where full attention runs out of memory. Engineers scaling long-context inference will find both the design and the speed numbers useful.
arxiv-2602-08221:
Search-boosted making fails when a model's learned knowledge beats found evidence, making false answers. Xuhua Ma and two co-authors trace this to memory squash: in deep layers, certain feed-forward layers cover context-sharp codes with learned priors.

Their method, CoRect, contrasts logits from in-context and non-in-context forward passes to find layers with high memory bias, without needing ground-truth labels, then fixes hidden states to preserve evidence-grounded information. Across question-answer and digest benchmarks, CoRect lifts faithfulness and reduces hallucinations over strong baselines. Search-system builders gain a label-free fix aimed at the mechanism of conflict, not just its symptoms.
arxiv-2602-08321:
Open science questions are hard for large language models, partly because training data and scoring are both shaky. Zijie Chen and five co-authors build a full pipeline to fix that. They turn mixed public science material into a dataset of one million questions across eight STEM subjects, each tagged by difficulty and by whether its answer can be checked exactly. Their 2026 arXiv paper calls the set Dr. SCI.

On top of it they reshape the usual train-then-tune recipe with three moves. First, wider exploration before tuning. Second, a curriculum that tracks the model's growing skill. Third, rubric-guided tuning for open-ended answers. A four-billion-parameter model trained this way scores 63.2 on a hard graduate-level test set and beats strong commercial baselines. Readers get a worked example of how careful data design lifts scientific reasoning.
arxiv-2602-09321:
Environmental sound classification helps smart cities listen for faults, supports acoustic surveillance, and aids factory quality checks. A 2026 paper by Parinaz Binandeh Dehaghani, Danilo Pena, and A. Pedro Aguiar compares two routes to the task: convolutional networks fed with stacked acoustic features, and audio spectrogram transformer models. Stacking pools complementary descriptors, such as log-mel spectrograms, spectral contrast, chroma, and cepstral coefficients, into richer inputs.

Trials on two widely used sound collections test the networks under varied training setups, including pretraining on one collection and fine-tuning on the other, against transformers pretrained on a large audio corpus. The stacked-feature networks hold up well when large-scale pretraining and large training sets are out of reach, offering a cheaper and less data-hungry option. The authors present them as a practical fit for devices with limited computing power and for edge-level listening tasks.
arxiv-2602-10221:
Denoising diffusion models struggle to pull out shape traits and to keep network symmetry, since the standard U-net only handles shifts in theory. A 2026 paper led by El Hadji S. Diop, with two co-authors, offers group morphological convolutions on curved Riemannian spaces, drawn from viscosity solutions for Hamilton-Jacobi-type flows that act as multiscale growth and shrinkage. A convection term is added and solved by tracing curves.

The approach better captures nonlinear effects, shows thin shape structures, and builds symmetry into learning. Tests on MNIST, RotoMNIST, and CIFAR-10 show clear gains over the baseline diffusion model, giving a denoising diffusion model rooted in the broader Euclidean group of rotations, reflections, and permutations.
arxiv-2602-10421:
Hing-Tong Cho and Bei-Lok Hu study a single quantum oscillator coupled to a large setting in a 2026 paper on open quantum systems. The coupling is uneven: the oscillator interacts with many harmonic oscillators through terms that square the setting factors. The work builds on earlier results by Hu, Paz, and Zhang on quantum Brownian motion.

Using a closed-time-path calculation, the authors separate the resulting influence into noise and dissipation parts. They then derive a fluctuation-dissipation relation and a uneven Langevin equation for the system. The results describe how non-Gaussian noise from the uneven coupling shapes the oscillator's motion. They extend the standard theory of quantum Brownian motion beyond its usual linear setting.
arxiv-2602-10721:
Zechun Hu and three co-authors study the range of a once-reinforced random walk on the half-line in a 2026 paper. A reinforced walk revisits its history: edges traversed before become more attractive, changing the walk's long-term wandering. The range, the set of sites ever visited, measures how far that wandering spreads.

The paper gives the limiting conduct of all moments of the range. Moment asymptotics describe not just typical spread but the full spread of extremes, distinguishing walks that explore steadily from ones that stall. The results add a precise quantitative picture of reinforced motion on a half-line. There, a edge at one end shapes every excursion the walk can make.
arxiv-2602-10921:
Matteo Giordano and two co-authors study Dirac mode localization in quantum chromodynamics near the crossover temperature in a 2026 paper. Using stout-smeared staggered fermions and an improved gauge action on the lattice, they examine low-lying Dirac key modes. They watch those modes as temperature rises through the chiral crossover region.

Localized low modes, absent at low temperature, appear at a localization temperature within the chiral crossover range. That range is set by the chiral condensate and light-quark susceptibility. Since neither the transition region nor the renormalized mobility edges change greatly on finer lattices, the conclusion should survive the smooth limit. The work links Anderson-like localization of quark modes to the chiral crossover, a connection with implications for hot QCD matter.
arxiv-2602-11221:
Images plus text make claims that text-only fact-checking cannot judge. Rui Cao and four co-authors describe the AVerImaTeC shared task, which advances systems that retrieve evidence and verify real-world image-text claims. Teams could use web search or a curated knowledge store supplied by organizers.

Scoring counts a verdict as correct only when its evidence score clears a threshold, tying judgement to proof. Fourteen teams entered growth and six reached testing, all beating the rival. The winning team, HUMANE, led the field. The paper reports full results and lessons, offering a shared yardstick for multimodal claim checks.
arxiv-2602-11321:
Humanoid teleoperation usually lags by about a human reaction time. Ziyan Xiong and five co-authors identify position-only control as the cause and propose ExtremControl, a whole-body frame that adds scaled velocity feedforward to low-level control. Feedforward alone cuts tracking delay greatly, with a provably optimal ratio.

Control acts straight on poses of selected rigid links, mainly extremities, avoiding joint-space retargeting in the loop. A closed-form Cartesian mapping, tuned once per tool, translates human motion to humanoid targets across body sizes. The resulting system, using motion capture or virtual reality tracking, reaches end-to-end latency well below the old floor, enabling ping-pong balancing, juggling, and live returns.
arxiv-2602-11421:
Integrated photonics promises compact, stable quantum light hardware. F. Baboux and two co-authors review curved integrated quantum photonics with AlGaAs. The platform combines mature fabrication, direct band gap for electrical injection, low loss, large electro-optic effect, and compatibility with superconducting detectors.

The review details quantum light sources that work at room warmth from the material's strong second- and third-order nonlinearities. It also covers circuits from beamsplitters and interferometers to modulators and tunable filters. It then covers quantum state engineering enabled by those advances and discusses open perspectives and remaining challenges. The paper serves as a map for builders choosing platforms for making, handling, and finding of quantum states on chip.
arxiv-2602-11521:
Serving large language models is bottlenecked by key-value operations, not just compute. Lian Liu and six co-authors propose PAM, a key-value-centric serving system that coordinates heterogeneous processing-in-memory devices across a memory levels. Single-level memory designs cannot meet bandwidth and capacity demands jointly.

PAM distributes key-value tokens across the levels by exploiting context locality, computes focus in parallel across devices with a new recipe, and balances workloads through mapping, migration, and online scheduling interfaces. Addressing bandwidth and capacity jointly, PAM greatly enhances speed and scalability for large-scale serving, paving the way for cost-effective high-results systems in the era of long contexts.
arxiv-2602-11621:
After soil turns to liquid in a quake, crews need to know how strong the failed ground stays. Old ways lean on simple physics and slow hand work. Yongjin Choi and one co-author automate the task with a graph network tool that models grain flows and works back from seen runout to the strength left behind. Gradient tuning drives the search, so no hand steps are needed.

The tool learns from runs shaped by real failure cases, so it can model slopes both small and large. Two well-known dam failures, Lower San Fernando and La Marquesa, serve as tests. In both cases the strengths it finds match past values closely and give runout shapes that make sense. It can also find several linked inputs at once, not just one. For ground work after quakes, that means fast answers from past flows that can be checked and run again.
arxiv-2602-12021:
Linear recurrent networks promise efficiency on long sequences, but diagonal state transitions limit what they can express. Igor Dubinin and two co-authors explore richer state mixing across time and channels that keeps efficiency competitive. They introduce two structured architectures: Higher-order Linear Recurrent Units, which generalize first-order recurrence to higher order by mixing multiple past states, and Block-Diagonal units, which enable dense mixing within channel blocks.

Per-channel or per-row normalization of selective gates stabilizes training and allows larger windows and blocks. A parallel-scan implementation keeps throughput competitive with diagonal networks for moderate orders and block sizes. In synthetic tasks, the block-diagonal design matches or beats linear state space models, low-rank recurrent networks, and LSTM baselines, while the higher-order design proves most parameter-efficient at compression. State mixing structure, the authors conclude, shapes expressivity more than width alone.
arxiv-2602-12221:
Most image systems split reading and making, or tangle their goals together, and editing by example stays fragile. Onkar Susladkar led this work with ten co-authors, proposing UniDFlow, one discrete flow-matching frame for reading, making, and editing alike. Small task adapters keep the two jobs apart, avoiding clashing goals and tangled internal codes.

A new preference method then tunes outcomes under identical prompts, lifting how true and how controlled results are, without large retraining. The system reports top scores across eight tests and works without task training on inpainting, in-context image making, example-based editing, and mixed image making. Readers get a single frame where one model can read, make, and revise images.
arxiv-2602-12621:
The shape of a number field is the class of its integer lattice under turns, flips, and positive scalings. Anuj Jakhar led this work with one co-author, Anwesh Ray, studying how shapes of octic Kummer extensions spread out. Here L equals Q(i, fourth root of m), where m in Z[i] is fourth-power-free.

Shapes are described by explicit invariants called shape params. A limit formula is given for their joint spread ordered by absolute discriminant. The limit measure factors as the product of a smooth measure and a discrete measure arising from local arithmetic rules. Readers get a precise statistical picture of how these degree-eight shapes spread as discriminant grows.
arxiv-2602-12821:
The top value of many convex functions shows up all through tuning, but giving its subdifferential tends to need extra shape tools. Caro and Abderrahim Hantoute give direct rules built straight from the data functions alone. Both active and non-active functions count on equal terms through their slope sets, so no extra build around the top value's domain is needed.

The rules are even and driven by data, which makes them easy to use. As a use for endless convex tuning, the authors derive sharp best-point rules of Karush-Kuhn-Tucker and Fritz-John type, stated only in terms of goal and limit functions. The rules cleanly show which limits are nearly active and which are not, a split that counts when checking best points in large problems.
arxiv-2602-12921:
Idioms rarely mean what their words say, and language models struggle with that gap most in low-resource languages. Adib Sakhawat and five co-authors release a large Bengali idiom dataset of 10,361 entries, each annotated across 19 fields covering meaning, syntax, culture, and religion, through expert consensus. The resource is designed to benchmark figurative understanding in Bangla.

Tests of 30 leading multilingual and instruction-tuned models find none above 50% accuracy on inferring figurative meaning, against 83.4% human performance. The gap exposes limits in cross-linguistic and cultural reasoning that scale alone has not closed. By releasing dataset and benchmark together, the authors provide infrastructure for grounding language models in Bengali culture and, by extension, other low-resource languages.
arxiv-2602-13021:
Symbol regression hunts for formulas behind data, but discovered formulas often fit well while violating basic science, a trap the authors call pseudo-formulas. Jing Xiao and nine co-authors propose PG-SR, a prior-guided system that bakes domain knowledge into discovery. A three-stage pipeline of warm-up, evolution, and refinement carries a prior constraint checker, coding domain priors as executable programs, plus a prior annealing testing workings that steers evolution toward scientifically steady regions.

Theory shows PG-SR shrinks the Rademacher complexity of the guess space, tightening generalisation bounds and guaranteeing protection against pseudo-formulas. Tests across diverse domains show PG-SR beating state-of-the-art plain rivals while staying robust to imperfect priors, noisy data, and scarce data. For formula discovery, the message is that priors, properly enforced, improve both trust and closeness.
arxiv-2602-13121:
Estimating recent strong population size from genetic data matters for ecology and conservation, most of all with sparse, unphased samples. Chris Smith presents LinkedNN, a neural model that learns linkage disequilibrium decay traits automatically as a function of genomic distance between variants. The tool guesses recent strong population size from those learned traits, without hand-crafted summaries.

Tests show the method beating current deep-learning and summary-statistic approaches while using relatively few individuals and variant sites. That leanness is the point: molecular ecology often cannot afford large, phased cohorts. LinkedNN is available as an installable Python package with documentation and open-source code, making the method immediately usable for researchers studying populations with limited data.
arxiv-2602-13321:
Clinical training chatbots must spot jailbreak attempts, where users steer the model off task or into unsafe replies. Earlier work on the 2-Sigma platform showed hand-labeled language traits could support detection, but hand labeling does not scale. This study automates the idea: expert labels for professionalism, medical relevance, ethical behavior, and contextual distraction train BERT-based models to score those traits straight from text.

The best scorer for each trait then feeds a second layer of classifiers that judge jailbreak likelihood, tested across tree, linear, probabilistic, and ensemble methods. Cross-validation and held-out tests showed strong performance, and error analysis points to richer labels and finer traits as next steps. Tri Nguyen leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13421:
Brains compute under tight energy budgets, yet most theories of computation treat energy as free. This paper argues that variational free energy minimization under a Poisson assumption points toward an energy-aware theory. In the Poisson variational autoencoder, the KL term becomes proportional to prior firing rates. That creates an emergent metabolic cost that punishes high baseline activity.

That link couples coding rate, an abstract information quantity, to firing rate, a concrete biological variable. It trades fidelity against energy. Tests across KL weightings and latent sizes show raising the KL weight steadily increases sparsity and cuts spiking in the Poisson model, while a Gaussian control model stays unchanged. Hadi Vafaii leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13521:
Asking a database in plain language should be easy. But agents translating language to SQL still stumble on large real databases: they miss what columns intend and form wrong ideas about the data. Prior fixes generate facts about the database, yet merely restating contents does not correct an agent's misconceptions. Tk-Boost takes a different tack, learning tribal knowledge from the agent's own mistakes.

The framework first has the agent answer a few queries, diagnoses its misconceptions from its errors, and writes knowledge that addresses them. Items are indexed by applicability conditions stating which query features each item suits. When new queries arrive, that knowledge feeds back during SQL generation. Accuracy lifts up to 16.9 percent on Spider 2.0 and 13.7 percent on BIRD. Shubham Agarwal leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13621:
The Hellings-Downs pattern is the benchmark signature for the gravitational-wave background in pulsar timing arrays under general relativity. But it assumes a smooth spread of sources without interference. Real backgrounds dominated by huge black hole pairs have discrete interfering sources, whose interference can mimic or hide altered-gravity signatures. This paper derives closed-form spatial patterns for backgrounds of any polarization with generic dispersion relations, including source interference.

Wave analysis shows interference reshapes patterns yet preserves each polarization's lowest surviving multipole. That multipole is quadrupole for tensor, dipole for vector, and monopole for scalar modes, with higher multipoles cut by pulsar distances and dispersion. The authors also measure the overlap between interference effects and altered gravity, concluding that a single realization of the universe sharply limits telling the two apart from spatial patterns alone. Yan-Chen Bi leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14121: Yiannis Fam, writing alone, widens a build of epipelagic representations to new supercuspidals in residue traits 2 and 3. Building on work of Gastineau and the Reeder-Yu build, the paper makes forms of higher depth that do not come from Reeder-Yu alone. The result adds to the known stock of rare supercuspidals in small residue traits.
arxiv-2602-14221:
The CMS Collaboration reports a 2026 arXiv measurement of charmed meson flow in lead-lead collisions. Prompt Ds mesons were studied at a nucleon-nucleon energy of 5.02 TeV, using CMS data with 0.58 inverse nanobarns of integrated luminosity. Their azimuthal anisotropy probes how charm quarks interact with quark-gluon plasma.

Anisotropy is captured by second- and third-order Fourier coefficients, v2 and v3. The v2 coefficient spans transverse momentum from 4 to 40 GeV across three centrality classes, while v3 spans 4 to 20 GeV in one class. Results are compared with earlier D0 meson measurements, testing coalescence and energy-loss pictures of charm in the plasma.
arxiv-2602-14321:
Saar Cohen, writing alone, models a 2026 arXiv coalition problem with overlapping groups and partial knowledge. Standard models assume disjoint coalitions and fully known preferences, but real agents may join several coalitions at once while their preferences stay partly hidden. Information arrives only as past interaction data and utility feedback in a fixed offline dataset.

The paper studies two feedback types: agent-level and coalition-level utility feedback. For each, it identifies conditions under which the dataset covers enough information for an offline learner to infer preferences. With those conditions met, the learner can recover a partition that is approximately Nash stable, meaning no agent gains much by switching coalitions alone.
arxiv-2602-14721:
Zikai Xiao and colleagues introduce WebWorld, the first open-web simulator trained at scale for web agent training. Real-world training is throttled by latency, rate limits, and safety risks, while older simulators stay closed with only thousands of trajectories. WebWorld trains on more than a million open-web interactions, supporting reasoning, multi-format data, and long-horizon simulations beyond thirty steps.

WebWorld-Bench, with dual metrics across nine dimensions, rates its simulation comparable to Gemini-3-Pro, and a Qwen3-14B model trained on WebWorld trajectories improves in extrinsic tests. The series aims to give web agents a world to practise in before they touch the live web.
arxiv-2602-14921:
Pedro Morin and others chart fit classes for uneven space-time mesh work, near full in scope. They fit Lp shapes on tube space-time zones with smooth uneven mesh on prism grids. They give a mesh-split trick that builds fine local grids with fair smoothness and the sought unevenness.

Hardness counts come with the split trick, and a quasi-interpolation tool on such grids lets the team pin fit classes by forth and back bounds in uneven Besov scales. Space-time fits thus gain a near-full chart, tying mesh build to shape smoothness.
arxiv-2602-15121:
Voit and colleagues explain how weak magnetic fields help hot gas around galaxies rain cold clouds. Circumgalactic gas around massive galaxies forms a volume-filling atmosphere whose temperature reflects the depth of the halo potential well. Near hydrostatic balance and stable against convection, such gas can stay nearly uniform, provided it is not too dense.

Past a density threshold, it grows prone to shedding cold clouds that fall toward the galaxy center and feed the central black hole. The paper shows how relatively weak fields boost that tendency and how the cold gas organizes into vertically elongated, highly magnetized filaments descending at sub-Keplerian speeds. The account is meant to complement recent numerical work and to guide reading of both models and observations of filamentary gas in hot halos.
arxiv-2602-15321:
Seadrow and colleagues recheck the spin period of NGC 1624-2, host of the top outer magnet field found on an O star. Across several epochs of looks, the now agreed spin period of about 158 days does not cleanly capture shifts of lines of magnet origin. They study Lomb-Scargle charts from new and old, multi-tool time series of Balmer H and He lines.

They find about 153 days, give or take under half a day, and about 307 days, give or take about one day. Both fit timing line and magnet time series data matching the Oblique Rotator Model. The about 307 day period means a magnet shape quite different from the earlier agreed one, where both magnet poles should be seen during a full turn. If so, the star's magnet South pole has yet to be seen, and more polar looks should check whether the south pole is visible.
arxiv-2602-15421:
Cruz Reyes and colleagues set the Tip of the Red Giant Branch using a list of even cluster spans. The cluster spans draw from a shared match to period-Wesenheit rules of RR Lyrae stars and type-II stars, tied by shifts. All readings come from Gaia's first third drop.

Using I-band readings in 48 clusters from Stetson's archive, they find an I-band tip brightness shy of minus 4. Tuning the tip using Gaia's RP light data of 53 clusters, they find an RP tip brightness about minus 3 and four parts. They gauge distances to the Large and Small swarms: 18 and a half brightness and about 49 kpc for the big swarm. The little swarm comes in at 19 brightness and about 60 kpc, in RP light data from Gaia's third drop. Their new tip spans, whose ruler is Gaia shifts, are wholly free of the well-known solo twin distances and match them.
arxiv-2602-15521:
Zhao and colleagues look for a cheaper road to sparse expert models. Mixture-of-experts models scale capacity while firing only a few experts at a time, but training good ones from scratch costs a great deal. Turning a trained dense model into an expert model is cheaper, yet current routes break the dense model inner activation patterns and so build weak experts. The authors argue that the gated linear unit, or GLU, already holds a blueprint for the conversion.

Fine-grained GLU activation patterns, they show, reveal a coarse structure: some neurons fire almost always, while others fire for special cases. Their training-free ExpertWeaver splits neurons on that basis into shared experts and routed specialists, tuned per layer. Tests show it beats prior methods both as a pruning route and as a start point for sparse expert training.
arxiv-2602-15821:
Jung and colleagues study interpolants for hybrid modal logics, modal logics with nominals. Recent research has established cost results for deciding whether they exist in logics lacking the Craig Interpolation Property. Proof techniques so far are non-constructive, with no meaningful bounds on their size known. Hybrid modal logics are a prime class without that property. In their case, the property cannot be regained without losing decidability. In uses, they can serve as exact descriptions and splits between positive and negative examples.

Using a new hypermosaic removal method, the authors show that in many usual hybrid modal logics, Craig interpolants can be computed in fourfold exponential time, if they exist. Existence of uniform interpolants, by contrast, is undecidable. That clashes hard with modal or intuitionistic logic, where uniform ones always exist. The paper thus gives the first built bounds for a long non-constructive area, plus that result.
arxiv-2602-15921:
Alpay and Sarioglu offer three algorithms with correctness proofs and complexity bounds for picking a diverse, multi-locale set of sources from ranked search results. First, weighted locale allocation becomes a constrained integer partition problem. An O(n log n) algorithm meets minimum-representation, budget-exhaustion, and proportionality-bound rules, with a tight deviation bound below 1.

Second, a cascaded country-code inference function runs as a priority chain over TLD structure, model-inferred metadata, and language fallback. It is proved deterministic with graceful degradation. Third, a kappa-domain diversity rule uses an O(|K| times R) algorithm with hash-map lookup, ending aggregator monopolisation seen in URL-level dedup. Latent Objective Induction, an environment-shaping operator over prompt spaces, steers later model acts without shrinking the feasible output set, and converges under mild assumptions. On 120 multilingual queries, first-party source ratio rises 62 percent and same-domain duplication falls 89 percent.
arxiv-2602-16021:
Blanco and colleagues design single facility service systems that must cope with shifting regimes, such as a clinic or call centre whose arrival and service rates change through the day. Regime dependent rates produce hyperexponential response times, and the design must choose capacities per regime to balance cost, congestion, fairness, and reliability.

Their framework is mixed integer exponential conic optimization, folding in service level chance constraints, conflict graph restrictions on design choices, and CVaR control of tail risk. The problem is NP hard in general, yet admits an efficient decomposition and tractable special cases. Experiments plus a large urban case study show large gains over the current system, with explicit trade offs laid bare between efficiency, congestion control, fairness, and robustness.
arxiv-2602-16121:
John Crosby leads a team of five researchers who improve heat flow between graphene and water while sparing graphene own conductivity. Chemical treatment can boost interfacial conductance, but it often harms in-plane phonon transport, forcing a trade-off. Using deep neural network molecular dynamics, the team compares edge-treated graphene nanoribbons against surface-treated graphene in water.

Treating only a tenth of ribbon edges with hydroxyl groups raises interfacial conductance more than eightfold. Stronger interfacial interactions and better wetting at edges drive the gain. Unlike basal-plane oxidation, edge treatment largely preserves in-plane conductivity. Hydroxyl edge groups pull two ways: they add boundary scattering that curbs conduction, yet they passivate dangling bonds at bare edges, cutting phonon localization. The net effect is non-monotonic, rising and falling as edge coverage grows, which points to edge chemistry as a precise design lever.
arxiv-2602-16221:
Zoltan Nemeth re-evaluates the link between the observed sunward electron cutoff energy and the depth of the Sun global electrostatic potential. Fluctuations of the variable interplanetary field form shallow mirror traps that move at roughly solar wind speed. They move outward against an attractive solar electrostatic potential and interact with these traps.

Electrons escaping one trap keep losing energy outward until later traps capture them. That prevents their return as sunward-moving particles. A derived cutoff velocity marks the limit beyond which particles cannot overtake a trap outer endpoint. The observed cutoff energy thus characterizes only the local voltage drop within a trap, not the total well depth. That well can run much deeper. Trapped ones also help form the solar wind core population. That makes the Sun electrostatic field a larger factor in solar wind acceleration than cutoff data alone suggested.
arxiv-2602-16321:
Leah Dickhoff and coauthors validate BRIGHT, a multi-objective tuning tool for brachytherapy treatment planning, with a custom GUI for cervical cancer. BRIGHT makes multiple treatment plans, each trading tumour cover against organs-at-risk sparing, and it had earlier proven useful and good in prostate cancer planning. Recently extended to this cancer, BRIGHT gains a novel GUI enabling plan navigation, pairwise comparisons, dose distribution visualisation, and adjustments, all essential for efficient clinical use.

End-user testing copying real practice in ten earlier treated patients tested the tool with its GUI. Results show the BRIGHT plan preferred over the standard plan in eight of ten patients, four with relevant differences. The standard plan won in two patients, neither with big gaps. The authors conclude that BRIGHT, with its GUI, is a clinically viable and user-friendly tool for treatment planning in cervical treatment.
arxiv-2602-16421:
Natsuki Akaishi, Nicki Holighaus, and Kohei Yatabe introduce SELEBI, a signal-adaptive phase vocoder for percussion-aware stretching. Phase vocoder time-stretching is widely used to change audio time scales, but standard implementations suffer smearing, an artifact that badly degrades percussive sounds. The authors trace it to a time-scale mismatch between the smeared magnitude spectrogram and the new phase.

SELEBI reduces that smearing while keeping stability, and unlike rule-based processing or component splitting, it uses the nonstationary Gabor transform. By varying analysis window lengths, giving short windows to parts with strong transient energy, it computes a localized spectrogram directly from the time-domain signal. That keeps phase structures more consistent. Its perfect reconstruction property guarantees stable, high-fidelity synthesis, unlike earlier approaches. Experiments show the method mitigates smearing and yields natural sound quality.
arxiv-2602-16521:
Giacomo Ascione and Luigia Caputo set out five queue models in which waiting times follow heavy-tailed Mittag-Leffler patterns rather than the usual short-tailed ones. Their models extend the classic single-server queue, and the classic case returns when the settings are chosen in a matching way. The paper gives the timing patterns for arrivals and service in both the older models and the new ones.

The main work then traces what happens to these queues when time and size are scaled up. The authors show how the limiting course of each model can reveal the traffic regime at work, whether arrivals tend to swamp service or stay in balance. For readers who model phone lines, servers, or other waiting lines, the paper offers a wider family of tools for bursts and long waits.
arxiv-2602-16721:
Bjorn Johnson and Jared Levy propose a Speech to Speech Synthesis Network for voice impersonation. Speech recognition and speech synthesis have each seen great success, but speech-to-speech processing is far less explored. The new model fuses the two fields to perform speech-to-speech style transfer, aiming to render one voice in the style of another.

Despite limits in capacity, the model generates realistic audio samples. It is benchmarked against a generative adversarial model for a similar task, and the authors report more convincing results. Voice researchers get a fused architecture for style transfer, along with a cautionary example of how readily voice identity can now be cloned.
arxiv-2602-16921:
Tran Duc Le and co-authors propose a frame for bringing cybersecurity contests into K-12 education for cognitive apprenticeship and ethical skill growth. Capture the Flag contests are powerful teaching tools for the cyber workforce gap, yet K-12 use faces barriers including educator preparedness gaps and equity concerns. The Ethical-Cognitive Apprenticeship frame, derived from systematic synthesis of literature and empirical proof, addresses those challenges.

It joins cognitive mentoring ideas with embedded ethical growth across five phases: foundational modeling, scaffolding the arena, coaching and articulation, ethical dilemma injections, and reflective exploration. The frame offers a low floor, high ceiling pathway to broaden participation among diverse students, including varied groups and women, while fostering deep, transferable skills. Teachers gain a clear plan. Students gain skills and ethics. By reframing the teacher as a lead learner, it also offers a sustainable answer to the teacher skill gap.
arxiv-2602-17521:
Benjamin Walker led a seven-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on how two-flagellum swimmers steer. Many tiny swimmers change their stroke to turn toward light or other cues, though their bodies show no clear left-right bias. The paper sets out a simple core idea. Pushes from the two flagella add up for forward motion, while they work against each other to make the body rotate.

The authors trace that idea from a rough back-of-envelope model to a full computer model of a sample swimmer. The trace yields a broad link between stroke asymmetry, such as beat rate, and the bend of the path. They apply it to the green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, which swims with a matched breaststroke yet may use the same trick to turn toward light. A robot model built on the alga backs the account, steering by closed-loop control toward light.
arxiv-2602-18021:
Agus Soenjaya studies schemes for the stochastic Landau-Lifshitz-Bloch equation, which models magnetization in a bounded ferromagnet at high temperatures in one or two spatial dimensions. It is a vector-valued quasilinear partial differential equation. If the initial data are smooth enough, the paper proves strong convergence for several semi-implicit and implicit finite element schemes, with stated rates.

The analysis rests on local error bounds and new exponential moment bounds. As a by-product, those bounds yield mean-square exponential stability of solutions and a single invariant measure in one spatial dimension under small noise. The work also sharpens earlier convergence-in-probability results for the schemes. Tests support the theory.
arxiv-2602-18121:
Marco D'Elia and one co-author revisit a 2017 claim about a family of graphs drawn in two outer layers. The earlier paper said every such graph with n points holds a large outerplanar piece. That piece can be drawn with all its points on the outer rim, and it covers at least two thirds of the points. The new paper finds a major flaw in that earlier proof.

The authors do not leave the claim hanging: they prove it again from scratch with a different route. Their proof is far more involved than the first attempt, but it saves the result. Readers get a corrected base for later work on layered graphs, and a warning that even published proofs in this corner of graph theory need a fresh check.
arxiv-2602-18621:
Dorian Smith computes sandpile groups for a family of trees. His 2026 paper notes the sandpile group of a connected graph forms a finite abelian group whose size equals the graph's spanning tree count. He computes the spanning tree number and sandpile group for the bi-coconut-tree cone, extending work of Reiner and Smith on coconut-tree cones.

He also answers one of their questions by showing a family of trees with all-cyclic sandpile groups but whose number of leaves grows without bound. The example separates cyclic sandpile structure from leaf-count bounds, extending the coconut-tree results to a broader tree family.
arxiv-2602-18921:
Proof assistants need a way to admit only programs that stop, and corecursive programs that keep producing. Bastiaan Laarakker, with two co-authors, investigates sized types in 2026 as a type-based alternative to the usual syntactic rules, which can be restrictive and hard to combine. With sized types, inductive and coinductive types carry extra size data, and well-founded induction on sizes proves termination and productivity.

Agda already has sized types, but adding a largest size broke its consistency. The authors instead extend intensional type theory by adding a large type of sizes, plus parametric quantifiers over sizes, and in that theory both kinds of types can be built. That goes past earlier work, which managed only finitely-branching inductive types. Consistency rests on an impredicative realisability model that treats the size type as an uncountable ordinal.
arxiv-2602-19121:
Consensus usually means agreeing on one point. Matthias Függer, with one co-author, relaxes that demand in 2026. Asymptotic subspace consensus asks outputs to converge onto a common subspace, while staying inside the convex hull of initial vectors. A single point is just the zero-dimensional special case.

The authors fully characterise solvability under oblivious message adversaries. A large class of standard consensus algorithms degrades gracefully to the subspace version. Weaker network assumptions thus still permit agreement, just on a subspace rather than a point. Bounds on the rate at which dimension drops below the initial level are also given. Distributed agreement gains a flexible middle ground.
arxiv-2602-19321:
On a general curve with a gonality structure, bundles with extra sections form loci whose shape is still being mapped. Youngook Choi and two co-authors study rank-two stable vector bundles of speciality 3 on such curves. They ask when the corresponding Brill-Noether loci exist and what their irreducible components look like. Their tools include universal extension spaces, modular maps, and recent work on rank-one Brill-Noether theory in Hurwitz spaces.

The authors give existence criteria and a full description of components, sorting them by regularity, superabundance, and the behavior of their general points. For certain degrees, they prove that several superabundant components coexist with a regular one. Specialization techniques reveal a stratification into locally closed pieces, with consequences for the birational geometry of these loci and for bundles with fixed general determinant.
arxiv-2602-19421:
Planning new transmission lines shapes, and is shaped by, how power generators bid in electricity markets. Tomonari Kanazawa and two co-authors propose a reinforcement learning framework that co-optimizes grid investment decisions and generator bidding plans in one unified training process. A multi-agent market model provides the setting, with a new design policy layer joining continuous and discrete growth choices to bidding plans.

Through repeated interaction between clearing the market and designing investment, the framework captures how each side influences the other. Case studies on the IEEE 30-bus network test the approach as a proof of concept. Readers get a design that treats grid expansion and strategic bidding as one coupled problem, not two separate ones.
arxiv-2602-19521:
Fatty plaques in artery walls are clumps of cells. Michael G. Watson's paper notes that early plaques hold macrophages, cells drawn in to eat locally bound fat. Growth reflects a gap between cell entry and exit. It can occur if macrophages die inside the plaque rather than leaving it, a process still poorly understood.

The paper builds a new spatial model of early plaques for studying how macrophages leave by chasing signals. That movement follows signals toward lymph vessels in artery walls. Math work and computer runs show how signal response traits shape the model's spatial traits and fat load. Transit time math adds a measured view of how long macrophages linger.
arxiv-2602-19621: Jeehoon Park and Junyeong Park give a systematic treatment of arithmetic BF theory, a framework introduced by Carlson and Kim. Their key observation is that the Cassels-Tate pairing can be read, in a natural way, as an arithmetic BF functional. Readers get a compact, unified account linking the pairing to BF theory.
arxiv-2602-20421:
One-dimensional anyons remain debated, though theory predicts exotic many-body phases and phase transitions for them, and experiments have begun to catch up. Brice Bakkali-Hassani and seven co-authors prepare two-body ground states of the one-dimensional anyon-Hubbard model with ultracold atoms in an optical lattice. They combine Hamiltonian engineering through quasiperiodic drives with adiabatic state manipulation.

The experiments reveal statistical interactions that produce pseudo-fermionization and chiral bound states when particles stay close together. The results link lattice and continuum versions of anyon models and mark steps toward precise control of one-dimensional anyons, both in equilibrium and out of equilibrium.
arxiv-2602-20621:
Half-metallic Heusler compounds attract interest for spintronics, above all those grown on III-V semiconductors for devices. Zefeng Cai and eight co-authors present a first-principles study of four cobalt-based and two nickel-based Heusler compounds matched to InAs. They compare density functional theory with semi-local and hybrid functionals against quasiparticle self-consistent GW. They add machine-learned Hubbard U corrections, tuned by a new Bayesian optimization objective, to best match GW band structure and magnetic moments.

The tuned DFT-plus-U method reproduces the key GW features adequately in most cases. Yet results show strong method dependence in spin polarization at the Fermi level, and in some cases even the dominant spin channel flips between majority and minority. Of the materials studied, the cobalt-titanium-tin and cobalt-zirconium-aluminum compounds emerge as the most likely half-metals, a finding builders can test.
arxiv-2602-20821:
Political polarization shapes how societies argue, and territorial disputes are among its sharpest settings. Julia Atienza-Barthelemy, Samuel Martin-Gutierrez, Juan Losada, and Rosa Benito study one such dispute, the independence of Catalonia, through Twitter data in this 2026 arXiv paper. They infer a continuous spread of opinion from retweet patterns, after first picking out elite users with fixed, opposing views.

Opinion falls mainly into two camps, with a smaller middle pole that makes the picture less stark than a pure split. The most active, engaged, and influential users hold the most extreme positions.
