Language tracks politics closely: users against independence write mainly in Spanish, while pro-independence users mix Catalan and Spanish freely. The middle pole leans pro-independence in opinion but resembles the against camp in language use.
arxiv-2602-21021:
The spectral type of a nilsystem tells how its motion spreads across tones. Felipe Hernandez studies Host-Kra factors and the spectral type of nilsystems in this 2026 arXiv paper, with no even-spread premise. In the even-spread case, the known result splits the spectral type into a discrete part and a Lebesgue part of endless multiplicity.

The paper's main result stretches that split to nilsystems that lack even spread. Readers working with systems that lack it thus gain the same spectral picture that ergodic theory already gave. The stretch matters for systems where even spread cannot be taken as given, whose study before lacked this clean split.
arxiv-2602-21221:
Long-context field use stalls between spread-out squeezing, which carries over poorly out of spread, and test-time training, which costs fake data and state-keeping weights. Zeju Li, Yizhou Zhou, and Qiang Xu shift the frame in this 2026 arXiv paper from tuning to building. A throwaway LoRA module acts as builder, boiling long contexts down into compact buffer tokens: state-free, portable memory for frozen base models.

A self-matched tuning plan removes the need for fake question-answer pairs, steadying rebuild with context-blind random queries so squeezed tokens stay within the model's prompt-obeying space. Tests with a popular eight-billion-dial model keep fine detail and thought where prior methods falter, even at 16-fold squeezing. Memory density is unlinked from model dials.
arxiv-2602-21621:
Jiexi Liu and one co-author study the Hopf-algebra-based formula for Yang-Mills-Scalar amplitudes. That formula expands a Yang-Mills-Scalar amplitude with massive scalars as a mix of propagator matrices joining massless scalars tied to gluons with the original massive scalars.

The note offers a recursive formula that expresses the Hopf-algebra-based formula with ease. In it, gluons turn into massless scalars. So a Yang-Mills-Scalar amplitude with massive scalars is expressed by amplitudes with fewer gluons, massive scalars, and massless scalars. The formula is verified with a soft behavior approach. In the massless limit, it turns into expressions for amplitudes with massless scalars earlier shown to satisfy another recursive expansion. The note shows the two distinct approaches match through explicit calculation on amplitudes with one and two gluons.
arxiv-2602-21721:
Cross-silo federated learning lets organizations train models together without sharing raw data, yet client updates can still leak sensitive facts through inference attacks. Secure aggregation hides individual updates, but that hiding blocks contribution scoring, which matters for fair rewards and for spotting weak or malicious participants. Shapley value scoring clashes with secure aggregation, while leave-one-out scoring is crude and relies on self-evaluation.

Delio Jaramillo Velez and four co-authors introduce two marginal-difference scores that work under secure aggregation. Fair-Private meets standard fairness axioms, while Everybody-Else drops self-evaluation and resists manipulation. Both carry theoretical guarantees for fairness, privacy, robustness, and efficiency, and on medical image data and CIFAR10 they beat baselines, track Shapley rankings better, and improve both downstream performance and misbehavior detection.
arxiv-2602-21821:
All gas-rich galaxies in clusters should face ram-pressure stripping from intra-cluster gas, yet only a fraction develop star birth in stripped tails. Alessandro Ignesti and 22 co-authors provide direct evidence that fields signal gaps in outer star birth, testing what creates a jellyfish galaxy. They first focus on JO147, with weak star birth in its tail.

MeerKAT radio data show aligned glow in only a small fraction of its tail, at 10 percent. Its low Mach number hints links among field draping, shock compression, and outer star birth. Testing the idea in 17 such galaxies from the GASP project, joining orbital models with cluster heat maps, they find a clear link between Mach number and tail star birth. They conclude supersonic motion must trigger star birth in stripped tails, with shock squeezing from fast motion blocking gas loss and likely boosting the nearby field and matter traits.
arxiv-2602-22221:
Search engines and AI answers now mediate factual knowledge, but their reliability in realistic settings is hard to pin down. Geng Liu and three co-authors build a fact-checking dataset from real Chinese search logs and compare nine systems, from classic search engines to standalone models and search-integrated AI overviews. They test factual yes-no questions against evidence-derived ground truth.

Systems prove similarly accurate when they commit to an answer, but differ sharply in how often they commit. Search engines answer definitively most of the time, while one leading model answers definitively less than half the time. All systems also show a polarity gap, doing better on yes-labeled questions. The study separates accuracy from answer rate, two virtues that are easy to confuse.
arxiv-2602-22321:
The supernova remnant N103B glows in X-rays from the shredded star's own elements, and Japan's XRISM mission now reads those lines with exquisite precision. Tyler Holland-Ashford and Brian J. Williams present the first XRISM analysis of the remnant, fitting spectra from the Resolve microcalorimeter across lines of silicon, sulfur, argon, calcium, chromium, manganese, and iron.

The fits demand a previously unidentified hot, highly ionized, iron-dominated plasma component rich in chromium and manganese, echoing a feature seen in another remnant. All ejecta show strong line broadening from thermal motion, rising from intermediate-mass elements to iron-rich ejecta, matching reverse-shock speeds of several thousand kilometers per second. The remnant's velocity structure and thermal state come into sharper focus.
arxiv-2602-23421:
Rathindra Nath Das and one co-author extend Krylov tools for spotting chaos from quantum to classical systems. Exact solvability in semiclassical string cases is strong but rare, and mapping the wide range of unsolvable string motion needs new tools. The authors introduce a Koopman-Krylov setup, built on the Koopman-von Neumann picture of classical motion.

The setup is built with a mode-based stand-in for the Koopman generator acting on measured traits. With it, the authors show how breaks in solvability shift spectral weight in distinct ways, causing spreading in Krylov space that depends on what is measured. The tools are shown on three kinds of unsolvable string cases, giving a firm toolkit for mapping chaos in classical string motion.
arxiv-2602-23521:
Ken-ichi Tadaki presents an archive-based catalog of high-J CO spectroscopy for high-redshift galaxies, the first paper in a series. High-J CO emission had been studied mostly source by source, blocking population-level conclusions about molecular gas excitation.

Combining ALMA archival data with published measurements, the catalog compiles CO spectral line energy distributions for 38 systems at redshifts 3.1 to 6.9, including 5 hot dust-obscured galaxies, 17 submillimeter-bright galaxies, and 16 optically selected quasars. Class-median distributions rise steeply to J = 9 and stay roughly flat through J = 11 to 12. SMGs show stronger low- to mid-J emission, Hot DOGs hint at higher excitation, and X-ray dominated heating or dense shock-heated gas may explain the extended high-J emission.
arxiv-2602-23821:
Jixiang Wang and seven co-authors present an acceleration-level control framework for fixed-wing drones, aimed at guidance uses such as proportional navigation. The 2026 paper notes that guidance laws command accelerations, but drones cannot command acceleration directly; they must realize it through attitude and thrust within flight limits.

The outer loop turns commanded tangential and normal accelerations into body-rate and thrust commands that standard autopilots accept. For the normal channel, a mapping turns desired normal acceleration into roll and pitch rates that steer the lift vector. For the tangential channel, an energy-based rule, fitted from flight data, links thrust to acceleration without a detailed propulsion model. Real flights on a vertical-takeoff fixed-wing craft show accurate tracking and working proportional navigation through those simple interfaces.
arxiv-2602-24021:
Zhaolin Cai and four co-authors present SteerVAD, an intervention framework that steers frozen multimodal language models for video anomaly detection. The 2026 paper notes that tuning-free use of such models inherits pretraining biases and cannot reshape their internal representations for specific video contexts, so subtle or ambiguous anomalies are missed.

SteerVAD shifts from passively reading model outputs to actively steering representations. A gradient-free separability analysis first identifies the attention heads most discriminative for anomaly detection, called latent anomaly experts. A hierarchical meta-controller then generates dynamic rectification signals from global context and those expert outputs, applying targeted scaling to the expert representation manifolds to amplify anomaly-relevant dimensions and suppress biases. Tests on mainstream benchmarks reach leading performance among tuning-free methods, showing that internal steering can adapt frozen models to anomaly detection.
arxiv-2602-24121:
Tyler Han and eight co-authors present the first inverse reinforcement learning method for visual manipulation in the real world, learned from observation alone, without hand-designed rewards, simulation models, or action supervision. The 2026 paper pursues observational learning, where only task observations such as video are given, a setting previously impractical for real robots due to reinforcement learning limitations.

Their method, MPAIL2, learns pick-and-place from scratch in under an hour to a high success rate. Reinforcement learning and behavioral cloning with equal interaction and demonstration budgets reach far lower success, despite their reward and action supervision. The work also gives the first demonstration, in the real world and from scratch, of positive online transfer across different visual manipulation tasks. By removing the need for expert rewards, simulators, or teleoperation, it lowers the labor and expertise barriers to teaching robots new manipulation skills from observation.
arxiv-2603-01621:
Inda Kreso, Mehran Tarif, Fatemeh Moradi, and colleagues guard factory control systems against stealthy data attacks. Their 2026 work targets false data that stays inside normal physical bounds, so it looks safe. Deep learning guards often smooth over such subtle fakes, while classic checks scale poorly on linked sensor data.

Their digital twin watches a live copy of the plant and flags shifts in the data pattern. A closed-form score measures how far the live pattern drifts from the twin in both mean and cross-links. Tests on two public plant data sets beat a deep learning rival on precision and on a balanced score. The math runs fast on plain hardware with tiny memory, which suits small edge controllers in plants.
arxiv-2603-01921:
Linnea Heitmeier and Jan Gabriel simulate a shaken box of plastic spheres and compare it with light-scattering experiments. Their 2026 work vibrates polystyrene spheres inside a cubic container at varied shaking strengths. Packing fraction tracks how densely the grains settle as shaking proceeds over time.

Simulations use the Discrete Element Method, which follows each grain and its contacts directly. Mean-squared displacement reveals whether grains diffuse normally, crawl subdiffusively, or surge superdiffusively. Simulated displacements run far above the values measured by diffusing wave spectroscopy in the lab. Rotational displacement, though, matches the measured scale closely, which flips the usual reading of the signal. The authors propose the lab signal reflects rotation, not translation, and note the system locks into a constrained state well before close packing.
arxiv-2603-02221:
Zizheng Zhang, Yiming Li, Justin Xu, and colleagues improve clinical prediction tables in this 2026 paper. Good features, built by hand from raw columns, often beat deep models on health data. Language models can suggest new features using medical knowledge. Older tools search blindly, ignoring how the final model learns and which features matter.

Their system, MedFeat, loops feedback from the final model back into feature search. Importance scores from a standard explainer guide which ideas to try next. Past wins and losses are tracked so search does not repeat dead ends. Across many clinical tasks, scores rose steadily over baselines. New features stayed meaningful and held up across years and patient groups, from intensive care to general wards.
arxiv-2603-02621:
Isaac Llorente-Saguer presents a GPU framework for testing Goldbach's conjecture in this 2026 paper. The conjecture claims every even number is a sum of two primes. It has been verified to huge ranges, but GPU tools hit a memory ceiling. A monolithic prime table consumed all video memory near a hundred billion.

His framework packs primes densely as bits, cutting memory sixteenfold. A segmented double sieve then removes the video memory ceiling entirely. Inverting the verification loop plus a fast primality oracle does the heavy lifting. Exhaustive checks reached a trillion on one consumer graphics card, with no counterexamples. Each segment needs only a tiny slice of memory. A rigorous CPU fallback guarantees completeness, and data-center tests scale cleanly across many GPUs.
arxiv-2603-02821:
Alphonse Duleau wrote this obituary for Augustin Fresnel, the French engineer and physicist known for his work on light. The preserved text opens with an editor's preface tracing Duleau himself, who was born in Paris in 1789 and trained as a bridge and road engineer. Duleau met Fresnel in 1810 while both were young engineers posted away from Paris.

The preface follows Duleau's postings to Bordeaux and the Garonne district, then back to Paris for canal work, including swing bridges. He later became a professor of construction and an editor of the engineers' annals. Read as a primary source, the obituary gains weight from this closeness: its author knew Fresnel personally from the start of their shared careers in French public works.
arxiv-2603-03321:
Nardine Basta and Dali Kaafar present DIALEVAL, a system for checking whether language models follow instructions. Judging that well means splitting an instruction into small checkable requirements, a job still done by hand with one-size-fits-all rules. Human judges, the authors note, actually apply different standards to different kinds of requirements. Their 2026 framework automates the job with formal types.

Two language model agents split the work: one extracts typed requirements under strict rules of atomicity and independence, the other scores each type its own way. Content items pass on matching meaning; numbers must match exactly. The method extends to multi-turn dialogue, where older tools fail. Validation shows about ninety percent accuracy and a much closer match to human judgment on complex instructions.
arxiv-2603-03421:
Shahar Hod proves a floor under the size of a black hole's shadow. The shadow is the dark disk framed by the photon ring, now photographed around real black holes by the Event Horizon Telescope. His 2026 paper asks how small that shadow can be, relative to the horizon, for black holes surrounded by matter fields, the so-called hairy case, in spherical symmetry.

Assuming the matter obeys the weak energy condition, Hod shows the shadow radius must be at least a fixed multiple of the horizon radius, more than two and a half times it. The familiar bald Schwarzschild black hole, with no surrounding matter, lands exactly on that floor, saturating the bound. The result gives observers a clean theoretical benchmark: any measured shadow smaller than the floor would break the assumptions behind it.
arxiv-2603-03521:
Jonathan Klawitter and four others ask how many truly separate trees a Bayesian evolution study has sampled. Such analyses explore evolutionary trees with Markov chain Monte Carlo, and consecutive samples resemble each other. The effective sample size corrects for that stickiness, but trees are discrete and high-dimensional, so usual estimators falter. Their 2026 study compares current tree gauges against new ones built on conditional clade distributions.

A further new gauge reads clade frequency differences between independent chains. Simulated chains with known answers grade every method, and real data sets test stability. The clade-distribution gauges match current approaches, and two of them vary less by averaging many estimates. The chance-based gauge and two previously recommended methods cost too much on long chains. Multimodality and poor mixing can badly distort all the gauges' readings, the authors warn.
arxiv-2604-00021: Fukui studies how language models process ethical instructions, in over 600 simulations across four models, four formats, and Japanese and English. Analysis matched a prior study's Llama Japanese dissociation pattern, but no other model matched it, marking it model-specific. Three metrics, Deliberation Depth, Value Consistency, and Other-Recognition, revealed four types: Output Filter, Defensive Repetition, Critical Internalization, and Principled Consistency. The central finding is a link between power and format: low-deliberation models show none, while high-deliberation models show opposite effects from norms and virtue framing.
arxiv-2604-00421: Mohamud and colleagues ask whether mixture-of-experts models really need a trained router. In these layers, each token wakes just a few experts, picked by a learned router from the token's hidden state. Self-Routing removes that router projection and instead reads expert scores straight from a chosen slice of the hidden state, leaving the rest of the layer untouched. Tests on language modelling across expert counts and model sizes, plus ImageNet-1K classification, compare it against the learned-router baseline, random routing, and dense models.
arxiv-2604-00721: Dupont-Bouillard tackles co-3-plexes in chordal graphs. A co-3-plex is a vertex subset inducing a subgraph of degree at most 2. Since chordal co-3-plexes induce triangles and induced paths, he reduces the search to maximum stable set search in an auxiliary graph of exponential size. That yields a variable-sized linear programming formulation for maximum weighted co-3-plexes. The pricing subproblem reduces to a maximum vertex-edge weight induced path problem, solvable in polynomial time.
arxiv-2604-00921: Lewis, Gregor, and Santos-Villalobos propose a simple training-free method to slim image vectors using a post-hoc canonical correlation analysis step. By using shared structure between two trained models, the method finds linear maps that keep shared meaning while dropping extra parts. Vectors shrink by more than 75 percent in size with better downstream results. They beat standard and PCA versions alike, with scores up to 12.6 percent.
arxiv-2604-01421: Saroha and colleagues present EgoFlow, a flow-matching system making plausible trajectories from first-person video. It uses a hybrid Mamba-Transformer-Perceiver design to model motion, scene shape and meaning. Gradient-guided steps enforce physics constraints such as crash dodging and motion smoothness. That yields smooth, steerable motion without post-hoc cleanup or extra labels. Tested on HD-EPIC, EgoExo4D and HOT3D, it beats diffusion and transformer rivals in accuracy, generalization and physical realism. It cuts crash rates by 79 percent.
arxiv-2604-01621: Li and colleagues present DWDP, an inference plan keeping split-data runs while shifting mixture-of-experts weights across peer GPUs and fetching missing experts on demand. By dropping joint inter-rank syncing, DWDP lets each GPU progress alone. They address real costs with two fixes for split-weight handling and early remote-weight prefetch. Built in TensorRT-LLM and tested with DeepSeek-R1 on GB200 NVL72, DWDP improves end-to-end output TPS/GPU by 8.8 percent at similar TPS/user under 8K input and 1K output sequence lengths.
arxiv-2604-01721: Sümer and colleagues design phase-shifted pilots for uplink sensing and communication networks with non-orthogonal access. Interleaved pilots with such access raise efficiency but blur sensing resolution through sparsity, and the nulling fix helps only little. Their phase-shifted design and its nulling variant puncture sensing signals at transmitter pilot spots to preserve early channel estimates and allow a dense data overlay. Adapted cancellation then untangles multi-transmitter interference, keeping sensing intact while cutting receiver computing cost by 18.8 percent against the older baseline.
arxiv-2604-01821: Ito and colleagues propose a two-stage method for sharing educational data under privacy constraints. But educational data are fragmented, small-sample and high-dimensional, so tailored methods demand engineering. Their method first generates synthetic data with LLM-based private generation, then offers on-demand validation, where researchers submit code for checks. It adapts to multi-shot synthesis across cohorts. Three years of tests plus a case study find LLM-based generation comparable to a deep baseline, cheaper. Yet only 36 percent of synthetic findings validate on real data.
arxiv-2604-02421: Bhandari, Borah and Saha give collapsing domain walls a new bias origin from matter antimatter gap. Spontaneous symmetry breaking spawns bad wall networks, made unstable by a bias term. Here the bias arises at finite temperature from radiative shifts of a Dirac fermion with a large number density gap. The case opens a new viable region for wall collapse and gravity waves within reach of future tests. Success also hinges on the temperature when it was generated, so future wave data could probe both its amount and its heat.
arxiv-2604-02521: Baiget Orts presents SESCC, which dates ancient star catalogues through the link between stellar speeds and position errors. At the true date the two are unrelated, so the best date is the trial date that minimizes their correlation. Validated against the catalogues of Tycho Brahe and Ulugh Beg, the method applied to the Almagest points mostly to pre-Christian dates, favoring a Hipparchan origin over a Ptolemaic one.
arxiv-2604-02621: Shen, Tu and Wang propose reinforcement learning for reasoning distillation that replaces ground-truth rewards with continuous scores from a judge language model. Their continuous chain-of-thought reward comes from a single-token logit of the judge, giving a scalable online signal for large volumes of unlabeled data. With a strong judge it matches verifiable rewards, and combining both in a semi-supervised setup beats either alone.
arxiv-2604-02821: Liu, Wang and Manchester present goal-conditioned neural ordinary differential equations for all-pairs motion planning, where start and goal may be any points in a safe set. Built from bi-Lipschitz diffeomorphisms, the model guarantees global exponential stability and safety. The safe set stays forward invariant for any goal, with clear bounds on convergence rate, tracking error, and vector field size. Demonstration data can be folded in. A 2D corridor task illustrates the method.
arxiv-2604-02921: Gao, Jiang and Yan propose debiasing language models by supervised fine-tuning to correct systematic extrapolation bias in forecasts. Prompt-based fixes appear limited against this bias. They train off-the-shelf models with low-rank adaptation on instruction sets built from rational benchmark forecasts. Intervening at the parameter level changes how models map observed information into forecasts. Fine-tuning corrects that bias out-of-sample in controlled experiments and stock return prediction. The method is low-cost and broad.
arxiv-2604-03221: Anagnostopoulos and colleagues build a fully noninvasive, patient-specific blood-flow model from a single cuff reading plus physics-informed neural networks. The inverse model solves flow and pressure across an eight-artery tree in minutes, training at least ten times faster than leading models. Validated against a reference solver and clinical data, it recovers cardiac output and central systolic pressure with strong agreement.
arxiv-2604-03421: Singh and Diamond show that nonlinear spectral back-transfer from zonal modes to turbulence limits how long zonal shearing fields stay coherent. Back-transfer bursts scatter the phase and amplitude of zonal shear, and the transfer distribution is non-Gaussian, with positive triangularity far more intermittent than negative. Negative-triangularity plasmas suppress back-transfer, gaining longer coherence and tougher turbulence regulation despite lower zonal energy.
arxiv-2604-03721: Luca Bergen and colleagues proposed a test for whether two factors stay linked once a third factor is held fixed. Older kernel tests lean hard on one fitting method that is slow when tuned and shaky when untuned. Their Generalised Kernel Covariance Measure works with many fitting methods. It maps the factors into a rich space, strips out what the third factor explains, and checks what is left. In simulations with tree-based fits, it often beat leading tests on false alarms and power.
arxiv-2604-04021: Shaikh Saad and Vasja Susič examined the minimal Yukawa sector of SO(10) grand unified theories with Higgs fields in the 10, 120, and 126 representations. Taking the 10 and 120 fields as real scalars, they derived reality conditions for their weak-doublet parts and found a sign difference between the two doublets in the 120 field. Four independent routes, including a Pati-Salam embedding map and an SU(5) oscillator calculation, all gave the same result. A broad numerical scan then matched observed fermion masses and mixings, including recent JUNO solar oscillation data.
arxiv-2604-04121: Leonardo Bitzki and team built NetSecBed, a box-native testbed for same-again security tests. Public data sets usually sit static, with weak support for set re-runs and tracking across rules. It packs 60 attack cases, 9 target services, and benign traffic makers into single-purpose boxes with plain-text specs. Its line does runs, packet capture, log grabs, probing, feature pulls, and data set merging, cutting day-to-day bias.
arxiv-2604-04221: Narayanan and Vaidya build a controller that helps four-legged robots walk blind over rough ground. Their RK-MPC method pairs a simple template model with a small data-learned correction for contact and terrain surprises, then runs the combined model inside a predictive controller at 500 hertz on board. Tests in simulation and on a Unitree Go1 robot cover grass, gravel, snow and ice, and the correction improves prediction over standard Koopman baselines.
arxiv-2604-04321: Hirst, Sá Earp and Silva introduce a neural flow that reshapes closed surfaces to minimize Willmore energy, the squared magnitude of mean curvature. Neural networks model maps from flat two-dimensional domains into three-dimensional space, trained with a physics-informed loss on the energy of the embedding. Training recovers the expected round sphere for genus zero surfaces and the Clifford torus for genus one. The genus two experiment offers a new route to hunt for minimal Willmore surfaces, an open problem.
arxiv-2604-04521: Illi and Qaraqe survey pinching antenna systems, a new channel-shaping technique for next wireless generations. Pinching antenna systems extend a base station's reach by linking radio-frequency chains to long guides, with aerials pinched at custom positions, overcoming missing line-of-sight and path loss. Channel tuning thus lifts sensing, coverage, data rate and resilience against snooping. The survey sorts research by objectives: reach, data rate, secure transmission, sensing, joint sensing-communication, and energy efficiency. It weighs schemes, drawing lessons on potential and limits, and future deployment directions.
arxiv-2604-04821: Cao and four colleagues model hidden-charm pentaquarks, exotic particles made of five quarks. They treat the Pc and Pcs states as loosely bound molecules. Solving the Bethe-Salpeter equation with coupled channels, heavy-quark spin symmetry, and a local hidden-gauge approach, they trace pole paths, wave functions, and sizes. For Pc states, full coupled-channel effects prove essential and shift decay widths, while the strange Pcs system behaves more simply, with its main bound channels coupling mainly to higher decay routes.
arxiv-2604-05621: Delitzas and ten colleagues rebuild usable 3D twins of indoor scenes from head-worn RGB-D videos of people handling objects. FunRec spots jointed parts, gauges joint motion, and rebuilds still and moving shapes with no staged setups or CAD priors. It tops prior work by up to 50 mIoU points on part segmentation with far smaller joint errors.
arxiv-2604-05721: Zhang and six colleagues grow 3D Gaussians from point clouds with text guidance, enforcing geometric accuracy from the start. A multi-view diffusion model supplies consistent appearances, view-fusion artifacts are curbed at overlap regions, and unseen areas are inpainted from the largest un-grown regions. Tests on synthetic and real-scanned clouds show strong text-guided generation.
arxiv-2604-05821: Lee and five colleagues improve cross-lingual retrieval with CLEAR, a reverse-training loss for multilingual embeddings. Standard contrastive adaptation misses deep alignment and can harm strong languages like English. CLEAR uses an English passage as a bridge to tie target languages to English, gaining up to 15 percent in cross-lingual tests, most in low-resource languages, with little English loss.
arxiv-2604-06021: In 2026, Gao and three colleagues made the first measurement of parity-odd kurto spectra in galaxy survey data. It tests whether the universe breaks mirror symmetry at cosmic scales. They use two composite-field spectra from BOSS and DESI luminous red galaxies. The method compresses the four-point signal so its covariance can be estimated directly from mock catalogues. Null tests and cross-patch checks find no parity-violating signal in either survey. DESI scatter runs about four times below BOSS, as its denser sample predicts.
arxiv-2604-06221: Dyck and five colleagues benchmark 13 lossless compression implementations for 4D-STEM microscopy, whose huge datasets strain storage and transfer. Across five datasets, gzip-9 gives the highest compression ratio but runs slow. Blosc-zstd matches its ratio while compressing and reading far faster. Compression follows a power law with sparsity, from 5 times to 35 times as data grows sparser. They name six top implementations and argue compression alone cannot sustain high-throughput workflows: future systems need inference-driven representations keeping only what an inference requires.
arxiv-2604-06421: Singh and eight others introduce Arabic-DeepSeek-R1, an open-source Arabic model on sparse experts. It tops the Arabic LLM board. Four-phase chain-of-thought distillation weaves Arabic checks and norms into a 372-million-token Arabic-English mixture. The model tops the seven-benchmark suite, with MadinahQA beating GPT-5.1. Sparse experts, culturally-informed distillation, and bilingual curation let an open-source model beat GPT-5.1 on most benchmarks, the first such demonstration for Arabic models. Arabic deficit stems from under-specialization, not architecture, and adaptation reaches without industrial pretraining.
arxiv-2604-06721: De Pas, Dipierro, and Valdinoci refine long-run bounds for minima of a far-reaching energy class with a weak wavy double-well shape. The shape obeys power control on its second slope near the wells, and the kernel belongs to a broad sized class modeled on the part Laplace. The authors prove their better bounds are optimal.
arxiv-2604-07121: Li and three colleagues propose Mixed Initiative Context, a way to treat chat context in human AI teamwork as a shaped object both sides can steer. Today, multi turn context is flattened into a time ordered list, so dead threads linger in a small window and clash. Users can only nudge context by rewording inputs, with no clear or checkable control. The new view lets the shape, scope, and content of context be rearranged as the task shifts, with humans and AI both shaping it.
arxiv-2604-07221: Ferreira and three colleagues compute the masses of light mesons, built from up, down, and strange quarks, with a symmetry-preserving method. Their approach feeds fully dressed quark-gluon vertices into the key equations, starting from a symmetric kinematic setup. From the gap equation they build a Bethe-Salpeter kernel with three diagram types, then find masses by tracking eigenvalues and extrapolating to the physical point. The results match experiment well and improve markedly on the rainbow-ladder approximation.
arxiv-2604-07821: Yadav, Black, and Sourbut test whether capable language-model agents cooperate when helping costs almost nothing. Many real coordination tasks are not dilemmas: sharing a document or unblocking a teammate costs the helper little and helps the group a lot. In a stripped-down turn-based environment where cooperation is free and plainly optimal, capability fails to predict cooperation. OpenAI o3 reaches only 17 percent of optimal collective performance, while weaker o3-mini reaches 50 percent, under identical instructions to maximize group revenue.
arxiv-2604-07921: Skuric, Von Werra, and Wolf survey sustainability awareness across nearly 50,000 open-access robotics papers from 2015 to early 2026. They count mentions of social, ecological, and green impacts and check alignment with the UN Sustainable Development Goals. A wide share of papers maps to goal-relevant domains, yet explicit green motivation stays very low. Impact mentions usually run below 2 percent, goal references below 0.1 percent, and green-motivated papers below 5 percent. The gap between the field's promise and its stated intent persists across the whole period.
arxiv-2604-08021: Mehta and Mankodi present SynQL, a deterministic framework for synthesizing SQL workloads. Data research and learned query tools rely heavily on SQL workloads. Real queries grow hard to obtain under strict privacy rules, and shared masked traces strip live query text. Older benchmarks offer too few fixed patterns for broad reach, while language-model methods invent fake columns and collapse toward simple join patterns that fail to stress tools. SynQL makes structurally diverse, ready-to-run workloads from rules, giving teams varied, runnable queries without privacy leaks or fake schemas.
arxiv-2604-08121: Qin and eight colleagues present Uni-ViGU, a framework for video making and viewing built on a video maker. Unified multimodal models face a gap: visual making costs far more compute than viewing, especially for video. Rather than stretching viewer models for making, the team inverts the approach, stretching a video maker as the base. A unified flow method matches smooth flow for video and discrete flow for text in one process, giving coherent generation. A mixture-of-experts design augments transformer blocks with lightweight text layers, keeping prior skills.
arxiv-2604-08421: Gelman, Krefman, Kennedy, and Hullman offer a way to form a realistic guess about an average treatment effect before a study runs. Instead of fixing on a single number, they start from how effects vary across people and build the average from that spread. Medicine, economics, and psychology cases show how the spread-first view shapes a more honest prior expectation.
arxiv-2604-08621: Jeunen, Hanna, and Wheeler track agentic personalization in marketing over 11 months in a real consumer app. They compare a phase of direct marketer control with a phase of autonomous agents running a fixed component library. Active human control gave the highest engagement lift, yet autonomous agents kept a real lift on their own afterward. The findings support a joint model: people drive discovery and setup, agents preserve and scale the gains.
arxiv-2604-08721: Cui and four colleagues design a linear feedback controller for homogeneous polynomial systems whose nonlinear term has a tensor form that splits along orthogonal axes. Their structure keeping design shares the tensor eigenbasis, yielding closed form paths and clear settling and escape thresholds. It gives sharp regions of pull, where local linear fits or Lyapunov sum of squares methods prove cautious and costly. Bounds for bounded disturbances follow, with numerical examples confirming the theory.
arxiv-2604-08921: Ao Li and five colleagues present TAIHRI, a vision language model built for close range human robot contact keypoint spotting. Whole body methods tune rebuilds against the root joint, but robots need exact spotting of task key parts under a head camera. TAIHRI reads motion commands, steers focus to task key points, and maps 3D keypoints into a finite contact space. It places key parts through 2D keypoint logic via next token guess. Head camera tests show top scores for task key parts, plus language control and mesh rebuild.
arxiv-2605-00621:
Christopher David Roberts and 4 co-authors assess what the oceans contribute to weather prediction at subseasonal range, weeks ahead, in Europe's leading forecast system. Coupling the atmosphere to a live ocean should help, through realistic air-sea exchange, but the interface can also grow biases that hurt. The team revisits that balance using forty-six-day reforecasts, hindcasts rerun with today's system.

Coupling significantly improved ensemble skill in the tropics, with benefits growing at longer lead times. Forecasts of the Madden-Julian Oscillation, a giant tropical weather pattern, gained about five days of skill over the uncoupled setup. In the extratropics the effect was marginal, barely moving major circulation indices. An experimental configuration with a much finer ocean grid, fine enough to resolve eddies, added little at this range. Accurate ocean initialization, the authors suggest, already captures most of the available benefit.
arxiv-2605-00721:
Anton Ratnarajah and 3 co-authors estimate how far a speaker is from a listener using synthetic echoes, in work from a room acoustics challenge at a major signal processing conference. Judging speaker distance from a recording depends on the room's impulse response, its acoustic fingerprint, and real datasets of such fingerprints are sparse. The challenge asks whether generated responses can supplement the few real ones.

The team generates impulse responses with an open-source fast generator that needs only the speaker and listener positions. A quality filter keeps synthetic responses that align with the challenge's real ones, and tuned fine-tuning does the rest. The augmentation cut the average distance error dramatically, roughly by two-thirds, in two simulated room families. Gains were largest at medium and long distances, exactly where estimation is hardest and where a system that knows how far away a voice sits becomes most useful.
arxiv-2605-01021:
Marcel Novaes generalizes the Kuramoto model of interacting oscillators so the particles move on the surface of a torus in D dimensions. The classic one-dimensional model is a standard tool for studying synchronization, where oscillators slowly lock into step. In the new version, the group behavior changes in a key way: the shift to synchronization becomes first order, meaning it is abrupt rather than smooth.

Novaes sets up the mean-field dynamics using a multidimensional Ott-Antonsen ansatz, a method that reduces the group equations. Synchronization arises through a saddle-node bifurcation, while the incoherent state remains always stable. Theory calculations are checked by numerical simulations. Readers get a clear picture of how higher-dimensional motion reshapes a classic model of synchronization.
arxiv-2605-01221:
Genki Osada proposes a new way to estimate the local intrinsic dimension of data, the number of directions that truly vary near a point. Diffusion models have opened new routes to this task, but older methods break down in high-dimensional spaces. Noise from the many normal directions drowns out the tangent signal that sets the local dimension, so estimates go wrong.

The method, called Local Hessian Spectral Dimension, filters the spectrum of the log-density Hessian. It cuts away the large eigenvalues tied to normal directions and counts the tangent directions with zero curvature. A stochastic Lanczos method makes the computation cheap, with cost growing only linearly in the dimension. Tests on synthetic and real data show stronger robustness than older methods. The method can also flag memorization in large diffusion models, where local dimension signals reveal overfitting to training data.
arxiv-2605-01321:
Yasuyuki Hatsuda and Tomohito Shiga compute the ringing tones of charged and spinning black holes at the extreme limit, where charge or spin is as high as it can be. These tones, called quasinormal modes, are the fading notes a black hole sounds after it is struck.

The pair use exact WKB analysis, a refined wave method that turns the tone problem into a set of exact conditions on complex frequencies. The key inputs, known as quantum periods, are summed to very high order and then resummed with a Borel-Padé step to get stable values. For scalar waves on extreme Reissner-Nordström and Kerr holes, the final tones match known correct values with high precision. That match checks the method on some of the hardest cases in the field.
arxiv-2605-01421:
Rosalba Garcia-Millan and six co-authors ask whether particles that only push each other away can act, in effect, as if they attract. Self-propelled particles that repel are known to clump into dense and dilute zones, a split often read as a sign of effective attraction.

The team test the idea in the smallest possible case: two soft run-and-tumble particles in a ring-shaped domain, handled with an exact microscopic theory. As the push between them grows, the leading effect is still effective repulsion. Attraction shows up only as a smaller, higher-order correction to the pair's effective interaction. The result refines the usual story told about this clumping: the phase split is real, but calling its onset an attraction effect skips the term that actually leads.
arxiv-2605-01521:
Paraskevas V Lekeas and Giorgos Stamatopoulos revisit cooperative games where a coalition's payoff depends on how the whole player set splits into groups. In this partition function form, what outsiders do among themselves changes what your group earns, which makes beliefs about outsiders part of the game.

Each coalition is assumed to hold probabilistic beliefs about how the outsiders will group, and those beliefs need not match what the outsiders actually choose. The pair apply the setup to symmetric games with positive or negative spillovers between groups. They derive conditions on the beliefs under which the core is nonempty, meaning some payoff split exists that no coalition can profitably break away from. The result shows how much shared expectation a stable grand outcome needs when groups watch each other guess.
arxiv-2605-01721:
Jacob Ginesin, Max von Hippel, and Cristina Nita-Rotaru automate the hunt for attacks that live in the wires between machines. Distributed protocols assume channels can insert, drop, replay, or reorder messages, yet verification projects each hand-roll their own fault model and prove safety against that alone.

Their tool, Tofu, flips the workflow. Given a protocol stated in linear temporal logic, it searches the whole state space for channel-fault attack traces, synthesizing a concrete attack when one exists and certifying absence when the search exhausts. The analysis is claimed sound and complete against its stated fault model, and general across protocols rather than tuned per case. TCP, the transport workhorse of the internet, serves as the demonstration target. The authors frame automatic fault analysis as a missing routine step for protocol design.
arxiv-2605-01921:
Yuan-Jun Gao, Gang Li, Shi-Dong Liu, and Qi Wu search for a proposed molecular state made of a B meson and its antimatter partner. The state, called Xb0, would be weakly bound and would test heavy-quark symmetry in the bottom sector. The team studies whether it could be found in a radiative decay of the Upsilon(10753) particle.

Working in nonrelativistic effective field theory, they treat the Upsilon state as a mix of two forms and let the decay proceed through meson loops. Loops with P-wave mesons dominate. The predicted width is small, giving a branching share around one in a million to one in one hundred thousand, but the authors call the channel promising for a search.
arxiv-2605-02021:
Santiago Thorup, Luca Castelletto, Zeyuan Feng, and Somil Bansal work on safe spacecraft docking, where a craft must reach its target while avoiding collision. Motion couples translation and rotation in many dimensions, which makes formal safety analysis hard. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability gives strong reach-avoid guarantees, but classic solvers only handle low-dimensional systems.

Their method learns a neural estimate of the Hamilton-Jacobi value function. Training uses physics-based losses plus supervision from model predictive control, which gives useful targets where physics losses alone fail and steadies learning. Online, the learned function guides control under that supervision. The aim is a scalable tube of safe states for docking and similar high-dimensional tasks.
arxiv-2605-02421:
Jinshi Liu and colleagues introduce AOCI, a symbolic-semantic index that lets a language model grasp a huge code repository in one pass. Models struggle once a codebase reaches hundreds of thousands of lines. Retrieval, summarisation, and agent exploration each build a different view at query time, varying between runs and leaving only ad-hoc traces behind.

An AOCI index starts with encoding rules, then gives one entry per code unit, meaning each file or database table. Each entry pairs a symbolic tag, which gives architectural coordinates, with semantic content covering function, dependencies, and constraints. The result is a structured blueprint of architecture, dependencies, and key design decisions that stays stable across tasks, instead of being rebuilt for every question.
arxiv-2605-02621:
Gabor Vattay writes a comment disputing a recent claim that the Schrödinger equation, the core equation of quantum mechanics, can be solved exactly using only classical action and a classical fluid density. The original article held that its method avoided the usual semiclassical approximations. Vattay argues that the derivation contains a basic error at its foundation.

In Vattay's reading, the derivation drops terms tied to how the probability density's amplitude varies in space. Dropping them removes the quantum potential, a term identified by Madelung and later stressed by Bohm. Without it, the claimed exact method is just the standard semiclassical approximation. The examples, Vattay adds, either sit in classes where that potential vanishes, or quietly import quantum results through their starting conditions.
arxiv-2605-02721:
Carlos Ruiz-Gonzalez, Mario Krenn, and Xuemei Gu build an algorithm that designs photon experiments to make entanglement with high success odds, not just high quality. Entangled photons are a workhorse of quantum technology. Sources that make photon pairs are probabilistic, and chasing perfect fidelity can make success vanishingly rare, a trade-off often ignored.

Standard treatments keep only the single-pair term and drop multi-pair emissions. The new design algorithm instead accounts for those higher-order events, explores different layout topologies under hardware limits, and tunes source settings to shrink the unwanted terms, or even use them. For widely used target states, including heralded Bell, W, and NOON states, the found designs beat prior proposals. The result points to more efficient photonic setups.
arxiv-2605-02821:
Haorui Li and nine co-authors measure how the same open-weight language model becomes a different service depending on who hosts it. Users rarely run the raw model; they call a provider's endpoint, which varies in variant, protocol behavior, context size, price, speed, reliability, and what tasks it can actually do. The paper argues the service, not the artifact, is the real unit.

Data come from a monitoring platform's request logs, provider records, compatibility probes, price snapshots, and steady latency measures over one quarter. Demand concentrates in a few model families, yet old versions stay active after new releases. A provider listing many models does not mean users adopt them, and prices stay steadier than speed, context, or error behavior. Task mix shifts token patterns, so the best provider depends on the job.
arxiv-2605-03021:
Florian Herren and Raynette van Tonder review what is known about semileptonic B meson decays that produce charm, and where the measured pieces still fall short. Adding up all measured exclusive rates should match the inclusive total, but a gap has long remained.

By adding rates measured against semi-inclusive decays, they show the missing part is mostly final states with no D meson at all. That points to sizable shares from baryon final states and from Ds mesons. They name candidate channels worth searching for and give simple models for two small missing modes.
arxiv-2605-03221:
Jiaxiang Jiang, Mahesh Subedar, and Omesh Tickoo use diffusion-generated images to lift rare-class accuracy in skin lesion classification. Medical datasets are heavily skewed, and the rarest classes often carry the highest risk, yet standard fixes give only small gains.

Their pipeline pairs an inpainting diffusion model with an out-of-distribution filter that keeps synthetic samples diverse and clinically plausible. On the large, skewed ISIC2019 benchmark, overall results rose substantially, with the biggest gain, over twenty-eight percent, on the class with fewest real samples. The work shows synthetic augmentation can directly ease long-tail imbalance in medical imaging.
arxiv-2605-03521:
Amanda Hirschi and Kai Hugtenburg construct open-closed Deligne-Mumford field theories, chain-level field theories built from moduli spaces of stable curves with boundary. Given a relatively spin embedded Lagrangian inside a symplectic manifold, they attach such a theory to it. The construction extends the Fukaya A-infinity algebra to curves of any genus and any number of boundary components.

The resulting theory is unique up to homotopy. Beyond its own interest, the construction is a first step toward proving Kontsevich's conjecture that the Fukaya category determines the Gromov-Witten invariants of the ambient space, following a strategy that Costello outlined. The paper supplies the basic construction that later steps of that program require.
arxiv-2605-03821:
Hao Wu and twelve co-authors present RoboAlign-R1, a framework that aligns robot video world models with what matters for decision making. Such models are usually trained on reconstruction and perceptual similarity. Those objectives say little about instruction following, manipulation success, or physical plausibility. Their errors also accumulate over long rollouts. The authors build reward-aligned post-training with stabilized long-horizon inference.

They built RobotWorldBench, ten thousand annotated video-instruction pairs from four robot data sources, and trained a multimodal teacher judge that scores generated videos on six dimensions. That judge is distilled into a lightweight student reward model for reinforcement learning post-training. A sliding window re-encoding step refreshes context during inference, and in-domain tests showed a double-digit percentage gain over the strongest baseline.
arxiv-2605-04021:
Sumit Rout, Aravinth Balaji Ravichandran, Paweł Horodecki, and Anubhav Chaturvedi show that Hamiltonian incompatibility is a thermodynamic resource for extracting work. Free energy caps the work of a single process once the state and Hamiltonian are fixed. But a work-extraction task is different. One device must perform across several preparations and Hamiltonian settings at once. A classical device is one whose Hamiltonian settings all mutually commute.

The authors place every branch at its best free-energy-limited envelope. They derive the resulting classical limit on the task's average work. The limit is optimized over arbitrary-dimensional classical devices. Incompatible Hamiltonian settings exceed that limit, even though every individual branch respects its own free-energy maximum. The advantage lives only in the average across the task. That identifies incompatibility itself as the resource.
arxiv-2605-04121:
Sonia L'Innocente, Francesco G. Russo, and Ilaria Svampa give Schur's classical theorem a dynamical interpretation for locally compact groups. Schur's 1904 result says an abstract group with finite central quotient has a finite derived subgroup, and it has many consequences and generalizations. The new viewpoint uses topological entropy, in the sense of Adler, Konheim, and McAndrew, to measure the complexity of group endomorphisms.

Working with groups whose central quotient is compact, the authors prove a conditional result. If the quotient has continuous endomorphisms of finite topological entropy, then the closure of the derived subgroup is also compact. It also has finite-entropy continuous endomorphisms. Connectedness is essential, since they construct a profinite counterexample without it. They also study Heisenberg groups over locally compact rings, where a dynamical Schur-type theorem persists even without compact central quotient, and derive new formulas for their p-rank.
arxiv-2605-05021:
Henrik Garde, David Johansson, and Thanasis Zacharopoulos extend a method for finding hidden inclusions inside a body from boundary electrical measurements, the Calderón problem. Their setting is harder than usual: the material can be direction-dependent, complex-valued, and not self-adjoint, a property many earlier results required. Only partial boundary data are assumed.

The monotonicity method is generalised to very general perturbations of this kind, in any dimension from two upward. The authors assume inclusion boundaries can be reached through a region where the background behaves self-adjointly, plus a definiteness condition nearby. Because uniqueness needs only the self-adjoint part, their method fits generic uniqueness results for this inverse problem.
arxiv-2605-05221:
Andrew Kiruluta develops a non-neural way to learn basis functions from data, keeping the clarity of classical expansions such as Fourier series and wavelets. Fixed dictionaries are easy to analyse but do not adapt to the structure of modern high-dimensional data. Neural networks do adapt, yet their layered form hides the basis and limits direct control over it.

His framework treats the basis pieces themselves as the variables to optimise, learning them jointly with per-sample coefficients and, when useful, a latent linear evolution rule. Kiruluta proves that minimisers exist, studies a blockwise descent algorithm, and gives conditions for recovering coefficients and identifying the basis. Manifold and dynamical regularisation can be added without neural machinery.
arxiv-2605-05521:
Decisions are often judged not only by what happened, but by what would have happened under another choice. Benedikt Koch, Kosuke Imai, and Tomasz Strzalecki give that idea, counterfactual utility, a firm formal footing. Critics had questioned whether such tastes can be consistent at all.

The authors extend the classic von Neumann-Morgenstern framework to the space of all potential outcomes. Expected counterfactual utility then meets the standard axioms there. Their framework also resolves the Allais paradox and a Russian roulette puzzle from the statistics literature, and it pins down when counterfactual values reduce to plain ones.
arxiv-2605-05721:
Single quantum emitters in two-dimensional materials could become the light bulbs of quantum networks, if they behaved like home gadgets. Sahil D. Patel and four co-authors review the push to wire such emitters into chips and light circuits. Today's best devices still need bulky optics, careful alignment, and hunting for a good working point.

The authors survey what turnkey use requires: on-demand triggering, steadying against noise, and efficient coupling into fibers and photonic circuits. Arrays multiply every difficulty through device spread and packaging costs. Their survey maps the gap between lab demos and deployable quantum-light engines.
arxiv-2605-05921:
Give expert mathematicians an AI discovery agent and the interesting question becomes how they steer it. Alex Bäuerle and seven co-authors ran a formative study with eleven experts using AlphaEvolve on advanced problems from their own fields. They identify a workflow they call intentmaking: discovering, defining, and refining one's goals through interaction with the system itself.

Intentmaking extends sensemaking, the building of understanding from data, into goal formation. Users cycle between the two as the agent's outputs reshape what they want to ask. The study offers a vocabulary for designing discovery tools around that cycle.
arxiv-2605-06021:
Tommy Carstensen presents PlotPick, an open source tool that pulls numbers out of scientific figures in batches. Systematic reviews often need values that papers report only in charts. Hand digitizing tools force a person to select and calibrate each figure one at a time, which is slow for large reviews.

PlotPick calls vision language models to extract tables from many figures at once. Carstensen benchmarks nine such models against DePlot, a dedicated chart to table model, on two synthetic chart sets. Vision models led clearly on one set, while results on the second were mixed. This version corrects the first, and withdraws its claim that every vision model beat DePlot on both benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-06421:
Mingfeng Lin, Jiakun Chen, Liang Han, and Liqiang Nie introduce FREPix, a flow matching method that generates images directly in pixel space. Pixel generation avoids the bottleneck of first compressing images through an autoencoder. Most methods, though, treat generation as uniform across frequencies, ignoring that coarse structure and fine detail behave differently.

FREPix splits generation into low- and high-frequency parts, gives each its own transport path, predicts them with a factorized network, and trains with a frequency-aware objective. On ImageNet it reaches competitive image quality scores at two resolutions. Gains are strongest early in training and when few sampling steps are allowed.
arxiv-2605-06521:
Clerico and three colleagues tackle a timing problem in sequential statistics, where late evidence can be useless even when it is strong. Their subject is anytime valid testing. It lets researchers check results while data still arrive and stop early without losing false alarm control. They build a testing by betting framework, where bets against a null claim build wealth as evidence grows, with rewards that favour quick rejection.

The authors turn the search for the best betting plan into a control problem whose answer depends only on the clock and the evidence so far. For hard deadlines, the simple case against one rival claim becomes a finite horizon Neyman Pearson problem. It comes with a matching optimal e process. They also derive an exponential decay optimal rule for shrinking rewards, a finite time cousin of the classic growth rate optimal view.
arxiv-2605-06921:
Yongliang Sun and five co-authors take a fresh look at hard counting and cutting problems known as Maximum Independent Set and Maximum Cut. Traditional step-by-step search finds good answers but grows expensive on large, dense problems. The authors explore smooth, gradient-based methods that can update many variables in parallel.

They show where plain gradient methods get stuck, and where a new formulation for Maximum Cut lets them escape weak solutions. Their framework adds partial resets, called differentiable mutations, to jump into new regions. Experiments suggest the approach scales well where ordinary local search becomes too costly to run.
arxiv-2605-07021:
Christopher Z. Cui, Taylor W. Killian, and Prithviraj Ammanabrolu tackle oversight of language model reasoning. Harmful plans may only become visible after a model finishes thinking, which makes monitoring hard. Their answer is Behavior Cue Reasoning, where the model learns to emit special tokens just before certain behaviors.

Those cues act as both signals and control points for an outside monitor. In tests, a monitor using only cue information cut wasted reasoning tokens by up to half on hard math problems. In a safety setting, cues let monitors recover safe actions from most traces that would otherwise end unsafely, with no loss in task performance.
arxiv-2605-07221:
Wei Jiang and three co-authors segment medical images using a frozen vision foundation model with only a light readout trained. Adapting such models usually means fine-tuning the backbone or building heavy decoders, both unreliable when labeled scans are few. The team found frozen DINOv3 features already carry structure and boundary cues.

Their readout trains small probes on the last three blocks, then views each image at several resolutions and augmentations, fusing the maps by confidence. Under fixed protocols on endoscopy, skin, and brain MRI benchmarks, scores were strong. With only five annotated brain patients, the method recovered nearly all of the performance of a forty-patient reference run.
arxiv-2605-07321:
Vijay Pratap Sharma and four co-authors design TREA, an edge chip for spotting and sorting objects. Edge vision platforms face tight limits on area, power, and delay. TREA uses a dual-precision multiply unit that computes most-significant digits first, supports runtime truncation, and avoids the usual multiplier cost.

A pruning strategy co-designed with the datapath keeps usage high at near half sparsity, and an adjustable unit handles several activation types through time sharing. One hundred such units are reused layer by layer across the network. Experiments show large gains in speed, usage, and energy use over fixed-width, non-adjustable chips.
arxiv-2605-07521:
Friedrich Hastedt and two co-authors tackle computer-aided synthesis planning, the task of finding routes to build a target molecule from simpler chemicals. Most tools stop once they find one workable route. Real chemists, though, must weigh cost, toxicity, sustainability, and yield against each other, so a single answer is rarely enough.

Their algorithm, MORetro*, searches for a whole Pareto front of routes, each best under some balance of the user's chosen criteria. It uses weighted scoring and guided sampling to search efficiently, and it carries a guarantee of recovering the true front under stated conditions. On standard benchmarks it surfaced strong routes that single-goal searches had missed.
arxiv-2605-07821:
Boyang Dai and two co-authors detect out-of-distribution images by reading the company objects keep. Detectors usually fight over entangled representations, ignoring context, and they struggle most on near-out-of-distribution cases, where a model's simplicity bias locks onto easy regions. Human vision, by contrast, uses object co-occurrence in natural scenes to understand what belongs.

Their framework, OCO, predicts disentangled representations for a test image, sorts its co-occurrence pattern into one of three scenarios learned from in-distribution data, and detects outliers within each scenario separately. Across challenging and full-spectrum test settings the method stayed competitive and handled both semantic and covariate shifts, precisely because it judges scenes by their object relationships rather than surface simplicity.
arxiv-2605-08021:
Jakob Wagner, Jeff Maki, Oded Zilberberg, and Kilian Seibold derive a fuller rule for driven quantum oscillators. Standard rules for how such systems lose energy assume no driving and no nonlinear terms. Real devices for quantum technology break both of those assumptions.

The authors keep the full driven motion inside the loss term itself. The loss paths then change with the drive. That change yields nonlinear damping, plus shifts in the drive. For a driven Kerr system, the theory predicts no bistability, lopsided resonance shapes, and strongly changed spread in the state.
arxiv-2605-08221:
Michael Jerge and David Evans present NoisyCoconut, an inference-time method that makes language model answers easier to trust without retraining. Instead of asking the model to reason in words, the method perturbs its internal latent trajectory with controlled noise, which produces several diverse reasoning paths inside the model.

Agreement among those paths becomes a confidence signal: when the paths converge on one answer, the model answers, and when they disagree, it can abstain. Across several reasoning benchmarks the method achieved effective coverage-accuracy trade-offs, needing no training data and no change to model weights. The design fits models already in service.
arxiv-2605-08321:
Lennart Wachowiak, Scott Blain, David Williams-King, and Samuele Marro test a watchdog for manipulative chatbots. In a preregistered study with one hundred twenty people across four decision scenarios, an adversarial language model with a hidden goal steered users' choices about two thirds of the time.

Their warden is a second model that watches the conversation live and sends the user private, non-binding warnings when it spots manipulation. Adding it cut the adversary's success rate to about thirty percent, while genuine interactions lost far less ground. The team also releases COAX-Bench, a simulation suite of fourteen scenarios and over sixteen thousand multi-agent interactions, to probe how the defense works.
arxiv-2605-08421:
Pascal Tilli and Mohsen Mesgar teach document retrieval models to see page layout, not just text patches. Late-interaction retrievers score a document as a bag of local patch embeddings. The patches are matched against query tokens. That is fast. But it is blind to the global arrangement of figures, tables, and columns. Relevance often lives in that arrangement.

Their encoder keeps the patch machinery. It adds one global layout embedding. The embedding is trained from textual descriptions of each document's layout. Inference itself does not change. On four ViDoRe-v2 datasets, the model beat the strongest comparable ColPali and ColQwen baselines. The gains were statistically significant on each dataset.
arxiv-2605-08521:
Nhut Le, Ehsan Karimi, and Maryam Rahnemoonfar estimate flood depth, not just flood extent, from aerial photos taken after a disaster. A flat flood mask tells responders where water is, but depth decides whether a road is passable and how badly a building is threatened.

Their pipeline segments the water with Mask2Former, a transformer segmentation model, then fuses the mask with a digital elevation model. The water-land boundary fixes a global water surface height, and each pixel's depth follows from local hydrostatic balance against the terrain height. Evaluated on the FloodNet and CRASAR-U-DROIDS datasets, the workflow turns strong segmentation into three-dimensional situational awareness.
arxiv-2605-09221:
Daniel Smola and Alex Smola recast fairness impossibility results as one geometry, showing several distinct scalar statements share a single RKHS picture. Fairness criteria become linear constraints on conditional mean embeddings, while unequal base rates push the law of total expectation to overdetermine those constraints. The Kleinberg Mullainathan Raghavan dichotomy then needs group conditional unbiasedness alone, rather than full calibration.

The Pokémon theorem shows a distinct group pair satisfying any finite set of linear mean fairness criteria still leaves a residual breach witnessed by the MMD. That violation decays at the Kolmogorov width rate under spectral regularity. Those tools also prove fair feature learning cannot escape: parity plus class conditional separation in representation space forces class collapse when base rates differ. Approximate relaxations yield signal and error frontiers, letting practitioners trade estimator performance against fairness goals, and experiments on standard fairness benchmarks agree with the bounds.
arxiv-2605-09321:
Zerhoudi presents OpenIIR, a simulation platform running hundreds of LLM-driven personas as parameterised experiments in information retrieval research. Researchers set up agents across four multi-agent study kinds: debate panels, social platforms, curated feeds, and co-evolution of content producers with credibility detectors. Action timings, mutation rates, persona budgets, retrieval policies, and ranker choices are set in advance, and the same study can re-run under different settings for side by side comparison.

Each run hands a downstream evaluator material it can use directly: argument graphs, exposure logs, fitness traces, and transcripts. A new study is a 200 to 400 line plug-in over a shared core. The work adds the shared core, a type interface for plug-in scenarios, four types with reference runs, and six modular extensions aimed at open IR research questions. Priors, rounds, and constraints vary explicitly rather than hiding inside prompts.
arxiv-2605-09821:
Long and three colleagues studied the online Steiner forest problem, where terminal pairs arrive one by one and the algorithm must keep a low-cost subgraph connecting each pair so far. If edges can never be deleted, the best possible competitive ratio, cost versus the optimal offline solution, is on the order of log n. That bound had stood as a wall.

The paper opens the study of low-recourse algorithms, which may delete edges sparingly. Its algorithm keeps a constant-competitive solution, cost within a constant factor of optimal, while changing only O(log n) edges per demand on average. Allowing a little recourse, the authors show, breaks the logarithmic barrier on cost without churning the solution.
arxiv-2605-10121:
Oliva and three co-authors make brain-computer interfaces both better and more transparent. P300-based interfaces read a typical brain wave from EEG signals, with uses in health, education and assistive technology, but person-to-person variation and opaque deep-learning models limit use. Their Post-Recurrent Module is an extra layer added to a recurrent neural network that classifies P300 signals.

The module enables dual analysis of space-time signals. Global techniques flag the most relevant brain regions and time windows, while local techniques explain single decisions in terms of EEG patterns matching established P300 neuroscience. Experiments show about nine percent better scores than the state of the art, with variability findings that match the literature. The framework generalises to motor imagery, steady-state visual potentials and cognitive workload assessment.
arxiv-2605-10321:
V. A. Dzuba, V. V. Flambaum, and G. K. Vong argue that hydrogen offers the cleanest atomic stage for hunting a hypothetical light Z-prime boson. Parity nonconservation, the weak-force mixing of opposite-parity atomic states, grows rapidly with nuclear charge for ordinary Z-boson exchange. For a light extra boson, that enhancement fades, so the extra boson's share grows as nuclear charge falls, faster than one over Z squared. Their 2026 paper quantifies the effect.

Hydrogen adds a second advantage: its theory is far cleaner than that of heavy atoms, allowing sharper interpretation of experiments. The authors calculate the ratio of the Z-prime contribution, for arbitrary Z-prime mass, to the Standard Model contribution in hydrogen and deuterium. Both nuclear-spin-independent and nuclear-spin-dependent interactions are included. Hydrogen and deuterium parity-violation experiments could thus disentangle a possible Z-prime signal from the Standard Model background.
arxiv-2605-10521:
Yiqi Tian and five colleagues address a hidden fairness failure in medical segmentation. Segmentation models perform unevenly across subgroups. Most fairness methods target average subgroup performance, treating each subgroup as internally homogeneous. That hides difficult cases where high-loss samples are masked by the subgroup mean. The authors call this intra-group hidden failure. Their 2026 paper proposes DuetFair.

DuetFair is a fairness framework covering inter-subgroup adaptation and intra-subgroup robustness. Built on it, FairDRO combines mixture-of-experts with subgroup-conditioned robust loss aggregation. The design adapts across subgroups while cutting hidden failures within each subgroup. FairDRO leads on equity-scaled performance on Harvard-FairSeg and lifts worst-case subgroup performance on HAM10000 for age- and race-based groups. On a 3D radiotherapy cohort, it improves worst-group Dice by 3.5 points under tumor-stage grouping and by 4.1 points under institution grouping over the best baseline.
arxiv-2605-10621:
Taha Entesari and Mahyar Fazlyab introduce hierarchical Taylor bounds for network verification. Reachability analysis seeks to compute or bound network outputs attainable over input domain. It matters for certifying safety and robustness in learning systems. Since reachable set computation is intractable, methods rely on overapproximations. Their 2026 paper introduces HiTaB.

For smooth, twice-differentiable networks, approaches exploit at most second-order information. They do not leverage higher-order information. HiTaB exploits second-order smoothness through the Hessian and its Lipschitz constant. The authors develop a hierarchy of zeroth-, first-, and second-order bounds. They give conditions under which higher-order approximations yield improvements. Their main contribution is a procedure for bounding the Hessian Lipschitz constant in networks. It uses layerwise propagation of curvature bounds. It extends to L2- and L-infinity-constrained input sets and integrates into branch-and-bound pipelines.
arxiv-2605-10721: De Marzo and four colleagues ask whether groups of AI agents stay safe when each agent alone is aligned with human values. Simulating opinion dynamics across nine big language models and a hundred opinion pairs, they find majority-following and intrinsic bias pulling against each other. Their statistical-physics theory predicts when populations get trapped in long-lived misaligned states, and how a few adversarial agents can tip a whole population irreversibly.
arxiv-2605-10921:
Huashuo Lei and twelve colleagues build RoboMemArena, a benchmark that tests robot memory over long, partly hidden tasks. Robots must lean on past sights and actions to finish jobs that stretch past a thousand steps, yet older benchmarks lack memory annotations, cover few tasks, and never leave simulation.

The benchmark spans 26 tasks, with over two-thirds of subtasks depending on memory, and pairs simulated trials with real-world memory tasks for physical checks. A vision-language model designs the subtasks, and the authors' PrediMem system, a dual planner with recent and keyframe memory buffers, beats all baselines. Roboticists get a demanding arena plus design lessons for memory that actually serves decisions.
arxiv-2605-11021:
Donghwan Lee and Han-Dong Lim develop a switching-system theory of Q-learning with linear function approximation, grounded in the joint spectral radius. With linear approximation, the Bellman optimality operator projects onto a feature subspace. The greedy action shifts as parameters move, so mean dynamics follow no single linear system.

The pair derives an exact linear switched model for mean dynamics and ties convergence to switched-system stability. The construction extends to stochastic linear Q-learning under independent and Markovian observations. Though exact joint-spectral-radius computation is hard in general, the certificate handles products of switching modes and improves on one-step norm bounds for conservatism. The framework also yields a joint-spectral-radius view of regularized Q-learning, unifying projected Bellman equations, stochastic-policy switching, and stability in one parameter-space picture.
arxiv-2605-11221:
Yaochen Rao and three co-authors augment targeted protein degradation databases beyond manual curation with agentic literature extraction workflows. Models in biomedicine depend on tidy assay data locked in papers, tables, and addenda, and TPD records must combine compound names, target, recruiter, assay context, and endpoint values across sections and files.

The team frames TPD record extraction as a domain task and presents an expert-in-the-loop LLM workflow, judged by three-way check among LLM outputs, standard baseline records, and expert ground truth. A lightweight cross-checked prompt-tuning module adapts task prompts from scarce expert notes. With only seven molecular glue papers, the workflow reaches record-level F1 near unity and transfers to PROTACs by wording swap alone, holding record-level F1 above ninety-three hundredths. Teams get record growth without hand-reading every paper.
arxiv-2605-11721: Koya Sakakibara develops a finite element method for constrained planar geometric flows, the evolving closed curves behind curve shortening and related motions. His stabilized dual-SAV form uses separate helper variables for physical energy and mesh regularization. The mesh term acts only on tangential motion, so mesh repair never invents a false driving force. The scheme shrinks global constraints to a tiny nonlinear system and, in tests on four flow types, preserved dissipation, constraints, and mesh quality.
arxiv-2605-12021: Ryota Yoshihashi and four colleagues split what from where in visual cores. Class-first cores stress looks while tangling or hiding place, making finding, spotting, and splitting harder. Their What-Where Transformer treats tokens as what and attention maps as where, handling them in joint feed-forward modules through a multi-stream slot design. Even under single-label ImageNet training it found multiple objects from raw attention maps, beating ViT methods on zero-shot finding and weakly guided splitting.
arxiv-2605-12321: Lakas, Ferrag and Debbah propose running road crossings without traffic lights, letting a language model arbitrate instead. Their LIDSA framework reads each self-driving vehicle's stated intent, together with priority class, queue pressure and energy wishes, and issues speed advice to resolve conflicting claims on the crossing. Earlier systems kept signals in place or used language models only as helpers, and slow model replies blocked split-second control. The paper argues that intent-driven arbitration can fill that gap.
arxiv-2605-12421: Wang and seven colleagues warn against asking language models to optimise search while they build combinatorial solvers. They release CP-SynC-XL, a benchmark of one hundred problems and over four thousand instances.
