Foresight restructures access so the structure skips over those misses, and it is designed as a surgical change that fits many existing skiplist designs.

Extending the idea to concurrent skiplists, where many threads work at once, raises synchronisation problems that the authors identify and solve. They apply Foresight to one sequential and three concurrent designs. Microbenchmarks show throughput improvements of up to forty-five percent. In a real test, they insert the optimised skiplist as the index of an in-memory database system. End-to-end performance there improves by up to fifteen percent.
arxiv-2606-13521:
Holmes studies what logical operations quantum codes can perform in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stabiliser codes protect quantum information by spreading it across many physical qubits. A transversal gate acts qubit-by-qubit across code blocks, which makes it fault-tolerant, so knowing which gates a code admits this way is fundamental. Holmes derives lower bounds on the circuit depth needed to generate a logical Clifford algebra, the standard set of basic logical operations. He also builds new transversal gates.

Highlights include a depth-one transversal phase gate in the rotated surface code, the leading practical code family. A depth-one controlled-phase gate inside blocks of the two-dimensional toric code generalises to all odd distances. Finally, he builds a high-rate code family, encoding many logical qubits per block, with a constant-depth transversal Clifford set. Such codes could sharply reduce the overhead of fault-tolerant quantum computing.
arxiv-2606-13621:
Achraf Hsain and Almuhammadi argue that safety shields for learning agents are worth more as design tools than as runtime guards in this 2026 arXiv paper. Shielded reinforcement learning compiles temporal-logic safety specifications into automata that restrict an agent's actions. The authors contend this is the wrong product: the same machinery, meaning specification compilation, product game construction, and winning-region extraction, more naturally serves as a design instrument. Its outputs are structural insights about a system, not constraints bolted onto a running agent. They call this reframing shield synthesis as defensibility analysis.

They show it in a two-player safety game for network defence. A defender specification defines unacceptable outcomes, while an attacker specification constrains the adversary, and the two are enforced asymmetrically. Solving the game reveals which parts of the network are defensible. For security architects, knowing a position is unwinnable before deployment beats a runtime shield.
arxiv-2606-14121:
Abubakar and the NOvA Collaboration ask whether a reactor experiment in China can tip their long-baseline experiment into settling the neutrino mass ordering. The ordering, which neutrino state is heaviest, is a fundamental unknown. NOvA currently prefers the normal ordering at only one point six sigma. JUNO will soon measure the atmospheric mass splitting far more precisely. Their 2026 arXiv paper explores how JUNO results may combine with ten years of NOvA data.

The headline is hopeful but conditional. Three sigma evidence for the normal ordering is achievable within five years over a range of plausible JUNO measurements. If JUNO's precision beats about zero point three percent, NOvA's own precision becomes the limit, so small gains there widen the winning range. But if JUNO's central value stays near the global average, its precision would not enable an early determination. The field would wait for better long-baseline data.
arxiv-2606-14521:
Rollier and Baetens derive exact Lyapunov spectra for a class of cellular automata in a 2026 arXiv paper. Cellular automata update grid cells by fixed local rules, and Lyapunov exponents measure how fast small disturbances grow, revealing chaos. For automata these spectra are usually approximated numerically, a delicate process prone to artifacts.

The authors show that affine rules, whose updates are an exclusive-or of chosen inputs plus a constant, admit an exact spectrum. Such a rule has one fixed Boolean Jacobian matrix, so the spectrum reduces to logarithms of that matrix's singular values, with no simulation needed. On periodic lattices the answer becomes a Fourier transform of the rule's stencil, and for the parity rule on any graph it is the logarithm of the adjacency spectrum. The exact results expose errors in previously published spectra.
arxiv-2606-14621:
Li, Pearson-Merkowitz, and Yokum evaluate a reemployment program in a 2026 arXiv paper. Rhode Island's RESEA program helps unemployment insurance claimants return to work faster. It also checks their eligibility. The authors ran a large preregistered randomized trial. It ran from February twenty twenty-two to September twenty twenty-three.

Over twenty-three thousand claimants took part. Selection into the program raised annualized wages. The gain was about one thousand one hundred fifty-three dollars per person. It lifted reemployment by one and a half percentage points. It shortened benefit duration by nearly two weeks. Most gains arrived within two quarters and lasted at least a year. Each dollar spent saved the state about two dollars and sixty-four cents. Effects were positive for everyone. They were especially large for older and lower-income workers.
arxiv-2606-15021:
Chan and Kao present Token Steering, a way to guide robot foundation models in a 2026 study. Vision-language-action models generate robot motion as action tokens. Small trajectory errors can ruin a task, yet language prompts are too coarse for live correction. Full teleoperation fixes errors but throws away the model's learned skill.

Token Steering converts a low-dimensional user input into steering tokens inside the model's action-token space. The policy then completes the motion on its own, keeping its smoothness and task knowledge. No training or fine-tuning is needed, since everything happens at inference time. Tests cover drawer closing after object placement and state-aware object swapping. Success climbs from about ten percent to over seventy percent on the first task, with a similar jump on the second. The authors note the interface could suit brain-computer control, where intent signals are low-dimensional.
arxiv-2606-15321:
Wei and coauthors generate flat-band materials from geometric motifs nobody had catalogued, in a 2026 materials design paper. Flat energy bands amplify electron interactions, enabling exotic quantum phases. Known flat bands come from a short list of named lattice patterns like kagome and Lieb nets. But flatness is a property of network linkage, so other geometries should work too. The authors map sublattice shapes continuously and pick motifs outside the known clusters. Their generator, SkeleGen, embeds those skeletons into crystals respecting crystal symmetry.

The pipeline produced over nine thousand candidate crystals passing stability and flatness screens. Full quantum calculations confirmed flat bands in the generated structures. The spectra matched tight-binding predictions for the skeletons closely. That match supports a shape-based origin for the flatness. The approach turns flat-band design from list search into open-ended generation. The same trick could target other traits tied to geometry.
arxiv-2606-15521:
Jain and colleagues examine a hidden symmetry of large language models in 2026: the same text can be split into tokens in many valid ways. Tokenizers normally return one canonical split, and models train on that split, so nothing guarantees they treat other splits of the same bytes alike. The team tests this retokenization symmetry through experiments on token composition, representation diversity, and benchmark tasks.

They find the symmetry emerges only in part during training. Retokenized prompts usually preserve task understanding, yet they still stir the internal computation enough to produce new solution paths. Used as a sampling trick, retokenization recovers solutions that temperature sampling misses, though it can hurt on easy problems. The effect is strongest in code generation, where many correct approaches exist. At matched compute budgets, though, retokenization is not a cheaper substitute for temperature sampling, so its value is as a probe and a diversity source.
arxiv-2606-16221:
Wagner and colleagues present QALM in 2026, a quantum circuit optimizer that escapes local minima without paying full search costs. Greedy rule-based optimizers apply any cost-cutting rewrite at once: fast, but easily trapped in local minima. Search-based optimizers accept worse circuits to explore, yet cannot cheaply tell whether a costlier point is truly promising.

That verification gap forces pure search to spend exponentially many steps checking whether a higher-cost point leads to a better basin. QALM interleaves the two styles in one control loop. Each exploration phase proposes candidates, and each exploitation phase immediately descends from every candidate with fast rules. Promising points are thus verified almost at once, instead of after blind wandering. The hybrid keeps rule-based speed while gaining search-like escapes from poor minima.
arxiv-2606-16621:
Singh and co-authors give a flying robot arm in 2026 a two-layer brain: reinforcement learning for the plan, and a dynamics estimator that cleans up reality's surprises mid-flight. Aerial manipulators work in hard-to-reach places, but whole-body control under rapid arm motion and payload changes remains largely unsolved. Their framework lets an RL outer loop map desired six-degree-of-freedom end-effector targets to coordinated whole-body commands, without needing an accurate coupled model inside the policy.

An inner loop then tracks those commands while an estimator compensates inertial shifts and uncertainty during execution. The team validates on a quadrotor carrying a three-degree-of-freedom manipulator, under payload conditions. Against RL-plus-PID and RL-plus-INDI-plus-PID baselines, the method cuts mean tracking error (RMSE) by up to 40.9 percent across conditions, per the report, with the smallest trial-to-trial variation.
arxiv-2606-16921:
Berger and Holzman settle the integrality gap for covering with triples in a 2026 combinatorics paper. The set cover problem asks for the fewest sets that cover every element, and with sets of size at most three it is still hard to solve exactly. A fractional relaxation, letting sets be used in fractions, gives a lower bound that real covers can exceed.

The ratio between the true optimum and the fractional one is the integrality gap. A classic Lovász bound capped it below two, later improved by Fujito and Okumura. Berger and Holzman prove the gap is at most three halves, and that this value cannot be improved. As a corollary, the vertices of any regular three-uniform hypergraph can be covered by at most half as many edges as vertices. That closes the three case of a problem posed by Moreira and Kohayakawa.
arxiv-2606-17221:
Escobar presents a 2026 arXiv paper on the Casimir effect in nonlinear field theories, where vacuum fluctuations between parallel plates produce a measurable energy. Earlier work on Lorentz-violating scalar fields found that a constant kinetic background rescales the plate separation and adds an overall factor. Escobar asks what deeper structure explains that simple pattern and how far it extends.

The answer lies in a shared Schur-complement structure, where one reduced quadratic form controls both the spectral denominator and the energy-density term. That insight turns the scalar result into a prescription for fluctuation sectors of nonlinear theories around constant backgrounds. For nonlinear electrodynamics, a magnetic background splits the modes into ordinary and extra branches, and the plate energy computed two ways agrees exactly. The energy also depends on the field's orientation, giving a concrete directional Casimir response.
arxiv-2606-17621:
Hrdina, Hildenbrand, and Rettig present a 2026 arXiv paper on Quantum Computing Algebra, a real algebra of geometry built to state quantum computing directly, with no detour through complex matrices. Earlier work of this kind used sign choices that make Dirac notation hard to translate into it. This scheme picks a split signature instead, which the authors argue gives quantum states and operators a natural home while staying friendly to existing software for such algebras.

An add-on to the GAALOP system shows gates and multi-qubit systems being built and run in code. Results come in a Witt basis whose change rules are simple and need no imaginary unit at all. A demo in quantum game theory shows the real form paying off when entangled strategies are modelled. The work links abstract quantum notation with fast, workable computation for those who build such systems.
arxiv-2606-18021:
Yadav and Gurugubelli audit how often legal AI systems invent contract facts, and in which direction, in a 2026 paper. Headline hallucination rates near one half hide where errors cluster, so compliance teams cannot tell a risky system from a safe one. Their framework, LegalHalluLens, profiles errors by claim type across numeric, temporal, obligation, and factual categories in real contracts.

Working over five hundred contracts and nearly a quarter million clause-level checks, they find a huge within-model gap between claim types that averages conceal. Two systems with the same overall rate can err in opposite directions, one inventing rights and the other dropping them, which their Risk Direction Index captures in one number. A calibrated multi-agent debate pipeline, tuned by that diagnosis, cut fabricated detections by nearly half while using a modest open backbone.
arxiv-2606-18221:
Wang and colleagues design a neural operator that can keep a shock wave sharp, in a 2026 paper. Hyperbolic conservation laws govern floods, gases, and traffic, and their solutions mix broad smooth regions with sudden jumps like shocks. The popular Fourier Neural Operator handles the smooth, long-range part well but smears the jumps with excess numerical dissipation, and errors compound over long rollouts.

Their Local–Global Neural Operator couples that global Fourier branch with a local multiresolution branch built to resolve discontinuities, joined by a multiplicative interaction. Training uses a one-step loss with a spectral penalty that damps fake oscillations near steep fronts. Across one and two dimensional benchmarks the model cut one-step errors by factors of two to five against parameter-matched rivals. Trained only on short high-quality simulations, it stayed accurate over long rollouts on coarse grids.
arxiv-2606-18621:
Li and the team tackle anomaly detection on relational databases, in a 2026 machine learning paper from Griffith and Guangxi Universities. Relational data is the default format for finance, commerce, and industrial monitoring, and fraud or risk often hides inside it. The clues are sparse, spread across mixed, wide tables. Some live in odd connection patterns along foreign keys, which tabular and graph detectors handle poorly.

Their system RelAD rebuilds both attributes and relational edges. A sparse-gated module cuts extra multi-table attributes and stresses abnormal semantic blocks. A dual-view module flags relation-specific abnormal connections, from built-in traits and behavior profiles. These parts fuse into one anomaly score. The authors also built six benchmark datasets with planned anomalies. On those, RelAD beat typical baselines throughout, at strong efficiency. It does not yet model how databases evolve over time.
arxiv-2606-18721:
Choi, Lee, and Kim fix a mismatch in how pointer-network models learn to recognize table structure, in a 2026 document analysis paper. Such models predict a table's HTML structure, while pointing each tag at its detected text region. Their error analysis shows failures are overwhelmingly local. Nearly eighty percent of pointing errors land on spatially adjacent cells, within a Manhattan distance of two. Standard cross-entropy training penalizes every wrong candidate equally.

Their Geometry-Aware Pointer loss reweights the objective by spatial proximity to the true cell, with inverse distance weighting. So immediate neighbors receive stronger gradients than distant cells, and training effort concentrates where the model struggles. On the PubTabNet and SynthTabNet benchmarks, the method consistently cut adjacent-cell errors and set new state-of-the-art performance. Gains in position accuracy were especially strong.
arxiv-2606-19021:
Dinkelacker-Steinhoff and colleagues model how silica glass compacts under pressure in a 2026 study. Under load, the glass can lose stiffness in a specific way and show complex inelastic behavior that is still not fully understood. The authors treat the odd S-shaped stress response as a sign of a binary phase change. Two volume fractions coexist while fine patterns like shear bands form between them at small scales.

Their variational model tracks only the volume fractions, not the fine patterns themselves. It assumes steady temperature during compaction and builds on earlier work on multi-phase change in inelastic materials. Even with that simplification, the model matches experimental findings very well. Numerical cases show clearly how shifts in elastic moduli track shifts in volume as pressure rises. The work gives engineers a simpler predictive tool for glass under extreme load, without resolving every micro-scale detail.
arxiv-2606-19721:
Daiki Yotsufuji and four colleagues tackle reinforcement learning when sensor frames go missing in 2026. Delays and sensor failures drop frames, hiding states and rewards from the agent. An earlier offline method, DeFog, patched Decision Transformers for such gaps.

Offline training, though, generalises poorly to states the dataset barely covers. OnDeFog merges DeFog's mechanisms with the Online Decision Transformer, which learns by direct interaction. Experiments compare all three methods across dropping rates and dataset mixes. OnDeFog beats the online baseline where dropping runs heavy. It also beats DeFog on datasets loaded with low-reward data. Online interaction repairs the blind spots that offline data leave behind. Agents on flaky hardware, from drones to field robots, face exactly this failure mode. Code for the study is released openly for replication.
arxiv-2606-20121:
Ghilain Bergeron and Vincent Trélat connect two worlds of formal software development with BARReL, a Lean 4 library serving as a modern backend for Atelier B. Their 2026 paper addresses a practical split. The B method, long used for safety-critical systems, has industrial tooling but aging proof support. The Lean proof assistant offers strong interactive proving with dependent types. BARReL lets users carry out full B developments, through refinement down to implementation, inside Lean while keeping standard B syntax.

B's partial operators are encoded so that every use generates explicit well-definedness conditions, which Lean's type system enforces by construction. Proofs therefore cannot silently rest on ill-defined terms, and built-in automation discharges the simpler conditions alone. The library rests on Lean meta-programming and stays modular, so extending the supported B fragment means adding syntax and encoding clauses. A case study illustrates the workflow.
arxiv-2606-20221:
Sergey Ostapchenko, Tanguy Pierog, and Günter Sigl probe how much trust to place in simulations of air showers. Their 2026 paper uses a new Monte Carlo generator, QGSb, to explore model uncertainties in extensive air showers. These are the cascades sparked when a high-energy cosmic ray hits the atmosphere. Experiments infer the primary particle's identity mainly from two shower features: the depth of shower maximum and the muon count at ground. Both come from models, not direct measurement.

The authors test several modifications of the collision model and trace the physics behind each change. For every variant, they check the impact on those two shower features and compare the altered model against accelerator data. The exercise maps which choices move composition-sensitive observables, and by how much. That matters because the muon puzzle, a mismatch between measured and predicted muon counts, may reflect model shortcomings rather than new physics.
arxiv-2606-20421:
Alexandru Dimca and Piotr Pokora study Ziegler pairs, two line arrangements that look alike numerically but differ homologically. Their 2026 paper asks how much of an arrangement's algebra is fixed by its intersection lattice, the record of which lines meet where. Ziegler pairs are the counterexamples that mark where combinatorics stops determining algebra.

For arrangements of fewer than nine lines, the intersection lattice does determine the exponent data studied here. At ten lines the picture flips: the authors list six distinct Ziegler pairs. Their examples share the same lattice, the same minimal degree of a Jacobian relation, and the same Hilbert function of the Milnor algebra. Yet their minimal graded free resolutions differ, so the abundance of such pairs is now clear.
arxiv-2606-20621:
Yang Feng and three colleagues introduce PEAR in 2026, a debate protocol that rearranges how language model agents talk to each other. Multi-agent debate can improve reliability through peer critique, but fixed layouts create positional bias, let weak agents gain lasting influence, and make results depend on who starts where. PEAR, short for permutation-equivariant adaptive routing, changes roles and sparse communication links across rounds at inference time.

By rotating agent-to-role assignments based on evolving states, PEAR stops any agent from holding a privileged spot and spreads influence more evenly. The authors characterize it as an equivariant sparse router, meaning relabeling agents preserves behavior while routing stays cheap and generalization improves. Tests across four benchmarks and six backbones show accuracy gains over strong debate baselines. Debate gains may come less from adding agents than from fair, shifting critique paths.
arxiv-2606-20821:
Habib Ammari and Clemens Thalhammer study a nonlinear wave system in 2026 with high-contrast inclusions in three dimensions. As contrast tends to zero, solitons emerge. A soliton is a self-reinforcing wave packet. Their tools include a Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator and a capacitance formalism. They build a step-by-step expansion in powers of the square root of contrast. Frequency and field are expanded together.

The main result links the continuous system to a finite discrete one in both directions. Every discrete solution lifts to a continuous soliton. Every continuous family with natural scaling reduces to a discrete one. The construction is algorithmic, giving higher-order corrections in two regimes. A frequency-dependent matrix handles the broader regime. Numerical tests illustrate the theory. A symmetric dimer also shows symmetry breaking. Such results help design tiny resonators, where simple discrete models must predict real wave behavior faithfully.
arxiv-2606-21021:
Muhammad Shahid and three colleagues add a learned corrector in 2026 to physics-based forecasts of spacecraft orbits, so that error bars come with the forecast. Long forecasts drift as errors build up. No new observations arrive to fix them mid-flight. Safety calls, such as warnings that two objects may collide, need honest error bars. Physics propagators are accurate but give point forecasts with no well-tested spread.

The corrector learns how forecast errors evolve over time. It wraps around an existing propagator as an add-on. Forecasts improve, and the full error spread stays sharp and well calibrated. The design handles irregular sampling and missing inputs with ease. Better error bars could cut false collision alarms, which cost fuel and staff time, while keeping true risks in view for the teams that manage crowded orbits.
arxiv-2606-21121:
Victor Lavrenko and Anastasiia Molodnitskaia propose answer engineering in 2026, a local editing method to keep language models inside required rules. Models can give confident but wrong answers when they skip steps in work where compliance is critical. Step-by-step work improves structure. Yet it often shifts errors rather than preventing them, because set rules stay underused. A clinical test case makes the effect stark.

Compliant outcomes for a target condition fall sharply under a step-by-step baseline. A contrast condition improves at the same time. Their fix steps in locally as text is produced. Valid paths are selected. Required tokens are enforced when violations occur. The method is a runtime layer, not a new decoding scheme. Trust under set rules matters in medicine and law, where a fluent answer that skipped a mandated check can mislead even an expert reviewer.
arxiv-2606-21321:
Antonio Mone and six colleagues argue in 2026 that multi-objective reinforcement learning hides important differences behind tidy score vectors. Such systems produce sets of policies that trade off competing goals, but decision makers usually see only expected returns per policy. Two policies with near-identical scores can behave very differently in practice, following distinct trajectories through the world.

The authors propose an exploratory diagnostic workflow that automatically highlights behavioral variation along the Pareto front, the set of best trade-offs, using quantitative measures and visual tools. Tests start on simple grid worlds and scale to continuous control benchmarks, where the workflow stays effective as problems grow. Better inspection tools help practitioners choose policies for what they actually do, not just what they score.
arxiv-2606-21621:
Qamar Bader, Sharief Saleh, Henk Wymeersch, Gonzalo Seco-Granados, and Aboelmagd Noureldin tackle positioning from low Earth orbit signals in 2026. Commercial LEO satellites are promising beacons when GNSS fails, but unlike GNSS they are not globally synchronized. Each satellite's clock bias and drift can badly distort a moving receiver's estimates and make them statistically inconsistent if ignored.

Their fix is a base-station-aided differential design. A fixed base station tracks each satellite's clock state and sends measurement-level corrections, each with its own uncertainty, to a compact eight-state rover filter. A scheme handles satellites constantly entering and leaving view, and a recursive Bayesian Cramer-Rao bound sets the theory limit. On real urban driving data plus simulated constellations, the rover's uncertainty tracks the bound and the inconsistency vanishes.
arxiv-2606-21721:
Anderson Melchor Hernandez proves limit theorems for a mixture-of-experts model generated by a quantum neural network in 2026. The model is trained by gradient flow on supervised problems, and as the number of experts grows, its parameter cloud becomes an empirical measure with a limiting distribution. The question is statistical: how does that cloud fluctuate around its limit?

Two classical pillars carry over. A central limit theorem describes the fluctuations, which turn out to solve a linear transport equation near the limit measure. A Sanov-type principle, the large-deviations law for empirical measures, governs the rare excursions. As a byproduct, the mixture converges to a limit function solving an evolution equation driven by the quantum neural tangent kernel. The results import the mature limit theory of classical wide networks into quantum machine learning, fluctuations and all.
arxiv-2606-21821:
Wei and colleagues ask, in 2026, which steps inside a language model's chain of thought actually cause its later steps. A chain of thought reads like an explanation, but the text may not reflect the model's real internal process. Their work takes a local approach, studying one specific reasoning trace at a time instead of averaging over many outputs.

The method, AttriCoT, builds a structural causal model over the trace's individual units and links each unit to the probability of the output that follows. It estimates each unit's importance with a number of model passes that grows only linearly with the trace length, and it needs no access to model internals. Across five datasets and four reasoning models, its attribution curves were more faithful to model behaviour than rival methods. The scores also exposed clear differences in how models and subject domains structure their thinking.
arxiv-2606-22221:
Koshkin and Lee study, in 2026, panmagic permutations and the structures that appear when several of them are multiplied together. A panmagic permutation's matrix is a panmagic square, constant along rows, columns, and all diagonals. The positions of its ones describe maximal placements of non-attacking queens on a toroidal chessboard.

Affine ones, described by linear formulas in modular arithmetic, are the focus. The authors show their sets are special cosets of the dihedral group inside the full affine group. Multiplying three or more of them stays inside the structure, making them N-ary, or polyadic, groups rather than ordinary ones. The authors also decompose them into disjoint cycles. That analysis connects with classical number theory: element orders, special primes, primitive roots, and quadratic residues.
arxiv-2606-22321:
Fathiyya Izzatun Az-zahra, Shinji Takeda, and Takeshi Yamazaki use tensor networks to study multi-particle states in this 2026 physics paper. Their test system is the Ising model in one space and one time dimension, a simple model of interacting spins. States holding one, two, or three particles matter for nuclear and particle physics, where particles scatter and decay into each other.

The team computes the energy spectrum from a transfer matrix estimated with the tensor renormalization group, which compresses a large network of numbers step by step. Since raw energies carry no labels, they identify each state's quantum number and momentum using matrix elements from an impurity tensor network. Watching how energies shift with system size reveals how many particles each state holds. From two-particle states they extract the scattering phase shift two ways, through Lüscher's formula and the wave function, and both agree with theory.
arxiv-2606-22421:
Yangjie Xu, Hui Huang, Li Ning, and Radu State propose a quantum version of hyperdimensional computing in this 2026 paper. That framework, inspired by how the brain works, stores data as long vectors and combines them with simple operations. Adding quantum effects promises faster and more compact work, but earlier quantum versions were hard to train.

Their system, QeHDC, trains in a single pass over the data. It uses sine-based and quantum encoding to turn plain data into quantum states. A new binding step, built on a reference state and run on quantum circuits, merges pieces of stored data. For grouping data into classes, the team uses density matrices and pulls out each matrix's main features to build sharper class summaries. On standard test datasets, the method beat both classical and earlier quantum approaches. It also stayed accurate when noise was added and proved feasible to run.
arxiv-2606-23121:
Henning Bruhn, Felix Joos, and Arthur Ulmer connect path problems to walls in a 2026 graph theory paper. Menger's theorem is a cornerstone result: either many vertex-disjoint paths link two sets, or a small set of vertices blocks them all. Gallai's theorem plays a similar role for paths through one set. Walls are grid-like subgraphs that serve as building blocks in structural graph theory. The authors ask what Menger-style statements look like when one side of the connection is a wall rather than an arbitrary set.

Bruhn and colleagues prove results tying the largest count of vertex-disjoint paths linking vertex sets to a wall against the smallest number of vertices hitting all such paths. Their treatment also covers paths that both start and end inside the wall itself. The results extend the classic min-max pattern of Menger and Gallai into wall-based territory.
arxiv-2606-23321:
Hamish Ivison and colleagues present TMax, an open recipe for training terminal-using agents, in a 2026 paper. Agents that work through a computer terminal have become a flagship use of language models. Academic work on training them with reinforcement learning lagged behind, held back by hard benchmarks, scarce data, and no simple baseline recipe. TMax generates its own training worlds using a taxonomy that mixes difficulty control, user personas, and varied verifiers. That yields large numbers of cheap terminal environments for both supervised and reinforcement training.

Ivison and colleagues release a terminal dataset over two and a half times larger than earlier public ones. Trained with a simple outcome-only reinforcement recipe, their nine-billion-parameter model scores twenty-seven percent on the Terminal-Bench 2.0 benchmark. That beats much larger models from prior work. Data, models, and code are all released as a baseline for future research.
arxiv-2606-23521:
Gan and colleagues present Concordia, a 2026 systems paper on keeping large language model services running when a graphics processor fails. Long-running AI agents store valuable state on those processors, including key-value caches that hold conversation memory, schedulers, and small adapter updates. A single hardware failure can erase minutes or hours of work, while restarting the whole service is slow and sometimes cannot replay actions already taken in the outside world.

Concordia runs an always-on checkpoint kernel, a small program living on the processor itself, that watches for dirty, meaning changed, memory pages. It compiles tailored handlers that save only the changed pieces into a log held in host memory. On the test hardware, processor-side saving runs up to two hundred nineteen times faster than scanning from the central chip. A two-processor prototype restores service in about one and a half seconds.
arxiv-2606-24021:
Huberman, Mokady, Patashnik, and Cohen-Or make text prompts for image generators behave like sliders, so images can be blended smoothly by arithmetic, in a 2026 paper on computer vision. Two prompts describing nearly the same scene in different words produce token sequences that sit far apart. Interpolating naively between prompt embeddings therefore jumps incoherently, blocking blending and gradual editing. The authors argue the structure is present but misaligned: corresponding concepts occupy inconsistent token positions across prompts.

Token to token alignment fixes the correspondence in two stages. Prompts are rephrased into a shared structured form, so the same concept lands in the same slot. Token embeddings are then matched across prompts by semantic similarity. Once aligned, plain linear interpolation traces a meaningful path: halfway points look like genuine blends, and edits can be dialed continuously.
arxiv-2606-24121:
Dharmawan and colleagues test a game-theoretic way to pick the most influential nodes in a network. Shapley values, borrowed from cooperative game theory, credit each node for what it adds across all coalitions. That captures collective sway, which simple degree counts miss. The 2026 study scores sphere-of-influence picks: small node sets meant to maximise coverage under one-hop, multi-hop, and multi-path reach rules.

Three real networks serve as testbeds: a European road system, a Facebook page network, and the Cora citation graph. Ratios in practice cluster near the top of the range, well past the classic guarantee. Shapley-based picks crush a degree-based baseline, most of all in hub-and-spoke layouts. On Cora, a few dozen nodes, under one percent of the graph, suffice to sway half of it within three hops. Influence, the team argues, is coalitional at heart.
arxiv-2606-24321:
Lin and Liu release a cleaned, machine-readable catalogue of old sunspot drawings from Chinese observatories. Sunspot records stretch back further than telescopes in China. The drawing archives of Yunnan Observatory and Purple Mountain Observatory have fed many published studies. This eighth part of the series merges years of stepwise corrections into one revised, hand-checked release, covering sunspot number, group number, and area measurements.

Comparisons with global reference data focus on relative sunspot numbers and group numbers from the two sites. Area measurements ship without a global comparison this round. Both raw and correction-adjusted values are analysed for sunspot numbers. Group numbers use raw counts, since the Chinese records carry no correction factor of their own. Every comparison correlates strongly and positively with the global series. Lin and Liu's 2026 catalogue aims at internal consistency and usability, for researchers rebuilding long-term solar activity.
arxiv-2606-24621:
Mahadevan builds a calculus for do moves so small they bend, rather than replace. Causal inference's do calculus rewrites such moves in picture syntax. Infinitesimal do calculus instead asks how tiny moves deform the copying and discarding structure that categorical probability assigns to what is observed, inside Frobenius Markov categories. To copy is to let one value feed two uses; to discard is to leave a value out.

The basic objects are new: Frobenius derivative defects and Lie bracket closure conditions. Two Frobenius structures must cooperate: the algebra one encoding copying, comparing, and discarding, and an integrability condition on the spread. Categorical causal sufficiency is defined as their fit. For structural causal models, this is the natural language, Mahadevan argues in 2026. The framework opens a tiny change layer of causal theory, asking not what a move sets, but which ways a system can change.
arxiv-2606-25021:
Richard Dyer, Adrian Ka-Wai Chung, and Christopher Moore test whether the direct wave in a black hole ringdown can serve as a probe of the event horizon. After a merger, the remnant rings down through quasinormal modes. Alongside them runs a direct wave: a signal travelling from the plunging object to the observer. Its properties may mirror the event horizon, promising a clean handle on horizon geometry. The authors pull direct waves out of numerical relativity waveforms, adapting techniques built for quasinormal modes.

The extraction works across various ringdown start times, showing the horizon mode model is useful. One number refuses to cooperate, though. The direct wave's frequency deviates from the horizon value it was predicted to carry. That mismatch limits the wave's usefulness as a probe of the event horizon, whatever its other merits. Dyer and colleagues report both halves plainly.
arxiv-2606-25621:
A hearing aid, a video call, and a voice assistant all clean speech in real time. Yet each allows a wildly different delay, and today each delay budget tends to demand its own trained model. Szu-Wei Fu and colleagues build one enhancement model in 2026 that serves them all. Delay comes in two kinds: how much future audio the model may peek at, and how long its computation takes. Parallel convolution branches handle different peek settings without wasteful retraining, while an early exit option lets the model stop at shallower depth when time is tight.

A two stage training recipe, moving from one shared decoder to several specialised ones, narrows the quality gap against single purpose models. One set of weights then covers diverse real time applications by turning two knobs. The model is released publicly for download, aimed at deployment across latency regimes.
arxiv-2606-25721:
Retrieval augmented chatbots answer from documents they fetch. An attacker who salts that library with crafted pages can steer the answers. Yan-Lun Chen, Pin-Yu Chen, Chia-Mu Yu, Ying-Dar Lin, Yu-Sung Wu, and Wei-Bin Lee present TRACE in 2026. The detector needs no extra classifier, no second model. It measures how much each token in fetched pages pushes the model's prediction. Then it looks for keywords whose influence repeats across documents. That repetition is the fingerprint of a coordinated poisoning campaign.

A second pass confirms whether those high influence tokens drive the output. Across three benchmarks and six language models, detection stayed strong and compute stayed light. A bonus falls out of the tracing. The method surfaces the answer the attacker planted as the target. It exposes not just that an attack happened, but what the attack wanted the system to say.
arxiv-2606-26121:
Mattia Consani and colleagues build Dot-Flik, a cheap insect monitoring system that thinks at the edge. Insect numbers are falling worldwide, and tracking them needs constant, wide coverage. Camera traps that stream everything to the cloud cost too much in hardware, energy, and bandwidth. Their design filters frames on the device itself. Motion detection, amplified and tallied in blocks, discards empty frames without any deep learning on the sensor.

Classification happens centrally, only on frames that pass the filter. The split design lets one central node serve five or six edge streams at once. Outdoor trials on commodity hardware test speed, scale, cost, and energy under shifting wind. Light wind brings frame cuts of sixty to eighty percent. Real-time operation holds at thirty frames per second with headroom to spare. Energy savings reach about a fifth, supporting dense urban biodiversity networks.
arxiv-2606-26421:
Cristiana Diaconu and six colleagues built Otter Weather. It is an artificial intelligence model for medium-range weather forecasts. Large AI forecast models beat traditional physics-based prediction on many scores. Yet their huge training budgets shut out smaller research groups. Otter was designed to open that work up at far lower cost.

Tests used ERA5, a standard record of past weather. Otter beat the best traditional baseline by about ten percent at one day ahead. Training took under three and a half days on a top graphics chip. A larger version, Otter-XL, also improved a standard probabilistic score by nearly ten percent. That score grades how well predicted chances match outcomes. Otter even handled an unrelated sound-scattering physics task well, with no retraining at all.
arxiv-2606-26521:
Yongjiang Wu and Lihua Feng settle a conjecture in extremal combinatorics, the study of largest possible structures under constraints. An intersecting family is a collection of sets where every two sets share an element. The 2017 conjecture of Suda, Tanaka, and Tokushige concerns biased measures, which weight each element differently when sizing such families. It claims the largest intersecting family is a star, all sets containing one fixed element.

Wu and Feng prove the conjecture in a stronger form. Their version covers families where every two sets share at least a given number of elements. Under the stated conditions on the weights, the family's measure cannot exceed the product of the largest weights. They also pin down exactly when equality can hold. Equality forces the family to be precisely all sets containing a fixed core.
arxiv-2606-26921:
U. Jena and eight colleagues report tests on a frustrated magnet where order and motion coexist. The material's manganese ions sit on a triangular lattice, a geometry that frustrates opposed magnetism because neighbours cannot all oppose each other. Such systems can show strange ripples and lasting dynamics instead of settling quietly.

Heat and magnetism tests mapped how the material behaves. Long-range order set in only at about one degree above absolute zero. Above that temperature, strong short-range links held up, with an odd power-law heat mark. Muon spin relaxation, a probe using implanted particles, tracked the spin dynamics directly. Neutron diffraction confirmed the ordered pattern. Basic theory supported the picture of dominant opposed coupling. Static order and restless spins share the same lattice.
arxiv-2606-27121:
Nozaki and Fujita return to chiral-induced spin selectivity, where electrons passing through twisted, nonmagnetic materials emerge with strongly sorted spins. Most earlier theory used single-band models, ignoring how electrons hop between energy bands. Their multi-band study asks whether coupling between bands, driven by spin-orbit effects, can explain the effect. Magnetoresistance measurements with magnetic microscopes supply the experimental setting being modelled in 2026 work.

Steady currents are simulated with the GKSL master equation, which tracks open quantum systems leaking into their surroundings. With realistic inter-band spin-orbit strengths and on-site Coulomb repulsion included, spin sorting passes a quarter of full polarisation in the runs. That level matches the scale experiments report. Single-band pictures missed this boost entirely. Inter-band coupling thus looks central to how twisted materials sort electron spins, not a minor correction.
arxiv-2606-27221:
Meni and colleagues search the atmospheres of four ultra-hot Jupiters for molecular fingerprints. These giant planets orbit so close to their stars that their air exceeds two thousand degrees. Transmission spectroscopy watches starlight filter through the planet's rim during transit. Near-infrared spectra from the GIANO-B instrument are cross-correlated against molecular templates. Six species are hunted, including water, carbon monoxide, and iron hydride, in an observational study published in 2026, covering WASP-189b and three companions.

Water shows tentatively in HAT-P-57b, at modest statistical strength. Iron hydride is detected in KELT-17b, only the third such detection in an ultra-hot Jupiter. No molecular signals appear in KELT-21b or WASP-189b, nor for other hunted species elsewhere. Results match the wider population pattern for these extreme worlds. More observations are needed to firm up the tentative cases.
arxiv-2606-27721:
Solving a hard problem by combining solutions to easier parts is a core skill. It underlies chain-of-thought reasoning in artificial intelligence. When does decomposition actually make learning cheaper, though? Nived Rajaraman and four colleagues study that question in 2026. Their test problem is learning to simulate semiautomata. That task captures state tracking, regular language recognition, and modular arithmetic. An autocurriculum recursively splits long sequences into shorter ones.

Two learning settings are analysed. The first mimics supervised fine-tuning with feedback on intermediate states. There, the curriculum needs only a subpolynomial number of supervision tokens. Direct simulation faces a linear token barrier. The second mimics reinforcement learning with a verifier. The curriculum weakens the demand on the reference model exponentially. Coverage is needed only at a short block length, not the full sequence length. Decomposition therefore provably beats direct learning in both regimes studied.
arxiv-2606-27821:
Traffic matrices record demand between every pair of points in a network. Forecasting the whole matrix is hard under tight memory and training budgets. Kuo-Chung Peng and five colleagues test compact quantum-inspired recurrent models in 2026. The task is forecasting of the Abilene network's traffic matrix. Each model predicts the next twenty five-minute frames of a 144-channel matrix. It sees only a two-hour history.

Three placements of a quantum-inspired Kolmogorov–Arnold module were benchmarked. Rivals included two LSTM networks and a classical fast-weight programmer. All trained under one fixed budget. The gated quantum-inspired variant achieved the best prediction error. It used only about twenty-two percent as many parameters as the larger LSTM. It beat the matched-size LSTM and the classical gated baseline. Convergence analysis agreed. The quantum-inspired variants reached lower validation loss faster and won on substantially more individual channels.
arxiv-2606-27921:
Flow past a circular cylinder is a classic stability problem. Geng Chen, Lian Gan, and Philip Gaskell add an aligned steady current to oscillatory forcing in 2026. The analysis uses a two-dimensional Floquet framework. Three parameters organise the study, the Keulegan–Carpenter number, the steady-to-oscillatory velocity ratio, and the oscillatory Reynolds number.

A steady current changes the picture qualitatively. When the velocity ratio exceeds about zero point five, a period-doubling subharmonic bifurcation appears. Purely oscillatory flow shows no such mode. At the highest Reynolds number studied, the neutral stability curve bends non-monotonically. A striking re-stabilisation region appears at high ratios. There the flow recovers a symmetric state, even though each part alone is unstable. Two unstable modes of different types can also coexist. Direct simulations confirm the linear predictions for single-mode cases. With coexisting modes, the quasi-periodic attractor tends to dominate.
arxiv-2606-28021:
Cavitation bubbles are too small for ordinary flow simulations to resolve one by one. F. J. Aschmoneit develops a multiscale sub-grid model in 2026 that treats them statistically. The bubble size distribution is treated as a linear stochastic process in radius space. The starting point is the integrated Rayleigh–Plesset equation for a single bubble. A population balance tracks how many bubbles sit at each size.

The balance becomes a transport equation for the number density per radius. Its solution, projected onto a histogram basis, yields a Markov chain over size bins. The transition matrix splits into two factors. One is a precomputable geometric part depending only on the mesh. The other is a local, pressure-dependent shift. Coupling to the surrounding flow compresses into one dimensionless vector per cell. Classical homogeneous-mixture closures are recovered in the single-scale limit. Coalescence and break-up effects are not yet included.
arxiv-2606-28521:
D. S. Almeida, A. S. Bibiano, W. M. da Silva, and R. R. Montenegro-Filho map the phases of magnetic ladders built from alternating spins of two sizes. Such mixed-spin Heisenberg ladders are laboratory models for quantum magnetism, and an applied field can freeze their magnetization at fractions of saturation, forming plateaus whose edges mark quantum phase transitions.

Combining density matrix renormalization group numerics with linear spin-wave theory, the team charts field against interchain coupling for the spin one-half and spin one ladder. A plateau at one third of saturation appears for positive coupling and survives in a limited range of negative coupling. The point where the plateau closes is a Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, an subtle unbinding transition, which they locate by finite-size analysis of transverse spin correlations. Estimates along several scan directions agree with the magnetic ordering picture.
arxiv-2606-28821:
Borel, Procacci, Sanchis and Scoppola settle a question about the Blume-Emery-Griffiths model. That model describes lattice spins that can point up, down or stay neutral. The authors focus on its FAD triple point. Three regions of behaviour meet there: ferromagnetic, antiquadrupolar and disordered. That point is singular. The model there admits infinitely many lowest-energy arrangements, which often signals unusual behaviour.

Their note proves the model has exactly one Gibbs measure at this point, at any temperature. A Gibbs measure is one consistent statistical description of the whole system. Uniqueness rules out phase transitions, the abrupt bulk changes seen elsewhere in the model. The proof builds a random-cluster picture, where linked sites form weighted groups. It couples that picture to simple coin-flip site percolation, the study of how randomly filled sites connect.
arxiv-2606-29121:
Hou, Hao, Park and Linzen test whether describing AI in human-like terms changes what the public thinks of it. Anthropomorphic language credits systems with human abilities and traits. Critics say such wording sets misleading expectations, inflates claims and fuels hype, which could distort public understanding and policy choices. The team ran an experiment with 815 participants who read passages about AI.

Some passages used anthropomorphic framing and others did not, in texts designed to mirror real public-facing AI discourse. Readers' views were measured across several dimensions prominent in current debate. The study covered two kinds of technology, large language models and recommendation systems. A separate text that spelled out AI's dangers did shift readers' views, proving opinions can move. But in the main comparison, human-like wording did not substantially affect perceptions. Any immediate effects look modest, the authors conclude, while leaving open slower effects from naturalistic, repeated exposure.
arxiv-2606-29221:
Guo, Yang and Shi tackle the problem of pairing robots with human teams online, when the robots' qualities are not known in advance. Over many rounds, a learner assigns robots from a fixed pool to distinct groups of human agents and learns from the outcomes. They frame this as a linear matching bandit problem, where each robot has unknown features and matches earn rewards.

Their algorithm, LinMatch, keeps confidence intervals for the unknown features and each round picks the matching that looks best under optimistic estimates. The optimistic matching step becomes a linear program for maximum-weight matching, solved efficiently by the Hungarian algorithm. They prove matching upper and lower bounds on regret, the loss versus an ideal matcher, that meet: the rate is optimal in rounds, feature dimension and matching size. The results also cover housing allocation and recommendation problems.
arxiv-2606-29421:
Moskal leads a large international team reporting the first imaging of quantum entanglement inside a living human patient. Entanglement links two photons, particles of light, so that measuring one constrains the other. Their photons come from positron-electron annihilation inside the body. The team used the J-PET scanner, built from plastic scintillators, which are materials that flash when radiation passes through.

A patient received a radiopharmaceutical labelled with gallium-68, a radioactive tracer used in cancer imaging. Compton scattering inside the plastic revealed each photon's position, timing, and polarization plane. Comparing the two polarization planes gave the degree of entanglement at each point. Values in the liver and spleen sat between the predictions for fully entangled and fully separable photons. The authors say this opens a new route for using quantum effects in clinical diagnostics.
arxiv-2606-29621:
Dong and Georgoulis design methods for the kinetic Fokker-Planck equations, which describe how a particle distribution evolves. These equations have degenerate diffusion, meaning smoothing acts in only some directions. Standard schemes can lose the fast decay toward equilibrium that the true solution shows, a property called hypocoercivity.

Their space-time Galerkin methods are built to preserve that decay. The design mimics Villani's framework, yielding a coercive form in a weighted norm despite the degeneracy. Proving coercivity needs new trace inverse inequalities for weighted norms on several domain shapes, . The fully discrete scheme couples the spatial method with discontinuous Galerkin time stepping of arbitrary order. It preserves total mass and provably converges to equilibrium at an exponential rate. Numerical experiments validate the theory.
arxiv-2606-29721:
Hwang and six colleagues redefine how maritime anomalies are detected and labelled. Ships broadcast Automatic Identification System data, and anomaly detection over those tracks supports safety, security, and traffic management at sea. Public datasets rarely carry labels. Prior work leans on statistical rarity or on expert labelling, which is costly and hard to scale.

Their taxonomy is grounded in equations and usable under a limited data schema. Three anomaly types are defined: unexpected AIS activity, route deviation, and close approach between vessels. A unified pipeline scores how plausible each pattern is, with language model guidance, creates anomalies, and assigns timestamp-level labels. Benchmark settings vary temporal window length and anomaly-type mix, and a broad range of time-series and anomaly detection models is evaluated. The authors release their code.
arxiv-2606-29821:
Nguyen, Märtens, and Chin build a benchmark for locating a planetary rover from its own surface views. Global position awareness is fundamental for exploring other worlds, since satellite positioning is unavailable and odometry drifts.

Their cross-view geo-localization benchmark uses rendered surface panoramas paired with overhead tiles from a high-resolution lunar terrain model. More than ten thousand ground views come as panoramas with matching overhead images. The team trains a leading transformer-based geo-localization method from scratch on this data and reports retrieval accuracy. Learning-based cross-view matching, they show, can work on such surfaces.
arxiv-2606-30021:
Kingshuk Adhikary, Darren Moore, and Radim Filip ask which interactions can bunch bosons, the energy quanta of quantum oscillators, into one high number state without fail. Linear setups paired with measurement can concentrate quanta only conditionally, and the success rate falls off sharply as the target grows. Bunching that is both reliable and energy conserving therefore needs a nonlinear interaction, and the authors work out which kinds can do the job.

They show that highly saturable systems, such as qubits, make the best nonlinear element, because a qubit can hold only one excitation and so saturates at once. That trait preserves the layered non-Gaussian features of the bunched states, and the states also hold up fairly well against pure loss, the slow leakage of quanta. The result points to a qubit-inside nonlinearity as a real advantage for preparing, processing, and detecting non-Gaussian quantum states on demand.
arxiv-2606-30121:
Jiaxuan Fan, Zhiyao Xiong, Xiaokui Yang, and Shing-Tung Yau construct special metrics on stable bundles by direct iteration. A Hermitian-Einstein metric is the preferred measuring rule for a vector bundle. The Donaldson-Uhlenbeck-Yau theorem guarantees one exists on stable bundles. Earlier proofs took a very different path. This team replaces that machinery with an iterative scheme.

Start with any Hermitian metric on the stable bundle. Their recurrence produces a unique sequence of improved metrics. A positive parameter and the bundle's stability constant drive each step. The sequence converges smoothly to a Hermitian-Einstein metric. The limit satisfies the defining equation with that constant. The proof works over compact Kähler manifolds, as expected. It also covers Gauduchon manifolds, which are non-Kähler. Independence from the variational route is the key advance claimed.
arxiv-2606-30321:
Paul Andreas, Torsten Schlett, and Christoph Busch squeeze a passport-quality face photo into a two-dimensional barcode's tiny budget. Travel documents store face images on RFID chips for automated checks. Temporary documents lack chips, excluding holders from automated verification. A barcode could substitute, but it holds only one thousand twenty-four bytes. The study optimizes every step toward that target size.

Seven image formats compete under the extreme compression constraint. JPEG, JPEG 2000, JPEG XL, JPEG AI, HEIF, AVIF, and WebP are all tested. Preprocessing choices like grayscale conversion, smoothing, and resizing are tuned. The newly standardized JPEG AI gives the best recognition performance overall. Its edge is clearest when compared images are high quality. AVIF and WebP also perform well in both scenarios tested. Grayscale helps for compliant reference images; color helps otherwise. Overall recognition losses from the harsh compression stay surprisingly small.
arxiv-2606-30621:
Oleksandr Masyutka and Mikhail Moklyachuk study how to estimate unknown values of a random field when its statistics are only partly known. A homogeneous random field is a random surface whose statistical rules do not change from place to place. The task is to estimate linear functionals, summary quantities, of unseen field values from noisy observations. Classical methods need exact spectral densities, the field's frequency profile, which practice rarely supplies.

The pair apply the minimax, or robust, approach. An estimate is judged by its worst error over a whole set of admissible spectral densities, not by one guessed density. For several special sets of admissible densities, they derive formulas for the least favourable densities, the worst cases an estimator must survive. They also derive the minimax spectral characteristics, which define the robust estimator itself. The results extend classical extrapolation, interpolation and filtering theory to realistic uncertainty about spectra.
arxiv-2606-30821:
Yujin Kim, Nidhi Soma and Sarah Dean fix a failure in weather downscaling, the task of turning coarse forecasts into fine-grained fields with uncertainty. A popular recipe predicts a mean field, then generates the leftover residual stochastically. In real deployments the ensembles come out biased and too narrow. The team show the cause is not generic miscalibration: the residual distribution learned in training systematically differs from the one needed at test time.

Their method, ReMatch, closes that residual gap. It pushes the training residual distribution towards the test-time regime using optimal transport, computed in a low-dimensional principal-component space. The mean-residual structure stays intact. On a synthetic benchmark with varying bias, and on a wind-field task pairing two weather datasets, ReMatch reduced under-dispersion and improved calibration scores. It beat the mean-residual model, its variants, and state-of-the-art super-resolution models.
arxiv-2606-30921:
Hai Duc Nguyen, Tekin Bicer, Kyle Chard, Ian Foster and Bogdan Nicolae ask whether a large language model can add checkpoint and restart support to a scientific program unaided. Checkpointing lets a long supercomputer job resume after a failure instead of starting over, but adding it by hand is slow expert work. The team assembled a benchmark of MPI applications from varied domains and computation patterns, then ran an iterative code-generation loop for each, driven by Claude Opus 4.7 through a command-line agent tool.

Across six applications, the model produced working checkpoint/restart code in about 50 minutes on average, using 3.4 million tokens per application. The generated code added negligible overhead in failure-free runs for five of the six. Recovery from injected failures matched the efficiency of human-engineered implementations.
arxiv-2606-31121:
Chen and six colleagues add a safety check to language model agents that learn from past tasks. Such agents keep an external memory and update it after each task. Most systems deploy every update at once. A change that helps today's task can still erase useful knowledge, add over-specific rules, or bias memory toward recent examples.

Their plug-in controller, Janus, decides whether each candidate update is accepted or the old memory stays. A Memory Momentum Trigger flags updates that veer oddly from the recent trajectory. Suspicious updates are judged on a compact test set of coverage, boundary, and fresh tasks, not the full history. Janus wraps existing updaters without changing their rules. Across six datasets, two backbone models, and two updaters, it raised average accuracy by 2.7 to 4.6 points.
arxiv-2606-31421:
Tomotaki-Dawoud and three colleagues ask whether video detectors truly use time, or just one lucky frame. Standard metrics reward right answers however they are reached, so a detector can look temporal while ignoring motion. Their TemporalLens diagnostic probes this with controlled damage: occlusions, frame shuffling, repeated frames, and resolution drops.

Stacked-frame 2D detectors collapse when the target frame is removed, betraying single-frame reliance. Spatiotemporal models rebuild the answer from earlier frames, the mark of real temporal use. Their YOLO-3D detector, built on YOLOv8, gains most from simply keeping temporal depth through the backbone, worth several points of accuracy at 32 frames. Together the tools turn a vague worry about temporal reasoning into a test any team can run.
arxiv-2606-31621:
Wilkinson and Ferro extend the idea of calibration for probability forecasts to sequences, where a forecaster updates a prediction for the same event repeatedly as new information arrives. A forecast is calibrated when the probabilities it assigns match how often events occur. One strict version, auto-calibration, demands that the forecast equal the true distribution of the outcome given the forecast itself.

For observations living in any Borel space, the pair show that auto-calibration of such a fixed-event sequence amounts to a sequence of random probability measures. Those measures obey the martingale property. That is the fair-game condition that future values equal the current one on average. They then propose a simple statistical test of that property, giving forecasters a first hands-on way to check whether such sequences, as they update, are truly calibrated.
arxiv-2608-00021: Unique axiomatisation of fractional integral operators on the real line, arXiv 2608-00021. The fractional calculus. The paper remains available to readers. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
bailey-english-dictionary-1721:
Nathan Bailey issued his Universal Etymological English Dictionary in 1721, the most complete English word book of its day. Bailey was a schoolmaster who gathered some 40,000 entries, giving each word's origin along with its meaning. Earlier English dictionaries had been small lists of hard words; Bailey aimed at the whole language.

The entries trace words to Greek, Latin, French, and other roots, and add notes on grammar and usage. The book sold through many editions and served writers and readers for decades. Samuel Johnson borrowed heavily from it when he built his own famous dictionary a generation later. Bailey's work marks the point where English lexicography became a serious, full-scale trade.
basden-among-the-ibos-of-nigeria-1921:
George Thomas Basden lived thirty-five years in Nigeria and wrote Among the Ibos of Nigeria in 1921, late in that long stay. Basden, an Anglican missionary and school builder, records the Igbo world he knew at close range and loved. Chi, the personal god of each person, ancestors, dibia diviners, and the village republic of elders fill his chapters.

Markets, marriages, funerals, and the rules of a stateless, democratic people come through in practiced, concrete detail. Basden writes as a friend of his subject within a missionary's frame, and both sides of him show on the page. His ethnography remains a first source on Igbo religion and society in the early colonial years.
berzelius-emploi-chalumeau-1821:
Jons Jacob Berzelius teaches the blowpipe's use in chemical trials in this manual, in its 1821 French version. A flame, a tube, and a steady breath reveal what a mineral hides. Prospectors and mineralogists learned the craft from the great Swedish chemist's clear, patient pages of instruction.

Tiny beads of melted ore tell their tale by color and change. Berzelius turns a camp skill into a exact field science for travelers. His methods traveled to mines and surveys on every continent in time. The little guide helped build mineralogy as a practical art, putting a laboratory, in effect, in a coat pocket.
bryant-poems-1821:
William Cullen Bryant published his first book, Poems, in 1821, when American poetry still had few names of note. Bryant had written its best-known piece, 'Thanatopsis,' while still in his teens. The slim volume gathered that poem with other early work on nature, death, and faith.

'Thanatopsis' urges readers to face death calmly, since all people return to the earth together. Other poems praise wild woods, open skies, and the quiet of country places. Bryant wrote in smooth, grave verse shaped by British models yet rooted in American scenes. The book was praised abroad and helped start a lasting American tradition of nature poetry.
carbonari-memoirs-1821:
Secret groups in the south of Italy drew wide fear after revolts shook Naples in 1820. An English book of 1821, turned from a French text, gave British readers their first full report on them. Its main subject is the Carbonari, a network of lodges with oaths, grades, and signs. No author is named on the title page.

Pages describe how the Carbonari met, how new men joined, and what their rites meant. Reports of trials from 1820 show how the state struck back at the groups. The book still serves as a first-hand source on the secret groups that fought kings in Italy.
cardozo-nature-judicial-process-1921:
The Nature of the Judicial Process, published in 1921, prints Benjamin N. Cardozo's Storrs Lectures at Yale, the most famous lectures ever given by an American judge. Cardozo, then on New York's highest court, answers a simple question: how do judges actually decide cases?

He names four methods: logic, history, custom, and sociology, and shows judges moving among them, often without knowing which is in command. Precedent guides but does not bind absolutely; the judge legislates in the gaps. Cardozo's candor and grace made the lectures a classic of legal writing. Lawyers still assign them to every beginner.
chahar-maqala-browne-1921:
E. G. Browne revised his translation of the Chahar Maqala in 1921 for the Gibb Memorial series. Nizami-i-Arudi wrote the Four Discourses in the twelfth century, treating the four men a king needs near him. The secretary, the poet, the astrologer, and the physician each get a discourse, salted with tales of courts and their servants.

Anecdotes carry the teaching: how a verse saved a life, how a doctor read a pulse and a fate. Browne, the great Cambridge Persianist, loved the book's lively mix of counsel and gossip. The work remains a window on Persian court life and letters at their most humane.
chekhov-cooks-wedding-1921:
The Cook's Wedding and Other Stories appeared in English in 1921, in Constance Garnett's translation. The title story is seen through the eyes of Grisha, a boy of seven. Grisha watches the household plot to marry off the cook Pelageya to a cabman she has barely met.

The Dependents shows an old peasant begging care for his starving horse, and finding none. The Orator mocks a pompous speaker hired to praise a man he barely knew. Chekhov moves easily here between comedy and quiet sorrow. Several tales take a child's view of adult dealings, with sharp results. The volume rounds out Garnett's long Englishing of his shorter fiction.
chekhov-horse-stealers-1921:
The Horse-Stealers and Other Stories reached English in 1921 through Constance Garnett's translation. The title tale follows a hospital watchman drawn into the company of horse thieves at a lonely inn. Drink, boasting, and a rising wind build the night toward theft and flight.

The Privy Councillor draws gentle comedy from a grand official's visit to a modest country estate. Other pieces in the volume range across the steppe, the road, and the village. Chekhov knew the open southern plains from travel and wrote them with love. Wind, grass, and distance shape the moods of these tales. The volume favors his stories of travel and open country.
chekhov-schoolmaster-1921:
Garnett's Schoolmaster volume of Chekhov stories appeared in English in 1921. The title story shows a worn schoolmaster honored at a dinner after twenty-five years of service. Praise rings hollow for a man spent by routine, and he dies soon after, little noticed.

The Man in a Case gives Belikov, a teacher so afraid of life that he wraps himself in rules and galoshes. His fear poisons a whole town until his sudden death frees it. The volume also reprints The Horse-Stealers, among other tales of school, town, and country. Chekhov's portraits of small, fearful lives remain painfully fresh. Few writers have matched his mix of pity and precision.
cia-0000009921:
American prisoners and their detention cells, north of Chavane in Saravane province, were sighted in a January 1971 report. Saravane sits in southern Laos, astride trail routes into Vietnam's center. Seeing the cells as well as the men gave the report unusual physical detail.

Cells describe a prison better than claims do: size, bars, and guards can be checked later. Such detail helped judge whether a site was a true camp or a stopping point. It also told planners what rescue would face. This file preserves the observed cells and captives together, a ground-level view of Laotian detention.
cia-0000012321:
Helms to the Director of Central Intelligence, January 1962: the summit correspondence on the Penkovsky case continues without pause. The subject, cut short in the file, concerns military matters in the colonel's channel. Principals traded these memos back and forth even as the year's crisis deepened. Berlin's tension and Cuba's approach formed the backdrop to every page.

The files keep the dialogue at the peak intact for readers today. Case management at this level balanced a spy's safety against a nation's hunger for his product. For readers, the memo shows the operation steered from the very top, month after month.
cia-0000013121:
How the Viet Cong used American prisoners, as policy rather than chance, is studied in a CIA paper from February 1967. In the south, captives were held in jungle camps. They answered to the southern movement's own command, not to Hanoi. The paper examines the doctrine behind their treatment. Prisoners served as sources of information and as labor. Above all, they served as propaganda, exhibits in a war for world opinion.

The study shows how systematic that use was. Captivity in the south followed rules written far from the camps. For readers, the paper is the enemy's prison theory read from inside, by the side that feared it most.
cia-0000013221:
Forty-two American prisoners were held by the Viet Cong in the border country, and a CIA report from November 1966 confirms the detention. The camps sat along the South Vietnam and Cambodia border area named in the title. Forty-two captives in one report made the southern system's scale plain. It was larger, and better organized, than Washington liked to admit in public.

The report counts and places the men as sources then knew them. Each number in it was a name to someone waiting at home. For readers, the page shows the southern captivity measured whole, years before its survivors came home.
cia-0000013621:
Brazil, titled with one word, gets a CIA country brief from February 1968. The brief sketches the giant's Cold War face at a hard season. The generals ruled with full force and full pride that year. Students and workers were filling the streets against them in protest. The regime was months away from the decree that closed congress. That decree opened the dictatorship's harshest years of rule.

Such briefs caught a country at a glance for busy readers above. This one catches Brazil at the hard-liners' peak, before the iron years deepened. For readers, it is the giant in brief: vast, rich, and governed by decree.
cia-0000013921: Policy toward American prisoners and a secret hospital for their care fill a CIA report dated November 2, 1967. A hidden hospital for wounded prisoners is a striking detail. It suggests the north set apart medical care for captives, away from public view. Reports like this fed debate over how the north really treated the men it held.
cia-0000014721: USSR intelligence activities are the broad subject of a CIA file dated March 5, 1954. The title names the whole field rather than one operation. Files at this level summed up Soviet spy work as the agency saw it. Such surveys helped set the watch lists and budgets of the early Cold War security state.
cia-0000014821: Major consequences of certain U.S. courses of action on Cuba fill a CIA paper dated September 6, 1962. The paper weighed the big results that might follow American steps. Like its twin of the day before, it came just ahead of the missile crisis. The pair show estimate work at full stretch on the eve of the Cold War's sharpest hour.
cia-0000049121: A trace reply on former members of El Salvador's revolutionary junta and their contacts survives in a CIA item from 1987. The junta had ruled at the war's start, and its scattered members still drew the file system's interest. Traces on yesterday's rulers show how long the paperwork of power follows the men who held it.
cia-0000049221: A draft letter to a Mr. Hamilton survives in a CIA item from 1985, kept with the Truth Commission records. Drafts preserve what officials almost said: the argument as first framed, before it was softened or sharpened. Who Hamilton was, and whether the letter was ever sent, sits inside the document and its file.
cia-0000049321: Terrorism Review is the short title of declassified CIA document 0000049321, dated July 4, 1990, and marked for the Truth Commission. The file presents itself as a review of terrorism rather than a report on one event. Readers get a dated agency survey item, preserved under a general heading that does not name a country or a single incident.
cia-0000098721: A Red Sea Security System: Political, Military, and Economic Issues is the title of declassified CIA document 0000098721, dated November 2, 1981. The subtitle sorts the study into three kinds of issues. Readers get a short declassified study whose heading promises a system examined from political, military, and economic angles at once. The record survives in the CIA Reading Room mirror collection.
cia-0000102921: Colony Settlement Prison Ya 38/10, Baku, with dates of information 1976 to December 1977, is declassified CIA document 0000102921, dated February 5, 1981. A coded designation and a city share the heading. Readers get a short single-prison record from Baku, companion to the Arkhangelsk colony settlement item in the same labor cluster. The heading and date are the firm facts the catalog gives.
cia-0000109821: Dr. a. Von Miorini is the whole heading on declassified CIA document 0000109821, dated September 1, 1945. The title is a name and nothing else: no topic, place, or charge is stated. A name-only heading leaves the file's subject to the pages inside. The brief record is a name file from the first month after the war in Europe ended.
cia-0000112821: Shanghai - Counter-espionage Summary is the short heading on declassified CIA document 0000112821, dated July 2, 1945. The title names a city and a form: a counter-espionage summary for Shanghai. Summary is the heading's own word for what the file holds. The brief record is a city summary item from the summer of 1945 in the China files.
cia-0000119721: A September 1956 CIA item notes a Hungarian newspaper backing Tito's position on ties with Moscow. Each such editorial marked Budapest's drift from the Soviet line, weeks before the revolution made that drift impossible to ignore. Praise for Tito in print was itself a political act, since his break with Stalin made his path a standing challenge to Moscow's rule.
cia-0000124321: A January 1952 CIA document covers preparations for exchanging United Nations prisoners in central and south China.
