Tushar Saini and colleagues present in 2026 a forty-seven-year-old man whose blocked stomach outlet looked like duodenal cancer but was groove pancreatitis instead. He drank heavily, and scans plus camera views first suggested a primary tumor of the duodenum. The rare condition sits in the groove between the pancreas head, duodenum, and bile duct.

Biopsies found no cancer, and a team review settled on segmental groove pancreatitis using the typical scan pattern. Treatment stayed conservative with stomach drainage, acid control, pancreatic enzymes, nutrition support, and stopping alcohol. Both the blockage and the lesion cleared within seven days. Careful checks before major pancreas surgery can spare patients a very large operation when this mimic is the cause.
pmc-13230321:
Ana Luiza Rocha Soares Menegat and colleagues pool in 2026 early evidence on a new keyhole operation for belly wall hernias. The PeTEP method repairs the hernia from outside the belly cavity and can also address separated stomach muscles. Four studies with ninety-nine patients formed the whole evidence base.

Average operating time was a little over two hours in the pooled results. Blood collections appeared in about one in ten patients, and about one in five had some complication, none needing another procedure. Slight bulging showed in a small share of cases, and no hernia returned during short follow-up of one to twelve months. Longer head-to-head studies are needed before the method can be judged against older repairs.
pmc-13230621:
Junhyeok Jeong and colleagues report in 2026 evidence that a copper oxide superconductor sits between two classic pairing regimes. Underdoped cuprates show only arcs of the electronic surface, leaving open whether electrons pair weakly or form tight pairs early. The team studied clean inner layers of a four-layer cuprate with light-based and magnetic methods.

Measurements revealed a small electron pocket coexisting with a surprisingly large superconducting gap. Ratios tying the gap and the transition temperature to the pocket energy reached near the top values expected for flat superconductors. Oddly, the crossover appeared as carrier numbers rose, within a very narrow doping window. The result gives a concrete footing for theories of pairing in these doped insulating materials.
pmc-13231721:
Xianzhong Zhu and colleagues test in 2026 a receptor-activating compound against skin scarring in a mouse model of systemic sclerosis. In that disease, helper T cells of the follicular type help drive the scarring process. Mice received a scarring drug under the skin for four weeks, with half also given the compound Ficz on a regular schedule.

Treated mice grew thinner skin with less collagen and lower levels of several scarring genes. Their blood held fewer follicular helper T cells, and skin levels of a helper signal from those cells also fell. Staining confirmed the helper cells sat inside the skin lesions of untreated mice. Turning on that receptor may calm both the cells and the scarring together.
pmc-13232621:
Xue-Ting Zhen and colleagues train in 2026 a deep learning tool that spots loose DNA circles in routine cancer slides. These circles, called ecDNA, carry extra cancer genes and help tumors resist drugs, yet finding them needs costly sequencing. Their platform, ecPICK, learned from thousands of stained slide images across twenty cancer types.

Predictions from ordinary slides matched lab-confirmed circle levels closely in validation checks. The tool also flagged patients with worse outlook beyond what standard factors explain. Circle-rich zones carried quiet immune activity, dense scar-like collagen, and altered cell energy patterns in spatial gene maps. Cheap slide-based mapping could sort patients faster and hint at how circles reshape their neighborhood.
pmc-13234021:
Anna G. Willocks, Ksenia M. Bykova, and Elena Moltchanova published a 2026 study building childhood reference values for a test of chewing and swallowing solids. The test counts bites, chewing cycles, swallows, and time while a child eats a cracker, and a phone-style application now administers it. The team tested 114 healthy children between four and nineteen years old, evenly split between boys and girls.

Age significantly shaped every efficiency measure, and the team converted the results into normative tables for clinical use. Scores from the app did not match the older hand-recorded norms, with the widest gaps in the youngest children, so the methods cannot be swapped casually. The authors offer the app-based norms as a first reference for spotting swallowing problems and oral motor delays.
pmc-13234121:
Seyed Reza Miri Shaktai and colleagues published a 2026 aquaculture study on feeding silymarin, a milk thistle extract, to Caspian trout larvae. Silymarin protects the liver and fights oxidation, but its free form absorbs poorly. The team compared plain silymarin against a nanomicelle version, tiny carrier droplets meant to deliver more of it. Each was mixed into feed at the same dose for sixty days. A third group got no supplement at all.

The nano form clearly outperformed. Larvae on the nano form ended heavier, gained more, and grew faster than both other groups. Plain silymarin did nothing that could be measured for growth. The nano group also showed stronger activity of one antioxidant enzyme and richer stores of valuable long-chain omega-3 fats in their bodies. Other measures did not differ. The authors back nano delivery for young farmed fish.
pmc-13235221:
Makoto Tsujita and colleagues followed in 2026 kidney transplant recipients in Japan to test whether lasting anaemia tracks declining graft function. Anaemia after transplantation is common and has been linked to worse graft outcomes. Records covered more than three hundred recipients at one hospital over two years. Kidney function was averaged repeatedly, while blood haemoglobin entered the models as it changed over time.

Kidney function declined steadily across the follow-up period in the main model. Higher haemoglobin at any point went together with better kidney function over time. Use of anaemia-stimulating drugs by itself showed no independent link to the function trend. Recipients receiving those drugs nevertheless lost function faster in supporting comparisons, including a matched analysis. The authors read persistent anaemia as a sign of underlying graft problems rather than a direct cause.
pmc-13235921:
Cheng and colleagues study how business analytics students engage with AI-supported learning. AI tools are now woven into coursework, yet little work has asked what keeps students using them over a whole course. The team treats AI use as part of the course itself, not a one-off choice to try a new gadget.

They ask how students' views of AI-supported learning shape their wish to keep using it. They then link that wish to interest in the subject and to plans for a career using analytics. The chain matters for teachers: a tool students abandon early cannot deepen interest, while one they value may steer both grades and ambitions.
pmc-13236721:
Damian M. Bailey and co-authors exposed in 2026 twelve healthy men to six hours of low-oxygen air and normal air on separate occasions. The study asked how organ systems coordinate to defend the brain's energy supply when oxygen falls. Blood markers of stress and vessel injury were measured alongside ultrasound estimates of brain oxygen and glucose delivery. Five participants developed acute mountain sickness symptoms during the low-oxygen session.

Brain fuel delivery stayed well maintained under low oxygen, including in those who felt sick. Slow rhythmic oscillations across body systems grew stronger and more synchronized during oxygen shortage. Those oscillations were even more pronounced and connected in the men with mountain sickness symptoms. Blood markers showed no extra oxidative damage or vessel unit injury in the sick group. The authors suggest mountain sickness may reflect a protective adaptation rather than simple failure.
pmc-13239121:
M. M. Guerisoli and colleagues ran the first multi-year survey in 2026 of the guigna, the Americas' smallest cat, in Argentine Patagonia. Thirty-five camera traps in a protected area logged over eight thousand trap nights and 176 independent guigna events, one of the highest detection rates recorded anywhere for the species. Models weighed landscape features against species-interaction factors, and activity patterns were compared across years, seasons, and coat types.

Guignas favored thick forest with plentiful prey and avoided open vegetation and places with rival predators. They were mainly nocturnal despite little human disturbance, and black-coated and spotted individuals kept the same schedule. The authors credit rich resources and low human impact inside the reserve. The study fills a near-total knowledge gap for Argentina and names what to explore next.
pmc-13239221:
Abebaw Hailu Fikire, Elena Viktorovna Korchagina, and Nidhi Chaudhary systematically reviewed forty-four studies from 2020 to 2024 in 2026. They defined what efficiency and sustainability mean inside food supply chains and built a framework that links their drivers. Inefficient food chains undermine food security and poverty reduction worldwide. The review followed PRISMA guidelines across two major indexing databases.

Publication in the area grew over the period, with one open-access publisher leading output and first authors from the United Kingdom and Italy most active. Efficiency, in their framing, means trimming cost and time, while sustainability adds environmental and social responsibility across the chain. The authors aim the framework at scholars choosing new questions, at policymakers, and at practitioners. Their closing claim is that the field now has clearer signposts for where the unsolved problems sit.
pmc-13239621:
Owais Dar and a large audit team summarise the first United Kingdom and Ireland audit of advanced heart failure referrals, published in 2026. Around a million Britons live with heart failure, and transplants or implanted pumps can save advanced cases, yet only a few hundred procedures happen each year.

Seven transplant centres reported roughly one hundred referrals a month for assessment. Referral rates differed sharply by region even after age was considered, and many referred patients turned out to have conditions ruling the therapies out. Distance and local deprivation did not explain the gaps, while women made up only a third of those assessed. The authors see unequal access needing national attention.
pmc-13239921:
Ali Moradi and colleagues report an unusual cause of episodic paralysis in a 2026 case paper. A 31-year-old woman with mast cell activation syndrome suffered repeated bouts of weakness, cramps, and near-fainting, often after carbohydrate-heavy meals or exercise, and one attack came with severely low blood potassium.

Her pattern fitted hypokalemic periodic paralysis, a muscle channel disorder usually seen in teenage boys with affected relatives. She had no family history and lacked the flushing that her other syndrome would predict during attacks. Genetic testing found an ultra-rare change in the CACNA1S channel gene whose effect remains uncertain. The authors urge suspicion when weakness pairs with low potassium and clear triggers.
pmc-13240121:
Anwu Huang and colleagues connect diet quality for gut microbes with survival in a combined heart, kidney, and metabolic syndrome in a 2026 study. The dietary index for gut microbiota scores eating patterns by how well they feed helpful gut bacteria, and its link with death risk in this high-risk group was unknown.

National survey data covered 13,562 American adults with the syndrome between 2007 and 2018, followed for about eighty-two months on average. The lowest scoring group died at the highest rate. Each extra point on the index came with roughly a tenth lower risk of death overall and a slightly larger drop in cardiovascular death. The pattern held across patient subgroups.
pmc-13240921:
Ratsavong's team in Vientiane asked why toddlers stay underfed where food is at hand in Laos's capital. 333 mother-child pairs filled out a structured survey. 47 caregivers also gave in-depth interviews. Two districts, one urban and one peri-urban, were covered.

About 27 percent of children under two were stunted, with low weight near fourteen percent. What set thriving children apart was not food access alone. Parents who gathered feeding advice from varied sources, and turned knowledge into daily practice, had better-fed children. The team advises hands-on, show-how feeding outreach for urban and peri-urban families in Laos.
pmc-13241521:
Pasvolsky and colleagues at MD Anderson report outcomes for older myeloma patients treated with a four-drug induction and stem cell transplant. Landmark trials of daratumumab-based D-VRD therapy excluded patients over seventy. The team reviewed one hundred twenty-five newly diagnosed patients treated between 2021 and 2024. Twenty-seven were aged seventy or older, with a median age of seventy-four.

Older patients often received gentler conditioning and lower lenalidomide doses than younger ones. Even so, response depth matched: nearly every older patient reached a very good partial response or better after transplant. No transplant-related deaths occurred in either group. Two-year survival was similar across ages, supporting transplant-based therapy for fit older adults.
pmc-13242121:
Stahl and colleagues at Ulm traced gut microbiome aging back to the immune system's own stem cells. Young recipient mice were rebuilt with either young or old blood stem cells. Their gut immunity then aged according to the donor, not the host. Fecal sequencing and blood vitamin levels completed the picture.

Old stem cells reproduced mucosal immune aging, with naïve T cells vanishing from the gut wall. The microbiome shifted, losing bacteria tied to vitamin B6 production. Blood B6 levels duly fell in the aged-immune animals. Stahl proposes an immune-microbiome-vitamin axis behind some aging changes.
pmc-13243321:
Mitsuaki Hirai and colleagues asked health workers how a water and sanitation improvement program actually landed in Zimbabwean facilities. Their qualitative study appeared in Discover Public Health in 2026. The WASH FIT program ran in one hundred facilities from 2021 to 2023, aiming to cut infections tied to poor water, toilets, and hygiene. The team interviewed facility staff and government officers across four provinces about their experience of the rollout.

Staff judged the tool practical and credited it with better services, happier patients and workers, and higher use of care. The constraints were concrete: too little money, missing supplies, and not enough staff time or skills. Training had not always been deep enough for teams to make the method their own. The authors argue ownership at facility level decides whether gains survive. Steady financing and fuller training are their two headline recommendations.
pmc-13245821:
Raja presents five clinical cases in this 2026 Cureus case series, all married women with years of bodily complaints such as pain, stomach trouble, dizziness, fatigue, panic, and broken sleep. Repeated scans and specialist visits had found little to explain their symptoms, and most had seen several doctors before reaching psychiatric care.

In long assessment sessions, including couple discussions led jointly by male and female psychiatrists, another story emerged: emotional loneliness, feeling unheard by their husbands, lost physical and emotional intimacy. Sexual concerns they had felt too ashamed to raise. Raja argues that careful, sensitive psychiatric interviewing can surface such hidden distress, while noting five cases cannot prove cause and effect.
pmc-13246421:
Zhiqi Yu and colleagues build a learning model to predict poor recovery after nerve fiber decay in a 2026 study. Wallerian degeneration follows nerve injury in the brain and often leaves lasting disability. No tool existed to flag which patients will fare badly.

Records from 285 patients at a Dalian hospital fed eight rival models. Ten candidate factors were weighed, from diabetes and stroke scores to scan features of the decay. Just over half the patients had a poor outcome at three months or later. The best model is explained with charts that show how each factor pushes the risk. Such a tool could guide early rehab choices.
pmc-13246921:
Vilela, Gomes-Andrade, and Silva review the cancer tubulin code in this 2026 Cancer Metastasis Reviews article. Microtubules, the cell's internal rails and division machinery, are built from tubulin proteins that come in many versions, and chemical tags added after assembly fine-tune their behavior. That variety, the tubulin code, differs between tumors and shapes how cancer cells divide, move, and spread.

Standard chemotherapy drugs that attack microtubules, such as taxanes, often fail through resistance, and no validated test predicts who will respond. The authors argue the code itself could become that test, marking prognosis and likely drug response, and that enzymes writing or erasing the tags are promising drug targets. They also warn that antibody tools for measuring the code need rigorous validation first.
pmc-13248421:
Peppler and colleagues studied how German nursing teams handle growing diversity, in a 2026 BMC Nursing paper. Hospitals and care homes increasingly recruit nurses abroad, mixing languages, training, and customs on one ward. Rather than study the newcomers alone, the team watched how whole receiving teams work with difference day by day.

Across six teams, the researchers logged two hundred three hours of observation plus interviews and group talks. Three patterns emerged: teams that treat diversity as routine, teams in active transition, and teams where friction builds around boundaries and competence. Managers, the authors argue, must match support to each pattern instead of using one fix for all.
pmc-13248521:
Brown and Shandas modeled future heat illness across the United States in this 2026 GeoHealth study. Hospital visits surge during extreme heat, yet how weather, housing, health, and income combine to drive those surges is poorly mapped. The authors built a system dynamics simulation covering the fifty-three largest metropolitan areas and their climate regions.

The model projects illness counts and costs through 2040 under lower and higher emissions paths. Results diverged by region, shaped by changing heat patterns and by where vulnerable groups live. The authors argue the approach lets officials test interventions at specific points in the chain, and time regional responses before heat waves arrive.
pmc-13249921:
Girasol and a Brazilian team simulated therapy lasers traveling through human skin, in a 2026 Lasers in Medical Science study. Using optical properties measured from real skin samples, they ran Monte Carlo simulations, a photon-by-photon lottery, for three common treatment wavelengths. Beam width and beam spread were measured from actual devices rather than assumed, then fed into a voxel model of tissue.

All three wavelengths faded with depth in similar fashion over the first millimeters. Beam width mattered most: wider beams lowered the surface peak but carried more light to depth at the same total power. Realistic beam spread barely changed anything in contact use, while exaggerated spread wasted light sideways. The results guide dose planning for light therapy.
pmc-13250221:
Ayele and a large team track severe bleeding around childbirth across two hundred four countries and territories. Their 2026 BMJ Open analysis draws on Global Burden of Disease data from 2000 to 2021, with projections forward to 2050. Maternal haemorrhage remains one of the deadliest risks of pregnancy worldwide.

Global rates of cases, deaths, and lost healthy years all fell across the two decades studied. The burden stayed heavily concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa, where rates in the west ran hundreds of times higher than in Western Europe. High-income Asia Pacific and Australasia recorded the lowest figures of all. Forecasts show further improvement by 2050, but the authors urge targeted local action because national gaps remain wide.
pmc-13250321:
Preethika Murugesan and Manimaran R report an easily missed diagnosis in this 2026 case report. A 22-year-old man came in with an upward curve of the penis that had bothered him since his teens, and standard checks, including a camera look inside the urine tube, were normal.

During corrective surgery, leaking gel revealed a hidden side channel in the urine tube that tests had missed. The team repaired it with a three-layer flap of nearby skin while also straightening the curve, and recovery went smoothly with good function and appearance. Old records suggested a childhood repair as the likely cause. The authors urge careful checks during surgery itself.
pmc-13251521:
Kadyan and co-authors show that a mother's fat choices during pregnancy and nursing shape her pups' guts and brains into adulthood. Their 2026 Gut Microbes study fed mice diets rich in saturated fat, omega-6, or omega-3 oils, then switched all offspring to a Western-style diet for ten weeks. Only the early-life window differed between the groups.

Pups of omega-3 fed mothers kept leaner bodies, healthier gut linings, and far less low-grade inflammation along the gut-blood-brain route. Their brains showed stronger synaptic plasticity signals, quieter inflammation, and lipid profiles tied to membrane health. Omega-6 also left lasting microbiome marks, distinct from saturated fat. The authors frame maternal omega-3 as long-term neuroprotection delivered through the gut-brain-immune axis.
pmc-13251821:
Adithya Sarma and colleagues rescue forgotten social memories in mice in this 2026 neuroscience study. Remembering who you have met matters for social life, and losing sleep right after a meeting can wipe that recognition away.

Using a new test, the team showed mice can tell apart several past meetings held in the same place on different days. Sleep loss after meeting blocked the memory from settling. An approved drug given during sleep loss protected it, and given just before testing it briefly restored access. Shining light on the tagged memory cells in the brain also brought the memory back, pointing to a recall failure rather than a lost trace.
pmc-13252821:
Shiqiong Yan and colleagues review machine learning for predicting bleeding during surgery in this 2026 paper. Bleeding mid-operation threatens patient safety, and prediction models are multiplying, but their quality and readiness for wards were unclear.

Searching seven databases to April 2025, the team kept 23 studies with sample sizes from 48 to over 48,000. Tree-based models were the most common, and accuracy varied widely. Feeding models both records and images helped. Only six studies tested their model on outside patients, and accuracy often fell sharply there. Every study carried a high risk of bias by a standard tool, so the authors urge stricter building and reporting.
pmc-13253221:
Hongfang Liu and colleagues hunt for predictors of new chromosome errors in embryos across three kinds of fertility testing in a 2026 retrospective study. Clinics screen embryos before transfer for inherited rearrangements, chromosome number, or single-gene disorders, and the three patient groups differ. The team asked which parent, treatment, and embryo features predict a fresh aneuploidy, an abnormal chromosome count arising in the embryo itself.

Error rates differed by testing type, from 19.5 percent in the rearrangement group to about thirty-two percent in the other two groups. Advanced maternal age predicted errors robustly everywhere, especially past thirty-five, while rates stayed near twenty percent at thirty or younger. How far the embryo had expanded and the grade of its outer cell layer also carried signal, the outer layer more than the inner mass. Whole-chromosome errors hit chromosomes 22, 16, and 21 most often, guiding individualized embryo selection.
pmc-13253921:
Aiman Waheed and colleagues sequence a drug-resistant bacterium in a 2026 study from Peshawar, Pakistan. The isolate came from a urinary tract infection and belongs to Klebsiella quasipneumoniae, a germ easily confused with a close relative. It resisted many drug classes, including colistin, a last-line antibiotic, but stayed sensitive to a few others.

Whole-genome sequencing found resistance genes on its chromosome, not on plasmids, plus many mutations tied to resistance. pmc-13254021:
Xintao Zeng and a large team review how alterations in the gene KMT2C reshape gastrointestinal cancers in a 2026 article. pmc-13254321:

pmc-13254721:

pmc-13255221:

pmc-13255421:
Jinghang Yu and colleagues ask whether an extra thigh-bone cut is needed in hip surgery for young children in a 2026 study. Walking-age children with developmental hip dysplasia often get open reduction plus socket reshaping, sometimes with a femoral osteotomy added. pmc-13255521:
Merve Koseoglu and co-authors use machine learning to predict dental student grades in a 2026 study. pmc-13255721:

Some plants supported the bug well and others poorly. pmc-13255921:

pmc-13256121:

pmc-13257121:

Sorting patients by mechanism could guide more fitting treatment choices. Clinicians get a concise map of causes spanning brain, psychological, environmental, and genetic factors. The subgroup idea is offered as a testable proposal, not settled fact.
pmc-13258121:

A moving average forecast tracked stockout patterns over time with a score of 0.883.
pmc-13259421:

Most plant fiber stayed whole for split use, and sugar goods came out too. Plants gain a route to sell lignin as a chem good, not burn it.
pmc-13259621:

Precision improves over conventional therapy in these designs. Stable colonization, immune reactions, factory-scale production, and missing rules still stand between prototypes and patients, the authors caution.
pmc-13259821:

The team fed MRI scans, lab values, and pathology data into the International Radiomics Platform.

pmc-13260021:

pmc-13260921:

pmc-13262421:
Benito Baldauf and co-authors track infections from implanted heart devices in Germany in a 2026 journal article. Pocket infections occurred in 1.91 percent, and wire-linked heart infection in 0.82 percent. pmc-13263021:

Shorter reported breaks oddly tracked with lower risk, which the authors say needs better measurement in future work.
pmc-13263121:

pmc-13263221:

pmc-13263921:

pmc-13264021:

pmc-13264121:

pmc-13264221:

pmc-13264921:

pmc-13266021:

pmc-13266221:

pmc-13266721:

pmc-13266821:

pmc-13267821:

pmc-13267921:

pmc-13268921:

pmc-13269121:

pmc-13269321:

pmc-13269521:

pmc-13269921:

pmc-13270021:

pmc-13270121:

pmc-13270221:

pmc-13270521:

pmc-13271921:

pmc-13272621:

pmc-13272921:

pmc-13273221:

pmc-13273421:

pmc-13273521:

pmc-13273721:

pmc-13274921:

Six related kinases, called PIKKs, run DNA-damage alarms, growth, and nutrient sensing, and a three-part helper complex called TTT matures all of them. The team found seven mutations in one helper gene, tti1, that made fission yeast sensitive to DNA-damaging chemicals.

One mutant, tti1-N18, selectively wiped out the function of the checkpoint kinase Rad3, the yeast version of human ATR. The other five kinases, including the ATM counterpart, worked largely normally. That surgical specificity suggests the helper grips each client differently. The authors note the human version of the complex is a known drug target, hinting at therapeutic openings.
pmc-13275721:
Junqi Ma and colleagues review COVID-19 mRNA vaccines and their future direction in a 2026 article. The pandemic turned mRNA from an experimental idea into a proven vaccine platform. First products in fatty nanoparticle carriers protected strongly against severe disease.

Protection against infection faded over time, and new variants partly escaped vaccine defences. Mucosal immunity in the nose and throat stayed limited, and responses differed in groups such as older adults. The review covers immune markers, repeated dosing questions, and new RNA formats such as self-amplifying RNA. It closes with uses beyond COVID-19, from other respiratory viruses to cancer therapy.
pmc-13276821:
Jens Verlinden and colleagues report a 2026 laboratory study that makes Sudan virus safer to study. Sudan virus is a deadly relative of Ebola, and work on it normally needs the highest level lab safety. The team removed a gene the virus needs, called VP30, so it can grow only in specially made cells.

The contained virus grew much like the wild type in those helper cells and stayed contained in other cells. VP30 proteins from related viruses worked in the system, while one from Marburg virus did not. The setup also allowed quick drug screening and confirmed strong action by remdesivir. Mutations tied to drug resistance were pinpointed along the way.
pmc-13278021:
Natalia Buenache leads a 2026 study of a blood test for leftover cancer cells in multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow. Checking bone marrow for residual disease predicts outcomes but is invasive and can miss patchy disease. The team tested a sensitive DNA sequencing method on cell-free DNA in blood from 84 trial patients, using 292 samples over time.

Detectable tumor DNA in blood predicted relapse more accurately than the standard bone marrow flow test, with far fewer false alarms. Patients with detectable DNA faced a much higher risk of progression or death. Automated sample preparation matched manual methods. A blood-based check could make repeated monitoring easier, the authors propose.
pmc-13278721:
Ibrahim Alharbi and colleagues report a new kidney finding in a child with a GLIS3 gene disorder, in a 2026 case. The ten-year-old Saudi girl carried the classic trio of newborn diabetes, underactive thyroid from birth, and congenital glaucoma. The gene shapes development of the pancreas, thyroid, kidneys, liver, and eyes.

Routine monitoring uncovered a complex mass in her left kidney that she had not felt. Biopsy after detailed imaging showed a benign multicystic nephroma with mixed tissue features. Such a tumour had not been reported in this disorder before, widening its known effects beyond simple kidney cysts. Doctors chose active surveillance over surgery, given the harmless nature of the lesion.
pmc-13278921:
Aidana Rakhmankulova and colleagues chart cervical cancer across Kazakhstan over a decade, in a 2026 nationwide study. HPV shots for girls began in 2024 in the country, so a pre-vaccine baseline matters. Registry data covered cases from 2014 to 2023.

Recorded cases climbed while incidence and death rates peaked around 2022. Five-year survival sat near sixty-five percent overall, with advanced-stage disease driving most lost years. Treatment with chemotherapy or radiation marked higher risk in adjusted models, reflecting more severe cases. Burden measures such as disability-adjusted life years also peaked in 2022. The authors offer the analysis as the benchmark for judging the years ahead.
pmc-13279321:
Hong Yang and colleagues published a 2026 analysis of how bacteria in the upper and lower airways change as ventilator-associated pneumonia develops. It strikes patients ventilated over 48 hours and carries high mortality. Reanalyzing gene sequencing data from 123 samples in public databases, the team compared intubated patients without pneumonia, a phase just before pneumonia appeared, and confirmed cases. They tracked diversity and makeup in both airway regions.

Bacterial diversity in the upper airway rose sharply in pneumonia groups, while lower airway diversity barely moved, yet their makeup differed across all three stages in both regions. Genera including Prevotella, Leptotrichia, and Peptostreptococcus emerged as candidate early warning markers with strong accuracy in their tests. Bacteria moving from upper to lower airway grew more in step by day seven, hinting at a window for action. The authors call for testing in fresh patient groups before any marker guides care.
pmc-13279421:
Mengying Mao and colleagues published a 2026 multi-site study building a prediction model for postherpetic neuralgia, the persistent nerve pain that follows shingles. The team followed 1,361 patients from two hospitals in Hangzhou and Zhejiang, of whom 511, about 37.6 percent, developed the outcome. They screened 36 candidate factors and focused on SIRI, a blood index combining several immune cell counts that reflects body-wide inflammation.

Inflammation measured by SIRI predicted who developed lasting pain on its own. Selection narrowed the model to six factors: age, SIRI, initial pain strength, delay before treatment, rash location, and a neutrophil-to-albumin ratio. Among eight machine learning methods, the XGBoost model performed best, with accuracy scores between about 0.86 and 0.90 across training, internal test, and external patient groups. The authors also converted the model into a simple paper risk score, aiming at a first-visit tool to flag patients for early, aggressive pain prevention.
pmc-13279921:
Yuqin Ye and colleagues give a 2026 review of a mixed cell death mode in brain and spinal cord trauma. Traumatic brain and spinal cord injury cause high death and disability rates in the world. The death mode, PANoptosis, blends three death types in one: pyroptosis, apoptosis and necroptosis. A hub complex starts all three at once. It links to rust stress, nerve swelling and second wave harm after trauma.

Mitochondria, the cell power cores, sit at the centre of the story. Their balance loss can start and run PANoptosis in many cell types. The review lists imbalance signs: poor new core growth, odd split and fuse acts, faulty clean up and shed vesicles. It then maps how each sign feeds the death hub. Drug ideas that guard power cores to block the death blend close the review.
pmc-13280221:
Mathieu Tiret and colleagues report a 2026 study of flea beetle resistance in cabbage kin. The cabbage stem flea beetle grows as a threat to winter Brassica crops in Europe, oil and vegetable plants of the cabbage family. Genetic basis of resistance was poorly understood. The team ran a genome wide association study, which scans the full genome for trait links. They joined pooled gene reads with a large feeding test on one hundred thirteen Brassica oleracea types.

Resistance showed moderate heritability with a mostly polygenic base, meaning many small gene effects. Types split sharply: cabbage head types were mostly susceptible, while cauliflower types and wild groups resisted far more. One major effect zone on chromosome C01 stood out despite the small effect back cloth. Resistance alleles piled up in wild groups, while susceptible alleles ruled in head cabbage. Wild kin hold the resistance stock for breeding.
pmc-13280721:
Diyana Muhammed and colleagues published a 2026 study of SelfCheck-Eval, a framework for catching made-up answers from large language models without needing reference data or model internals. Hallucination is an obstacle to using these systems in medicine, finance, or education. Existing detectors lean on general questions, so the team built a test set from an American mathematics examination, where wrong reasoning can sound convincing. Their framework combines three checks covering meaning, specialized checks, and consistency with context.

Evaluation exposed a sharp split. Detectors handled life stories well but stumbled on math reasoning errors. The weakness persisted across three improvement strategies: fine-tuning on inference data, preference learning, and guided reasoning steps. The authors conclude the failure is structural rather than a matter of more tuning. They argue for specialized black-box detectors for any model, open or closed, before such systems can be trusted in high-stakes work.
pmc-13281321:
Camille Wirth and colleagues shared a 2026 case report on a heart fix that backfired in a very sick patient. The patient was on a heart and lung support machine for severe lung artery pressure. The heart then weakened under stress, and fluid backed up into the lungs. Doctors made a small hole between the heart's upper chambers to drain the pressure. The step is used to ease lung pressure in some patients and to unload the heart in others.

Here it did the reverse. Blood slipped the wrong way through the hole, starving the body of oxygen. Pressure also loaded the weak heart further, and the patient got worse. The authors say the balance of pressures on each side of the heart decides whether the hole helps or harms. They urge great care before using it in like cases.
pmc-13281421:
Temesgen Gebeyehu Wondmeneh measured anemia in toddlers across nine African countries for a 2026 study. Anemia in this age group can slow growth and brain gains. The study used fresh health survey data from 2021 to 2024. It counted more than fourteen thousand children aged six to twenty-three months. Rates were judged by new 2024 global cutoffs, which are stricter than the old ones. The author weighed severity, from mild to severe, against family and health factors.

Even with the new cutoffs, about six in ten toddlers had anemia. Most cases were mild or moderate, and severe cases were few. Girls tended toward milder anemia than boys. Schooling of the mother, health cover, worm care, and varied food all guarded against severe anemia. Fever, low weight, and being a twin or triplet made anemia worse. The author urges action on food, care access, and mother schooling.
pmc-13281821:
Killian Sheriff and colleagues taught software to model metal mixes at any recipe in a 2026 study. A metal's traits swing with its recipe, from neat ordered mixes to jumbled ones. Simulating each recipe from scratch is slow and costly. Learning models can help, but they often fail outside the recipes they trained on. The team used information theory to pick the most telling atom patterns to teach. The model then learned the full landscape of each mix.

They tested it on four mixes, from two-metal pairs to a four-metal blend. It foretold fault energies, local atom order, heat storage, and phase maps across recipes. Its calls matched lab data closely throughout. The authors say smart sampling, not brute data, is the key step. The method could speed the hunt for alloys built for heat, strength, or wear.
pmc-13282321:
Sedra T Alabed and Diana Finkel wrote a 2026 narrative review on tuberculosis that shows only as eye inflammation. Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection best known in the lungs, but it can inflame the uvea, the eye's middle layer. Diagnosis is uncertain because no test directly proves the eye disease. The authors set out how doctors weigh eye patterns, exposure risk, blood immune tests, and the exclusion of look-alike diseases.

Certain eye patterns raise suspicion more, including a snake-like retina pattern, blocked retinal veins, and lumpy iris or choroid lesions. A positive immune blood test shows past exposure, not that tuberculosis caused the eye problem. A negative test does not fully rule it out either. Guidance supports tuberculosis antibiotics in selected patients. The review urges lower treatment thresholds for high-risk eye patterns, and caution when findings are vague and only the blood test is positive.
pmc-13283121:
Fluid racing over a sensor skin, spiked with nanoparticles and swimming cells, is modeled in 2026 by Muhammad Azhar Iqbal's group. The flow mixes tiny metal grains, heat, magnetism, and living cells that swim. Good models can aid drug delivery tools, chip labs, and plant sensors.

A trained neural network learned to predict flow traits with high accuracy. Inputs covered squeeze flow, heat source effects, and chemical change in the fluid. The model also fits ore slurry lines, mine water units, and coating tasks. Magnetic control and grain mix can tune heat flow and sensor response. The authors offer the model as a design aid for engineers who build smart sensor systems for harsh settings.
pmc-13283421:
Calcified shells around old brain bleeds form an armoured-brain picture in Aasim Ali's 2026 shunt case from Pakistan's literature. The shunt was placed in childhood for high brain pressure. New headache after 20 days prompted brain imaging for shunt problems.

The patient was a 35-year-old man with a mild, diffuse headache at arrival. Brain checks showed no clear nerve deficits or eye signs of pressure. CT scans showed crescent collections with thick calcified shells on both sides. That shell pattern is called armoured brain in the report text. MRI confirmed the collections and showed a mild shift of the brain midline. A small fresh bleed may have triggered symptoms.
pmc-13283621:
Stephanie Tow, David Bell, and Shana Harrington surveyed young para sport athletes in 2026 about early specialisation and injuries. Little is known about specialisation in this group, whose medical and body factors may reshape what counts as early or risky. The web survey, tested first by five young para athletes, went out through national para sport bodies to athletes aged eight to eighteen.

Twenty-five athletes replied, average age thirteen and a half. Most played several sports all year, averaging more than eight months in a main sport. Among the youngest group, all played multiple sports year-round. About four in ten of all respondents reported a sport injury in the past year. Injury shares looked much alike whether the main sport ran past eight months or not.
pmc-13283921:
Blood cell shredding after a pit viper bite was diagnosed without key lab tests in a 2026 Nepal case from Prabhat Kaphle and colleagues. The complication, called MAHA, is extremely rare with green pit vipers. Rural clinics often lack the blood smear tools that confirm it.

The 47-year-old woman developed swelling, bruising, blood in urine, and clotting failure. Low red cells and low platelets tracked over time fit the MAHA pattern. No species-matched antivenom was available at her treating facility. Supportive care plus blood product transfusions carried her to full recovery. Kidney harm never developed, and syndromic vigilance got the credit.
pmc-13284421:
Noam Shalem and colleagues report a 2026 imaging study on personal targeting for focused ultrasound treatment of tremor. Standard care aims at a thalamic site using fixed landmarks, yet up to one fifth of patients get poor tremor control. The team tested whether maps of brain tracts could guide a better target for each patient.

Scans from 81 patients treated between 2014 and 2021 were reviewed, with outcomes tracked for up to two years. Good lesions sat in one front-side zone of the dentatorubrothalamic tract, while poor lesions ringed that zone. A model using tract features predicted the best target well. The authors propose a shared sweet-spot map, while noting more testing is still needed.
pmc-13284521:
Won Ro Park, Yong Jae Kwon, and Dong Ha Lee compared in 2026 two ways of gauging bone strength: the standard DXA scan and density readings taken from ordinary CT scans. CT values, called Hounsfield units, had matched DXA fairly in the spine, but other bones were barely studied. The team reviewed 214 patients who had both scans, measuring CT values at five spots in four limb bones.

Inner bone readings in the upper and lower shin bones correlated moderately with the lowest DXA scores. One outer region of the upper arm bone also tracked the scores. Average CT values at several spots differed clearly between osteoporotic and normal groups. The authors suggest routine CT scans can supplement bone checks when DXA is unavailable.
pmc-13284721:
Yuna Miyachi and Kenta Nakai built a deep learning model in 2026 that predicts where RNA gets spliced, reading DNA stretches up to one hundred thousand letters long. Splicing trims non-coding segments from gene messages, and errors cause disease. Older tools miss far-away control signals because long sequences cost too much to process, and many models cannot explain their calls.

Their model, SpliceSelectNet, stacks transformer layers in a hierarchy, mixing local and global attention to catch near and distant signals at single-letter precision. It topped benchmark tests for splice site prediction and for spotting harmful splicing changes. Systematic fake mutations showed the model's attention scores track real functional importance, and long-range perturbation tests confirmed it senses distant regulators. The authors present it as both accurate and biologically readable.
pmc-13285221:
Mario Gilberto Siqueira and co-authors report long-term results, published in 2026, for a nerve transfer that restores shoulder outward rotation after upper arm nerve injury. Turning the shoulder outward is vital for daily tasks, yet repair efforts often focus on lifting the arm and bending the elbow. Seven patients had a radial nerve branch rerouted to power the infraspinatus muscle.

All seven regained some outward rotation after follow-up with a median near five years in this small series. Five reached the level the authors count as a good result. The team argues the transfer works and should join the set of options nerve surgeons consider for upper plexus injury, where each added motion widens what patients can do.
pmc-13285621:
Why does Bundibugyo ebolavirus still lack a licensed vaccine? Aniso Mohamed Abdi and co-authors press the question in a 2026 letter after fresh outbreaks in Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Licensed Ebola shots guard only the Zaire species, leaving Bundibugyo and Sudan species bare despite repeat deadly outbreaks.

Animal proof for Bundibugyo and mixed-species shots exists, so the block is not science, the writers argue. Weak profit pull stalls late trials for germs that strike rarely in poor lands. Even Zaire shot access lags where risk runs high. The letter calls the gap a structural failure of preparedness and urges funding paths that do not wait for rich markets.
pmc-13285921:
Yuki Suzuki reviews DNA origami for drug delivery and cell control in a 2026 survey of intelligent nanomedicine. Folding a long DNA strand with short staples builds tiny shapes with exact size and spots for cargo. Such structures can sense signals, make simple choices, and move, which sets them apart from plain carriers.

Shape and stiffness steer how cells take the structures in and where cargo ends up inside. Loaded drugs and gene-like agents can be freed on cue by chemical, light, or molecular triggers at the right place and time. Other designs gather cell surface receptors into set patterns to steer cell behavior and fate. Glue-like linking and surface coats help the shapes survive in the body, and Suzuki sees smart sensing as the next leap.
pmc-13286221:
Jinlong Huang and colleagues price a second-line pancreatic cancer regimen for China in a 2026 economic study. The drug wraps a proven chemotherapy agent in fat bubbles so more of it reaches the tumor, and a large trial showed it stretches life after first treatment fails. A three-state model weighed lifetime costs against quality-weighted years of life, from the health system's side of the ledger.

The wrapped drug bought only a small slice of extra quality-weighted life at a very steep cost per unit. Its cost ratio landed many times above the national yardstick the authors applied, and chance-based reruns gave it no shot at passing at that price. Only a price cut near nine tenths would bring the regimen within the yardstick. The verdict guides talks on price and cover for a cancer where extra months are dear but budgets stay finite.
pmc-13286321:
Jun Yu and colleagues test whether two blood inflammation scores can predict death among people with fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. Their 2026 cohort study uses United States survey data from 1999 to 2018 linked with death records, covering 6,252 patients followed for a median of just over nine years.

During follow-up, 1,154 participants died, including 373 from cardiovascular causes. People in the highest quarter of either score faced clearly higher death rates than those in the lowest quarter. Risk rose steeply only after each score passed a threshold level, while heart-related death climbed in a straight line. The scores discriminated well between outcomes. External testing is still needed before clinics rely on them, the authors caution.
pmc-13286521:
Hanna Plischke and co-authors set out a scoping review plan on vitamin C and the pancreas in a 2026 protocol article. Pancreatic cancer kills most patients within five years, and inflamed pancreas tissue shares the scarred, immune-heavy surroundings that help tumors grow. Vitamin C might calm inflammation in benign disease and poison tumor pathways in cancer, but its effects on the supporting and lining cells remain scattered across journals.

Following standard scoping rules, twin reviewers will screen PubMed, MEDLINE, and Web of Science plus gray sources. Early screening had already sifted 475 database hits by April 2026, with the full sweep running through the year and results due in early 2027. Rather than grading study quality, the team will chart cell types, doses, and outcomes to expose the gaps preclinical work should fill next.
pmc-13286821:
Sunyi Zheng and fellow editors introduce a 2026 journal collection on artificial intelligence in lung cancer screening and treatment. Lung cancer kills more people than any other cancer, largely because it is found late. Low-dose CT screening catches it earlier but floods clinicians with images and uncertain nodules to judge.

Contributions in the collection widen screening beyond CT alone, pairing scans with blood markers or ultrasound in selected cases. Others turn images into numbers, measuring texture inside and around nodules to separate cancer from look-alike infections and to distinguish cancer subtypes. The editors see a shift from stand-alone algorithms toward tools woven into clinical decisions, including treatment choice and prognosis.
pmc-13286921:
Ngoc Bich T. Nguyen and Linh Thuy Nguyen describe braces-only treatment of a thirteen-year-old boy with a Class III bite, where the lower jaw sits ahead of the upper. The 2026 case report notes that his upper jaw was also narrow, causing crossbites front and back plus facial asymmetry, and that the family declined jaw surgery. Three-dimensional imaging confirmed a major width mismatch.

Skeletal expansion of the upper jaw widened it by six millimeters. The lower jaw then settled into a better position on its own, and facial balance improved. Standard angle measures showed the jaw relationship nearing normal while height measures stayed stable. Later braces and elastics finished the bite. The authors credit treating the width problem, while warning against generalizing to severe cases.
pmc-13287121:
Vanessa Bundle and a large team test yoga against physiotherapy for stiffening spine disease in a 2026 prospective controlled study. Axial spondyloarthritis inflames the spine, eroding movement and mood together, and exercise is a pillar of care. Seventy-six people took part: patients chose eight weeks of weekly online yoga or standard one-on-one physiotherapy, and healthy volunteers completed the same yoga course for comparison.

Spinal mobility scores improved in the yoga patients while the physiotherapy group clearly worsened over the same span. Yoga patients also gained in movement confidence, mental quality of life, and fear of movement, and their disease activity dipped slightly. Physiotherapy produced no meaningful shifts on those scales. Healthy yoga volunteers moved in the same directions with smaller effects. The authors back yoga as an add-on therapy spanning body and mind.
pmc-13287821:
Okasha Zulfiqar and co-authors compare two drug families for ulcerative colitis in a 2026 systematic review. Ulcerative colitis is a long-term inflammation of the colon lining. Biologic drugs are large proteins usually given by injection or infusion, while small-molecule drugs come as pills. The review drew on eight landmark publications covering pivotal phase 3 trials in adults with moderate to severe disease.

Across the trials, the pill-based therapies matched the biologics in a clinically meaningful way for starting and keeping remission. The drug classes differed in how fast they worked and how well gains held over time. Pills also avoid injections, which some patients prefer. The authors argue that doctors should pick treatments by mechanism, patient risk, and personal priorities rather than cycling within one class. Safety profiles still need care when matching a drug to a patient.
pmc-13288721:
Kaisa Kujansivu and co-authors profile chat clinic users in Finland in 2026. Their study uses linked national records. Years ran from January 2022 to February 2025. The set held 1,599,588 residents. Eight service counties fed the data. Older, poor, and jobless groups got close looks.

Public chat users skewed young. They were more often women. They lived in cities more often. They had fewer chronic diseases than in-person users. At-risk groups did use chat care too. They leaned on in-person care more, though. Chat topics were often simple. Chronic care needs also came to chat. Fairness effects need direct tests.
pmc-13289021:
Rebecca K Kelly and colleagues study heart risk by wealth and sex in the UK. Their 2026 study uses UK Biobank data. It holds 500,769 adults with one risk read. Wealth was split by a town score. Women made up 54.4 percent of the group.

Poorer adults had higher body weight and waist size. Their blood fats and sugar ran worse too. One swelling marker also ran higher. Blood pressure gaps went the other way. High blood pressure was more common in poor areas. Kidney disease was also more common there. Smoking gaps were wider in men. Weight gaps were wider in women. Care plans should weigh both wealth and sex.
pmc-13289221:
Liane B de Azevedo headed a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis on what shapes mobile device use in young children. The review covered tablets, smartphones, and problematic smartphone use in children aged six or younger. Searches ran across ten databases through March 2026, with two reviewers screening and rating study quality.

In total, 39 studies with 32 927 children from 17 countries met the rules for inclusion. The team sorted 115 correlates into child, family and social, and wider environment levels. No factor showed a clear link with problematic use in the pooled results so far. The work gives parents and researchers a map of which child and family traits most often track with early screen habits.
pmc-13289921:
Yency J. Forero and colleagues offer a 2026 study on repeated measures of CYFRA 21-1, a lung cancer blood marker, in people with lung nodules. Single readings of this cytokeratin fragment separate cancer from benign nodules poorly. Inspired by serial prostate marker use, the team asked whether change over time sharpens the test for nodule clinics at Vanderbilt.

Samples came from 132 patients in a thoracic biorepository, narrowed to 121 untreated patients with 91 benign and 30 malignant nodules. Serial lab measures were modeled with mixed effects on log-transformed values to trace paths. Starting levels ran higher in malignant nodules than benign ones at baseline. Trend modeling then tested whether slopes diverged with time.
pmc-13290121:
Electrical muscle stimulation before play sped up badminton lunges in a 2026 experiment by Xuerui Li and Yi Sheng. The forward lunge demands quick starts, controlled landings, and fast recovery, so the pair tested whether stimulation combined with weighted squats could prime players.

Thirty-six male players were assigned to weighted squats alone, sham stimulation with squats, or real stimulation with squats, then performed shuttle trials while muscle activity was recorded from 14 sites. The real stimulation group finished fastest and showed stronger activation in key leg and trunk muscles, plus greater co-activation and coupling between muscle pairs. Li and Sheng propose stimulation as a short pre-competition priming tool.
pmc-13290321:
David Escalante Raz, Javier Cantón Castillo, and Alberto Alcaráz Romero test tropical grasses in sheep diets in a 2026 feeding study. Rising grain prices push tropical sheep farms toward local forages. Two trials ran at a research field in Yucatán, Mexico, with Katahdin cross Pelibuey sheep. Rams first tested digestibility of concentrate alone or with thirty percent of one of three grasses. Lambs then ate the same diets for 84 days.

Concentrate alone digested best, and one grass, CT-115, cut fiber digestion the most. Forage groups still ate more total feed than the concentrate-only group. Growth, slaughter weight, carcass yield, and muscle area did not differ between diets. Meat traits stayed in normal ranges across all groups. Concentrate-only lambs stored more fat inside the muscle, while forage lambs' meat held more moisture. The authors conclude that thirty percent forage swaps in without hurting performance.
pmc-13290521:
Different ball sports sharpen different corners of children's thinking, Tongyan Zhang and colleagues find in a 2026 network meta-analysis. They pooled randomized trials in children and adolescents to compare how football, tennis, table tennis, and other ball games affect executive function subdomains.

Twelve studies covering five sports entered the network. Football ranked best for the accuracy of inhibitory control, while tennis led for reaction time and table tennis for reaction time in cognitive flexibility tasks. Working memory accuracy, oddly, ranked highest under control conditions rather than any sport. Zhang and colleagues caution that several rankings flipped when the analysis was limited to typically developing children, and with thin, mixed evidence the domain-by-domain verdicts should be read as provisional.
pmc-13290721:
Plant essential oils attack gum-disease bacteria on several fronts at once, Yan Huang and colleagues summarize in a 2026 review of alternatives for periodontitis care. With standard drugs facing resistance, the review gathers what is known about oils' antibacterial strength and how they work.

Many oils suppressed key plaque pathogens, including Porphyromonas gingivalis, often at minimum inhibitory concentrations below 100 μg/mL, and some blocked biofilm formation at even lower doses. Their weapons include tearing bacterial membranes, jamming metabolism, switching off virulence genes, and interrupting quorum sensing. Single components such as carvacrol, thymol, and eugenol carry much of the punch, and carriers like nanoemulsions and liposomes can steady the oils and deliver them better. The authors flag poor water solubility, leftover toxicity, and instability as the work that remains.
pmc-13290821:
Adding a diode laser to scraping improves inflamed gums around dental implants, Akif Nalbant and colleagues report in a clinical study from 2026. Peri-implantitis threatens implant survival, and the team tested whether a 940 nm laser, alone or combined with mechanical cleaning, beats cleaning alone on clinical signs and a fluid biomarker.

Thirty-nine patients split into debridement-only, laser-only, and combined groups, with pocket depth, attachment level, plaque and gum indices, and fluid volume checked at baseline and weeks 4 and 12. Every group improved, but the combined group cut plaque and gum inflammation most, with the largest numerical gains elsewhere too. The biomarker S100A8, however, did not move significantly in any group. Nalbant and colleagues endorse the combination for calming inflammation while doubting the marker's short-term sensitivity.
pmc-13291021:
Robots placed in older people’s homes might flag who needs depression care, according to a 2026 real-world study led by Han Wool Jung. Participants used a social robot called Hyodol, which asked daily health questions, held free conversations, and logged how people touched and used its content.

Data came from 215 community-dwelling older adults, split into a 2024 training group of 170 and a 2025 test group of 45, with depression judged by surveys and expert video consultations. A random forest model caught most people who were symptomatic and most who needed referral, though it also raised many false alarms. Quiz use, chat frequency, meal regularity, and physical contact with the robot ranked among the strongest signals.
pmc-13291221:
Deep space travel strains the heart in ways still unclear. Agnieszka Brojakowska leads a 2026 review of heart risks for Moon and Mars crews. Space flight brings weightlessness and strong radiation. Long trips add isolation, poor sleep, and scant medical help.

Known effects include rhythm faults and stiffer blood vessels. Control of blood pressure by nerves also shifts. A body-wide inflammatory state may develop. What these changes mean over years away from Earth is unknown. Particle radiation from deep space adds new danger. The review gathers all known risks in one place. Planners can use it to design safeguards for long missions.
pmc-13291321:
New brain cells in mice may soften social rank fights. Birte Doludda leads a 2026 study of female mouse groups. Genes and homes were held the same across groups. Yet each mouse still acted as an individual.

Groups mixed normal mice with mice lacking new neurons. A tracking system watched them for three months. Stable rank orders formed in all groups. Mice without new neurons grew more rank-bound over time. They also took higher ranks than normal cage mates. Social rank in normal mice tracked new cell counts. Flexible social skills may need fresh neurons. Flat groups may rest on that flexibility.
pmc-13292321:
Kim L Vockert and co-authors run a 2026 five-year imaging follow-up of people with inherited nerve diseases, hunting for measures that track slow decline. Fourteen patients with genetically confirmed Charcot-Marie-Tooth types and related conditions received muscle MRI of the legs and high-resolution nerve ultrasound twice, about 4.75 years apart. Clinical scores, strength, sensation, and nerve conduction studies ran alongside.

Clinical examination scores worsened significantly, driven by motor symptoms, yet nerve conduction and MRI muscle volume barely budged. One MRI measure, normalized signal intensity in the lateral calf muscle, rose clearly and matched fat fraction readings, exposing creeping fat replacement. The ultrasound pattern score also climbed in demyelinating forms and tracked with slower conduction speeds. The authors nominate fat fraction and the ultrasound score as trial-ready progression markers.
pmc-13293121:
Andrew A Davinack and co-authors introduce, in 2026, a free Python package that turns genetic distance data into smooth maps. Standard population genetics often forces data into set groups, which can hide steady shifts across a landscape.

The package, called pygenoscape, takes distance tables or aligned DNA and blends embedding, map projection, gap filling, and interactive viewing in one workflow. Trials used genome data from an invasive bumblebee and DNA from a marine worm, matching earlier findings in both. Tests with made-up data also rebuilt known patterns, such as slow drift with distance and sharp breaks at barriers. Anyone can install it from PyPI.
pmc-13293721:
Linqin Xie and colleagues make, in a 2026 study, a foam dressing loaded with copper-bearing bioactive glass for chronic diabetic wounds. Such wounds need dressings that soak up fluid, kill germs, and actively support tissue repair at the same time.

The foam soaked liquid well, let vapor pass at a fit rate, and held its strength in tests. Copper glass gave germ killing above 99% against two common bacteria, values the authors report, and boosted growth of vessel lining cells. In diabetic rats, the dressing sped wound closure with more vessel growth and collagen than shop dressings. Physical and biological gains came in one product.
pmc-13293921:
Jintao Zhu and colleagues test age-friendly room design with virtual reality in a 2026 framework study. Interviews with 50 older adults named seven design features, including ceiling height, openness, daylight, and noise. Those ideas became variables in 18 virtual scenes tried by 40 older participants, whose skin conductance, heart rate, and mood scores were recorded.

Early results link daylight strength, noise level, and openness to short-term body and mood responses. The authors warn that repeated measures and a screening design make the work exploratory only, fit for forming hypotheses rather than proof. Still, the participatory tuning method offers a practical way to test rooms before building.
pmc-13294921:
Dong Gao and colleagues predict coal self-heating risk when oxygen is scarce in a 2026 study. Coal left in worked-out mine areas can slowly oxidise, build heat, and catch fire. Oxygen levels there fall well below normal air, changing how different coal ranks behave.

Three coal types, from lignite to fat coal, were heated at oxygen levels from 18 percent down to 3 percent. Higher rank coals reacted less readily, while falling oxygen slowed weight loss but raised the energy barrier for reaction. Heat release peaked at a different oxygen level for each coal. Grouping methods then sorted conditions into risk and no-risk classes for practical mine warnings.
pmc-13295421:
Silvana Aparecida de Souza and colleagues review plant-based insecticides and bee safety in a 2026 article. Botanical sprays are often sold as gentle on nature and people, but proof about pollinators is thin. Harm can hide below death, in changed behaviour, growth, or breeding.

Most safety testing still uses honey bees alone in lab settings, missing stingless bees, bumblebees, and solitary species entirely. Effects on foraging and colony upkeep may matter as much as outright kills for farm pollination. The authors call for testing that spans bee diversity and realistic field exposure, so natural labels rest on evidence rather than assumption.
pmc-13295621:
Nan Wang and colleagues examine an enzyme that quietly guards the gut's stem cell nursery, in a 2026 study of PRMT5. The enzyme decorates proteins with methyl marks and is abundant in intestinal crypts, where stem cells renew the lining every few days. It is also a cancer drug target, which makes its normal gut job worth knowing. The team blocked it with an inhibitor in mice and organoids and deleted it in models of radiation injury.

In healthy guts, blocking PRMT5 changed the lining's cell mix and raised a nitric oxide enzyme in stem cell zones. After radiation, missing PRMT5 stalled stem cell division, soured the Paneth cells that nurse them, and left organoids feeble. The cause traced to a jammed urea cycle, which flooded tissue with nitric oxide, fats, and reactive oxygen. Guarding that cycle, the authors suggest, is how the enzyme keeps regeneration possible.
pmc-13295721:
Yueyan Huang and co-authors pool what is known about body-based effects in verb learning, in a 2026 meta-analysis. Verbs name actions and changes, so they lean on sight, sound, and movement more than most words. The team merged thirty-seven studies with 265 effect sizes and 12,357 people from the past fifteen years to test how strong that body link is.

A real effect stood out, of modest size. How concrete a verb is and which layer of the verb is in play changed the effect's strength. Task depth and language status played smaller parts. The authors suggest that teaching verbs with body action mixed in, plus rich context, may help learners grip new verbs faster and keep them longer.
pmc-13295921:
Upeka Senanayake, Phoebe Aubugeau-Williams and Gemma Barnard evaluate, in 2026, debrief support for junior children's cancer doctors after a patient dies. The work is rewarding yet draining, and one centre had set up private debrief sessions led by a pastoral doctor.

Local and national surveys of trainees and new consultants found universal agreement that the role takes an emotional toll, with varied effects on wellbeing. Respondents valued regular wellbeing sessions offered by their trusts. The evaluation supports structured debriefing as part of wider efforts to curb burnout and keep staff in post.
pmc-13296621:
Liu Wen and colleagues map, in 2026, nurse-led diet advice for bowel problems after rectal cancer surgery that spares the sphincter. Searching four databases to May 2025, they find just five small studies, mostly pilot trials, testing such programmes.

Advice covered fibre management, food diaries, symptom-tailored changes and fibre supplements, sometimes alone and sometimes inside wider nurse care. Benefit varied across studies, and timing and delivery differed a lot. The authors call for standard, evidence-based programmes and for research on remote and more precise nurse-led diet support after rectal surgery.
pmc-13297921:
Three immune molecules may help read a tumor's prognosis and likely drug response across many cancers, propose Christos Panagiotis Rigopoulos and co-authors in a 2026 data study. They profiled CD70, CD80, and TIGIT through cancer genome data spanning gene expression, methylation, mutations, and single-cell records.

All three molecules were widely misregulated, with joint overexpression standing out in clear-cell kidney cancer. Higher levels tracked with advanced stage and worse survival in selected cancers, including uveal melanoma and kidney tumors. Expression also lined up with immune cell mixes, TIGIT marking T-cell-inflamed tumors, and with sensitivity to several anticancer drugs in cell lines. The authors present the trio as candidate biomarkers for precision immunotherapy.
pmc-13299321:
A mint-family plant's scent repels a disease-carrying mosquito, and Jinfeng Xiong with co-authors traced the molecular handshake behind the effect in a 2026 study. They distilled Mosla chinensis leaf oil, identified its main components, and tested them on Culex quinquefasciatus.

The oil strongly repelled the mosquitoes. Two odorant-binding proteins from the insect bound five oil components tightly, including citronellal, citronellol, and geraniol, and a blend of the five also repelled well in behavior tests. Docking and mutation experiments pinpointed two amino acid positions, Phe123 and Gln77, as key contact points. The authors propose the blend as a candidate natural repellent.
pmc-13299621:
Neslihan Cansel and others survey healthcare workers one year after the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes, in a 2026 one-time study at a hard-hit tertiary hospital. Checked scales gauged burnout, anxiety, depression, trauma symptoms, and plans to quit for 640 workers. Hierarchical models weighed disaster exposures against workplace factors.

Over half showed depressive symptoms or trauma risk, and low personal accomplishment was the commonest burnout feature. Low job satisfaction proved the strongest, most consistent correlate of poor outcomes, and distant colleague relations added harm. Very few workers had sought psychiatric help since the disaster. The authors urge workplace improvements plus accessible mental health support for retention.
pmc-13299721:
Yesennia Sánchez-Pérez leads a large team surveying airborne particles as a possible driver of stomach cancer, in a 2026 survey. Chronic inflammation sits at the centre of this cancer, and epidemiology ever more links particle exposure to higher incidence and deaths. How particles reach and linger in the stomach remains poorly understood, so pathways receive close focus.

Particle size, chemistry, and surface reactivity shape biological activity. Studies across tissues show particles switching on several inflammatory pathways, although stomach-specific evidence is thin. The authors propose particles may amplify bacteria-driven inflammation into a persistent tumour-friendly setting, positioning exposure as a plausible and modifiable risk factor worth direct study.
pmc-13299821:
Ant communities inside farm-country forest fragments answer to the landscape around them, not just the fragment itself, find Helivelton H M Araújo and colleagues in a 2026 field study from Brazil's Cerrado. Using baited traps, they sampled ground-dwelling and tree-dwelling ants across fragments and compared richness and composition with fragment structure.

Community makeup shifted significantly under the study conditions, and the signal pointed beyond fragment-level traits to the surrounding agricultural matrix. Because ants carry out many ecological jobs, from seed dispersal to predation, altered communities imply altered ecosystem processes. The authors endorse ants as cheap, fast bioindicators for judging fragment quality in converted landscapes.
pmc-13300621:
P Ollitrault and co-authors report primary results from the VAMPIRE registry on leadless pacemaker implantation through the neck's internal jugular vein, published in 2026. The route promises easier early movement and possible same-day discharge compared with the usual leg vein approach, yet clinical data are scarce. The prospective multicenter registry enrolled consecutive patients planned for this access, treated by operators experienced in the femoral route but new to the neck route.

Of 193 patients enrolled from May 2024 to November 2025, the approach was attempted in 176, with success in ninety-eight percent. Failures came from vein clotting or a sheath that would not advance. Minor bleeding and bruising each affected about two percent and settled on their own. Sixty-four eligible patients went home the same day with no complications or readmissions within a month. The authors see a feasible first-line option taking shape.
pmc-13301921:
Predicting which proteins a fungus ships out in tiny vesicles can be done from sequence alone, João Neves-da-Rocha and colleagues show in a 2026 computational study of Mucor circinelloides. The fungus matters twice over: it causes dangerous mucormycosis in vulnerable patients and yields useful enzymes for industry. The team first catalogued its full secreted protein set in silico.

A random forest trained on trusted vesicle datasets from other organisms then sorted the fungal proteins for vesicle cargo. The predicted vesicle proteome echoed patterns seen in human vesicles, suggesting the model reads real sorting signals. Carbohydrate-cutting enzymes featured richly in the secretome, feeding both the virulence and the biotechnology sides of the story.
pmc-13302021:
Friendly fungi can guard picked tomatoes against rot, Lobna Hajji-Hedfi and colleagues show in a 2026 biocontrol study. Local strains of three Trichoderma species faced two rot fungi, Alternaria alternata and Curvularia spicifera, in dishes and on fruit. The team also checked growth-boosting traits and the chemistry of treated fruit.

Two species led the pack, shrinking Alternaria sores on fruit by roughly half and Curvularia sores by similar margins. Both made the plant hormone IAA and freed phosphate from soil compounds, though none fixed nitrogen. Treated seedlings grew better and fruit stayed firmer with less cell damage, making the case for living storage guards.
pmc-13304021:
Ke Xie and co-authors compare soil microbes under tree plantations on the Yellow River floodplain in western Shandong, China, in a 2026 field study. Planted forests aid land recovery there, yet what shapes their underground microbe communities is unclear.

Four stand types mixed or grew alone two tree species, poplar, willow, and black locust. Gene sequencing mapped bacteria and fungi alongside soil chemistry. Mixed poplar and locust soil held the richest bacteria, while mixed willow and poplar soil held the richest fungi. Soil carbon, nitrogen, acidity, and moisture best explained community shifts between stands.
pmc-13304421:
Qing Li and co-authors test rare earth additions to marine steel in a 2026 corrosion study. Low-alloy steel dominates sea engineering, yet salt air eats it fast, shortening service life and risking major failures.

Steels with varied lanthanum and cerium doses were melted, rolled, and put through lab cycles mimicking tropical sea air. Electric tests and rust analysis tracked the damage. Both additions improved even corrosion resistance, and the richest mix cut corrosion current by roughly one third. The rust layer grew denser and more stable, with fewer cracks and pores to let attack continue.
pmc-13305521:
Cátia Moreira de Carvalho leads a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of programs that fight false information to curb violent extremism. False stories now spread faster and wider, feeding division and possibly easing paths into radical groups.

The planned review will gather programs that reduce or counter exposure to misleading, false, or harmful information and measure effects on extremist attitudes and behavior. Studies of many designs and settings will be combined, gaps mapped, and strong practices extracted. Results aim to give policy makers, teachers, and practitioners workable steps against harmful narratives.
pmc-13305921:
Amelia-Naomi Sabo and co-authors model how hydroxyurea moves through the body in sickle cell disease in a 2026 analysis of trial data. Plasma samples came from 22 patients, mostly children, taking a daily oral dose. Response to the drug varies widely between patients, and the team looked for traits that explain that spread.

Two absorption patterns emerged: rapid absorbers reached higher peak levels than slow absorbers, although total exposure was similar. The absorption pattern explained about half of the variation in absorption rate between patients. Rapid absorbers also showed stronger gains in red cell size and fetal haemoglobin trends, without added toxicity signals. The authors propose adding absorption pattern to dosing algorithms so treatment can be tuned earlier for each patient.
pmc-13306021:
Silvana Alfei and co-authors test charged phosphonium salts against drug-proof staphylococci in a 2026 lab study. One compound, a benzyl triphenyl phosphonium bromide, worked at low doses against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and related skin species. The team checked particle size, killing speed, and biofilm blocking.

That compound killed drug-proof staphylococci within eleven hours, with no regrowth over the next day. It also blocked biofilm growth fully in the strongest biofilm-making samples tested. It did nothing against Gram-negative drug-proof samples, which limits its range. Harm to mouse fibroblasts and human skin cells stayed low at working doses. The authors propose the salt as an option for infections that current drugs can no longer treat, pending animal studies.
pmc-13307621:
Dimitrios Kouroupis and co-authors review in 2026 tiny parcels called exosomes that stem cells release, and their promise for easing pain from worn joints. Knee osteoarthritis touches about 500 million people worldwide, and pain plus stiffness drive much of the burden for those who live with it.

Joint fat and lining tissue feed swelling and send pain signals through agents such as substance P and CGRP. Exosomes can carry calming signals into that setting without placing live cells in the joint. The review weighs how such parcels might quiet nerve driven swelling and protect joint balance, while noting that dose, targeting, and proof in patients still need much more work.
pmc-13307921:
Linglin Wang and colleagues scan enterovirus B genomes in silico in 2026 to flag the mutations most likely to matter before they spread. Four representative serotypes, including coxsackieviruses and echoviruses, were mutated exhaustively in computer models of their shell proteins. Stability, receptor binding, and fitness effects were combined into one risk view.
