The ends of the VP1 protein and a surface loop of VP2 carried the highest variation risk. High-risk changes found in the scan had also played notable roles in the virus's natural history, which supports the approach. Deep mutational data from one serotype trained a fitness model that transferred to relatives. No drug or vaccine exists for these viruses, which burden children with meningitis, heart inflammation, and hand, foot, and mouth disease. The authors offer their framework for surveillance teams watching viral evolution.
pmc-13308321:
Altynshash Rakhat and Gulzhanat Aimagambetova pool in 2026 studies of self taken urine and vaginal samples for high risk HPV, a cause of cervical cancer. Their search covered four databases for work from 2015 to 2025 and drew 22 studies with more than 9000 people in total.

Vaginal self samples caught 91.3 percent of true cases and cleared 86.9 percent of true non cases in the pooled figures. Urine samples scored lower on both counts, yet they stay a kind option for women who skip clinic checks. DNA based tests beat RNA based ones, and warm storage hurt urine results. Self sampling could widen screening where clinic access is thin.
pmc-13308721:
Huiyun Fan and co-authors measure in 2026 calprotectin, a swelling linked protein, in people with HIV at two stages and in healthy controls in Chengdu. Groups held 15 patients with AIDS, 15 with silent infection, and 10 controls, with blood, stool, and gut lining samples from each.

Blood and stool levels ran high in both infected groups and peaked in the AIDS group in this small set. Gut lining scores rose with the protein signal, and both tracked against falling CD4 counts in mirror form. Blood and stool tests thus offer a needle free way to gauge gut swelling and immune wear, which could steer daily care for patients.
pmc-13310421:
Tian-Ming Fu and a large imaging team present in 2026 a single microscope built to watch biology from single molecules up to whole living animals. Their device, called MOSAIC, merges light-sheet, label-free, super-resolution, and multiphoton imaging behind adaptive optics that correct sample warping. Older scopes usually excel at one scale and fail at others.

The system images subcellular motion inside grown cells and living creatures without cutting prep. It maps molecule-level layout at nano scale across wide, stretched tissue samples. Neural structure and signals can also be caught inside live mice. Because one sample can move between modes, matched studies across scales become workable in a single session. The authors offer the platform as shared kit for broad life-science work rather than a single-purpose tool.
pmc-13310621:
Jitendra Singh, Thomas D Grant, and Andrew M Gulick solve the structure in 2026 of OaaC, a stand-alone enzyme from gut bacteria. It builds fatty acid amides, signalling molecules that act on host receptors. Unlike textbook assembly-line enzymes, OaaC works alone rather than as part of a giant multi-domain protein. Scattering, crystallography, and mass measurements probed its shape and behaviour.

OaaC forms an unusual two-copy complex whose joined shape blocks the surface where carrier proteins normally dock. The paired form stayed stable without substrates and ignored free fatty acids and free amines. Loaded carrier protein, however, selectively broke the pair apart into an active complex. Test-tube reactions confirmed the enzyme makes fatty acid amides from varied chain lengths. Gene family analysis placed these enzymes in their own branch with a distinctive active-site motif. Regulation by pairing and splitting, the authors propose, controls gut chemical signalling.
pmc-13310721:
Yujie Guan and colleagues map links between looks based worry and mental health in teens with curved spines in a 2026 study. Young people with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis often feel anxious about appearance and fear harsh judgment. Past work looked at single traits, not how traits connect as a web.

The group surveyed 349 patients aged 10 to 18 years at a hospital in northeast China. Worry about lacking good looks sat at the center of the web. Control of feelings acted as the main bridge between risk traits and helpful traits like support and strength. Guiding care toward looks worry and feeling control may help most.
pmc-13311021:
Qian Yang and colleagues study sleep quality among troops posted at high altitude in a 2026 survey. Thin air and long stays disturb sleep, which can hurt health and duty fitness. Added oxygen and trips down to low land may help or harm, so their joint roles were tested.

A poll covered 1,316 troops in high regions with a standard sleep score. Longer total stays and more frequent returns to low land linked to worse sleep scores. More frequent and longer oxygen use linked to better scores. The worst pattern paired long stays with short oxygen sessions and frequent returns. Steady oxygen plans may guard sleep best.
pmc-13311321:
Yuriko Kiriya and co-authors offer a 2026 case of heart sac removal aided by a microwave device in IgG4-related constrictive pericarditis. The stiff, scarred sac squeezed the heart, and dense sticking made surgery risky.

The patient was a 79-year-old man with repeat heart failure from the condition. Surgeons worked off the heart pump and used the Acrosurg microwave tool to cut the sac widely while sparing the phrenic nerves. No heat injury, rhythm trouble, or nerve palsy followed. His heart output rose and vein pressure settled, with no return of disease and no steroids needed.
pmc-13311621:
Bettina Schwind and co-authors lay out a 2026 study protocol, GiveCare, on fair end-of-life care in Switzerland across gender and diversity lines. Palliative care is among the least equal areas of health care.

The project runs four linked parts. A national survey gauges how aware palliative staff are of gender and diversity issues. Close field study in two specialist wards follows patient and family journeys. Network analysis and event modeling in Zurich map how care paths tangle across settings. Findings feed teaching, policy, and practice, with knowledge shared throughout rather than only at the end.
pmc-13312021:
Venetia Koidou and co-authors describe, in a 2026 methods study, a lab test built to measure double-stranded RNA pesticides in soil and in lab preparations. These sprays use RNA interference to silence a chosen gene in a pest, but until now there was no standard way to track how much of them remains in the environment.

Working with a 297-base-pair RNA aimed at the Colorado potato beetle, the team tuned a reverse-transcription PCR assay. Enzyme treatment sharpened the test's specificity, while a chitosan coating lowered sensitivity yet helped the RNA persist longer in soil. Because the RNA sticks fast to soil particles, the method recovers both loose and bound fractions, and matched calibration let them measure it in three soils of differing acidity. The workflow gives regulators a way to monitor these new pesticides.
pmc-13312721:
Bahar Hassantabar and colleagues survey, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, how mothers in Tehran decide to stop breastfeeding entirely, what methods they use, and where they turn for support. Stopping altogether is a distinct step from adding complementary foods, and evidence on the decision process in lower-income settings has been thin.

An online survey run through 28 public health centers gathered 420 mothers of healthy children aged six months to under four years. Stopping was mostly the mother's own choice, reported by 86.4 percent of respondents, and over half finished between 18 and 24 months. Traditional discouragement practices were common: 41.2 percent used bitter or sticky substances on the breast, and 32.9 percent used medicines without prescription, while only about a third consulted professional sources. The authors organize the influences through a social ecological lens.
pmc-13312921:
Jonathan Tersigni, Edward B James, and Aaron W Reinke describe the first year of Worms About Town in a 2026 report. The citizen science project hunts microsporidian parasites of wild nematodes around Toronto. Microsporidia are fungal parasites of many animals. The laboratory worm C. elegans offers a model host. Yet almost nothing was known about how geography, season, or substrate shape natural infections. Volunteers collected samples from plant material across the city during 2024.

Of 127 samples, 60 contained wild nematodes and four carried the parasites. Two finds were Nematocida homosporus, a known generalist. The other two belonged to undescribed species in genera distantly related to human-infecting microsporidia. The survey also turned up C. elegans itself, never before reported wild in Ontario. One parasite isolate could infect a laboratory strain. The authors present the network as a repeatable framework for studying this host and parasite system.
pmc-13313021:
Ziyi Wang and colleagues compare, in a 2026 prospective observational study, long versus standard courses of dual antiplatelet therapy after coronary stenting in patients whose blood still shows high inflammatory risk. A C-reactive protein level of 2 milligrams per liter or more marks this group as prone to further ischemic events, yet the best length of blood-thinning treatment for them was unsettled.

At Fuwai Hospital, 2,440 patients, 69.5 percent of the cohort, stayed on dual therapy past twelve months. Three years out, their combined rate of death, heart attack, stent thrombosis, and stroke was 1.5 percent against 4.2 percent for the conventional group in the reported analysis, with net adverse events also lower. Serious bleeding did not differ significantly between the strategies. The authors conclude that, in inflamed high-risk patients, longer therapy buys protection without a bleeding penalty.
pmc-13314321:
Amal M. El-Feky and colleagues profile, in a 2026 study, the leaf chemistry of Schefflera arboricola and test its extract against Cryptosporidium parvum, a zoonotic gut parasite with few good treatments. Lab tests catalogued the leaves' pigments, sugars, and protective compounds. Fifty mice in five groups tested the extract in living infection: untreated infected controls, low and high extract doses, a standard drug group, and uninfected controls.

The chemistry proved rich, with 51 compounds identified, dominated by thirty flavonoids alongside fourteen acids. Both extract doses significantly cut parasite egg shedding compared with untreated infection. Treated mice also showed gentler intestinal damage, less DNA damage in tissue, and improved liver and lipid blood markers. The authors present the leaf extract as a genuinely promising natural candidate against this gut infection, notable because the parasite, tissue, and blood evidence all point the same way.
pmc-13314521:
Jiuli Zhao and colleagues test how heart rate skews heart function readings in small animals in their 2026 study. Ultrasound checks under anesthesia drive most rodent heart research, yet the rate itself can shift the numbers, blurring comparisons between healthy and failing hearts.

The team made heart failure in rats by tying a heart artery. The model group held 11 rats and the control group held 11 too, as counted in the report, and both were checked at days 7 and 28. Mice got a two-hit model of failure with kept ejection fraction, using a nitric oxide blocker plus a high-fat diet. By varying anesthesia depth, they set different heart rates and read function at each load. The aim was to name safe rate windows for fair measures, so labs can trust their ultrasound data.
pmc-13316221:
Yuan Yuan and colleagues, in 2026, compare how six industrial strains of Escherichia coli regulate their genes. These bacteria are workhorses for protein production and chemical synthesis, yet strains perform very differently for reasons that genome notes alone cannot predict. Regulatory networks, which control movement, stress responses and metabolism, may explain much of that gap.

The group assembled 433 matched RNA sequencing profiles for BL21, C, Crooks, MG1655, W and W3110 grown under similar conditions. An iModulon analysis, which groups genes that vary together, showed that core programmes with similar jobs are wired differently in each strain. Strains also switched those programmes on in distinct ways under the same challenges, giving engineers a clearer basis for choosing and tuning a host.
pmc-13316621:
Olyad Erba Urgessa and colleagues mined, in a 2026 computer study, bacterial genomes from horse feces for phytase enzymes that could free locked-up phosphorus in animal feed. Phytic acid in grain blocks nutrition for chickens, pigs, and fish, and better enzymes would cut waste.

Screening 162 genomes yielded 69 distinct candidate enzymes in two families, spread across familiar gut bacteria. Scoring of predicted traits picked a few standouts, and shape modeling plus docking tests ranked how tightly each grips phytic acid. One candidate bound most strongly. Safety screens flagged possible risk factors in some sources, so the authors warn that lab and animal tests must come before any feed use.
pmc-13318821:
Yue Sun and co-authors report a 2026 cross-sectional study of meaning, emptiness, and depression in Chinese teenagers. Students at one senior high school completed standard questionnaires in May 2022. Scales measured depression, presence and search for meaning, and feelings of emptiness. The authors tested how these inner states connect.

In total, 2,230 students were included in the analysis. Depression was classified in 726 students, or 32.6 percent of the sample. Depressed students reported more emptiness and less felt meaning. Correlation between depression and presence of meaning reached r = −0.46 in their data. Emptiness and low presence of meaning each predicted depression status. Searching for meaning did not predict it. A combined model reached an AUC of 0.74 for screening.
pmc-13318921:
Angela Clemens and co-authors report a 2026 methods study on monitoring transplanted hearts in mice. Feeling the graft beat by hand is the usual check, but it says little about immune attack strength. Results also vary between operators. The team tested ultrasound imaging against palpation.

Mismatched donor hearts were transplanted into recipient abdomens. Ultrasound judged rejection more accurately than hand palpation. Motion-mode changes also matched the size of the anti-donor T cell response. Immune tests timed by imaging gave cleaner readouts than fixed time points. The authors argue imaging should replace touch for rejection calls. That change would improve reproducibility and the value of this widely used model.
pmc-13319721:
Jie Yu and co-authors build tiny copper based capsules for cancer immune care in a 2026 study of tumors that hide from the immune system. Many tumors block immune attack by keeping warning signals weak. Their capsules aim to start a chain where copper stress inside tumor cells spills cell DNA, which then trips a strong alarm path in the cell.

The capsules free their load in the sour fluid around tumors, and a second metal in the mix boosts the alarm signal while also lighting up scans so dosing can be timed. A drug that blocks a growth path is packed in to stop tumors from dodging the stress. In a mouse tumor model the chain woke immune cells, shrank tumors, and slowed spread.
pmc-13320021:
Jack H Ratliff and co-authors study a fat handling protein in lung immune cells in a 2026 mouse study tied to chronic lung disease. Lung guard cells must eat dead cells and calm swelling for lungs to heal, and in this disease that clean up falters. Past gene work flagged the protein as low in patients, so mice lacking it were tested after germ or sterile lung insults.

Guard cells without the protein ate far fewer dead cells and took in and burned less fat for fuel. Their power houses slowed, waste products piled up, and gene access shifted toward stress pathways. Without the protein the cells never switched into repair mode. Raising its levels may help lungs settle after swelling.
pmc-13320421:
Mina Owrang reviews gut microbe products and immune balance in a 2026 narrative review covering live germs, dead germ brews, and paired mixes. The gut microbe crowd talks to the immune system in ways that shape health and disease far past the gut. Many gains once tied to live helpful germs in fact flow from the compounds those germs make. That fact has swung focus toward their brews and toward mixes that pair germs with their food.

Proof for live germ effects on immunity runs deep, while proof for brews and mixes stays thinner and still grows. How each class calms or wakes immune arms, and where they may beat live germs on safety or shelf life, is mapped from the past literature. Sharper trials could turn these tools into real care options.
pmc-13320521:
Pu Liang and co-authors reflect on the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in a 2026 perspective. The prize went jointly to Mary E. Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell, and Shimon Sakaguchi for work on how the immune system tolerates the body's own tissues. Their findings centred on regulatory T cells, a group that calms immune attacks.

Older teaching stressed a central check in the thymus that removes self-reactive cells early in life. The laureates showed a second, outer system also matters, since some risky cells escape the first check. Regulatory T cells police those cells in the tissues and help explain why severe self-attack is rare. The piece traces how that view of tolerance grew.
pmc-13322221:
Monika S Patil and colleagues test, in 2026, whether variants in inflammation genes track with type 2 diabetes in a rural population in southwestern Maharashtra, India. Diabetes involves chronic inflammation that damages insulin response and insulin-producing cells. Local genetic data for candidate cytokine variants were limited.

The hospital study matched 260 diabetes patients with 260 healthy controls of similar age and sex. Four variants across three inflammation-related genes were typed from blood samples. Distributions differed significantly between groups for all variants. One interleukin-4 variant was linked to higher risk after adjustment, while one interleukin-18 variant appeared protective. The strongest signals came from a tumour necrosis factor receptor variant, where both mixed and variant genotypes carried several-fold higher odds. The authors present regional risk markers for further study.
pmc-13322921:
Vahid Akbari and a large team build a blood immune encyclopedia called HuBIE, reported in 2026, covering T-cell and B-cell receptors in infection and cancer. The resource holds repertoire data from 2,614 samples taken from 1,941 participants, including bloodstream infections, several cancers and controls, with repeat samples for many people.

Using a Roche targeted sequencing platform, the team read heavy chains for T-cell receptors and antibodies in all participants at once. Analyses cover repertoire diversity, gene use, chain shares and CDR3 features. Small cohorts, narrow diversity and uneven lab methods have held this field back, and the authors offer HuBIE as a shared base for diagnostic, prognostic and treatment work.
pmc-13323821:
Jin Young Hong and co-authors review devil's claw for musculoskeletal pain against standard anti-inflammatory drugs, in a 2026 structured narrative review. The plant Harpagophytum procumbens is a traditional remedy whose use grows as long-term NSAID harms to gut, heart and kidneys limit care.

Lab work suggests its key compound harpagoside can damp inflammatory paths such as COX-2, NF-kB, cytokines and oxidative signals, though that proof is indirect. Clinical studies, mostly in osteoarthritis and low back pain, hint at symptom relief for some patients, yet trials are small, formulas and doses vary and follow-up is short. The authors judge NSAIDs still far better proven, with devil's claw generally well tolerated.
pmc-13324221:
Anas M Barabrah and co-authors pool 218 cases of heart chamber clots in Behcet's disease, in a 2026 systematic review of case reports and cohort studies to December 2024. This rare autoimmune disease can clot inside the heart, with high illness and death risk.

Cases clustered in young men from historic Silk Road regions, and the clot was the first sign of Behcet's in over half the cases in their count. Fever, breathlessness and coughing blood were common, and the right heart chambers were hit most. Steroids, immune suppressants and anticoagulants formed the main treatment, with full resolution in about two thirds of treated cases. Surgery carried high recurrence and death rates, so the authors favour medical care first.
pmc-13324321:
Lanzhuang Chen, Liming Guan, and Taiji Adachi hunted for the gene behind apomixis in guineagrass, a trait that could transform plant breeding. Their 2026 study explains the prize: apomixis passes only the mother's genes to the next generation, so fixing hybrid vigor in seed could slash seed production costs. The team aimed to isolate the aposporous apomixis gene and trace how it is expressed in aposporous guineagrass.

They devised a new staging method using ovary length to sample ovaries and buds at matching developmental stages in sexual plants and apomicts. From a cDNA library built at the stage when aposporous initial cells appear, differential screening yielded four stage-specific clones, 577 to 1,182 base pairs long, matching the apomixis-specific gene ASG-1. Signals appeared in initial cells, derived embryo sacs, root tips, and shoot meristems, marking a first step toward isolating an apospory gene.
pmc-13325321:
Yaqi Zhu and colleagues report four beef tapeworm cases in Hunan Province in a 2026 case report. Taenia saginata spreads through raw or undercooked beef, and Hunan is not a usual hotspot for the parasite.

Cases surfaced in 2023 and 2025, and worm segment checks plus PCR sequencing confirmed the species. Every patient had eaten raw or undercooked beef at mid-to-high-end restaurants, and some were healthcare workers. Cases clustered within households, hinting at shared meals as the source. The authors urge stronger food safety teaching, tighter meat inspection, and clear public warnings about raw beef dishes, even in regions where the worm is rare.
pmc-13325421:
Tomislav Bracanović argues that parts of AI ethics overreact to new technology for evolved mental reasons in a 2026 essay. The field has grown fast, and many papers treat broad AI trends as urgent moral threats.

Three habits from Stone Age psychology anchor his case: seeing agency where none exists, moralizing charged scenes too fast, and spreading moral alarms widely. Fresh technology, moral shock value, and career rewards for finding new problems all feed those habits. Even training in ethics shields experts only weakly from such bias. The essay builds a framework of testable claims about why some worries swell beyond the real risk of present systems.
pmc-13327021:
Soon Kyu Lee and co-authors present a 2026 case report about a liver lump that looked like cancer on scans. A 74-year-old man with metabolic and alcohol-related liver disease had a 5.3 cm nodule found on ultrasound. Blood tumor markers were normal, yet scan features met top-level criteria for liver cancer.

Surgeons removed the left half of the liver, both to treat the lesion and to learn what it was. Under the microscope the growth held spindle-shaped cells, and staining for c-KIT and CD34 showed it was a gastrointestinal stromal tumor starting in the liver, not liver cancer. He then took imatinib and stayed free of recurrence, a reminder that look-alike lesions need tissue proof.
pmc-13327321:
Angelo Bartsch-Jiménez and team used mild ear pulses to probe brainstem paths after one-sided stroke weakness. Their 2026 study set fourteen right-weakness stroke survivors against fourteen age-matched controls. It tracked muscle links in neck and arm muscles at rest and during a reach-like move, with shoulders flat or raised, under no pulses, fake pulses, or real pulses.

Stroke survivors showed no rise in muscle links between arm or neck muscles with pulses. Links even fell with the raised shoulder, arguing against brainstem balance output as the main driver of faulty teamwork during willed moves. Neck muscle links on the strong side fell during pulses at rest, hinting at shifts in same-side brainstem balance output. The team flags unexplored opposite-side brainstem-spine paths and muted same-side links for rehab plans.
pmc-13327521:
Eusebi Chiner and team looked for early small-airway trouble in smokers with normal lung tests. Their 2026 snapshot study took in ninety current smokers with kept lung function, set as pre-inhaler FEV1/FVC at or above 0.70. A single-breath nitrogen washout caught uneven airflow. Smoke-linked small-airway trouble may come before lung test blockage shows. No healthy control group was signed up at the same time, so results were set against published reference values.

Washout scores rose step by step with smoking load. Closing volume ratios rose with pack-years. In men aged 30 to 70, the phase III slope averaged 327.1% of predicted, with 83.3% topping the proposed upper limit of 180% predicted. Male sex stayed tied to higher slope values alone after change for pack-years, age, and body mass index. The team backs washout testing as a keen early spotter of outer airway trouble, with sex-aware reading.
pmc-13327821:
Eunsun Lee and team reviewed the first year of South Korea's National Center for Injury Prevention and Control. Their 2026 study traced injury care rule growth, reading rule papers, law frames, national injury data, and writings on shifts since the 2000s. Injury rules started split up, but growing watch and standard stats since the 2010s built the base for joined-up work.

The Act on the Prevention and Management of Injuries, passed in 2024 and in force in 2025, set the law base for a joined-up national system. It set up the National Injury Management Committee and the Center itself. In 2025, steps forward were naming the trusted body to run the Center and sealing the First Comprehensive Injury Management Plan for 2026 to 2030. The team calls the Center's first year a shift from rule shaping to system running, spanning watch, stats, rule backing, staff growth, public messages, and multi-sector teamwork.
pmc-13327921:
Lei Zhang and co-authors tune a seaweed gel dressing so its calcium speeds wound repair in a 2026 study. Alginate gels form when calcium links their chains, and the same calcium can steer cell behavior. Gels were made with calcium chloride at 20, 50, 100, and 200 mM and tested for strength, calcium release, and cell response.

The 100 mM recipe balanced firmness with bioactivity best, driving fibroblasts to multiply, move, and lay down matrix in dishes. On full-thickness skin wounds in rats, that gel sped closure and tissue regrowth, and gene profiling showed calcium signaling switched on in fibroblasts. Dose of the cross-linking ion, not just the gel itself, is the design lever.
pmc-13328021:
Yanhui Wang and co-authors sort children with appendicitis into inflammation types in a 2026 cohort study. Single blood markers miss how varied the body's response can be, so the team applied latent class analysis to nine indicators in 402 children who had keyhole appendix removal. Learning models then forecast complications after surgery.

Three types appeared: low inflammation at 29.4 percent, moderate at 40.8 percent, and high at 29.9 percent of the group, differing in markers, perforation, stay length, and complications, which hit 17.4 percent overall. Perforation alone independently predicted trouble, with an odds ratio of 3.03 in their model, while the XGBoost model forecast complications with an AUC of 0.911 on held-back cases. Phenotype plus algorithm could guide watch intensity.
pmc-13330521:
Lee Wha Gwon and a large team improve twin prime editing for large genome changes in a 2026 study. Twin editing uses two editor complexes with matching guide RNAs to write bigger changes. The team reworked the editor by adding a La domain and tuned the guides, then tested the system in human-derived cell lines.

Editing efficiency rose by a fold gain of 1.75 in the reported results, without more stray cuts or faulty edits. The system placed a green marker gene of about 2.8 kb at target sites. It also removed the expanded repeat tract in the ATXN3 gene in a cell model of spinocerebellar ataxia type 3. Simpler guide design may widen use in research and therapy.
pmc-13331221:
Ismail Aslam, Masood Sadiq, and Asma Aslam review artificial intelligence in brain tumour diagnosis and surgery planning in a 2026 article. Searches of two databases covered peer-reviewed English work from 2015 to 2025 on learning systems, image traits, and planning tools for neurosurgery.

Learning systems have sharpened tumour spotting, sorting, and outlining on scans, the review finds. Image trait methods can guess molecular type without tissue sampling. Planning uses span brain shift models, fibre maps, live tissue checks, and smart navigation. Hurdles include scarce data, opaque logic, mixed datasets, and approval and setup needs. Firm prospective proof must come before safe wide use, the authors conclude.
pmc-13331421:
Shahad Al Jebeli and colleagues review clot removal for stroke in pregnancy in a 2026 article. Pregnancy raises stroke risk through heart, vessel, and clotting shifts, yet treatment proof is thin. Searches of four databases to May 2024 followed standard review rules, taking any study design that reported such cases.

From 785 first records, 16 studies with 26 cases in total met the rules in the reported flow. Mean mother age was 32.6 years in the pooled cases. Strokes split most between the first and third thirds of pregnancy. Techniques mixed stent retrievers and suction, alone or with clot drugs. Mother function, vessel reopening, harms, and baby outcomes were charted for each case.
pmc-13332621:
Elnaz Ghajar-Rahimi and colleagues refine a 2026 mouse model for studying heart recovery after aortic narrowing is released. Models that narrow the transverse aorta and later remove the band are standard for recovery research. Yet the standard version needs two separate chest operations in a row, raising surgical risk and variability. The team built a reproducible change to the procedure that allows timed, minimally invasive band removal after a single initial operation.

Eight-week-old male mice were anesthetized, intubated, and given a left chest opening to expose the transverse aorta, under animal-care rules from the University of Montpellier and European guidance. A fine suture was placed beneath the vessel as part of the modified setup. The model lets researchers control when the heart is unloaded and then track recovery with less surgical noise. It should make recovery studies more consistent and less burdensome for the animals used.
pmc-13333221:
Li Chen and colleagues comment in 2026 on a study testing multimodal large language models in neuroradiology. The study under discussion, by Suh and colleagues, used 401 neuroradiology and head-and-neck quiz cases from RadioGraphics. It judged not only diagnostic accuracy but lesion localization, imaging findings, hallucinations, and overall acceptability. Chen and colleagues commend that broader framework as more clinically meaningful than simple answer matching alone.

They raise several points to contextualize the findings, starting with training data independence. The claim that RadioGraphics cases ensure independence from model training data may need more cautious phrasing. Source figures and text could overlap with training material in ways the study cannot fully exclude. The comment helps readers weigh AI neuroradiology results with proper skepticism about benchmarks, leakage, and what accuracy on quiz cases really proves.
pmc-13334121:
Wafaa A Mohamed and co-authors gauged the accuracy of custom-made titanium plates for repositioning the upper jaw in a 2026 surgery study. Computer planning promises precise orthognathic surgery, but the plan must survive transfer into the operating room.

Ten patients had digital simulation, and their cutting guides and customized plates were designed and built by computer, replacing the classic splint. After surgery, the team overlaid actual jaw positions on the virtual plan and took shifts in three directions plus rotations. No landmark differed by much between plan and outcome across the sagittal, coronal, and axial planes. The largest wobble showed at the posterior nasal spine in the axial plane, at 1.7 mm of deviation. The results support splint-free, plate-guided jaw surgery.
pmc-13336021:
Jianhua Wang and co-authors foretold a giant light-to-current effect in atom-thin ferroelectric metals in a 2026 computing physics study. Materials that are simultaneously ferroelectric and metallic are rare, and their switchable polarity could control electron topology.

First-principles math and symmetry analysis picked three candidate monolayers, the XO family with X as niobium, tantalum, or rhodium, each with notable out-of-plane polarization and only modest switching barriers. Rhodium oxide's polarization of 5.68 picocoulombs per meter exceeds most known two-dimensional ferroelectric metals. The layers also host protected Weyl points and edge states, making them topological semimetals. Their broken symmetry and topology yield a large bulk photovoltaic effect, which doping and strain can enlarge further, pointing to solar and sensing uses.
pmc-13336421:
Oscar O'Dwyer Lancaster-Jones and co-authors set quality benchmarks for blood vessel tissue assembled by sound in a 2026 tissue study. Acoustic handling can pattern cells without touching them, but nobody had defined how good the patterning must be for complex tissues to form.

The team made sound-patterned 3D vascular tissues and followed them for seven days. The tissues built their own vessel networks, secreted their own matrix, and shifted angiogenic gene activity in response to the acoustic patterning. Most tellingly, the quality of cell alignment tracked positively with the vascular structure that followed, so pattern quality predicts tissue growth. The method gives bioengineers measurable requirements, spanning biological and physical parameters, before acoustic assembly can be trusted for medical use.
pmc-13336721:
Joeri Bordes and colleagues tested in 2026 whether blocking the stress protein FKBP51 can prevent lasting harm from early life adversity. Such adversity raises risk for psychiatric illness, yet preventive treatments are scarce because the biology is unclear. FKBP51 tunes the stress hormone receptor and is a key driver of stress vulnerability.

Male mice exposed to early adversity showed lasting social problems, including subordinate behaviour in youth and adulthood. Early treatment with the selective blocker SAFit2 fully reversed those social deficits. Gene activity across six stress related brain regions also returned toward normal, most clearly in the prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens. The work points to a possible early window for preventing stress related illness.
pmc-13337821:
Gaiyan Du, Ping Zhang, and Qiaojun Liu sort pregnant women with hepatitis B by knowledge patterns in a 2026 study. Passing the virus to the baby remains a worry despite good prevention tools. Education helps, but treating all women as alike can hide groups with stubborn false beliefs.

Survey data from 203 women in Taiyuan from 2020 to 2022 were reanalyzed with latent class methods. Two groups appeared: a large low-error group and a smaller group at 9.8 percent that knew true spread routes yet also believed casual myths such as spread through food in the reported profile. That smaller group was younger and needs targeted teaching.
pmc-13338821:
Ferhat Bozkurt and colleagues review fifteen years of skin squamous cell cancer cases in a 2026 single-center study. This common skin cancer can return or spread, and reliable warning signs guide follow-up intensity. Records covered surgically treated primary lesions from 2008 to 2022.

A total of 428 lesions entered the analysis, with average patient age 71.5 years as reported. Local return occurred in 4.5 percent of cases, spread to nodes in 4.7 percent, and distant spread in 1.9 percent in the reported counts. Larger tumors, especially above 3 cm, returned and spread more often. Poor cell grading also raised risk, supporting closer watch for big, poorly graded tumors.
pmc-13339621:
Tyler W. Hines and colleagues squeeze a terbium crystal to force a rare oxidation state in a 2026 study. Terbium normally sits at +3, and +4 chemistry is sparse. Crystals of a cesium terbium chromate were pressed in a diamond cell to gigapascal levels.

Color shifted from yellow toward dark red and black under pressure as reported. X-ray absorption spectra gained a second edge feature near 7528 eV starting at 19.62 GPa in the reported measurements, the signature of Tb4+. Diffraction, Raman, and light spectra tracked the change. Pressure thus opens a new route to tetravalent terbium chemistry.
pmc-13341421:
Liver involvement in Prader-Willi syndrome is examined through new lab models by Romar Guintu Dabban and colleagues in a 2026 review. The genetic disorder pairs extreme obesity with oddly mild insulin resistance and fewer liver complications than expected.

Faulty fat storage and burning in fat cells appear to shift lipid burden toward the liver, and blood profiling shows a distinct pattern of altered phospholipids. Fatty liver disease stays comparatively uncommon. The authors highlight stem-cell-derived liver-like cells and organoids as tools that carry patient-specific gene regulation, letting researchers connect molecular defects to whole-body metabolism in this rare condition.
pmc-13341521:
Immune checkpoint drugs appear usable in people with HIV and cancer, in a 2026 retrospective study by Xiaola Xue and colleagues. Ninety patients treated with PD-1 inhibitors between January 2022 and December 2024 were enrolled, including some with very low CD4 counts or detectable virus.

After matching, 56 patients were compared across HIV-positive and HIV-negative groups. Response and disease control rates were comparable, with the HIV-positive group at 16.2% response, and side effect profiles were tracked alongside survival. Data on this population have been scarce because trials often exclude them. Real-world evidence of this kind helps oncologists weigh treatment for a group long left out.
pmc-13341721:
Sleep protects rosacea patients from acne while sunscreen may aggravate it, in a 2026 cross-sectional study by Shiyu He and colleagues. Questionnaires on lifestyle, skincare, and diet covered 300 rosacea patients, and regression models hunted factors tied to also having acne.

Acne appeared in 30.33% of these patients versus 14.83% in the general population. Enough sleep lowered odds (OR 0.738), with a smooth dose-response as sleep lengthened. Sunscreen use raised odds notably (OR 2.602). The counterintuitive sunscreen signal may reflect product choice or skin sensitivity rather than sun protection itself, but it gives dermatologists a concrete habit to ask about.
pmc-13343221:
Rose-Marie Lindkvist, Anders Håkansson, and Lars Garpenhag study the ethics of routine violence risk screening in Swedish emergency psychiatry in 2026. Two units in Malmö introduced the V-RISK-10 screening tool, and the authors interviewed developers and staff about whether general screening feels ethically acceptable in daily care.

Six interviewees welcomed the tool's promise of uniform and fair judgments, yet worried about accuracy, how scores get read, and how results turn into risk management steps. Acceptability, they found, rests on balancing personal and shared interests. Screening can fit staff values, the authors conclude, if knowledge spreads well and clear rules govern how scores are used.
pmc-13345321:
Khaled Abu Baker and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare bloodstream infection in a 54-year-old man with a normal immune system. He had a long-term arm catheter for treatment of bone infection, and first developed a resistant Klebsiella bloodstream infection, followed by a yeast infection linked to the same line.

The yeast, Cryptococcus laurentii, is usually viewed as harmless in people, and the patient had no diabetes, cancer, transplant, or immune-suppressing drugs, with a negative HIV test. He had tampered with his catheter and showered without protection. After blood cultures confirmed the yeast, the line was removed and targeted therapy began. The case warns that even low-risk yeasts can infect lines when catheter care breaks down.
pmc-13345821:
Tuba Eda Arpa Zemzemoğlu and co-authors tune a gentler juice process for broccoli in 2026, pairing heat with ultrasound. Standard pasteurization drains the drink's phenolics and antioxidants, so the team optimized thermosonication with response surface methods checked against two swarm algorithms.

Best settings landed at 40 degrees for 6.75 minutes at about 64 percent amplitude, holding strong agreement across all three optimization routes. Treated juice kept more phenolics, chlorophyll, and vitamin C than pasteurized juice, led by gallic acid and naringin. Simulated digestion then recovered 30.45 percent of phenolics from the treated juice against 26.22 percent for pasteurized, meaning more of the good compounds survive to be absorbed.
pmc-13349921:
Yafei Ge and Ting Gao reviewed the complement system in preeclampsia in 2026. They argue it helps explain why this pregnancy disorder takes such varied forms. Preeclampsia is a major cause of illness and death for mothers and babies worldwide.

Complement is part of the immune defence system. It must stay tightly controlled for a healthy placenta to form. The authors describe distinct patterns by subtype. One pathway dominates in early disease driven by placental failure. Another runs at a low level with metabolic disease. Faulty control defines a severe group that overlaps with vessel clotting disorders. Matching these patterns to subtypes could guide targeted care instead of one-size treatment.
pmc-13350021:
Joanna Konkol and fellow authors pooled research in a 2026 meta-analysis on poverty and death risk in people with diabetes. Nineteen studies reporting income, education, job, or area deprivation links to death were gathered from four databases through September 2025.

Low social and economic standing came with 67 percent higher odds of death from any cause, and the pattern held across each separate measure. Study results varied greatly, yet removing any single study barely moved the total. The finding underlines that diabetes outcomes depend on more than medicine: money, schooling, and housing shape who lives longest with the disease.
pmc-13350321:
Reto Engeli and colleagues studied babies who had heart surgery before six weeks of age in a 2026 Swiss registry analysis of 240 infants operated between 2020 and 2024. The question was how often a heart-lung machine, ECMO, was needed around surgery and what it meant for survival and development at one year.

Overall one-year mortality was 5.8 percent. ECMO supported 34 babies, whose mortality reached 29.4 percent against 1.9 percent for the rest. Development was scored with standard infant scales for thinking, language, and movement. The stark gap marks ECMO babies as a group needing close follow-up, even though the machine itself may reflect illness severity.
pmc-13353021:
Ragnhild Nicolaisen and others matched how nursing students in Lebanon and Norway perceived illness stopping in their training hospitals after COVID-19, ran the story-based study in 2026. The climate for illness control covers the shared views, habits, and support that shape whether precautions are followed on the ward. Social and institutional gaps might change how students experience that climate.

Semi-structured interviews with eight Lebanese and seven Norwegian students continued until no new themes emerged, and the transcripts were studied inductively over three months. Four themes captured the students' perceptions. The study helps educators see where training hospitals support safe practice and where students still feel exposed or unsure.
pmc-13353821:
Gabriela Fioranelli leads a 2026 scoping review of reporting gaps in the BREAST-Q outcome survey. The tested tool measures satisfaction and quality of life after breast surgery, but reporting habits vary worldwide. Five sources were searched from January 1, 2009 to September 16, 2022, and 307 of 6,921 records qualified.

Studies covered reconstruction after mastectomy plus cosmetic enlargement and reduction, grouped for contrast. Most-reported domains in both groups were satisfaction with breasts, at 91.21 percent and 96.36 percent, plus mental-social and sexual well-being. The weighted global mean score ran higher in cosmetic patients, at 81.99 versus 74.49 in the reconstruction group. Uneven domain use limits fair contrast across studies.
pmc-13353921:
Kakhramon Shomurodov led a 2026 full review of intraoral scanners for measuring soft tissues around dental implants in three sizes. Precise, repeatable tracking of gum shape matters for implant health, and digital scans promise more aim numbers than visual checks alone. The question was how accurate and dependable scanner tests actually are in medical studies.

Following PRISMA guidance and a registered plan, the reviewers searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, judging studies on truth, trust, repeat use, and useful use. The making shows where scanners perform well and where method or tissue movement still limits them. Implant doctors gain a realistic basis for adopting digital soft-tissue monitoring.
pmc-13355321:
Yongsheng Chen writes a 2026 commentary on a design idea for cheaper organic solar cells. Light, bendy solar films could be made cheaply with simple materials, but those materials twist into many shapes, which disorders them and weakens power output. Costly ring-fused materials avoid this but are hard to make at scale.

A study he discusses borrowed a lesson from protein folding: cut the number of shapes a molecule can take, a measure called conformational entropy. The tuned molecule settled into one flat shape, packed neatly, and hit a record efficiency near 19 percent for its class, at a far lower cost. Chen presents the measure as a guide for future solar materials.
pmc-13358621:
Eduardo de Souza M Fernandes and Orlando Jorge M Torres wrote a 2026 letter on a major trial of pancreas surgery. The trial, called MAPLE-PD, compared two ways to remove the head of the pancreas in patients with pancreatic cancer. One way starts at the gut's main artery and isolates the tumor early, aiming to stop cancer cells from spreading during surgery.

The trial found that this artery-first method did not improve survival. Fernandes and Torres weigh what the result means for a technique that many Japanese centers treat as standard. Their letter helps surgeons judge where the method still earns its place, such as checking artery involvement early.
pmc-13358821:
Xiao Sun and co-authors map how lung cancer spreads to chest lymph nodes in a 2026 study. Node spread decides how much tissue surgeons should clear. The team paid special attention to subsolid nodules, tumors that look partly hazy on scans and often act less aggressively than solid ones.

They reviewed 6,273 patients treated from 2014 to 2018 and charted spread by tumor site and stage. Spread followed the lung lobe in a regular pattern, more so in early lesions. In small hazy nodules with little solid core, spread was almost nil, under one percent. Such maps can help surgeons clear enough nodes without over-cutting low-risk patients.
pmc-13359521:
Russell J. Diefenbach and co-authors test a two-in-one blood test for cancer in a 2026 study. Tumors shed DNA into the blood, and reading it can reveal both gene mutations and chemical methylation tags that mark cancer. The Avida Duo assay reads both from one sample of this floating DNA. The team checked its performance in patients with advanced melanoma.

Using plasma from two separate patient groups, they tuned the workflow for steadier output and sharper mutation detection. Methylation results matched a rival established assay closely. A single sensitive test for both signal types could simplify how doctors detect cancer, track it, and pick treatment.
pmc-13359721:
Anh Duc Vu and co-authors review a versatile protein in a 2026 paper. RNF126 is an enzyme that tags other proteins with ubiquitin, a small label that can order a protein's destruction or change its job. Working with helper proteins, it clears misplaced and misfolded proteins, keeping the cell's protein stock healthy. It also helps repair damaged DNA through several partners.

Beyond housekeeping, the protein supports embryo growth and male fertility, and many cancers exploit it to grow faster. The review gathers these roles and the tumor-driving tricks the protein performs. Such a hub, with one clear working part, draws interest as a possible drug target.
pmc-13359921:
Zaher Merhi studies sugar-damaged proteins and ovarian insulin resistance in a 2026 paper. Women with polycystic ovary syndrome often show high levels of advanced glycation end products, compounds formed when sugar sticks to proteins. These build up in the ovaries and may disturb insulin signaling in the cells that nurse the egg. Merhi tested that idea in human cumulus granulosa cells from IVF patients.

Cells fed the glycated protein raised the gene for its receptor more than threefold and the gene for an insulin signaling protein, IRS-1, more than fourfold. The results support the theory that these compounds help drive ovarian insulin resistance in the syndrome.
pmc-13360021:
João Rocha-Gomes and co-authors review the economics of a harsh cancer group in a 2026 paper. Biliary tract cancers are uncommon, aggressive, and usually found late. New immune and targeted drugs have widened choices but raised costs. The team gathered the published economic evidence: studies of value for money, illness costs, and resource use.

Twenty studies qualified. Older chemotherapy plans looked better value in several settings, while most immune combinations and targeted drugs exceeded local value thresholds at current prices. Real-world care proved heavy on hospitals, above all in later treatment lines. Evidence on prevention and screening was thin, the review notes.
pmc-13361321:
Fuge Cai and co-authors mapped the genetics of rice grain clarity in a 2026 study. How clear a rice grain looks drives buyer preference and price, yet its genetic basis was poorly known. The team grew 450 rice varieties in two places and scored their grain transparency. A genome-wide scan tied the trait to spots across nearly all rice chromosomes.

Nineteen regions linked to clarity were found, and four showed up in both growing places. Two steady regions sat right at known grain shape genes, GS3 and GW5. For one new region, the team narrowed the search to a short DNA stretch and named candidate genes, including an F-box protein gene. Breeders can use these markers to select rice that looks better in the bag.
pmc-13361721:
Lattawat Eauchai and co-authors review vision-language models in medical diagnosis in a 2026 paper. These AI systems read both images and clinical text at once, much as a doctor does. The review asks whether this dual input truly improves diagnosis over single-input models. It also weighs how the tools perform alone versus as helpers to physicians.

Across studies, multimodal models beat models using only text or only images. Doctors assisted by such a system reached higher diagnostic accuracy than doctors without it. But proof for the models as standalone diagnosticians conflicts between studies. The authors advise building AI as a co-pilot that backs human judgment, easing fatigue and cutting mental load rather than replacing doctors.
pmc-13362521:
Charalampos Voros and a large team offer a 2026 review on the immune balance inside the ovarian follicle, the small sac where an egg matures. They focus on the PD-1 and PD-L1 pair, a brake system that keeps immune cells from attacking the body's own tissue. The authors argue this brake may shield the growing egg from swelling and immune stress during its development.

If that shield slips, they suggest, egg quality and embryo growth could suffer, which may matter in conditions like endometriosis and in cases where IVF fails without a clear cause. The idea is fresh and largely untested in the follicle. The review lays out the logic and points to studies that could confirm or refute it.
pmc-13362921:
Dilara Tüfek Öztan and colleagues present a 2026 study on intensive care planning after major lung surgery for cancer. Care level is usually set before the operation, yet events during surgery often change what a patient needs. The team screened 1,060 patients at one center and focused on 159 who had a written plan for intensive care watch after surgery, then checked who actually went there.

Fewer than a third of the planned patients used intensive care in the end. Long operations and problems during surgery were the strongest signs of real need. A model that adds surgery events beat a plan based on pre-surgery facts alone. The authors argue for a second triage check right after the operation to place patients more fairly.
pmc-13365221:
Miguel Padilha and co-workers test in 2026 a drug named anle138b in cell and mouse models of Huntington disease, a gene ill that wastes the brain and has no cure. The drug reshapes harm clumps of the ill protein. Treated brain cells made few clumps and took less harm.

Mice on the drug by mouth showed late clump build, less brain waste, calm swell, and betters steps and life span. Brain marks and nerve links lost in the ill came part way back. Human stem cells from patients also clumped less. No harm shows in well mice, a hope for trials.
pmc-13367921:
Rexford Gyamfi leads a team that polls in 2026 fresh stroke kin in Ghana on what they know of high blood press, the top stroke risk. Near five hundred folks from ten care sites take a 14 part test at sign up to a phone aid trial. Scores run mid, with wide spread.

School rank lifts scores most: each school tier adds more than a point. Faith group and a stroke weight score pull scores down, while body weight adds a trace. The gaps tell phone aid teams where to aim press teach for stroke kin.
pmc-13370021:
Gábor Apjok and others probe how common gut viruses latch onto human gut lining in a 2026 study. Bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria, are major members of the gut community, yet their direct contact with human cells is poorly known. A high-throughput screen was built to find phages that stick to epithelial layers and the proteins behind that grip.

The sticky phages carry proteins with antibody-like parts. When placed on a non-sticky phage, those parts gave it the power to bind and enter cells in lab tests and to linger longer in mouse guts. pmc-13371021:
Siquan Zhou and colleagues isolate the genetic roots of pregnancy diabetes that do not overlap with type 2 diabetes in a 2026 study. The team subtracted type 2 diabetes genetic effects from pregnancy diabetes results, using FinnGen data and a second large data set for replication.

The findings may sharpen risk prediction for mothers and point to pathways that act only during pregnancy.
pmc-13372821:
Maria Clara Fagundes Lucio and co-authors summed up exercise trials for weak muscles of age in a 2026 review. Weak, thin muscles raise falls, need for help, and death risk in old age. The team searched eight data banks for trials up to May 2025, with no bar on tongue or year.

Trial types still vary a lot, so pooled means need care. The sum-up helps clinics pick the drill types with the best proof so far.
pmc-13374821:
Colin Jones and Ambalangodage C. Jayasuriya sum up six gene bone ills in a 2026 review. Each ill is rare, but each can shape a whole life of pain, breaks, and care. The search held peer work from 2020 to the end of 2025, and 36 studies made the cut.

pmc-13378021:
Aso Navaee and co-authors made a copper frame by spark craft in a 2026 study. The frame links copper to a glow coal ring, a type prized for light and charge acts. Their way runs a two-pole spark in a bath for 150 minutes at a set push.

The made stuff was checked, then tried as a light-aid to split water for its fuel gas. It woke at a low push and gave more flow as the push grew. No salt bath was in the test, a hard mode it still won in. Spark ways may build next frames and films with less fuss than heat ways.
pmc-13379721:
Canthiya and colleagues interviewed pre-medical students in 2026 about how they form views of what medical school admission demands. The process is widely seen as grueling, and beliefs about it can push students toward extreme steps and burnout. Twelve students recruited through online forums and personal contacts described how their views formed and steered their choices.

Four themes emerged from the interviews. Formal and informal sources together shape how students read the process, and many begin early, polished self-presentation to match a felt sense of rivalry. Students test, adjust, and rethink their approach in cycles, slowly building an image of the ideal applicant. A lasting tension runs through the accounts between being genuine and giving the system what it seems to want. The authors urge clearer outreach from medical schools to break echo chambers and ease needless strain.
pmc-13380521:
Deya AlWady and co-authors wrote a 2026 systematic review on choosing back surgery when a worn, curved spine also narrows the spinal canal. Surgeons may relieve pressure alone or also fuse the spine for stability. The size of the curve, measured as the Cobb angle, informs that choice but does not settle it alone.

The team searched major medical databases for adult surgical studies that reported curve size before surgery and outcomes afterwards. Mixed patient groups were excluded unless the relevant patients could be separated. Because the studies differed, results were combined in narrative form. The review aims to show how curve size should be weighed alongside symptoms and other factors.
pmc-13383421:
Ananya Mathur's team asked whether lung cancer screening itself improves surgical outcomes, in a 2026 matched analysis. Screening trials show survival gains, but screened patients may simply be healthier or caught earlier. The team compared 370 patients who had curative lung resection, 35 through screening and 335 through routine pathways, then matched 34 per group.

Before matching, screened patients looked more favorable at baseline. After matching, length of stay, overall complication rate, complication severity, and comprehensive complication scores showed no significant differences. The result suggests screening's benefit runs through earlier stage at diagnosis, not through a smoother operation itself.
pmc-13384721:
Frederick F. Strale and co-authors compare SPSS 31.0 with GPT-5.5 across common statistical procedures in a 2026 study. Fourteen analyses, from simple descriptions to multi-way variance models, were run on real datasets drawn from published papers. Prompts for the AI model were copied in with the original variable names intact.

Most descriptive and inferential results agreed closely between the two tools, the team reports. Some notable mismatches did appear, though the summary leaves their exact pattern to the full results. The study adds a fresh replication check on whether newer language models can match trusted software for research statistics.
pmc-13385621:
T. Shobha's team proposes a multi-layer airport security system combining X-ray AI, video analysis, sensors, and blockchain logs, in a 2026 framework paper. Manual baggage screening suffers from fatigue, clutter, and overlapping items. The framework layers three detectors: YOLOv11-s on X-ray images trained on the CLCXray dataset, a 3D-CNN autoencoder for video anomalies, and an LSTM autoencoder for IoT sensor anomalies.

A blockchain-secured log stores security events tamper-proof. Outputs from the three modules combine for threat decisions, aiming at reliable real-time detection in busy terminals. The paper offers airports a modular design where each layer covers the blind spots of the others.
pmc-13390221:
Mingqian Yu leads a 2026 study of how vision prescriptions change over time after orbital decompression surgery for thyroid eye disease. The operation relieves pressure by expanding the eye socket, but moving the eyeball can also shift focus.

Following 57 eyes from 46 patients with moderate-to-severe disease, the team tracked eyelid position, refraction, eye length, and corneal shape and stiffness, and compared paths across surgical techniques. Eye length configuration and globe position played the dominant role in prescription change, with technique and corneal behaviour adding smaller effects. Eye surgeons gain predictors they can check before surgery to warn patients whose glasses prescription is most likely to change afterwards.
pmc-13392021:
Zakery N Baker's team discovered that the energy-unit inner-membrane protein Fmp30p acts as a phosphatidylinositol phospholipase, shaping coenzyme Q making. Organelle membranes carry tailored lipid mixes, but the enzymes crafting them and their effects on membrane proteins were poorly understood.

Deleting FMP30 substantially raised energy-unit phosphatidylinositol species, and raising energy-unit phosphatidylinositol by either route boosted coenzyme Q biosynthesis, related enzyme expression, and metabolon formation. The work establishes Fmp30p in energy-unit lipid biology and reveals inner-membrane phosphatidylinositol as a regulator of energy-unit function.
pmc-13392221:
Jinfeng Deng's team asked whether AD blood markers predict later blood-pressure swings, studying 470 local older adults from the Health and Aging Brain Study-Health Disparities cohort. Vessel factors influencing AD are studied, but whether AD damage conversely disturbs blood-pressure control was unclear.

In fully adjusted models, total tau alone model higher upper-number swings, with stronger links in men, non-Hispanic White people, clear-minded adults, and APOE e4 non-holders. The findings suggest AD damage may feed back on heart control well before memory loss. The cohort came from the Health and Aging Brain Study-Health Disparities.
pmc-13392521:
Yi Tai, Zhihao Chen, Yuping Zhu, and Weidong Han survey GLUT1, the transporter that carries glucose into most cells and across the barrier guarding the brain. Having too little working GLUT1 from birth causes a severe syndrome in which the brain runs short of fuel. Having too much, driven by cancer signals, feeds tumour growth through the glucose-hungry pattern known as the Warburg effect.

Blocking the transporter everywhere harms healthy tissue, and tumours adapt, so older drug plans stalled. The review charts newer tactics meant to hit cancer cells only. Among them are sugar-coated carriers that smuggle cargo inside, tools that tag the transporter for destruction, and immune cells reworked to thrive in glucose-poor tumour surroundings. Framing GLUT1 as the hub of a suppressive tumour setting, the authors map routes toward sharper metabolic cancer therapy.
pmc-13392621:
Tran Thi Thao, Nguyen Tran Phuoc Chien, and Tran Ngoc Bich ran a forward-looking survey of liver and bile disease in dogs seen at a university clinic in southern Vietnam during 2025. From well over a thousand visits, one hundred eleven dogs met the entry signs for closer checks, and sixty-three had confirmed problems on ultrasound. Blood tests accompanied the scans in every enrolled dog.

Older age, obesity, and being underweight all raised the odds of abnormal scans, as did exotic breed status. Hepatitis was the commonest pattern, followed by fatty liver change and cirrhosis. Among hepatitis cases sent for infection testing, more than half carried an infectious agent, most often germs spread by biting insects. Dogs with fatty livers showed a different picture, which the authors use to argue for routine infection screening alongside imaging.
pmc-13393321:
Masahiro Ishikane and five colleagues ran a randomised crossover trial testing whether a large language model speeds the tedious data extraction behind evidence reviews for emerging infections. At Japan's national reference centre, five seasoned reviewers pulled set items from mpox articles twice over, once helped by OpenAI's o3 model producing set summaries and once reading PDFs by hand. Twenty task-level checks were completed.

Assisted extraction averaged about eight minutes faster per article, near a quarter saving, with accuracy at one hundred percent either way and no adverse events. The time gap did not reach the bar for statistical proof, and its confidence interval crossed zero, so the authors stay cautious. Still, they argue the practical value for rapid evidence gathering during outbreaks looks real as tools and prompting improve.
pmc-13394021:
Hasegawa and team examine, in 2026, regional gaps in Japanese gut surgery using the National Clinical Database, which captures over 95 percent of operations across Japan. They tracked three major ones from 2013 to 2023: colectomy, gastrectomy, and pancreaticoduodenectomy, a complex surgery on the pancreas and nearby organs. The team compared prefectures by population density and measured case volumes, surgeon numbers, and cases per surgeon.

The registry held 955,168 colectomies, 514,155 gastrectomies, and 126,008 pancreaticoduodenectomies across the decade studied. Colectomy and pancreaticoduodenectomy volumes rose even as surgeon numbers fell, pushing more work onto each surgeon. Gastrectomy volume declined across Japan over the same period. By 2023, workload per surgeon had largely converged across dense and sparse regions. One concern stands out: surgeons with at least 20 years of experience are disproportionately concentrated in low-density areas, leaving rural surgical care dependent on senior doctors nearing retirement.
pmc-13395321:
Farhana Ahamed Shanila leads a 2026 trial on salt levels for giant freshwater prawns. Salt shapes shell shedding, growth, and stress in shellfish. Young prawns lived for 56 days in water from fresh to mildly salty, across five set levels. The team weighed growth, feed use, and survival, and read gene activity for stress, immunity, and shell work.

Prawns grew best at a low salt level, three parts per thousand. Feed use, body condition, and survival also peaked there. Genes for shell shedding woke up, stress genes quieted, and immune genes rose. Fitted curves put the ideal near that same low level. The authors back mild salt for prawn farms seeking faster growth.
pmc-13395421:
Yi Huang, Wei Li, and Mohammed Misbah Ul Haq catalogue, in 2026, harms linked to camrelizumab, a cancer immune drug. Reports came from a world safety database covering 2019 to 2025, plus published case reports. Six hundred and one database reports were logged, almost all from Asian patients and mostly men. Eighty case patients from China added detail.

Blood and skin harms led the list, from marrow suppression to rash and a drug-typical growth of tiny skin vessels. Grave events included heart muscle swelling and a blistering skin emergency. Harms struck at a median of eight weeks but could arrive far later. The authors urge early spotting and steroid care for immune harms.
pmc-13395521:
Adam Swanson and co-authors report, in 2026, a gut drug that cleared a severe bowel standstill in a young man with liver failure. Ileus, where the bowel stops moving, plagues critical care and resists standard steps. The 28-year-old had decompensated alcoholic hepatitis and brain fog from liver failure. His small and large bowel both stalled despite usual care.

The team tried prucalopride, a drug that wakes a serotonin receiver to drive gut motion. The bowel soon restarted, and scans and symptoms improved in step. The drug is cleared for long-term constipation, not for this crisis use. The authors call for trials to test safety and gain in like patients.
pmc-13395821:
Enoch A. Appathurai and co-authors survey, in 2026, work-related aches among Australian optometrists. Eye doctors spend long hours bent over lamps and lenses. An online survey in two states drew 119 replies. Most reported neck, shoulder, or lower back discomfort, with neck pain scoring worst.

Repeated tasks, still poses, and awkward angles were blamed most. Lamp work at the slit lamp stirred pain most often. Only one fifth knew their workplace safety rules, and almost none had employer training on injury cuts. Aches spilled into work quality and home life, replies said. The authors call for posture training, safety rules, and better gear in clinics.
pmc-13395921:
Fangquan Chen and seven colleagues published a 2026 review on how cancer cells control acidity in separate compartments, and whether changing that balance could help treat tumors. Healthy cells keep their inner fluid near neutral, but cancer cells keep theirs mildly alkaline while the space around them turns sour.

The authors sort findings by compartment, covering the tumor surroundings, the cell interior, and small inner structures such as lysosomes. Forcing these spaces to become more alkaline can upset ion balance, damage organelles, and trigger a form of cell death called alkaliptosis. They also weigh immune effects and warn that benefits depend heavily on tumor type, so gains in the lab may not carry into care.
pmc-13396221:
Ning Liu and co-authors engineered a ceramic that stores an unusually large amount of energy for use in capacitors, and report it in 2026. Capacitors release power far faster than batteries, which suits advanced electronics, but they usually hold too little energy per volume to take on bigger jobs.

The team used a high-entropy recipe, mixing many different metal ions into a sodium niobate base so the crystal's neat order breaks down. What remains is a tangle of thread-like polar regions only a few nanometers wide. That tangled state lets the material take a strong charge without locking it in place, so more of the stored energy can be recovered when the capacitor discharges.
pmc-13396521:
Xueyao Chen and co-authors worked out the maths of electric fields under Arctic-style seas, where a layer of ice caps the water, in a 2026 paper. Ships and underwater targets carry electric signatures, and knowing how those fields spread through layered water helps others detect and locate them.

Their model stacks four layers: air, sea ice, seawater, and seabed. Starting from the equation for a steady field, they used a repeated image method to reach an exact formula for field strength inside the seawater. That method mirrors the current source across each boundary in turn. A numerical model built on small volume cells checked the formula, giving engineers a tested tool for ice-covered waters.
pmc-13397521:
Published in 2026 with no author named, the study asks whether nicotine from vapes and other non-tobacco sources harms healing after body contouring surgery. Smoking is long known to slow wound repair, but the risk from nicotine alone has drawn far less study. Contouring lifts and shifts large areas of skin, so blood flow matters a great deal.

Patients with nicotine dependence from non-tobacco products were matched against similar patients without it. The team then compared wound problems and other bad outcomes after surgery, testing whether nicotine by itself carries the same danger as smoke.
pmc-13397721:
Kabali Bwogi and others describe HPV patterns in rural Ugandan women living with HIV in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. Persistent HPV infection precedes cervical abnormalities and cancer, yet type spread in this high-risk group was little known.

Reviewing women tested at Mityana and Kiboga Hospitals between July 2021 and July 2022. The team used GeneXpert HPV DNA testing to spot types 16, 18 and 45, plus other pooled high-risk types. Cases were grouped as single or multiple infections. Age and antiretroviral history were read with robust regression. Cervical screening programs gain rural Ugandan type patterns for vaccine and screening planning.
pmc-13398521:
Xinhang Zheng and colleagues find a self-limiting switch inside a rice immune receptor. A phosphatase named SIPP1 removes the tag and stabilises the receptor, until a rival, SIPP2, pushes it aside and lets destruction proceed. pmc-13398721:

Their 2026 work presents the hexaploid Actinidia valvata type Zhongmikangzhen No. 2, the first rootstock of its kind granted plant variety protection in China. pmc-13398921:
Roland Kotolloshi and co-authors test a drug that breaks a growth-signal partnership inside bladder cancer cells. Bladder cancer is the commonest urinary tract malignancy, yet its progression machinery still hides drug-worthy weak points.

The partner protein BCL9L pushed bladder cells to grow and invade, and silencing its sibling BCL9 slowed growth, movement and invasion too. The inhibitor ZW4864 shut down a subset of Wnt target genes and curbed cell proliferation in the experiments. Jamming this one protein handshake, the authors argue, could become a bladder cancer strategy distinct from broader Wnt blockade.
pmc-13399121:

Without added magnesium, mineral deposits covered the construct by day two, though the cells stayed alive. pmc-13399221:

The team wanted to know what long-term capsinoid treatment does to the heart, while their cardiac effects remain unclear. The animals were then regrouped into control, obese, and obese-plus-capsinoid groups, the last receiving capsinoids by oral gavage at 10 milligrams per kilogram. Obese rats carried more fat than controls, and capsinoids did not reduce that fat or improve the metabolic and lipid changes of obesity. Heart size did not differ between groups. The treated obese rats, though, showed a reduced shortening fraction, a sign of weaker heart-muscle contraction. The authors conclude capsinoids failed to help metabolism here and harmed heart muscle function.
pmc-13399421:
Raquel Brito Elmescany and co-authors set out to examine how the brain's electrical activity relates to slow motor reactions in older women with differing degrees of sarcopenia, in a 2026 study. Sarcopenia is the age-related loss of muscle mass and strength. Reaction time lengthens with age, and some of that slowing happens in the brain rather than the muscles. The authors reasoned that women with more advanced muscle loss might show distinct patterns on the electroencephalogram, the scalp recording of brain waves.

Postmenopausal hormone changes accelerate muscle quality loss in women, especially in the legs. Against that backdrop, the study compares electroencephalogram measures across women grouped by sarcopenia severity while they perform reaction tasks. The aim is to separate the brain's share of slowness from the muscles' share.
pmc-13399621:

It also adds a natural suture repair for the zona orbicularis, a ring fiber band usually cut in the approach, to restore its link and strength. The work gives hip surgeons a full technical option, while head-to-head tests against standard capsulotomy remain ahead.
pmc-13399721:

Gout appeared in 6,910 patients, 3.0 percent of the cohort, and 16,296 ischemic strokes occurred during follow-up. Patients with gout suffered strokes at higher rates: the incidence rate ratio was 1.35 before adjustment and 1.12 after. Among patients who had both conditions, time spent on urate-lowering therapy came with a stroke rate about 30 percent lower in the reported models. Crude stroke rates in untreated gout patients climbed with the standard risk score. The authors argue gout deserves a place in stroke risk thinking for fibrillation patients, not least because it can be treated.
pmc-13400721:
Alessia Canevotti and colleagues analyze, in 2026, a DNA-unwinding factor called HLTF across human cancer cohorts, asking whether it suppresses or promotes tumors. Evidence pointed both ways. Distinct regulatory setups appeared in different cancers, shaped by gene dosage changes and loss-of-function events. Methylation at both nearby and distant control regions helped set HLTF activity in each context. Several tumor-specific patterns tied HLTF changes to patient outcomes, supporting its promise as a biomarker. The work argues that HLTF role depends on the molecular setting, not a fixed label.
pmc-13400921:

Four themes emerged, starting with trust: building credibility in rural communities, offering meaningful incentives and fielding well-trained staff. Partners also stressed explaining the value of acupressure clearly, with detailed guidance and motivational messaging. The regional sample limits generalizability, the authors note.
pmc-13401321:

The German study interviewed ten health professionals who manage the condition, watched them run simulated patient consultations, and interviewed eight patients for thirty minutes each. In the simulated visits, most professionals recommended long-term prophylaxis when attacks were frequent. Quality of life had to suffer badly too. The interviews showed how clinicians usually open the prophylaxis conversation. They also surfaced barriers that block shared decisions and treatment starts, plus strategies meant to beat them.
pmc-13401521:

The claimed benefit to plant growth was judged unconvincing, and the authors could not give a satisfactory explanation, so confidence in the article was lost. Six authors disagree with the retraction; Najla A Alshaikh did not respond to the publisher.
pmc-13402621:

pmc-13403621:
