Signals that build these structures include chemokines, tumor necrosis factor family members, and interactions with gut microbes. Early experimental strategies try to grow them deliberately, using immune-stimulating drugs, nano-sized vaccines, or focused radiation schedules. The aim is to turn quiet tumors responsive and rescue treatments that resistance had blunted. Clinical proof, the authors note, is still developing.
pmc-13459321:
Ping Xie and co-authors report the first human trial of an iron loaded carbon nanoparticle injection designed to revive drug sensitivity in resistant solid tumors. The particles, injected directly into tumors, flood cancer cells with iron to trigger ferroptosis, a rust like form of cell death that resistant cells usually evade. Their 2026 cohort analysis covers nineteen heavily pretreated patients in a phase I trial. It tracks safety, imaging changes, tumor growth rates, and survival after treatment.

The injections proved acceptably safe and consistently hollowed out tumors from the center, producing marked internal necrosis on scans even when overall shrinkage looked minimal by standard criteria. Four patients, about a fifth of the cohort, with ovarian, pancreatic, vulvar, and thyroid cancers survived roughly twenty nine to thirty six months afterward. Strikingly, those four regained responses to chemotherapy or targeted drugs that had previously stopped working for them.
pmc-13459621:
Annelies M Baart and colleagues test urine dipstick hit rate for bladder infection in older adults in a 2026 test study. Dipsticks are widely used, yet silent bacteria and white cells in older adults, especially women, undermine trust. The study drew 368 cases from 199 people, mean age 73.8 years, each with dipstick, cell counting and culture, judged against an agreed yardstick standard.

The usual cut-off gave 93.6 percent catch rate but only 58.6 percent clear rate, risking needless bug drugs. A higher cut-off, a total of at least 2 plus, lifted clear rate to 75.7 percent while keeping catch rate at 82.2 percent and improving the positive odds ratio from about 2 to about 3. Doctors gain a stricter cut-off to consider before giving bug drugs to patients aged 60 and older.
pmc-13460021:
Yang Yang and co-authors explored why older Chinese adults living in the United Kingdom exercise less than guidelines advise, interviewing them about what blocks and what enables activity. Their 2026 study ran sixteen interviews with twenty seven self identified Chinese residents over sixty, recruited by convenience sampling. Transcripts were mapped against the COM-B framework, which sorts influences into ability, chances, and drive. Participants ranged from fully active to inactive by World Health Organization standards.

Barriers clustered on every side of the framework. Poor health, pain, and low energy limited ability, alongside weak knowledge of activity guidelines and low confidence in how to work out safely. Social chances were thin: many lacked workout partners or community support for activity. Drive suffered when workouts felt culturally unfamiliar or pointless against chronic conditions. Facilitators mirrored the barriers, pointing to group based, culturally familiar activities with social support as the most promising design.
pmc-13461021:
Min Yan and Xiaowei Jiang link cardiovascular health to overactive bladder in a US population sample in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Overactive bladder burdens quality of life, yet whether broader heart health tracks urinary symptoms was incompletely understood. The study drew 6,042 participants from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, scoring cardiovascular health by Life's Essential 8 and testing associations with bladder symptoms.

High cardiovascular health cut overactive bladder odds by 41 percent versus low health, and each 10-point score gain lowered odds by 13 percent. Protective effects plateaued near a score of 73, while inflammation mediated 4.8 percent and plasma osmolality 12.8 percent of the link, with body mass and sleep the strongest components. Clinicians gain modifiable targets, especially weight and sleep, for bladder symptom prevention.
pmc-13461321:
Kartali and colleagues presented in 2026 Cardio-FL, a smartphone system for spotting heart rhythm faults outside clinics while keeping heart data private. Wearable ECG sensors and phone cameras can track rhythm at home, but a usable system must handle messy real-world signals, guard sensitive data, adapt to each user, and limit false alarms. Their prototype streams ECG from a chest wearable to an Android app for on-device analysis.

Kartali's model is tiny, with only about five and a half thousand parameters, and sorts beats into normal, early upper-chamber, and early lower-chamber types. The phone's camera adds a pulse check after alerts. Learning adapts on the device itself using unlabelled beats, and updates are shared in a federated way, meaning data stay on phones while model gains are pooled. Activity sensing gates when recording and training run, to save power and cut noise.
pmc-13461421:
Qiming Zhao and colleagues tested whether a combined inflammation-metabolic index predicts new heart disease in rectal cancer survivors. The index, CTI, merges C-reactive protein, triglycerides, and glucose into one score of body-wide inflammatory and metabolic strain.

The main cohort held 1,160 survivors from a Chinese hospital, with 1,752 UK Biobank survivors as an outside check. Each standard-step rise in CTI came with 18 percent higher odds of new heart disease after full adjustment. Risk climbed in a near-straight line and concentrated in the top quarter of scores, above all in younger, non-hypertensive survivors. In the UK cohort the link faded to nothing after adjustment, Zhao notes, so the index fits high-burden clinic settings best.
pmc-13461521:
Sidneva, Lobanova, and Vysotskaya presented in 2026 a way to design story-based tasks that show whether preschool children truly use counting, not just recite it. Many young children can count formally yet never use counting as a tool inside other activities. The team set five design principles for narrative tasks and built a battery that sorts counting mastery into formal, reasonable, and functional levels.

Sidneva piloted the battery on 56 older preschoolers, about 69 months old on average. Scores fell in a clear staircase from the formal level to the reasonable and then the functional level. Formal and reasonable scores tracked executive skills such as working memory and self-control, as expected. Functional scores did not, which hints that using counting inside a story task leans on different mechanisms. The authors say purpose-built stories are needed to test real use, though more validation is required.
pmc-13461621:
Huang and co-authors pooled a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis comparing ultrasound with plain X-ray for spotting signs of necrotizing enterocolitis in newborns. That disease inflames and can kill sections of a baby's intestine, so early imaging signs matter greatly. Six databases were searched for studies comparing the two scans head to head.

Twenty studies covering 1,793 newborns with confirmed or suspected disease entered the pooled analysis Huang led. Ultrasound found gas in the portal vein, a danger sign, more than twice as often in odds terms as X-ray did. Ultrasound also trended ahead on gas within the bowel wall, while X-ray trended ahead on free air and bowel widening without reaching significance. The authors suggest combining both scans for earlier recognition and tracking of the disease.
pmc-13461821:
Zhang, Zhang, and Liu reported a 2026 case report of a newborn boy with cblC-type methylmalonic acidemia combined with high homocysteine, an inherited fault in handling vitamin B12. The disease blocks normal processing of certain amino acids and fats. From birth the baby fed poorly, responded weakly, and had floppy muscles and muted reflexes.

Blood screening showed raised homocysteine and a pattern of carnitine markers pointing to the disorder, and urine carried extra methylmalonic acid. Brain imaging lit up in two deep structures called the globus pallidus on both sides. Genetic testing found two faulty copies of the MMACHC gene, one from each parent, confirming the diagnosis. The authors urge metabolic screening for any newborn with unexplained feeding trouble and abnormal tone.
pmc-13462121:
Man Gao leads a 2026 study of a mitochondrial protein, METTL17, in stomach cancer, formally gastric cancer. Stomach cancer is widespread and carries a poor outlook. METTL17 belongs to a family of proteins that tag other molecules. It had been shown to drive colorectal and mouth cancers. Its role here was unexplored. The team measured it in tissue and cells, then raised and lowered its levels in tests.

It ran high in stomach tumors, and high levels went with worse patient outlook. Lowering METTL17 slowed cell growth, movement, and invasion, and weakened tumor formation in mice. Raising it did the opposite. Protein surveys showed how it works: METTL17 holds down a protein, GSK-3beta, which restrains a growth pathway, Wnt/beta-catenin. With the brake weakened, the pathway switches on and fuels the cancer. The authors present METTL17 as a drug target for stomach cancer, pending checks.
pmc-13462221:
Shalini Gakhar and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how generative AI could turn farm science into advice fitted to each rice farm in India. Agriculture produces oceans of data, yet farmers rarely get guidance shaped to their plot. Old expert systems gave stiff, general answers. Newer language models can reason and handle images, and rice-specific versions trained on science texts make fewer errors.

The strongest designs pair a language model with a knowledge graph, a structured web of facts that grounds answers, and with crop growth simulators. Satellite, drone, and phone images with vision models could give near-instant diagnosis for small farms. The authors are clear about the conditions. Connectivity gaps must close, farmers' data rights must be protected, and a human adviser must stay in the loop. Only then can such tools make precision farming fairer rather than a privilege of large farms.
pmc-13462321:
Ame Stephanie Ayemere and Jeanny B Aragon-Ching discuss, in a 2026 commentary, estradiol skin patches as an alternative way to lower testosterone in advanced prostate cancer. Standard hormone treatment uses injections crushing both testosterone and estrogen, bringing bone loss, fractures, hot flashes, and muscle wasting. An older oral estrogen worked, yet raised clot risks by passing through the liver. Patches bypass the liver, keeping estrogen's benefits without that risk.

The commentary covers a randomized trial in 1,360 men treated between 2007 and 2022, which compared patches against injections. The question was whether patches controlled cancer as well, measured by time free of spread or death. Cancer control proved no worse with patches. Side effects differed: fewer problems tied to estrogen loss, yet more breast growth in men and more patch-related skin trouble. The authors present patches as an option whose trade-offs suit some patients better than others.
pmc-13462921:
Suhail Sayed and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a scoring chart to predict dangerously low blood calcium after parathyroid surgery in patients with secondary hyperparathyroidism. The condition, where overactive parathyroid glands follow severe kidney disease, is treated by removing all four glands and reimplanting a fragment. Severe calcium drops strike a quarter to a half of patients, driven by hormone loss and hungry bones soaking up minerals.

The study gathered 227 patients treated at two centers between 2019 and 2024, all on intensive calcium plans after surgery. Just under half developed severe low calcium by the study's definition. A screening method picked four predictors from data available before surgery, including age and two blood measures taken a month ahead, phosphate and an enzyme, alkaline phosphatase. Repeated internal resampling corrected the model's optimism. The authors offer the chart for risk planning around surgery, while noting it needs validation at other centers.
pmc-13463321:
Zufiria-Gerbolés and colleagues mapped in 2026 the wiring of the locus coeruleus, a tiny brain stem hub. The hub sprays a wake chemical through the brain, and stacks Alzheimer's tau first. Two scan banks fed the work. The team traced the hub's white tract links and weighed them by age and ill.

The tracts sort in a top to base plan no one had shown in man. Some link shifts come with plain age, some with the ill alone. Link shifts tracked gene maps, mind scores, and tau in a memory zone. The team built a gap mark for stray links. In sound folk at high risk, a wide gap went with slow tau growth.
pmc-13463521:
Park and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a handheld six-lead heart tracing device can stand in for the standard twelve-lead electrocardiogram. Their patients all had rhythm disorders. In a single hospital, both tracings were recorded at the same time. Patients were tested lying down and sitting up. A heart rhythm specialist, blinded to the source, then read each pair.

The team analyzed 229 usable paired recordings. The handheld device matched the standard machine's rhythm diagnosis in about 99 of every 100 cases. That held in both postures. Each time, it missed one case of atrial flutter by calling it atrial fibrillation. Measured intervals differed only slightly, with most gaps under 20 thousandths of a second. Heart rates were nearly identical. Agreement slipped to about 97 in 100 when postures were mismatched between devices. Timing and posture, the authors conclude, clearly matter.
pmc-13464321:
Li and co-authors asked in 2026 whether the retina can forecast depression. The retina is the light-sensing layer at the back of the eye. It grows from the same tissue as the brain and can be photographed noninvasively. UK Biobank scans from 36,220 adults aged 40 to 70 supplied the data. Six retinal layers were measured. New diagnoses of depression and anxiety were tracked over a median follow-up beyond twelve years.

During that time, 1,340 participants developed depression and 1,373 developed anxiety. Each standard-step thickening of the ganglion cell layer came with about eight percent lower depression risk. That layer carries visual signals toward the brain. Greater overall macular thickness came with about nine percent lower risk, even after full adjustment. The protection looked stronger in women. No retinal measure predicted anxiety once other factors were counted. Eye scans might one day help flag people deserving closer mental-health watching.
pmc-13465721:
Sunggyun Park, Kyoungbo Kim, and Jung-Sook Ha compare two lab methods for measuring how much of a blood sample carries the JAK2 V617F mutation, in a 2026 study. That measurement guides care in a group of blood cancers that lack the Philadelphia chromosome change. Their chip-based digital PCR test, built in the lab, went against a commercial real-time PCR kit.

Both methods ran on leftover DNA from 76 mutation-positive patient samples. Detection limits sat close together, slightly favoring the digital test, which also varied less between repeats, above all at low mutation levels where precision matters most. Straight-line accuracy was strong for both. The authors also checked how mutation levels related to routine blood counts and diagnosis groups.
pmc-13466421:
Tianqi Cao, Hongyu Cui, Junyi Liu, and Chuanhui Zhang dope a cobalt oxide catalyst with rare earth elements to speed oxygen reactions in rechargeable zinc-air batteries, in a 2026 study. Both oxygen uptake and oxygen release at the air electrode run sluggishly, which holds the battery type back. A citric acid gel method produced equal-share doping with four different lanthanides for comparison.

The samarium version won, showing the smallest voltage gap between the two reactions and a clean four-electron pathway. Doping warped the crystal lattice, opened oxygen vacancies, and shifted the balance between cobalt charge states. The authors tie those structural facts to performance, building a structure-activity map for later catalyst design.
pmc-13466721:
Muhammed Dogukan Aksu and co-authors chart the genomic landscape of colorectal cancers carrying mutations in ERBB2, the gene for the HER2 growth receptor. Their 2026 analysis compares these mutated tumours with cancers where the gene is instead amplified, meaning copied many times.

Drawing on the cBioPortal database, the team analysed 4,348 patients and found driver mutations in 95 and amplifications in 87. Mutated tumours were enriched for KRAS alterations and for microsatellite instability, a marker of faulty DNA repair, and tended to sit on the right side of the colon with high mutation counts. Amplified tumours favoured the left side, avoided KRAS mutations, and often carried TP53 alterations. Clustering confirmed the two groups are distinct, which the authors say supports different treatment strategies for each.
pmc-13467521:
Mehtap Ertekin and Salih Gozmen compare in 2026 the sleep of children treated for leukemia or lymphoma with that of similar children seen for harmless blood conditions. Sleep problems are now recognized as part of good supportive cancer care, yet their pattern in this group is poorly described. The study enrolled 54 young patients and 56 comparison children of similar age and sex, using a standard parent questionnaire on children sleep habits.

Patients scored worse overall on sleep disturbance, averaging 53.56 points against 49.07 for the comparison group. The clearest gaps appeared in sleep anxiety and parasomnias, unusual behaviors during sleep, while sleep duration barely differed. Within the patient group, the authors modeled recent hospital stays and steroid treatment, both common in cancer care, as possible drivers. The results argue for routine sleep screening during treatment.
pmc-13467821:
Huang and colleagues quantify how frailty drives hospital costs and stay length for older patients having colorectal cancer surgery, in a 2026 multicenter study. Frailty means reduced physical reserve from aging. The team analyzed 4,936 patients aged 60 or older who had elective surgery between 2014 and 2024. They then decomposed the frailty effect to see how much ran through other illnesses the patients had, and how much through complications arising after the operation.

Frail patients faced higher odds of expensive admissions, with an odds ratio of 1.274 in the adjusted model. Their odds of adverse events were far higher still, at an odds ratio of 3.317 against non-frail patients in the same analysis. Stays also ran longer for frail patients. Existing comorbidity burden explained 28.6 percent of the frailty-linked cost difference, the decomposition showed. Postoperative complications explained only 3.8 percent of the stay difference and not significantly. Huang urges frailty screening before elective cancer surgery.
pmc-13468021:
Nuria Aide López Hernández and colleagues compare in 2026 two remote sensing routes for scheduling irrigation in forage maize: satellite images and drone flights. Both feed a vegetation index that tracks crop greenness, which the team converted into crop water-use coefficients during the 2023 season and then tested in real fields in 2024. Two maize hybrids were grown under farmer practice, satellite-guided watering, and drone-guided watering.

The drone model fit the water-use data more tightly, with an R-squared of 0.9414 against 0.8278 for the satellite. Drone scheduling applied 23 to 30 percent less water and kept water productivity high, but the crops grew less and yielded lower-quality forage. Satellite scheduling produced the biggest harvest, reaching 59.8 tonnes per hectare in the best case. The trade-off between saving water and maximizing yield sits at the heart of the comparison.
pmc-13468121:
Danila Maltsev and colleagues make silk fibroin gels in 2026 that change color when squeezed, pointing toward soft mechanical sensors. The silk protein, extracted from silkworm cocoons with a calcium-based reagent, was dialyzed against an ethanol-water mix to trigger a slow, controlled setting into gel. Higher starting protein levels gave stiffer gels that stayed stable in water, with a uniform network of physical crosslinks.

Gels that retained calcium ions kept a different, more transparent silk conformation and conducted ions better. The sensing trick came from soaking the gel in a fatty acid building block and polymerizing it with ultraviolet light into polydiacetylene, a famously color-shifting polymer. The resulting blue gel blushed red under compression. A biodegradable, silk-based material that visibly reports force could serve in wearables, wound dressings, or soft robotics.
pmc-13468321:
Muhammad Tayyab Noman and co-authors examine in 2026 the fiber-matrix interface in polymer composites, the thin boundary where load passes from resin into reinforcing fibers and where performance is often decided. Many surface treatments improve the interface on paper, yet those gains do not reliably become stronger finished parts. The review connects surface chemistry, interphase structure, nano-scale modification, and processing conditions into one account of load transfer and damage growth.

Unlike surveys that simply catalog treatments, this one stresses that interfacial performance is made during manufacturing, not baked into the material. Reported gains are checked against real structural results, exposing limits from poor particle dispersion, resin flow behavior, processing defects, and scale-up trouble. The authors propose a multiscale framework to carry interface design from chemistry to factory floor, a bridge the field has lacked.
pmc-13468521:
Xiaobing Hu and co-authors review in 2026 the circadian clock of cyanobacteria, the simplest organisms known to keep true daily time. Their clock is a trio of proteins, KaiA, KaiB, and KaiC, that ticks out a near-24-hour rhythm through cycles of phosphorylation, without needing genes to switch on and off. The review analyzes how the three proteins change shape together, how temperature compensation keeps the period steady, and how the design varies across cyanobacterial lineages.

Input pathways that reset the clock by light and metabolic signals are mapped, as are the output routes that schedule photosynthesis and cell division across the day. The cyanobacterial system matters beyond microbiology: it proved a clock can be pure protein chemistry, and it remains the test bed for understanding how all circadian clocks stay robust yet adjustable. The authors also look ahead to engineering timing into industrial microbes.
pmc-13468721:
Wei Gao and colleagues build in 2026 a shore-based instrument that watches river carbon almost continuously, filling a gap between sparse satellite passes and finicky underwater sensors. Their ground hyperspectral system photographs the water surface with three miniature spectrometers. It measures the light coming off the water, the sky, and the incoming sunlight, deriving the water reflectance every ten seconds at best.

The unit runs on solar power, reports over a 4G link, and covers wavelengths from 400 to 900 nanometers at one-nanometer resolution, allowing long solo deployments. Models for dissolved and particulate organic carbon were built and checked against 90 paired water samples taken in place. Rivers carry a major, poorly counted share of the global carbon budget, and a cheap always-on watcher at a riverbank could tighten those numbers.
pmc-13469021:
Dotan and colleagues build a fishing platform for antibodies against targets hidden inside tumour cells. Their 2026 paper addresses a blind spot: antibody discovery has largely ignored intracellular antigens, assuming antibodies cannot usefully reach them. The team combined classic hybridoma generation, fusing B cells into immortal lines, with flow-cytometric enrichment steered by the antigen itself, using tumour B-cell receptors as the bait.

In a mouse breast cancer model engineered to make a glowing intracellular protein, tumour growth triggered a class-switched B-cell response against that hidden antigen. The selected hybridomas kept both surface receptors and secreted antibodies, enabling efficient selection. The resulting monoclonal antibodies recognised native intracellular targets that conventional screens missed. Given system-wide, one antibody slowed growth of early established tumours. The team also demonstrated the approach with human B cells from tonsils and blood, supporting translational use.
pmc-13469121:
Vishal Kumar U Shah and colleagues combined plant biochar with ozone in 2026 to clean real textile wastewater of colour and chemical oxygen demand. Dyes block light, resist breakdown, and foul rivers, yet single treatments often fall short. Canna indica biochar treated with potassium or sodium hydroxide was tested across dose, pH, time, and ozone flow.

Potassium-treated biochar cut chemical oxygen demand by 96.90% at 2.5 grams per litre, pH 8, 17 hours, and 100 millilitres per minute, while sodium-treated biochar best removed colour at pH 8.5 and lower ozone flow. Acidity mattered most among factors, and adsorption followed pseudo-second-order kinetics with chemical sorption dominant. The paired process offers a practical route for dye works to meet discharge limits.
pmc-13469621:
Fangfei Wang and colleagues built a prognosis model in 2026 for resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma from tumour biology plus host nutrition. Anatomy-based staging predicts poorly for this lethal cancer, whose five-year survival sits below 10%. The study followed 105 patients after pancreaticoduodenectomy from 2019 to 2024, measuring KRT6A in tumours and a nutritional index from albumin and lymphocyte counts.

KRT6A ran high in poorly differentiated tumours and drove migration and invasion in dishes, while KRT6A and nutrition emerged as the only independent predictors of disease-free survival. Their combined nomogram scored 0.838 for one-year prediction, 0.836 for two-year prediction, and 0.969 for three-year prediction, splitting patients into low, intermediate, and high risk with three-year disease-free rates near 52%, near 39%, and near 12%. The model should sharpen personalised treatment choices after surgery.
pmc-13470521:
Sato and colleagues in Japan told in 2026 of six hip swaps redone with a graft trick that packs crushed donor bone round a fresh stem. The classic form of the trick glues the stem with cement. Reports with glue free stems are rare. Their stems wore a full coat of hydroxyapatite, a bone like mineral that bone grips well, plus a collar at the top. Patients bore full weight from the first day.

At a mid check near four and a half years, the set looked strong. A joint score rose from mid range to near top marks. No joint grew loose, wore, slipped, or caught a germ. Stems sank a hair, just over a millimeter, well shy of worry marks. Scans showed new bone growth in all six, and one deep scan showed bone fused to the stem.
pmc-13470721:
Lorraine L. G. C. de Araujo and colleagues test in 2026 whether modified corn starch can coax extra oil from carbonate rock. Carbonate reservoirs resist enhanced recovery because their surfaces start out oil loving and uneven. Three starch derivatives, decorated with charged groups at different levels and chain lengths, were pushed through carbonate rock plugs after ordinary water flooding.

The starch floods recovered an extra six to eleven percent of the oil in place. Heavier decoration and longer chains displaced oil better, by shifting the rock surface toward mixed wetness and sweeping more evenly. Ultra detailed mass spectrometry of the starting and recovered oils showed shifts in their polar compounds, especially nitrogen and oxygen bearing ones. The authors read those shifts as selective sticking and sorting at the rock surface.
pmc-13471421:
Trabelsi-Mescheloff and co-authors present a faster version of a peptide docking program. Their 2026 paper improves PatchMAN, a tool that predicts how short protein chains called peptides bind to target proteins. The original method borrows structural fragments as templates, then refines many of them at high computational cost, including many that lead nowhere.

The new version, PatchMAN2, adds strategic filtering that discards poor fragments before the expensive refinement step. It also adds local docking modes that concentrate the search on relevant surfaces or known binding regions. In benchmark tests the filtering removed roughly 30 to 70 percent of unnecessary fragments while keeping prediction accuracy. The authors report substantially shorter runtimes, making global peptide docking more practical for everyday use.
pmc-13471521:
Huang and Lin built a bedside risk model to flag severe psittacosis, the pneumonia caught from birds, using two ordinary blood tests. Their 2026 double-center retrospective study covered 36 hospitalized patients with confirmed Chlamydia psittaci pneumonia, split into 11 severe and 25 non-severe cases.

Lung scans followed a set rhythm, peaking in severity at two weeks with a median total CT score of 7 before gradually clearing. Creatine kinase, a muscle enzyme, and direct bilirubin, a liver pigment, separated severe from non-severe cases and stayed stable under bootstrap re-testing, with small relative biases of −8.9% and −7.5% respectively. With only 36 patients, the authors frame the model as hypothesis-generating and warn against clinical use until larger prospective studies confirm it.
pmc-13471621:
Yu Pan, Lixun Wang, and Yanle Zhang evaluate in 2026 a corpus based course that teaches medical students to write about patients with more humanity. Language teaching in medical schools rarely targets how students express care and ethics in writing. Sixty students at a medical university in southeast China were split into experimental and control groups for a technology assisted course built on collections of real medical language.

After accounting for starting scores, the experimental group finished with significantly higher writing marks. Frequency counts tracked how often humanistic expressions appeared in their texts, and close reading showed shifts in how clinical and ethical concerns were voiced. Interviews with the experimental students explored how working with real language samples changed their sense of ethical responsibility and patient perspective. The authors present the design as one route to humanistic training.
pmc-13473521:
Jiahao Kong proposed in 2026 a faster, lighter detector for prohibited items in X-ray security screening. Airport and checkpoint scanners must find hidden objects through heavy overlap and clutter, in real time, yet existing models trade accuracy against speed. The new framework, GSA-YOLO, builds on the small YOLOv8n detector and adds three parts. Group lasso sparsity in the network neck gives robust features. Sparse structure selection in the detection head slims the model, and adaptive knowledge distillation recovers accuracy lost to pruning.

Tests on two X-ray datasets, HiXray and PIDray, gave a leading speed of about 190 frames per second. Computing cost trimmed from 8.7 to 8 gigaflops. Accuracy at the standard mAP50:95 measure reached 0.531 on HiXray and 0.679 on PIDray, improving on the baseline by 2.4 percent and by 1.8 percent in turn. The authors present the model as a practical balance of speed and accuracy for live security lanes.
pmc-13473721:
Ciancio and colleagues in the United States read in 2026 the charts of 107 child kidney swaps done at their hub since 2014. All had no stent left in the new urine pipe. A stent is a thin tube that props the join while it heals, and many teams leave one by rule. Their side sewn join was built to skip that step. The team logged each urine snag in the first year.

Snags were rare: four children in all had one, a rate under four in a hundred. Just three needed a fresh operation to fix theirs. Two snags were blocks high in the pipe, and one was a low block from stones. No child leaked urine at all in the first year, the snag stents are most meant to stop. The authors call the stent free way safe for child swaps.
pmc-13475521:
Julia Hawthorne and co-authors review calcium use in 2026 during resuscitation for heart arrest inside hospitals. Calcium was long given for its hoped heart-boosting effect, despite thin proof. Records covered 599 arrest events at one academic center from 2011 to 2024, all lasting at least five minutes. About thirty-nine percent received calcium during the event.

Calcium use tracked with far lower rates of restored pulse, survival to discharge, and good brain outcome. Adjusted math kept the link strong on all three outcomes. Longer resuscitation time did not explain the pattern. The authors urge restraint and fresh trials before routine in-hospital use.
pmc-13476321:
Lorenzo Onorato and four colleagues pooled in 2026 studies on preventive antibiotics of the fluoroquinolone class for high-risk patients with low white-cell counts and blood cancers. They combined 18 trials and observational studies covering 12,586 patients, comparing preventive treatment with ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin against no preventive treatment.

Death rates did not differ between groups, even after excluding low-resistance settings. Preventive treatment did cut fever episodes and bloodstream infections, with a strong effect on the latter. Resistant strain counts did not differ. The authors conclude that preventive treatment reduces fever and bloodstream infection but offers no survival benefit.
pmc-13476621:
Yi Chen and co-authors show in 2026 that a tag system for proteins is required to build kidneys before birth. The system, UFMylation, had been tied to kidney shrinkage in adult mice when its ligase failed. Pups lacking that ligase in the kidney grew malformed kidneys that mimicked loss of a growth switch called YAP. Lab work found YAP itself receives the tag at one key site.

Tagging shields YAP from the cell shredder, letting it enter the nucleus and switch genes on. One of two tag-removing enzymes proved to be the main brake on YAP. Removing that brake steadied YAP and lifted its activity. A fresh cause for birth kidney faults is named.
pmc-13478521:
Alwabli presents a task offloading strategy in 2026 for the Internet of Vehicles, where connected cars generate computing jobs too heavy to run on board. The four-tier design spreads work among the vehicles themselves, roadside units, edge servers, and the cloud, weighing delay against energy use for every assignment. Learning agents, trained centrally but acting independently in each vehicle, decide where each task goes as traffic and channels shift.

Against nine rival methods, from simple rules to rival learning systems, the strategy posted low average delay and low energy use in the simulations run. It also achieved a high task success rate and settled into stable behavior faster than the competing approaches tested alongside it. Tuning the balance between delay and energy shifted the system between safety-style services, which prize speed, and tolerant services that prize saving power, which the author frames as sustainability.
pmc-13479221:
Jeremy Howick and colleagues present a 2026 proposal for a model of empathic leadership aimed at crises in modern management. Business writing celebrates empathic leadership, yet two gaps persist. Evidence that empathy benefits patients and practitioners in healthcare has never been carried into leadership theory, and no formal model of empathic leadership exists for teaching or testing.

The proposed model imports what healthcare research shows about empathy: understanding another's perspective, communicating that understanding, and acting on it. The authors argue this sequence can guide leaders facing staff burnout, conflict, and rapid change. A defined model also lets organizations train the skill deliberately instead of treating it as a personality trait. The paper offers the model as both an explanation of good crisis leadership and a teaching foundation.
pmc-13479621:
Tina Nanyangwe-Moyo, Laura J. Rosa Pereira, and Mathieu Jean-Patrick Poirier published a 2025 evaluation of how well tobacco control research handles gender. Smoking behavior is shaped by gender norms, yet policy studies often proceed as if gender were irrelevant. The team applied a European gender impact assessment toolkit to forty-three peer-reviewed studies using national data published after 2005.

Each study was scored on whether it named its gendered target group and assessed how policies land differently by gender. Forty of the forty-three studies did identify specific target groups and their challenges, a stronger showing than the authors' framing might suggest. The full coding still exposes gaps in impact assessment practice. The exercise gives tobacco researchers a structured mirror for designing studies that treat gender as a variable, not a footnote.
pmc-13480521:
Daniel C Cano-Blanco and co-authors present a 2026 catalyst study on breaking down nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas. The team dotted a cobalt oxide base with tiny rhodium oxide and cerium oxide patches. Each additive alone helps somewhat, yet the pair together did far more than the sum of the parts.

Live X-ray probing during reaction showed the gases cycling through a shared pathway where the cobalt-cerium base stores and releases oxygen while rhodium sites turn over. The three-way border between the oxides flexes oxidation states with ease and frees lattice oxygen for the work. Rate studies matched that shared cycle picture. Designing oxide borders on purpose, guided by live spectroscopy, may yield cheaper gas clean-up catalysts that use less precious metal.
pmc-13480921:
Ren and colleagues set side by side in 2026 three decades of ischemic stroke data for China and the United States. Ischemic stroke, the kind from a blocked brain vessel, is a top cause of death and lost function in both lands. They drew counts from the Global Burden of Disease bank for 1990 to 2023. Trends were split by age and birth group, and the team cast counts ahead to the year 2035.

The two lands part ways. China's new case rate by age ticked up, while death rates by age fell by more than half. In the United States, rates by age fell across new cases, deaths, and lost years. Rates of living with past stroke rose in both. Raw case loads will still swell by 2035 in both lands, as crowds age. The authors urge more stroke proofing and care funds.
pmc-13482621:
Barre and Mohamud survey Mogadishu households in 2026 on what would make them pay for renewable energy, modeling the decision with the theory of planned behavior. They handed a set questionnaire to 300 home bill payers who understood energy costs, and 255 clean responses survived into the analysis. The model links readiness to pay with attitudes, social norms, personal control beliefs, green concern, cost beliefs, and buying intention.

The model explained 42.8 percent of the spread in readiness to pay, a moderate showing its adjusted figure of 40.2 percent roughly confirms for this sample. Five drivers pushed readiness upward significantly: intention, green concern, perceived control, social norms, and attitude toward green power among households surveyed. Beliefs about the cost of green energy showed no significant link, and intention strengthened several of the other drivers, a pattern the authors hand to policy makers planning adoption campaigns.
pmc-13483521:
Yingxuan Rong and co-authors compare three keyhole surgery routes for pinched neck nerves in a 2026 network meta-analysis. The routes differ by channel: a single slim scope, a two-portal scope, and a wide-channel scope. Twelve retrospective studies covering 939 patients fed a statistical web that mixes head-to-head and indirect comparisons.

The wide-channel route finished operations fastest, beating the slim scope by about twenty-six minutes and the two-portal route by about sixteen. Neck pain, arm pain, daily function scores, and complication rates stayed statistically even across all three. Rankings crowned the wide channel only on speed. Because every study looked backward rather than randomising patients, the authors warn the speed edge may reflect bias. Fair prospective trials remain the missing proof.
pmc-13486721:
Bozorgzad Fahadan and colleagues pitted two exercise therapies against each other for women with chronic low back pain that has no specific structural cause. Core stability training strengthens trunk muscles, while postural control training retrains balance and position sense. Their 2026 trial randomly assigned 51 middle-aged women equally among the two programs and a control group, scoring pain, disability, balance, and position sense before and after.

Both programs cut pain by roughly two and a half to three points on the scales used in this trial. Disability scores fell by about fourteen points under both programs, far beyond the control group's change. Postural training pulled ahead specifically on lumbo-pelvic position sense, the ability to feel where the lower back sits. Bozorgzad Fahadan recommends blending both approaches, matched to each patient's particular deficits.
pmc-13486821:
Hosseinnezhad and Sabri designed a portable radon sensor around a cadmium telluride crystal, simulating the whole tool before building it. Radon gas seeps from soil and its decay products cause lung cancer in non-smokers, so homes and workplaces need tracking. Their 2026 study coupled particle-transport model run with electronics model run and a computer-modeled housing, testing performance across radon levels, heat and damp ranges expected indoors.

The design reached a response of 0.15 counts per second for each unit of radon level in the model runs. It distinguished decay energies sharply, with resolution better than two percent at the main alpha energy tested. Significant concentration changes registered within fifteen minutes, fast enough for practical alerts. Hosseinnezhad presents the coupled model run method as a reusable recipe for designing compact radiation sensors.
pmc-13487821:
Makoto Nojo and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 35-year-old woman with repeated night-time anaphylaxis that was first blamed on Anisakis, a fish parasite. Careful history showed every attack followed condomless intercourse, while condom use prevented symptoms entirely. Skin prick testing and a basophil activation test, which measures allergic cell responses in blood, both supported allergy to proteins in her partner's semen.

Clinicians describe how seafood avoidance failed to stop the attacks, which helped rule out the first explanation. They explain the simple semen preparation used for testing in a routine clinic. In vitro fertilization avoided exposure to seminal plasma and led to a healthy birth, which the authors present as a practical route to pregnancy for similar patients.
pmc-13488021:
Ahmet Yuce and colleagues study a blood ratio as a marker of erectile dysfunction in a 2026 retrospective analysis. The ratio divides fibrinogen, a clotting protein tied to inflammation, by albumin, a common blood protein. Records covered men seen between 2020 and 2025, with 214 patients in the erectile dysfunction group and 210 controls who had full measures and lab results available for comparison.

The ratio averaged clearly higher in patients than in controls, and higher values tracked with worse scores on a standard five-question erection scale in the reported analysis. A high cutoff was very specific but missed many cases, so the authors frame the ratio as support for diagnosis rather than a stand-alone test. They argue the link fits vessel and inflammation theories of the condition.
pmc-13488221:
Chun-Yan Sun and colleagues build a scale that gauges how well caregivers can support teenagers who self-injure without suicidal intent in a 2026 scale development study. No standard tool existed for this supporting ability, which spans knowledge, attitudes, daily practice, caregiver health, relationships, and use of resources. Fifteen experts refined draft items over two rounds of advice, and 431 caregivers filled in the scale so its structure and consistency could be tested.

The final scale holds thirty-two items across five dimensions, after weak items were cut by factor analysis. Scores hung together well, the five parts split cleanly, and a second model backed the structure in the reported checks. The authors offer the tool for assessing families and targeting support programs.
pmc-13490021:
Zengpeng Sun and others describe an exceptionally rare liver tumour containing two distinct cancers side by side. In 2026, the case report concerns a fifty-four-year-old man with hepatitis B-related liver scarring and three liver lesions, two cancers and one benign growth. Imaging suggested different findings for each lesion, and biopsy showed one as hepatocellular cancer and another as cholangiocarcinoma.

Surgery was not feasible, so the patient received interventional therapy, immune care, and chemo. By nine months, both cancers had shrunk a lot, by roughly sixty percent and seventy-two percent, with good general condition and normal routine blood tests. The authors review only two earlier definitive cases and offer this outcome as a reference for treating unresectable collision tumours.
pmc-13491821:
Yunanji Zhou and four colleagues quantify in 2026 the hidden cost of delivering liquid traditional Chinese medicine to older rural patients with chronic lung disease. The decoctions are bulky and heat-sensitive, needing cold-chain handling across long distances. Lacking real route data, the team built a four-stage simulation from national survey microdata, facility statistics, machine learning, and cost modeling.

Modeled distance to care averaged roughly ten kilometers for rural residents against under three for urban ones, and one in nine rural patients sat beyond fifteen kilometers. Delivery costs for rural areas beat urban benchmarks under every assumption tested, with the most expensive rural deliveries reaching several times city prices. No subsidy level in the scanned range produced stable cooperation among all parties, so the authors demand local pilot data before any national scheme.
pmc-13492321:
Yunjuan Sun and others describe implanting a leadless pacemaker in a pregnant woman without iodinated contrast and with minimal X-ray contact. In 2026, the case concerns a woman thirteen weeks pregnant with intermittent complete heart block, pauses up to 5.2 seconds, and repeated fainting. As a dancer, she declined a standard transvenous pacemaker.

Guided mainly by transthoracic echocardiography, the team tracked the guidewire, sheath, giving catheter, and device in real time, using belly shielding and only a low dose of fluoroscopy in the end. The approach shows that sound scans can largely replace contrast and X-rays for leadless pacing when fetal safety demands it.
pmc-13492421:
Lee, Cho, and Park wrote in 2026 a commentary on a fresh study of blood thinners and hidden cancer. The study they discuss used Korean health records for close to seven thousand people with atrial fibrillation, a shaky heart rhythm, who had just started oral anticoagulant drugs. These drugs cut stroke risk but can unmask slow bleeds. The study team tracked shifts in hemoglobin, the red blood protein, in the year after the drugs began.

About one in thirteen patients lost a large chunk of hemoglobin with no clear bleed to blame. Those patients went on to get a cancer diagnosis at a higher rate than peers whose levels held steady. The link ran strongest for gut cancers, and the same group also faced higher death and major bleed risks. Lee and co-authors frame the drop as an early alarm bell that should spark a search for hidden tumors.
pmc-13492521:
Sonja Hoover and four colleagues price out in 2026 what a community cancer support center actually spends guiding patients through their illness. Michelle's Place, a California nonprofit, offers navigation plus education and support groups to patients and families. The team collected salaries, staff time diaries, and non-labor costs, then split spending between core navigation work and extras aimed at relatives.

Helping one client cost about six hundred thirty-nine dollars in total. Core activities such as intake assessments and hunting down financial assistance consumed roughly four hundred sixty-four dollars of that figure. Family-oriented extras added about one hundred seventy-five dollars per client. Published cost figures for nonprofit navigation programs are rare, and the authors offer theirs as a budgeting anchor for funders and planners.
pmc-13493821:
Diella and co-authors tested intensive robot-assisted walking training for people with hereditary spastic paraplegia, an inherited condition that stiffens the legs and weakens walking. Forty patients, including 20 children, joined the 2026 pilot programme in Italy. For three weeks they trained five days a week, mixing sessions in a robotic gait device with conventional therapy. The team measured walking, balance, motor skills, and quality of life before and after, plus three months later.

The clearest gain came in the six-minute walk test, where patients covered more ground after training, a change the authors found statistically significant. Timed walking, balance scores, and a broad motor function scale also improved, and a severity rating suggested symptoms eased. Detailed gait analysis, however, showed no significant change in how the walking pattern itself looked. Patients reported better perceived physical health. The authors call for studies in more uniform patient groups.
pmc-13494221:
Scull and Benitez review bovine leukemia virus, a widespread cattle infection, through a One Health lens that links animal, human, and environmental wellbeing. The virus infects more than four fifths of dairy herds in many regions. Yet most infected cows never show the cancer it can cause, so its costs get ignored. Their 2026 review gathers evidence on milk output and composition, udder health, farm economics, and the unresolved question of whether the virus reaches people.

Infected cows give less milk with reduced fat, protein, and protective components. That thins the food value of a staple that poor households and young children depend on. Immune weakening from the virus also invites mastitis, compounding losses. Reports of viral traces in human tissue recur but fall short of proving transmission, the authors stress. They call the virus a silent drag on food security deserving coordinated control.
pmc-13495321:
Pengchao Zhang and colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, two platelet-rich plasma protocols for mild meniscal tears in the knee. The meniscus is a cartilage pad that cushions the joint, and low-grade tears often ache without needing full repair. One protocol gave a series of ultrasound-guided shots around the meniscus over six weeks. The other paired scope surgery with a single shot inside the joint.

The review covered forty patients, twenty per protocol, followed for six months. No serious problems occurred. Both groups improved strongly: pain scores fell by about five points, and knee function scores climbed steeply. Pain paths matched between groups. Function scores leaned higher at six months for the surgery-plus-shot group. The authors stress the gap is descriptive only, a hint for a proper trial rather than a verdict, since patients were not assigned by lot.
pmc-13495521:
Dene Betz leads a large team comparing, in a 2026 mouse study, gene activity in the brain cortex beside a stroke and on the opposite side. Recovery peaks in a brief window after stroke, and repair was thought to center on tissue near the injury. The team sequenced RNA from both regions seven days after a clot-based stroke in male and female mice.

Both sides, injured and untouched, switched on the same inflammation program, rich in signals tied to reactive microglia, the brain's immune cells. The far side showed no distinct profile of its own; it echoed its injured partner. The shared response held in both sexes, and six weeks later both sexes grew comparable new wiring from the far side toward the injury. The authors argue that stroke recovery is a whole-cortex affair, not a local one, which widens where therapies might aim.
pmc-13495921:
Deng and co-authors use Denmark's national registries to ask whether a mother's thyroid disease, or the medicines used for it, raises her child's risk of cancer. Thyroid problems are common in women of childbearing age, but earlier evidence was patchy. Their 2026 case-control study matched 2,521 children diagnosed with cancer between 1973 and 2016 against 63,014 children without cancer. It then pulled mothers' diagnoses and prescriptions from national registers.

One condition stood out: children of mothers with goiter, an enlarged thyroid, had roughly double the odds of any childhood cancer in the adjusted analysis. Higher odds again appeared for leukaemia and lymphoma in particular. Neither underactive nor overactive thyroid showed a clear link, though the authors caution those analyses had limited statistical power. Reassuringly, mothers' thyroid medication itself carried no increased risk. The team stresses the small numbers behind the goiter finding and calls for replication first.
pmc-13499921:
Cierra M Keith leads a 2026 study asking whether memory failure works the same way in Alzheimer's disease that begins early in life as in the usual late-onset form. Holding onto new memories, called episodic memory, is the hallmark problem in both, yet onset groups might lean on different brain regions. Using memory clinic data for 180 people with the amnestic, memory-led form of the disease, the team compared several memory measures and their ties to volume and thickness in signature brain areas.

No difference appeared in memory performance between early-onset and late-onset groups on any examined measure. Links between memory processes and brain structure were likewise mostly similar across groups. One exception stood out, since memory consolidation tied more strongly to thinning in a left parietal region in the early-onset group. That region helps integrate senses and language, hinting it carries extra weight there.
pmc-13500721:
Rahul Biswas, Rakesh Salunke, and Sadik Khan present a 2026 remote-sensing study of ground movement across the Mississippi River Delta. The team processed 461 pairs of Sentinel-1 radar images from 2020 to 2024, covering about 22,043 square kilometres of southeastern Louisiana and coastal Mississippi. They used a small-baseline interferometric method that tracks slow surface change over time. A key step filtered the radar signal using different quality thresholds for each land cover class, such as developed land, farmland, forest, and marsh.

Measured line-of-sight speeds ranged widely, from sinking near 43.71 millimetres per year to rising near 30.23 millimetres per year. Marsh and wetland ground sank fastest, especially organic-rich, low-lying areas, while parts of the southwestern coast rose where sediment accumulates. Readings at two NOAA stations were checked against satellite navigation measurements for validation.
pmc-13501721:
Razan Ahmed Alawaz leads a three-author team reporting a 2026 case of chronic oculomotor nerve palsy in a teenager, traced to an old sphenoid sinus lesion. A 16-year-old boy had a long outward drift of the right eye and growing limits on eye movement from early childhood. Examination showed restriction of inward, upward, and downward gaze, a wide outward squint, and a fixed dilated pupil, matching third cranial nerve palsy. The right eyelid did not droop despite the motor deficit.

His history included a sphenoid sinus lesion treated years earlier with endoscopic surgery and partial removal. Tissue study had shown a histiocyte-rich lesion wrapped in fibrosis. MRI showed surgical changes and arrested development of that sinus, with no returning mass. It also showed fatty wasting of two eye muscles from denervation. The authors stress that sinus disease near the cavernous sinus can damage eye nerves in children.
pmc-13503021:
Jason Liew reports a 2026 lung case in which a year's worth of tuberculosis investigation ended with a steroid prescription instead. A 65-year-old non-smoker with diabetes and hypertension carried a waxing and waning cough for twelve months, with chest infiltrates that migrated between scans and a stubborn right upper lobe opacity. At a specialist centre, sputum smears, gene assays, and cultures all came back negative, ruling the infection out rigorously.

Attention then shifted to the blood and the pattern: a peak eosinophil count of 3.8 billion per litre on the reported scale, IgE of 729 international units per millilitre, and edge-heavy consolidations on high-resolution imaging. Vasculitis, fungi, and parasites were excluded. The patient declined the airway scope that would have sampled his airways, so chronic eosinophilic pneumonia was diagnosed clinically. Prednisolone at 30 milligrams daily produced dramatic relief within 48 hours and complete clearing of the shadows in four weeks.
pmc-13503721:
Siva Venkadesh and ten colleagues present a shared brain atlas that lines up regions across five species, in a 2026 paper. The set spans mouse, rat, marmoset, macaque, and human brains. Past atlases were built one species at a time, which blocked fair comparison across them.

The team built the atlas from averaged brain forms with matched tissue maps, then checked it four ways. Checks covered match with known human maps, fit inside species maps, steady placement across species, and dye-tracer links in mouse and marmoset. Each region got a score for how sure its match across species is. Sense and movement links held up well across species, while links for higher thought drifted more. The atlas is free for others to use.
pmc-13503921:
Caio Márcio Vasconcellos Cordeiro de Almeida leads a team selecting cacao clones for farms in Rondônia, Brazil, in a 2026 study. Brazil could grow its share of world cacao as output slips in the top producer states. Local clones must yield well and hold steady across years under tree shade.

The team tracked 30 clones in shaded plots over seven harvests. Yields ranged widely, nearly sevenfold from worst to best, with a mean near 476 kilos of dry beans per hectare. Genetic spread and heritability were high, which favors selection gains. A factor model best captured how rankings shifted across years. Two years of harvests sufficed to pick clones in late breeding rounds. Five clones combined top yield with the steadiest record.
pmc-13504821:
Marco Carfagno leads a team exploring how people with eating disorders rethink illness and recovery during group therapy, in a 2026 interview study. Recovery is often counted as symptom loss alone, which can miss what change means to the patient. Group settings may reshape those meanings.

Ten adult outpatients spoke at the end of a group program set within broader care. Early on, most framed their illness through food, weight, and control. Over time they spoke more of feelings, relationships, and self-worth. Recovery became a winding path of awareness, acceptance, and connection rather than a finish line. The group gave belonging and a mirror for reflection, though it also stirred shame and fear of judgment. The authors name feeling skills and identity work as recovery targets.
pmc-13505021:
Saime Esin Güney leads a team comparing mouth health in child leukemia survivors at early and late stages after treatment, in a 2026 study. Cancer drugs given in childhood can scar growing teeth and dry the mouth. Whether those harms fade with time was the open question.

The study covered 38 survivors aged five to eighteen and 20 healthy siblings. Tooth decay scores ran higher and saliva flow lower in survivors seen within about three years of treatment than in those seen later. Tooth shape faults, like small teeth and odd roots, appeared in most survivors but few siblings, and they did not fade with time. Age and time since treatment each predicted decay scores. The authors urge close dental watch in the first years after treatment.
pmc-13505121:
Aykut Can Balkanlıoğlu and Izzet Acikan test cold plasma surface treatment for early dental implant hold. In 2026, the forward-looking single-center randomized within-patient trial compares untreated implants with cold atmospheric plasma, vacuum plasma, and argon jet plasma, each applied sixty seconds before placement. The trial analyzed forty implants in ten patients. Implant hold dips transiently before biological secondary hold takes over.

All implants remained in place with no adverse events, and baseline stability quotients were comparable. Controls dipped at day twenty-eight while plasma-treated implants rose steadily, with a clear group-by-time interaction. At day fifty-six, plasma groups exceeded controls by 10.0, 8.9, and 8.3 stability units respectively. The authors call for larger forward-looking, site-standardized trials.
pmc-13506121:
Justin Hyde and colleagues review how aneurysmal bone cysts behave when they grow in the spine or sacrum rather than long bones. These blood-filled cysts are benign yet locally aggressive, and in the spine they often start in the rear elements and push toward the canal. The review, built mainly on the last ten years of literature, covers diagnosis, biopsy, surgery, and add-on treatments.

Imaging can hint at the diagnosis through fluid levels inside an expanding lesion, but scans cannot rule out cancer look-alikes, so biopsy stays essential. Treatment is tailored to nerve pressure, stability, deformity, and lesion size. Options run from scraping the cyst out to wider removal with stabilisation, sometimes helped by blocking its blood supply, injecting doxycycline, or giving denosumab. Cyst return links most strongly with incomplete removal and younger age, and the authors ask for prospective spine-specific comparisons.
pmc-13507021:
Bing Sun, Jieyang Zhu, Yi Jiang, Sihui Chen, and Tao Zhang build, in 2026 work, a survival forecast for osteosarcoma based on genes tied to cell organelles. Osteosarcoma is the most common malignant bone tumor, often seen in teens. The team screened gene data from patient cohorts and kept three genes linked to outlook: ACSS2, CLTCL1, and PLD3.

Their three-gene score divided the cohort into high-risk and low-risk groups whose survival differed clearly, and it held up in a second cohort. Risk groups also differed in response to four drugs in lab data. Cell tests supported a real role for ACSS2 in tumor behavior. The score could help sort patients and point to new treatment targets.
pmc-13507221:
Junkyu Park and colleagues explore, in 2026 work, side-effect patterns of GLP-1 obesity drugs in real-world reports and search computationally for herbs linked to those patterns. Reports came from the United States adverse event system for 2015 to 2025, totaling 142705 reports, with 4090 tied to obesity use. Stomach and gut events dominated, and most reports involved female patients.

Onset clustered in the first month, while one drug showed more late cases after a year. Strong signals appeared for gallbladder, pancreas, kidney, and clotting events for some drug pairs. Network models ranked familiar medicinal herbs as top candidates for study. The authors stress that all herb links are hypotheses needing lab and clinical proof.
pmc-13507821:
Ayushi Saxena and six co-authors review whether a fast form of brain stimulation works as well as the standard daily form for hard-to-treat depression, in 2026 work. Standard treatment uses magnetic pulses over several weeks of daily visits. The faster option, called accelerated iTBS, compresses sessions into a much shorter span. The review gathered 25 studies that compared the two approaches in adults whose depression had not eased with usual care.

Across those studies, the fast approach matched the standard one on easing depression symptoms. Effects on thinking skills looked just as safe in both groups. Shorter schedules also lowered the travel and time burden that can block access to care. The authors present the fast option as a practical choice for clinics and for patients who cannot manage weeks of daily visits.
pmc-13508221:
Meng Zhou, Liru Zhao, Dongbo Li, and Zhongle Cheng combine a rapid lab fingerprint method with machine learning to spot drug-resistant bacteria, in 2026 work. The target germ, Acinetobacter baumannii, causes hospital infections, and its carbapenem-resistant form limits treatment choices. Standard resistance testing is slow. The team collected 301 bacterial samples, over half of them resistant, and took two spectra from each. Five learning models were trained on part of the data and judged on a held-out set, split by sample to avoid leakage.

A flexible way of slicing the spectra into bins beat fixed slicing for every model. The best model reached near-perfect sorting scores on the test set, with accuracy above nine in ten. An explanation method highlighted which parts of the fingerprint drove the calls. The authors argue this pairing could flag resistant infections sooner, guiding drug choice and infection control while tests still run.
pmc-13508321:
Xuan-Geng Deng and five co-authors compare two ways to stop spinal fluid leaks during neck disc surgery, in work published in 2026. The surgery, called ACDF, treats worn or injured neck discs. A tear in the membrane around the spinal cord is a rare but serious slip during the operation. Standard care patches the tear and seals it with glue. The newer method plugs the space around the implant with bone wax, walling the leak off. Records covered patients with such tears from 2020 to 2025.

Among 1,311 operations, twenty-three patients had a leak, and all tears were small. Twelve were patched and eleven were sealed with wax. The patch route failed twice, needing extra drainage for lasting leaks. The wax route had no failures and no other complications after surgery. The authors suggest wax sealing is a dependable backup when patching proves awkward.
pmc-13508621:
Furkan Bahar and five co-authors compare clotting and bleeding risks between the two first-line drug routes for advanced melanoma, in 2026 work. Vein clots are a leading cause of illness in cancer patients, and both immune therapy pairs and targeted tablet pairs are standard openers. Adults starting either the immune pair or the targeted pair were matched one to one on background traits, giving 1,043 patients per group. Clots, bleeding, and death were tracked for six months.

The immune pair carried clearly higher clot risk: seven percent against about four percent in six months. Lung clots and leg vein clots each ran higher too. Bleeding, including brain and gut bleeding, did not differ between the groups. Deaths ran slightly higher with the immune pair, though that gap missed statistical firmness. They suggest clot prevention planning should weigh which melanoma opener a patient receives.
pmc-13510721:
Kotova and colleagues tested in 2026 whether two anti-inflammatory drugs ease the effects of long stress in zebrafish, small fish widely used to study mood disorders. Stress that lasts for weeks can inflame the brain, and that swelling is tied to anxiety and depression. The team wanted to know if calming the swelling also calms behavior.

Fish went through two weeks of unpredictable stress, with or without drug treatment. Minocycline, given for the full two weeks, cut depression-like freezing in a tail test and lowered both pro- and anti-inflammatory gene signals in the brain. Nimesulide, given for one week, had a narrower effect: it eased anxiety-like behavior and brought two stress-raised inflammatory genes back to normal levels. The contrast shows the two drugs act on stress in distinct ways.
pmc-13511721:
Sab Siddiq, Shabnam Cheetham, Clare E. Pain, Eve M. D. Smith, Sizheng Steven Zhao, Liza J. McCann, and David M. Hughes gather evidence on extra health conditions that travel with rheumatic diseases starting in childhood, in a 2026 systematic review. The three diseases covered are juvenile idiopathic arthritis, childhood-onset lupus, and juvenile dermatomyositis, a muscle and skin condition. Three major databases were searched without limits, following standard review guidance.

Patients faced a higher risk of a wide range of added conditions in both childhood and adult life. That extra burden reaches beyond the primary disease and weighs on quality of life across the whole life course. The authors urge proactive, multi-specialty watch and care for these added conditions. Current studies show weak spots, above all thin long-term follow-up, so firmer risk figures for childhood-onset disease still need building.
pmc-13515321:
Li and colleagues published a 2026 study on a bird flu virus taken from chickens in Jiangsu, China. H9N2 flu circulates widely in poultry and can infect people occasionally. The isolate, gathered in March 2025, came from a chicken flock. The team read its genes and tested it in mice, chickens, and ducks.

Gene trees placed the virus in a fast-spreading Chinese lineage mix. Key changes hinted at stronger copying power inside mammal cells after infection. In mice, the virus grew in lungs and noses with no prior training rounds. Chickens caught and passed it more readily than ducks did. Chicken-to-duck spread worked better than duck-to-duck in their pens. Stronger farm surveillance is the team's closing plea to authorities.
pmc-13517021:
Gabriela Christina Kuhl and four colleagues engineer a safer therapeutic bacterium in a 2026 proof-of-concept study. Live bacterial medicines need two things regulators demand: they must not escape control, and their added genes must stay put. The team used CRISPR-based editing to swap one gene in a standard E coli strain. The swap removed the bacterium's ability to make certain amino acids, so it starves without supplements, and inserted a therapeutic gene in the same step.

The built-in starvation worked and lifted when the missing nutrients were fed. The chromosome-based strain kept its therapeutic activity, the red-cell-bursting effect of its cargo protein, and grew as well as the plasmid version. Both versions delivered DNA into those cells. Kuhl's team presents the single-step design as a cleaner chassis for future live medicines.
pmc-13517121:
Guillermo Eduardo Cuéllar-Nevárez and five colleagues review how to diagnose tuberculosis in people living with HIV in a 2026 article. The pairing is deadly because weakened immunity makes TB hide: fewer bacilli, odd symptoms, disease outside the lungs. Standard tools, sputum smears, cultures, and chest X-rays, miss many such cases. The authors walk through each option's accuracy, practicality, and barriers to real-world use.

Rapid molecular tests now catch the germ and drug resistance early, though sputum-free and body-wide disease still slip through. A urine test helps the severely ill, and a newer version promises more. Blood signatures and computer-read chest images may sharpen screening and triage. Cuéllar-Nevárez's team argues no single test suffices. They propose combined algorithms matched to local resources, stitching microbe tests, urine tests, imaging, and host-response tools into one pathway.
pmc-13519021:
Sejoong Ahn and a large team mine a Korean emergency department registry in 2026 for clues on steroids in septic shock, a debate usually argued from intensive care data. Records covered 5,127 adults treated between 2015 and 2023 across many centers. Timing and dose were examined among patients given hydrocortisone after blood-pressure drugs began.

After adjustment, steroid use linked to lower 28-day mortality, with odds reduced by about a quarter. The benefit concentrated in patients also receiving vasopressin. Among 1,529 hydrocortisone patients, waiting longer to start, starting at higher pressor doses, and exceeding 300 milligrams per day each linked to higher mortality. Ahn and colleagues stress the findings are observational and hypothesis-generating, not proof.
pmc-13520121:
Siddiq and colleagues trace how a yeast gene's control region evolved in this 2026 study. The gene, TDH3, helps yeast process sugars. Its promoter became more active in the baker's yeast lineage. A promoter is the DNA stretch that sets how strongly a gene runs. The team compared promoters across Saccharomyces species to find which DNA changes caused the rise and how they acted.

Much of the increase came from changes sitting between the well-known binding sites of two regulator proteins, not at the sites themselves. Those changes raised expression levels while leaving the timing pattern of the response untouched. Their effect appeared only when a third regulator, TYE7p, was present, suggesting the changes work by shaping how the whole regulator complex assembles on the DNA.
pmc-13520321:
Chenjiao Hou and colleagues describe in 2026 miniature heart tissues grown from reprogrammed human stem cells, used to test drug harm and benefit without animal hearts. The tissues beat on their own and copy key features of real heart muscle.

Known heart-damaging and heart-protecting drugs were applied to the tissues, including a cancer drug noted for heart injury and a birth-defect drug used as a harm check. Beating, survival signals and injury models for heart attack and thickened heart muscle were tracked. Responses matched expected drug effects, supporting the tissues as a screening platform. Further validation would be needed before routine drug decisions rely on them.
pmc-13520521:
Kai Zhao and Xiangcai Meng test in 2026 whether a brief hydrogen peroxide soak can raise medicinal compound levels in peony roots used for two traditional remedies. Farmed roots have lost quality as demand grew, while mild stress is known to switch on protective chemistry in plants.

Fresh roots from two peony lines were soaked at several peroxide strengths. At the middle strength on day two, eight measured compounds rose markedly in one line, with gains ranging from roughly one fifth to over three quarters. Six compounds rose in the other line as well. Follow-up tests with blockers probe whether reactive oxygen signalling drives the gains.
pmc-13521021:
Chen and colleagues studied in 2026 the blood ratio of heterophils to lymphocytes, a simple immune marker in poultry, in Yellow-legged Ma chickens. The basis of this ratio inside tissues was unclear. The team picked birds with very high or very low ratios from 113 chickens and split them by sex. They combined liver and spleen tissue checks with blood chemistry and gene and metabolite profiling.

Chen found no clear differences between high- and low-ratio birds in tissue structure, liver enzyme levels, or oxidative stress markers. The molecular picture split sharply by sex, though. Hens with low ratios showed stronger immune gene activity across T cell and cytokine pathways. Roosters differed instead in chemokine, Toll-like receptor, and related signalling. One gene, CCR2, stood out as a shared node. The authors frame the ratio as a sex-dependent window on liver immune state, useful for breeding.
pmc-13522421:
Firew Tekle Bobo and co-authors examine, in a 2026 Australian study, how national data sources define and count psychosocial disability, meaning disability linked to mental health conditions. Five sources were compared, including disability and health surveys, a mental health survey, the Census, and records from the National Disability Insurance Scheme. Definitions were reviewed first, followed by a comparison of prevalence figures.

The sources proved inconsistent, because each was built for a different purpose and covered different conditions. Broad surveys included developmental and degenerative conditions, while the insurance scheme covered only severe illness with major limits on daily function. Reported rates ranged widely, so the authors warn researchers and policymakers to account for these differences before using the figures for planning or funding choices.
pmc-13522521:
Ibrahim Aldawood, Ahmad Althumali, Syed Mansoor Ali, and Saad Aldawood grow nickel oxide films of different thicknesses on flexible plastic in a 2026 materials study. Nickel oxide conducts positive charges and is transparent, making it useful as a charge-transport layer in solar cells. Films from ten to forty nanometers thick were deposited on plastic coated with a clear conductor and then examined by several methods.

Thin films formed scattered islands, while thicker films became compact and much smoother, with roughness falling sharply. Light emission peaked at thirty nanometers, and electrical resistance fell as thickness grew, reflecting more charge carriers. The authors identify films in the thirty to forty nanometer range as the most promising for flexible solar and light-based devices.
pmc-13523221:
Ella Petter and colleagues use tumor size dynamics to find mutations that shape treatment response in lung cancer in a 2026 study. Standard genetic studies rely on survival outcomes, while clinicians in practice follow how tumors shrink and grow on scans. A new framework was built to model repeated tumor readings from roughly seventeen thousand radiology reports at a major cancer center.

The method found twenty-seven mutations linked to uneven response to common treatments, with both protective and harmful effects. Two findings were validated in an external drug sensitivity screen. Thirteen further mutations tracked rates of growth and response across the whole treatment course, nine of them invisible to conventional survival models. Results held in an advanced-stage subgroup, supporting tumor dynamics as a complement to survival analysis.
pmc-13523321:
Ngwa Niba Rawlings, Mark Stephen Bailey, and Orin Courtenay pool evidence on volatile pyrethroid spatial repellents in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. These devices release insecticide vapor to protect a surrounding space from mosquitoes and sand flies. Forty-nine studies with more than one hundred fifty datasets were included, covering human infection trials and trap-based insect studies, mostly testing one active ingredient.

Trial data suggested protection of about half against malaria parasites and about one third against dengue and Zika viruses, with a single trial giving similar protection against leishmania. Trap studies showed substantial falls in captured insects, with estimates varying by trap type. Outdoor use looked no worse than indoor use. The authors present spatial repellents as a promising complement to existing vector control tools.
pmc-13523521:
Shuai Yang and others test, in a 2026 imaging study, whether pairing two magnetic resonance mapping methods can grade knee cartilage wear and meniscus injury in knee osteoarthritis. Standard scans show structure late, while mapping reads tissue chemistry earlier. One method, sped up by AI compressed sensing, was paired with conventional mapping.

The study took in 56 patients with knee osteoarthritis and 30 healthy volunteers between August 2025 and February 2026, all scanned at 3 tesla. Both measures were higher in patients than controls across regions, and values separated mild from severe subgroups. Joint mapping reached the strongest accuracy for cartilage wear and slightly better accuracy for meniscal injury than either method alone.
