The authors propose the pairing for earlier, stage based management decisions.
pmc-13524921:
Victor Miguel Sierra Marquina, Maria del Carmen Pardo, and Alba Maria Franco-Pereira develop an overlap measure for judging biomarkers. Their 2026 statistical methods paper targets markers that must separate three stages of Alzheimer's disease. Tests sort people into probable Alzheimer's, mild cognitive impairment, or normal aging, and the usual scoring tools were built for two groups.

Their overlap measure extends a known index to three groups, with both parametric and nonparametric forms plus bootstrap confidence intervals. Practice runs checked how well the estimators behaved. They set it against the volume under the ROC surface, the standard three-way accuracy measure. A longitudinal neuropsychological data set on biomarker tracking of disease stages shows the method. The authors aim to speed drug work by finding markers that track progression earlier.
pmc-13526721:
Xiaoli Chen, Zhuo An, Changhong Li, and Jinxia Zhao test, in a 2026 lab study, whether pooled antibodies from rheumatoid arthritis patients can drive the bone eating cells behind joint erosion. These anti-citrullinated protein antibodies mark the disease, yet their direct effect on osteoclast growth was debated. Antibodies were purified from pooled blood of 37 positive patients.

Purified antibodies kept an intact structure and bound citrullinated vimentin. Monocytes from healthy donors and patients were then grown into osteoclasts with standard growth factors, with or without the antibodies. Antibody treatment did not clearly raise osteoclast numbers, marker gene expression, or bone resorption pit area against controls. The authors conclude any bone effect likely needs a richer tissue setting or special antibody properties their setup missed.
pmc-13527121:
Christopher F. Sharpley, G. Lorenzo Odierna, Vicki Bitsika, and Christopher B. Watson review, in a 2026 systematic narrative review, sensory hyposensitivity in major depression, meaning dulled responsiveness across the five senses. Individual studies had reported blunting in single senses, yet no review had covered vision, hearing, taste, touch, and smell together.

The search gathered fifty-one individual studies and five reviews focused on smell. Findings were organized by the form the blunting takes, the brain processes proposed to underlie it, and its possible function. Explanations split between peripheral sensory dulling and central cognitive dysfunction. The authors propose hyposensitivity may serve as an escape from an aversive environment, giving the depressed person a form of relief. Clinical translation ideas and future research directions close the review.
pmc-13527921:
Esa Ala-Ruona and eight colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for a randomized trial of integrative music therapy for adults with depression-related problems, including anxiety, work stress, and exhaustion. Participants aged 18 to 65 will receive improvisational music therapy twice a week for six weeks, starting each session with slow paced breathing.

Four groups will compare the core therapy with versions adding music listening, vibroacoustic treatment, or both; one group waits as a control. The main outcome is psychological distress, with depression, anxiety, burnout, quality of life, and difficulty naming emotions also measured. Registered in advance, the trial aims to show which combination of elements helps and who responds best.
pmc-13528021:
Ning Yao and seven colleagues chart chickenpox in Chongqing, China, in a 2026 study of disease patterns, immunity, and costs. Routine records from 2011 to 2024 held 301,714 cases. Over half were in children under fifteen. A 2024 blood survey of 960 people measured protection levels. Cost data came from thousands of clinic and hospital cases.

Overall, about seventy-eight percent of people carried antibodies. Children showed a clear gap, at about seventy-one percent protected. Two vaccine doses protected far better than one dose. Adults over fifty had the highest levels and the lowest recent case rates. Hospital care for children cost more than for older patients. The authors recommend wider two-dose coverage to cut both illness and costs.
pmc-13531621:
Jakub Chmiel and co-authors link in 2026 the tally of cardiovascular risk factors to dangerous plaque features across all heart arteries. Light-based imaging inside the vessels of 131 patients catalogued 534 plaques and their traits. Risk factors split into changeable habits and conditions versus fixed traits such as age and family history.

More risk factors meant more plaques, more thin-capped fatty plaques, and more fragile features such as cholesterol crystals and tiny vessels. After adjustment, only the changeable burden predicted higher vulnerability. The message supports aggressive control of pressure, lipids, diabetes, weight, and smoking.
pmc-13532221:
Anastasia Lambropoulou and colleagues find in 2026 two soil-bacterium peptides that restore frontline antibiotic power against enzyme-armed resistant gut bacteria. Screening natural products surfaced pinensin A and B from a soil species. These bacteria-killing enzymes, metallo-beta-lactamases, shrug off nearly every beta-lactam drug and have no approved blocker.

Both peptides returned the drug meropenem to full effect in 30 resistant clinical strains, dropping needed levels below the treatment threshold. The secret is tight zinc grabbing: the enzymes need zinc, and the peptides bind it at extremely low amounts. Further work as drug boosters is warranted.
pmc-13534421:
Ritu Gauraha, Ayush Kumar Agrawal, and Parul Dubey present in 2026 a hybrid framework that classifies sentiment in deepfake social media posts while showing its reasoning. Fake text is hard to judge, and most accurate models act as black boxes. Their dataset held 25,572 tweets split evenly between human and machine writing.

The method pairs transformer text embeddings with fuzzy rules that people can read. Across ten-fold checks it reached high accuracy and F1 scores, beating a strong baseline by a clear margin. Readers gain both performance and explanations that help analysts trust each call.
pmc-13534521:
Ozge Gundogdu, Erol Egrioglu, and Eren Bas propose in 2026 a forecasting method for nonlinear time series that blends Pythagorean fuzzy sets with a hybrid neural network. Fuzzy methods capture uncertainty well, yet their inputs grow large and lag choice is often unsystematic. Dimension reduction first compresses membership data into cleaner inputs.

A modified network paired with simple smoothing then models both linear and nonlinear patterns, with swarm optimisation setting all parameters. Tests on rolling windows of two major stock indices beat existing approaches. Readers in finance and engineering gain a systematic, ready-to-build forecasting framework.
pmc-13536621:
Shuang Zhang and colleagues compare in 2026 ultrasound cycloplasty with Ahmed valve implants for neovascular glaucoma, a severe eye pressure disease driven by abnormal new vessels. Eighty patients, one eye each, were split evenly between the two treatments and followed for six months. Pressure, drug counts, pain, vision, and complications were tracked over time.

Both methods lowered eye pressure well, and success rates were similar across the groups. By six months the ultrasound group showed steadier pressure and lower pain scores. The valve group had more complications, mainly tube blockage and plate exposure, favouring ultrasound on safety and comfort.
pmc-13536721:
Haoyu Wei and Xinhong Yang describe an inherited low fibrinogen case in a 2026 family report from China. Fibrinogen is a blood protein needed for clotting, and low levels can cause bleeding. A 28-year-old pregnant woman and her mother both showed low fibrinogen levels on lab tests. Gene sequencing searched for the cause, and delivery care was planned around the clotting weakness.

Testing found a new single-letter deletion in the FGA gene carried by both women, matching their low activity and low protein levels. Before a planned cesarean birth with spinal anesthesia, the patient received extra fibrinogen by vein. The baby girl was delivered safely without heavy bleeding. The authors stress combined lab and gene testing for diagnosis, counseling, and safe birth planning.
pmc-13536821:
Wei-Zhi Huang and co-authors probe how lidocaine, a common numbing drug, affects human mouth cells in a 2026 laboratory study. Beyond pain control, the drug may influence cancer growth and healing after surgery. Two cell lines were tested, one mouth cancer line and one normal gum line, using growth, flow, gene, protein, and electrical measures. Combinations with two standard cancer drugs were also checked.

Cancer cells grew less under lidocaine, with shifts in cell cycle, cell death, energy membranes, low-oxygen signals, and self-cleaning activity. Gum cells responded differently, with distinct cycle, death, and stress patterns. Lidocaine strengthened both cancer drugs in both cell lines. Electrical patterns for the drug alone resembled those for a drug pairing. The authors suggest wider roles for numbing drugs in oral cancer care.
pmc-13538221:
Franck Zekre and co-authors test blood antibodies to two gum bacteria in early spine arthritis in a 2026 cohort analysis. Both bacteria drive gum disease and have been linked to joint arthritis, raising questions about spine disease. Serum from 554 people in a French early back pain cohort was tested and sorted into spine arthritis types, with or without skin or bowel features, plus chronic back pain controls. Smoking was also considered.

Antibody levels overlapped strongly across all groups, with no clear gap between any arthritis type and controls for either bacterium. Adjusting for age, sex, weight, and smoking changed nothing, and smoking itself showed no sway on patterns. The authors conclude that blood responses to these two bacteria show no major link to early spine arthritis, while wider mouth imbalance remains possible.
pmc-13538521:
Esperança João Rafael and colleagues survey self-medication for COVID-19 among health students in Maputo, Mozambique, in a 2026 online study from November 2022. Students from three health training institutions answered questions on herbal and standard medicine use during the pandemic. Among 390 eligible respondents, most reported treating themselves, raising concern about habits that future clinicians may carry into practice and patient advice.

Herbal use dominated, led by eucalyptus steam inhalation, lemon, ginger, garlic, and onion across twenty-three plant types. Standard medicines reached about one third of students, led by an antibiotic also used without prescription. Three in ten students mixed both approaches. The authors call for curriculum teaching that confronts false beliefs, flags resistance risks from stray antibiotic use, and promotes evidence-based care.
pmc-13538821:
Jonas R Schaarup and colleagues test whether nerve damage to heart control tracks early heart failure in type 2 diabetes in a 2026 Danish clinic study. Two hundred patients from two outpatient clinics underwent reflex tests for the nerve condition, blood tests for a heart strain marker, and risk scoring, with symptom grading by a standard scale. Adjusted models probed the link overall and in symptom-free patients.

Forty percent of tested patients had the nerve condition, and over half of them showed raised heart strain marker levels versus under a quarter without it. Full adjustment tied the nerve condition to about sixfold higher odds of raised marker levels. The link held in patients without symptoms and at low-to-moderate risk scores. The authors suggest nerve testing could flag earlier heart failure stages.
pmc-13540321:
Elisa Buzzatti and a large Italian team report a 2026 letter. The subject is infection during treatment with gilteritinib. That oral drug treats a form of acute myeloid leukaemia. The cancer has returned or stopped responding in these patients. Trial reports lump infections into broad labels, leaving clinicians short on detail.

Eighteen centres tracked 123 adults from April 2020 to January 2025. Sixty percent had at least one documented infection. Lung infections came first, then bloodstream sepsis. Most episodes arrived within ninety days of starting treatment. Fungal disease clustered in patients with a stem cell transplant. Death from infection reached eighteen percent, far lower among responders.
pmc-13540921:
Leilei Zhang and six colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a deep learning model that predicts how candidate drugs will be absorbed, distributed, broken down, excreted, and whether they will prove toxic. Such ADMET traits decide clinical success, yet traditional models generalise poorly when data are thin.

Their model fuses a language-style network reading molecular sequences, a second network digesting global property descriptors, and fingerprint encodings of local substructures. It outperformed traditional methods and most rival pre-trained models on standard benchmarks. Fine-tuning on a self-built database of nearly half a million entries produced ninety-seven property predictors. A free online tool now offers 133 prediction endpoints.
pmc-13542121:
Xiong Li and colleagues simulate a drug carrier question in 2026. The compound is wogonin, from a traditional Chinese medicine herb. The carrier candidate is graphene, a flat carbon sheet. How the compound grips the sheet guides carrier design. The study works at atomic level throughout.

Quantum calculations ran alongside molecular dynamics runs. The dynamics lasted twenty nanoseconds of simulated time. Both agreed the molecule lies flatter on graphene. Its electron cloud spreads wider across the surface. Charge transfer was negligible between the pair. Gentle stacking forces dominate the grip. Binding energies were strongly favourable at two levels of theory. In simulated water, the pair stayed together throughout.
pmc-13542421:
Pound, Ainslie, and Wolf price out two technical rule changes in America's federal milk marketing orders, the Depression-era system that sets minimum dairy prices by end use. In 2025 the agriculture department dropped 500-pound barrels of cheddar from the cheese price survey and restored an older formula, the higher-of rule, for pricing fluid milk's skim component. Their 2026 analysis estimates what each change does to the prices farmers and processors actually face.

Removing barrels nudges the cheese survey price, and with it protein values, modestly upward, with the effect strongest when margins are thin. Restoring the higher-of rule lifts average class I skim prices by roughly a quarter of a dollar per hundredweight compared with the averaging rule it replaced. It hands the asymmetric risk of price spikes back from processors to producers.
pmc-13543521:
Zilin Wang's team published a 2026 study building a prognostic score for kidney cancer from genes tied to mitotic catastrophe, the cell-death route triggered when division goes badly wrong. Using cancer atlas data and outside cohorts, the team distilled a nine-gene signature and scored patients with two survival-learning methods. Scores were checked against stage, scan features, immune makeup, and mutations, and one standout gene, CCNF, was tested in cells and mouse tumours.

The signature separated high- and low-risk patients, with accuracy above 0.9 for one-, three-, and five-year survival in the main cohort. High scores tracked with advanced stage, blood-vessel growth, suppressive immune cells, and higher levels of the checkpoint proteins LAG3 and TIGIT. CCNF contributed most to the score; boosting it made cancer cells grow, move, and invade faster, through the mTOR pathway. It is offered as both marker and possible target.
pmc-13543621:
Li Xiao and colleagues published a 2026 survey of whether China's tuition-waived medical students, trained free in exchange for contracted rural service, actually intend to honour their contracts. The programme exists to staff underserved countryside clinics. Questionnaires based on the theory of planned behaviour reached 1,130 students in Hubei Province in 2023, and 1,114 valid replies were analysed for attitudes, social norms, and perceived control.

About seventy-five percent intended to comply. All three theory components mattered significantly. Several things nudged intention upward: voluntarily choosing the programme, believing rural work has value, family support, and a mother with more education. Peer compliance and familiarity with rural practice helped too, as did feeling that rural systems need highly trained doctors. Winning hearts before graduation, the authors argue, matters as much as the contract's legal weight for keeping doctors in the countryside.
pmc-13544721:
Ngokwe and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a lipoma, a benign fat tumor, inside the mouth of a 52-year-old woman. Oral lipomas are rare compared with lipomas elsewhere, and this one grew slowly without pain, pushing her face out of symmetry. The team removed it through the mouth under local anesthesia.

Tissue study after removal confirmed the diagnosis of a simple lipoma. At follow-up the facial asymmetry had faded and the wound healed well. Working through the mouth leaves no visible scar, which matters on the face. The report walks the full path from first exam to final check. It reminds clinicians that a soft, painless, slow mouth swelling in a middle-aged adult is often this harmless tumor, best confirmed by removing and testing it.
pmc-13545721:
Daniela Denier led a 2026 study of children with primary sclerosing cholangitis, a liver disease whose course varies widely from child to child. Instead of judging risk from a single blood test, the team modeled how one enzyme, GGT, moved over three years in 782 children from an international consortium. Statistical grouping sorted the children into four patterns of change.

The four groups fared very differently, with five-year survival without a transplant ranging from 74 percent to 98 percent. Children whose high GGT fell back to normal within a year did nearly as well as those who stayed low throughout. Baseline and six-month readings predicted group membership well, which could help doctors judge early whether treatment is working.
pmc-13546521:
Beibei Hua and colleagues examined in 2026 the role of FANCI, a protein from the Fanconi anemia DNA repair pathway, in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Using several public cancer datasets plus single-cell data, they found FANCI switched on at high levels in tumors, where it separated cancer tissue from normal tissue with high accuracy. High levels also tracked with shorter survival.

In cell experiments, raising FANCI pushed cancer cells to grow, spread, and resist death, while silencing it slowed tumors in mice and stalled the cell cycle. The protein was found physically bound to its pathway partner FANCD2 inside the nucleus. The authors propose FANCI as a possible marker for diagnosis and prognosis, and as a candidate drug target.
pmc-13546721:
Seikh Masudur Rahman and colleagues surveyed in 2026 what Bangladeshi consumers believe about broiler chicken meat and what shapes how much of it they buy. Interviews with 369 consumers in rural, semi-urban, and urban areas measured common fears on a five-point scale and linked purchases to income, schooling, job, and place of residence.

Concerns about hygiene at processing points scored highest. Next came beliefs that broiler meat carries unsafe chemicals, growth hormones, heavy metals, and even cancer risk. Many also saw it as less nutritious than local Deshi chicken. City living and more schooling raised consumption, while higher income and professional jobs lowered it. The authors urge better food safety communication to correct misconceptions.
pmc-13547221:
Junchen Liu and colleagues asked in 2026 how deep a residual neural network should be when forecasting electricity demand a short time ahead, a task grid operators depend on for scheduling. They tested two versions of the architecture across many depth settings on two real datasets, one from New England with strong seasonal swings and one Malaysian dataset rich in weather variables.

Depth helped in a bent, dataset-dependent way rather than a straight line. Medium-depth networks suited the seasonal New England data best, while shallower networks did better on the Malaysian data, where extra layers added complexity without gains. Squeezing the weather inputs through principal component analysis made the Malaysian models steadier across depths. The authors advise choosing depth together with the data's character.
pmc-13547321:
Hamza Tahiri and co-authors built in 2026 an automatic tuning method for a sliding mode controller, a robust but fiddly controller for robot arms, applied to a three-joint manipulator. Their optimizer adds three tricks to an existing stochastic algorithm. A chaotic shuffle spreads starting guesses, a learning step flips candidates to speed convergence, and periodic long jumps near the best solution escape traps.

On a standard benchmark suite the tuner ranked first among twelve algorithms. In the robot test, tracking a looping figure-eight-style path, it produced the smallest tracking error of all rivals, settled fastest, and repeated its performance almost identically across runs. The authors present it as reliable automatic tuning for nonlinear robots facing disturbances.
pmc-13547421:
Yuanyuan Wang and colleagues fed mice a combined supplement of Rosa roxburghii fruit and kiwifruit for 28 days in 2026 to test claims of better stamina and faster recovery from fatigue. Fifty mice were split among resting controls, exercised controls, and three dose levels, then put through a swimming endurance test. Blood and tissue chemistry captured the usual fatigue markers and the body's fuel stores.

Supplemented mice swam longer, stored more glycogen in liver and muscle, and cleared exercise waste products faster, with lower urea nitrogen, lactic acid, and muscle damage enzymes. Oxidative stress markers fell while protective enzymes rose. No organ damage appeared. The authors credit fuel storage and oxidative balance for the effect, at least in mice.
pmc-13547621:
Do Thi Cat Tuong and colleagues reviewed in 2026 plant bioactive compounds as feed additives that might replace antibiotic growth promoters in livestock and poultry. These plant chemicals span phenolics, terpenoids, polysaccharides, and sulfur compounds, and studies link them to better growth, improved nutrient use, calmer gut communities, and antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial effects in farm animals.

The appeal is doing all of that without feeding drug resistance or endangering food safety. Practical hurdles remain: the right dose varies, absorption is inconsistent, compounds can break down during feed processing, and ingredients are hard to standardize from batch to batch. The review maps what is known, names the gaps, and sketches what must be solved before plant additives take a routine place in sustainable production.
pmc-13548621:
Mustafa Güneşdoğdu and Samet Hasan Abacı test a bay leaf oil preparation against the Varroa mite, the honeybee parasite behind many colony losses, in a 2026 field and modeling study. Beekeepers need alternatives to synthetic mite killers. The team turned laurel essential oil into a nanoemulsion, a fine droplet mix that stays stable and spreads well, then measured its chemistry and performance in real colonies.

The oil was dominated by 1,8-cineole at about forty percent. Droplets averaged roughly seventy nanometers and held together well. Mite numbers fell with dose, reaching about seventy percent control at the highest strength, clearly beating the standard drug used for comparison. Computer docking suggested the oil's parts grip a mite nerve enzyme tightly, supporting a poisoning mechanism. The authors present the preparation as a greener candidate for mite control.
pmc-13548721:
Seung-yoon Han and colleagues test whether the angle of the head relative to the neck can flag nonspecific neck pain in women factory workers, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Forward head posture is measured by this cervicovertebral angle from a side photograph. Among 135 workers, sixty-four had neck pain and seventy-one did not, and the team ran both logistic regression and decision tree models to find useful cutoffs.

Workers with pain held their heads about two degrees further forward on average. Each added degree of angle lowered the odds of pain slightly, even after adjusting for body size and age. Both models settled on a cutoff near fifty-one and a half degrees, with a second, lower tree threshold. Accuracy was modest, however. The authors advise treating the angle as a supplementary screening hint, never a diagnosis on its own.
pmc-13551721:
Wei Zhao, Rongjie Tang, Jing Tian, and Dengfeng Gao published a 2026 prospective cohort study of insulin resistance markers and heart disease risk in Chinese adults with early metabolic problems. Direct insulin resistance measurement is impractical in large groups, so eleven substitute scores built from glucose, lipids, and body measures were tested. Data came from a national aging study spanning 2011 to 2020, with marker levels in 2012 and 2015.

The authors compared single measurements, cumulative exposure across both time points, and trajectory patterns grouped by clustering. Survival models estimated risk of newly diagnosed cardiovascular disease, and curve analyses checked for nonlinear links. Their aim was to show whether long-term exposure and changing patterns predict risk better than one baseline reading in people with prediabetes, prehypertension, or early lipid problems.
pmc-13551821:
Xinchang Lun and ten colleagues tracked a fungal infection in mainland China in a 2026 study. The fungus, Talaromyces marneffei, was tracked in hospital patients from 2022 to 2024. Past work focused on HIV patients in narrow regions. Here the data came from sequencing tests on patients with acute lung infections. The team mapped where and when detection rose and what germs appeared with it.

The study covered 2,316 reported cases. Detection clustered in space and peaked twice a year. Men and people aged 41 to 50 were hit most. A yeast-like fungus was the top co-detected germ. Dew point, a humidity measure, explained nearly half the spatial pattern. Paired factors explained more than single ones. The team aims the results at surveillance in humid areas.
pmc-13551921:
Markus Harboe Olsen, with a large trial team, published a 2026 report on data checks in a trial of preterm infants. The SafeBoosC-III trial enrolled 1,601 infants at 70 sites. Site visits for data checks are costly and were strained by the pandemic. The trial used central checks instead. Staff ran monthly data reviews and completeness checks. Most errors were spotted by eye.

Central checks kept missing data near one percent of all data. Reviewers looked at close to 44,000 data points. They flagged a few hundred points for review. About a fifth of the flagged points were fixed after checks. The team argues that human review plus statistics guards trial truth. They call for standard rules for central checks in future trials.
pmc-13554021:
Yang Yang and Leilei Fan scan a fat-carrying protein, APOC1, across thirty-three cancers in a 2026 study. The protein had been tied to several cancers, yet its wider role stayed unclear. The team combined gene, protein, and drug data from large public banks. They also used tissue maps and single-cell data to find which cells make the protein.

High levels appeared in most cancers and meant worse outcomes in kidney, brain, and stomach tumours even after other factors were weighed. The source proved to be macrophages, immune cells that settle inside tumours. High levels came with both immune attack signals and immune brakes, plus more cells that suppress attack. Tumours rich in the protein answered some drugs poorly yet may suit others, a lead for paired immune therapy.
pmc-13554121:
Routhu Srinivasa Rao and three colleagues build a two-part learning model to find gut diseases in scope images in a 2026 report. Gut diseases carry a heavy global burden, and early spotting improves outcomes. Their design pairs a small image network, good at fine detail, with a larger one that reads the whole scene. An attention block then stresses the regions that matter most while muting background noise.

Tricks such as mixed training images and averaged weights steadied the learning. The finished model sorted images with accuracy above eighty-four percent overall. It beat single-network versions and other standard models on the same tests. Scores for rare classes also rose, which matters when some diseases appear far less often than others in clinic sets.
pmc-13554221:
Aflah Hanafiah leads a ten-author team uncovering a surprise role for a silencing protein group in waking genes up in a 2026 study. The group, a Polycomb complex, usually keeps genes quiet by folding DNA into loops. At genes marked as ready-but-waiting, those loops held the genes poised for action. Removing a key part of the complex broke the loops and stalled nerve cell growth.

A second protein, CTCF, gathered at the loop anchors and at Polycomb clusters. As stem-like cells became nerve precursors, loops passed from the Polycomb group to CTCF, switching genes on. The hand-off suggests poised loops are a planned first step, not mere silencing. The work reframes how cell identity changes are staged in the genome.
pmc-13558321:
Shan Zhuang, Peihua Zhang, and Yujie Feng charted in 2026 the burden of pancreatic cancer that strikes adults aged 20 to 54 in low- and middle-income countries. Data for this early-onset group are scarce even as overall cases climb. Drawing on the Global Burden of Disease 2023 study, they tracked cases, deaths, and years of life lost from 1990 to 2023. Trends were broken down by national income band, and rates were projected to 2050.

Cases rose by about one hundred twenty-five percent and deaths by a similar margin over the period. Lower-middle-income countries saw the steepest surge, and young women in poorer settings carried a heavier burden than their peers in rich regions, reversing the usual pattern. Inequality between countries widened, and the models expect age-adjusted rates to keep rising. The authors call for prevention and resources aimed deliberately at younger adults in poorer health systems.
pmc-13558721:
Demi Both and eleven colleagues showed in 2026 that engineered T cells kill lymphoma cells partly through a bursting form of death called necroptosis. The tidy apoptosis of the textbooks is only part of the story. The team exposed malignant B cells to bispecific antibodies that redirect T cells and to CAR T cells. Test material came from cell lines and from chronic lymphocytic leukaemia patients. Candidate death pathways were then blocked one by one.

The usual executioner enzymes proved dispensable, and familiar death signals from the T cells were ruled out. Microscopy showed a mixed appearance, and knocking out or chemically blocking the core necroptosis proteins confirmed that arm of the killing. Dying cells released a nuclear alarm protein, and the T cells released a blend of immune activators alongside calming molecules, in amounts that shifted with which death pathway was blocked. Tuning the balance could become a therapy dial.
pmc-13560221:
Sonoka Ichikawa and colleagues profile knee muscle characteristics in adolescent female soccer players, hunting for traits tied to injury risk. Their 2026 cross-sectional study tested 97 girls, 62 soccer players and 35 recreationally active controls, split into older and younger age bands. Dynamometer measures captured hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios in both static torque and dynamic power, while ultrasound graded the quality of two thigh muscles.

The soccer group showed a higher isometric strength ratio, 55.3 percent against 51.0 percent in controls in the pooled comparison. Dynamic power ratios, though, did not separate the groups, and neither did ultrasound measures of relative muscle quality. Age and leg dominance moved the dynamic ratio but not the static one. The authors conclude the two ratio types capture different aspects of knee function. Trained players, they note, do not automatically show distinct dynamic or resting muscle profiles.
pmc-13560421:
He Baixu, Wang Qing, and Xie Chunming argue that retinal infection with Chlamydia pneumoniae opens a window into Alzheimer's disease. Their 2026 perspective builds on a postmortem study of 104 cases spanning the full Alzheimer's spectrum, which found bacterial clumps in both retinal and brain tissue. The retina-brain parallel anchors their argument.

Bacterial load in the retina tracked closely with load in the cortex in the cited work. Retinal load ran nearly threefold higher in Alzheimer's dementia than in controls, tracked with the APOE ε4 risk variant and advancing Braak stage, and rose as mental test scores fell. The authors link the germ to inflammasome firing that could define part of the disease process. They pitch retinal infection as a low-burden test lead beside the amyloid-first view, and as a hint toward infection-inflammation treatment routes.
pmc-13561621:
Koji Matsushima and Fumi Saito report two women who ended up with airway narrowing after immediate reconstruction of both recurrent laryngeal nerves during thyroid surgery elsewhere. Their 2026 case report examines a complication of a technique that serves unilateral nerve injury well. Both women arrived with tracheostomies, referred for closure.

Muscle recordings explained the paradox: the rebuilt nerves fired during breathing in rather than during speech, a miswiring that pulls the airway shut. The team widened the rear airway with a laser technique that trims the rear airway cartilage from inside while sparing its surface. Breathing got better in both patients, both tracheostomies closed, and no narrowing came back over more than a year of follow-up. Voice and swallowing suffered little. The authors warn against bilateral immediate reconstruction in benign thyroid disease and suggest staging the sides instead.
pmc-13562721:
Su Ya Han and two colleagues ask what turns a casual online encounter with traditional culture into active efforts to pass that culture on. Their case is the Morin Khuur, the Mongolian horsehead fiddle, whose music now circulates on digital platforms. Reach alone does not guarantee participation. The 2026 study surveyed people who had recently met Morin Khuur content online, keeping 520 valid answers. A structural model tested two platform qualities, how interactive the experience feels and how present the viewer feels inside it, against flow, the absorbed state.

Both qualities fed flow, with path strengths of 0.410 and 0.521. Flow in turn predicted inheritance behaviour, sharing, learning, and promoting the tradition, at 0.551, and it carried the effect of both platform qualities. Prior cultural involvement did not act directly, yet it strengthened the flow-to-behaviour link. Designers of heritage platforms, the authors suggest, should engineer for absorption, not mere exposure.
pmc-13563821:
Yongguo Xie and five colleagues engineer a nanoparticle that fights acute lung injury on three fronts: inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death. The three feed each other in a loop that tears the barrier between air sacs and blood vessels, and no drug breaks it. Their 2026 platform loads esculin, an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant, into a porous crystal cage called ZIF-8, then coats the particle with polydopamine, a polymer that mops up reactive oxygen. The coating answers acidity, releasing cargo where injured tissue turns sour.

In cell and animal models of lung injury, the particles pooled in the lungs. Inflammation eased, oxidative damage fell, and lining cells survived, so the barrier held and breathing improved. Tracing the signals pinned the effect to the PI3K/AKT/GSK3β axis, which the treatment nudged toward calm. The authors present the design as a template for inflammatory lung disease.
pmc-13563921:
Jiapan Wang and many colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, how a circular RNA called circCDR1as may drive harmful heart muscle thickening that can lead to heart failure. Work in a mouse model of pressure overload, created by narrowing the aorta, was paired with protein studies and blood findings from patients.

The circular RNA was higher in patients with thickened hearts, and lowering it in mice eased heart dysfunction and reduced thickening after surgery. Raising it had the opposite effect in the experiments described. The RNA was found to interact with SERCA2a, a protein that handles calcium in heart cells. Readers get a step-by-step case for one molecular pathway worth testing further.
pmc-13572521:
Ronghao Yang, with eight colleagues, reports a 2026 investigation of the value of water ecosystems in Chuzhou, a city in the Jianghuai watershed of China. The area guards ecology along the middle and lower Yangtze River. The team priced what its lakes and rivers do for people, then weighed that value against economic growth from 2000 to 2022.

Satellite images yielded water maps through a snow-water index and an automatic threshold. A dynamic model then priced the services year by year. Water value first wobbled downward, then recovered across the two decades. The northwest of the city held high values, while the southeast ran low. Coordination between water value and output stayed healthy in the northwest. In the southeast, building land took water space and the balance worsened. The maps aim to guide growth that puts ecology first.
pmc-13574921:
Ivana Vecurkovska leads a 2026 pilot study on a blood protein in pancreatic cancer. The protein, TIMP-1, has links to tumour spread, yet its value in this cancer was not well defined. Pancreatic cancer is most often found late, after spread has already occurred and cure is unlikely.

The team measured TIMP-1 in blood and tissue from 154 patients, 108 with malignant tumours and 46 with benign growths. Levels ran higher in cancer, and blood levels ran higher still in patients whose disease had spread to distant sites. Blood testing separated groups somewhat better than tissue testing. The authors stress the gaps were modest, so TIMP-1 suits combined marker panels rather than use on its own.
pmc-13575021:
Mario Escobar Gómez leads a 2026 study of how pill features shape prostate cancer treatment choices in Mexico. The drugs in focus block the androgen receptor pathway, a key driver of this cancer. Features such as pill size, shape, count, and dosing schedule may affect whether patients keep taking them.

The work mixed a literature review, expert surveys and interviews, focus groups, and statistical modelling. Clinicians put dosing frequency at the top, with pill count next, among influences on adherence when drug effects were equal. Regimens of two pills or fewer per day, taken once daily, were favoured. Model results matched the expert views. The authors suggest patient-friendly formulations deserve a place in shared treatment decisions.
pmc-13575121:
Santosh Kumar Majhi and four colleagues present a computer method for spotting glaucoma from eye images in a 2026 paper. Glaucoma damages the optic nerve and is a leading cause of blindness that cannot be reversed. Reading retinal photos by hand is slow and can miss early signs.

Their method pulls two kinds of features from fundus images: texture patterns and a measure based on white pixel counts and fractal shape. Nine standard classifiers were tried, with four tuning methods used to sharpen the best two. The top pairing reached 97.55 percent accuracy using CatBoost and LightGBM classifiers. The authors offer the pipeline as a basis for automated screening of retinal images.
pmc-13575221:
Halil İbrahim Akçay reports a wire-free clot removal technique for stroke in a 2026 case series. Direct suction through a large catheter is now a first-line way to clear blocked brain arteries. The SNAKE technique advances the catheter without a guidewire or inner microcatheter, and this report tests it with a newer 0.071 inch catheter.

Fourteen patients with blocked arteries at the front of the brain were treated. Blood flow was restored to the target level in every patient, and over half cleared on the first pass. The average procedure took 12.1 minutes with a median of one pass. Stroke severity scores fell sharply within a day, and 78.6 percent of patients were functionally independent at 90 days. Clots did break off downstream in 42.9 percent of cases, yet final flow held in all.
pmc-13575321:
Halison Correia Golias warns in a 2026 commentary that dengue vaccination in Brazil could quietly weaken mosquito control. Brazil was the first country to offer dengue vaccine through its public health system, starting in February 2024 and reaching 1,921 municipalities. Two vaccines are approved, with a third still in trials.

His concern is risk compensation: people who feel protected may stop clearing breeding sites and join clean-up efforts less. Officials might also scale back campaigns. The mosquito Aedes aegypti spreads chikungunya and Zika as well, and no widely available vaccines exist for those diseases. Golias argues vaccination must be paired with sustained vector control, not treated as a replacement, or mosquito numbers and other diseases could climb.
pmc-13578021:
Enno Schmidt and three colleagues compare four itchy skin diseases that look unrelated on the surface in a 2026 review. The set is bullous pemphigoid, a blistering disease of older adults; chronic spontaneous urticaria, with recurring hives; prurigo nodularis, with hard itchy nodules; and chronic prurigo of unknown origin. All four carry heavy burden and few good long-term treatments.

The review traces a shared thread: type 2 inflammation, an immune pattern also seen in allergy, woven together with nerve circuits that drive itch. Each disease reaches that pattern by its own route, from autoantibodies and complement in pemphigoid to overactive mast cells in urticaria and a self-feeding itch-scratch loop in nodular disease. Drugs that block type 2 drivers are now being tested or used across the group. The authors map which targets fit which disease.
pmc-13578221:
Shareefa Mohammedali and co-authors set out a 2026 lab method for cloning top coconut palms without a callus stage, the lump of loose cells that can scramble genes in new plants. The team took young flower spikes from West Coast Tall palms aged 25 to 30 years and cut them into tiny segments for culture in the dark.

Three base media and varied growth chemicals were tried over eight months of culture. One mix on a woody plant medium sparked the most buds with the least browning, and a later mix drove shoot growth and leaf number. Roots formed best on a weaker salt mix with two rooting chemicals. DNA checks showed the new plantlets matched their mother palms closely.
pmc-13578321:
Flurin L. Brand and colleagues pitted seventeen dermatologists against four freely available general-purpose AI chat systems on diagnosing nail disorders from clinical photographs. Dermatologists named the leading diagnosis correctly in 70.6 percent of cases, rising to 80.3 percent when their differential diagnoses were also counted. Accuracy climbed with experience, from residents at 68.3 percent to nail experts at 96.0 percent on the broader measure.

The AI systems managed only 25.0 percent on the leading diagnosis and 35.0 percent on the broader measure, with tumors identified far less often than non-tumors. The authors conclude that current general-purpose AI tools are too unreliable to diagnose nail disease alone and should be used, if at all, only under clinical supervision.
pmc-13578721:
Ceilidh Jenkins and colleagues ask whether an aging stallion sires slower racehorses, in a 2026 study of Australian Thoroughbred records. Breeding data covered 35 retired stallions and more than thirty three thousand offspring. The team linked each foal to the sire's age at conception, then tracked whether the foal raced and how it fared in top grade stakes races.

Foals conceived when sires were eight or younger were far more likely to reach the track than foals of sires aged nineteen or more. The young sire edge grew even larger for placing or winning in stakes races. The pattern is a population link, not proof of cause, and the records cannot show the sperm level changes that may drive it. Breeders weighing long careers for popular sires get a clear signal here.
pmc-13579721:
Dayan Liu and colleagues build a calculator that flags heart bypass patients likely to linger in intensive care, in a 2026 study. Long ICU stays after bypass surgery strain beds and budgets, and the call must be made at the one day check. Records came from two large critical care databases, one used to build the model and one held back for a cold test.

Eight bedside facts from the first day fed the model, led by fluid intake, overall illness load, and a rhythm fault. A boosting model won a nine way race. It sorted risk fairly at home, with well matched odds, and kept its calibration abroad though its sorting dipped. A web calculator shows each patient's drivers one by one. The authors pitch it as honest decision support, not a verdict.
pmc-13579821:
B Doğan and colleagues test whether a bedside score, read twice, can warn that mask ventilation is failing in emergency care, in a 2026 study. One hundred six adults with sudden breathing failure got noninvasive support in the emergency department. A five part score covering heart rate, oxygen need, breathing rate, and alertness was taken before the mask and again one hour in.

Half the patients ended up failing the treatment. Starting scores could not split winners from losers. The one hour score and, even better, the change over that hour did sort them well. Patients whose score flatlined or rose failed at over twice the rate of those whose score fell. Each point of rise added clear risk. The authors urge repeat scoring in the first hour, not a single snapshot.
pmc-13582221:
Graziano Onder and a large national team count unmet comfort care needs in Italian hospitals and care homes, in a 2026 snapshot study. A validated checklist flagged needs in 5,389 adults across 235 sites on a single census sweep. Hospital patients averaged eighty one years old; care home residents averaged eighty six.

Well over half of hospital patients flagged positive for palliative needs, as did about half of care home residents. Cancer patients flagged highest, yet half of those without cancer flagged too, which breaks the hospice only stereotype. Function loss led the sign list, with feeding trouble, confusion, sores, and clear pain all common. The authors call for routine screening and comfort care woven into wards and homes, not bolted on at the end.
pmc-13582721:
Riley Leckie and colleagues tested if watch on one's own thought helps people handle feelings. In a first test with 226 people, scores on how well faith matched truth in a sight task were set beside scores on a test of feeling-handling know-how. Good match went with better feeling-handling, while broad over-faith went with worse scores.

A second test with 200 people gave half the group a nudge to rate their faith while they did the feeling-handling test, and half no nudge. The nudged group scored far better, which shows cause, not just a link. A plain faith-rating nudge may thus give a cheap way to boost feeling skill.
pmc-13584521:
Xu Tian and colleagues survey moral resilience among cancer nurses in China in this 2026 study. Oncology nurses face hard choices daily around strong treatments, which can leave lasting moral strain. Moral resilience names the capacity to hold to one's values under that strain. An online survey reached 466 nurses in 2023 and scored both resilience and burnout with standard scales.

Resilience landed near the middle of its scale, while burnout scores ran fairly high. The two moved in opposite directions with a strong tie: nurses with more burnout showed far less resilience. Sex and schooling also shaped resilience scores. The authors argue that managers should build resilience on purpose, since it may shield nurses from burnout and keep care quality steady for patients who need it most.
pmc-13584821:
Jamie Swaine and colleagues teach a language-style AI model to invent new layered materials in this 2026 study. The materials are MAX phases, hard ceramic-metal mixes that can be peeled into thin sheets called MXenes with many uses. The possible recipes number in the thousands, so testing each one in a lab would take far too long.

Their model was tuned on more than six thousand known recipes with two metal sites. Given target settings for sheet-forming promise and bond strength, it produced new recipes at double the rate of untargeted runs. Ten fresh recipes were checked with detailed physics calculations, and five held up as stable or nearly stable. The authors present the method as a scalable way to aim invention at the parts of a design space that matter most.
pmc-13590121:
Lucas E Sainburg and nine colleagues offer, in 2026, a brain scan measure that may find the seizure source in drug resistant epilepsy without extra gear. Finding that source guides surgery, yet the usual method pairs brain scans with scalp recordings and needs rare skill. The team instead tracked how links between brain areas shift over time in scan data. Sharp drops in those links seemed to mark seizure like activity between seizures.

They turned the rate of such drops into an index and tested it in 62 patients. Scores ran high in the inner temporal lobe of people with temporal lobe epilepsy, matching known seizure zones. Patients whose surgery removed high scoring tissue fared better afterward. The gain held even when scans showed no clear lesion.
pmc-13590521:
Daniel J. Ford and colleagues recalculated the world's surface-ocean carbon dioxide atlas to a single consistent temperature and depth. SOCAT gathers CO2 measurements from ships, buoys, drones, and yachts, but different platforms sample different depths, and some sensors warm the water they measure. Those quirks bias estimates of how much CO2 the ocean absorbs. Their 2026 study recalculated the SOCATv2025 database to a reference temperature at 0.2 metres depth using a satellite climate record.

The recalculation kept each CO2 reading paired with its temperature and captured temperature-driven chemistry changes. Removing the warm bias raised the estimated 2024 ocean CO2 sink by about 0.4 petagrams of carbon per year, roughly 12 percent, to 3.4 petagrams. The authors will routinely provide recalculated products with each annual SOCAT release for carbon assessments.
pmc-13591521:
Sabina Kumar and colleagues report a registry analysis, published in 2026. It asks whether a Michigan quality programme raised imaging-guided heart procedures equally in both sexes. The procedures are called PCI. They open blocked heart arteries. Guidance uses imaging from inside the vessel. It improves outcomes. Uptake had been low before the statewide BMC2 initiative began in 2020.

More than 170,000 procedures were covered. They ran at 51 hospitals from 2019 to 2024. Imaging guidance rose sharply in women and men. It rose from under ten percent toward the mid-forty percent range. Annual trends did not differ significantly by sex. The authors read this as equitable uptake under a system-wide push.
pmc-13592021:
Fábio J N Ferreira and two colleagues simulate how a cancer fighting plant derived compound slips through a cell membrane without help. Crossing the fatty wall passively decides how much drug reaches its target. Their test compound, a lab tweaked naphthoquinone, had shown cell killing power in early work. Using heavy computer sampling on a four part model membrane, they mapped both the energy cost and the local speed of crossing at each depth.

The compound settled happily at the membrane surface yet faced a steep energy hill at the center. Energy unevenness and depth dependent slowing each raised crossing resistance more than tenfold. Two cousin compounds showed contrasting patterns. Ferreira and the team say separating energy and mobility maps can sharpen drug design.
pmc-13592321:
Mohamed Niyaz Vellala Syed Ali and six colleagues report, in 2026, a ruthenium catalyst that upgrades only the end double bonds in a mixture, sparing inner ones entirely. The reaction, hydroformylation, adds carbon monoxide and hydrogen to make aldehydes for plastics and scents. Industry leans on pricey rhodium with phosphorus ligands. Their system pairs simple ruthenium carbonyls with a common base, no phosphorus at all, and works under mild settings.

Spectroscopy caught the active form: a four ruthenium cluster carrying hydrogen, isolated and reused with the same behavior. Inner and crowded double bonds sat untouched even in messy factory feedstocks, a discrimination the team calls unmatched. Cheap, air stable parts plus that sharp aim make the system a strong rival to the rhodium standard.
pmc-13592421:
Marvin Krüner and eight colleagues write, in 2026, phase patterns into atom thin molybdenum disulfide films made by a low heat layer by layer process. The crystal can sit in a semiconducting phase or a metallic one, and devices gain when each patch can be chosen. Focused beams of lithium and gallium ions flipped treated zones into new phases with fine accuracy. The written films stayed stable over the long term, a must for factory use.

An ultrashort pulse laser then rewrote the zones back to the semiconducting phase. Krüner and the team frame the pair of tools as a reversible pen and eraser for phase. Such direct writing could let future flexible circuits define function by crystal phase rather than by stacked materials.
pmc-13592721:
Matthieu Marfoglia and five colleagues present AlloPool, a deep learning system that reads protein motion from simulation movies. A protein's job depends on shape shifting, and distant parts of the chain talk to each other through allostery, yet training data for such motion stays scarce. Their graph network treats amino acids as nodes, then prunes links again and again to expose the smallest interaction webs that drive each transition. Time aware attention tracks how those webs evolve.

Across binding domains, force sensors, signaling receptors, and enzymes, the system rebuilt motion paths more faithfully than rival learning methods. It also mapped communication routes and predicted how binding, force, or mutation would ripple through a protein. Marfoglia and the team offer it as a general lens for drug design and protein engineering.
pmc-13595521:
Huan Yu and colleagues followed twenty-five geriatric service management undergraduates through a nine-week course on death-related topics, tracking how their attitudes and self-view shifted. Their 2026 mixed-methods study, framed by terror management theory, measured death attitudes, self-esteem, and life purpose at three points and then interviewed the students.

Overall death attitude barely moved, yet its parts churned: fear rose early in the course, then fell below its start by the end, while calm acceptance steadily grew. A belief-based form of acceptance dipped early and recovered. Self-esteem improved at every step, the most consistent change in the study, and purpose in life rose as well. Interviews helped explain the arc, suggesting students first wrestle with the material before integrating it. The authors see structured death education as ultimately strengthening for students headed into elder care.
pmc-13597021:
Kapil Goel and colleagues lay out a two-phase feasibility study for getting Indian adolescent girls to adopt reusable menstrual products, menstrual cups and period underwear, against the drag of taboo and misinformation. The plan trains forty community health workers and female teachers first, then sends them to educate 912 girls at two contrasting Indian sites.

A subset of 406 girls will receive a cup or the underwear and be followed for a year through diaries, home visits, and discussion groups, recording acceptance and lived experience. The study also measures several other things. It tracks whether training changes the workers' own knowledge and attitudes. It tracks whether the campaigns shift girls' readiness. It also prices the products per unit of health gained, using a standard quality of life questionnaire. Behavior change frameworks structure the analysis. The authors aim to learn whether community-led promotion can scale.
pmc-13597521:
Nicole C. Strock and co-authors reviewed which fitness measures actually predict how well astronauts perform simulated spacewalk tasks, groundwork for keeping crews safe on the Moon and Mars. Their 2026 review gathered twelve studies with 366 participants, astronauts and stand-ins, linking heart-lung and muscle fitness to task outcomes.

Thirty-eight fitness metrics appeared across the studies. Eight heart-lung and twelve muscle measures showed real links with simulated spacewalk performance or its intensity. The quality of the studies behind them was checked with a standard tool. With Artemis missions planning longer and more frequent surface excursions than Apollo ever attempted, and suits growing larger, the authors say the identified metrics can guide exercise countermeasures. They can also guide the monitoring systems that watch crew fitness through a mission.
pmc-13598021:
Wen-jie Huo and co-authors argue that an embryo's growth path from day two to day three predicts its future better than a day-three snapshot of cell count. Their 2026 study built a ranking from more than twenty-seven thousand embryos at one center. It was validated on 1,691 single embryo transfers at three centers.

Trajectory reversed the usual pecking order. Embryos reaching nine to sixteen cells by day three outperformed textbook eight-cell embryos. The winners had started from a normal four cells on day two. They posted the highest top-quality blastocyst rate of any path. Four tiers were distilled from the trajectories. The top tier carried roughly double the second tier's adjusted odds of clinical pregnancy. The trajectory score beat day-three counts at predicting both blastocyst quality and pregnancy. The authors offer it for women up to thirty-eight choosing which embryo to transfer.
pmc-13601421:
Shoba Ekambaram leads a large team reporting in 2026 that blood from time-restricted eaters can reprogram brain blood vessel cells in the lab. Time-restricted eating improves metabolic and vascular health, but how it might protect the brain's small vessels was unclear. Damage to those vessels feeds vascular cognitive impairment and dementia. The team tested whether blood-borne factors carry the benefit.

Serum from older adults on a restricted schedule was applied to human brain microvessel cells, and gene activity was profiled. The treated cells switched on stress-response and metabolic pathways, raised the stress signal GDF15, and quieted growth programs driven by the mTORC1 pathway. Mitochondrial energy genes rose without a full cell-building response, pointing to remodeling rather than growth. Vessel repair and barrier upkeep programs did not switch on as a group. The pattern reads as stress adaptation shipped through the bloodstream.
pmc-13601621:
Ángela González-Cebrián and four colleagues release PituPhase65 in 2026, a public dataset of pituitary surgery videos labeled by surgical phase. Systems that recognize which step of an operation is underway could coach trainees, coordinate operating rooms, and draft procedure notes. Pituitary surgery through the nose is less standardized than many operations, so models need plenty of labeled examples to learn from. Recordings came from Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre in Madrid.

The dataset holds 65 endoscopic pituitary operations averaging 90 minutes each. Every recording is divided into eight phases, from the out-of-patient start to dural closure. The authors describe it as the largest labeled collection of its kind for this surgery. They offer it openly so research groups can train and compare phase-recognition models on shared material, a step they see as necessary before such tools can support real operating rooms.
pmc-13601821:
Joseph Matthew Holden and David John Calkins describe a surprising structure inside the support cells of the mouse retina. Voltage-gated sodium channels are famous for carrying electrical signals in neurons and muscle. Using super-resolution microscopy, electrical recordings, and gene activity analysis, the pair found dense NaV1.6 channel clusters inside retinal astrocytes, the eye's star-shaped support cells.

The clusters sit in pockets facing the retinal ganglion cell neurons, in zones lacking a protein that usually spreads throughout the astrocyte. These pockets are packed with oversized mitochondria sitting close against the channel clusters. The same compartments accumulate high levels of GABA, a signaling chemical better known from neurons. The authors argue this channel-mitochondria complex gives astrocytes a metabolic role no one had assigned them, beyond firing electrical signals. The finding may matter for diseases where retinal support cells are involved.
pmc-13609621:
Mariel Monrroy and four colleagues catalog the tiny eukaryotes living in Panama's farm soils. These tiny organisms, from fungi to single-celled grazers, drive nutrient cycling and soil fertility, yet tropical farmland communities were barely described. Using DNA metabarcoding, the team characterized them in soil samples from 44 sites across three farm regions of the country.

Sequencing turned up 7,714 distinct sequence groups. The high-altitude region held much richer communities apart from the lowlands, and ordination split samples into two major clusters along that altitude line. Diversity tracked soil phosphorus, electrical conductivity, and slope. The authors caution that species-level names from single-gene barcoding rest on operational groupings. Even so, they present a first map of tropical farm soil microeukaryotes and a case for folding nature checks into soil management.
pmc-13612221:
Mina Kashima leads a fourteen-author team introducing a chart to help counselors judge if a tumor variant was inherited. Tumor-only gene panels often flag variants in hereditary cancer genes, but telling a born-with-it germline variant from a tumor-acquired one is hard, and confirmatory testing is costly and often uninsured. Their graph plots each variant's allele frequency against the tumor's purity, with lines from the classic two-hit model.

The team reviewed patients tested with tumor-only and paired tumor-normal panels between 2018 and 2025. Of 103 patients, 35 carried confirmed germline variants. Patterns matched the two-hit model in 18 of those 35 cases, including loss of the second copy in 12 of 22 BRCA1/2 variants. Four of eight cases in other genes carried two variants along the germline and somatic lines. Hypermutated tumors scattered along the somatic line instead. The authors offer the graph as a shared visual language for counseling.
pmc-13612921:
Etsuko Yoshikawa and colleagues describe in 2026 how an international training program for workplace health facilitators was rebuilt after the COVID-19 pandemic broke up its long-running network. The training style, called participatory action-oriented training, teaches people to lead practical fixes for safer and healthier workplaces. The study followed the rebuilding through two rounds of action and reflection.

Organizers, 79 participants, and researchers shared reports, meeting notes, and committee papers, which the team compared across sources. Lessons from the first post-pandemic course reshaped the second one. Readers who run cross-border training get a concrete account of what restarting a network takes. They also learn what new facilitators gain, and which supports keep such programs alive after a long forced pause.
pmc-13614821:
Shweta Singh and colleagues describe a 2026 case of a newborn whose right adrenal gland burst shortly after birth, causing bleeding that threatened his life. Adrenal bleeding in newborns is rare. This boy, born at full term by vaginal birth, fell ill on his first day with breathing trouble and shock. Checks found severe paleness, a swollen belly, and a tender lump in his flank. Scans showed a large pool of blood beside the kidney and no clear adrenal shadow.

The team weighed kidney swelling, cysts, tumors, and clots before settling on adrenal rupture as the cause. Fast fluids, drugs to support blood pressure, and four units of transfused red blood cells steadied the infant. Careful watchful care without surgery led to a good outcome. Clinicians should keep adrenal bleeding in mind when a newborn arrives in shock with a flank mass, since it can look much like a kidney disorder.
pmc-13615121:
Anas Bassam Barnawi and colleagues gather in 2026 what is known about platelet-rich plasma squirted into the nose as a treatment for lasting loss of smell. The plasma, drawn from the patient's own blood, is rich in growth factors that may help damaged smell tissue heal. Their review and pooled analysis of studies from 2010 to 2025 covered smell loss lasting over six months.

Seven studies with 473 people qualified. In the controlled studies, with 314 people, smell test scores improved by a moderate, clear margin over controls. The average gain of 7.73 points on the smell scale beat the 5.5-point mark classed as noticeable to patients. Few options exist for this frustrating condition, so a simple clinic treatment with gains patients can feel deserves the careful testing the authors call for.
pmc-13616121:
Chunhui Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a six-year-old boy whose jaw cyst around an unerupted first molar shrank and vanished without surgery. He was referred because a lower left back tooth was late to appear. Scans showed a clear hollow area, about 22 by 18 millimetres, around the crown of the buried molar, diagnosed as a dentigerous cyst. The tooth still had power to erupt, and no solid bone blocked its path.

The team chose watchful follow-up over an operation. At six months the cyst had shrunk, and after two years the tooth had erupted on its own and the cyst was gone. Surgery remains the standard for such cysts, yet this case shows that careful waiting can spare some young children an operation when the tooth is well placed to break through.
pmc-13616621:
Jindan Hou, Hanyi Zheng, and Shaoshuo Cai study a cute Thai-boxing chicken character, the Muay Thai DunDun Chicken. They ask how it wins fans across cultures on Douyin and TikTok. Those are China's and the world's sister video platforms. Cute intellectual property travels globally, yet why it resonates was unclear. The team analysed 446 high-engagement videos and about 332,000 characters of user comments, sorting feelings and themes and comparing the two platforms.

Cuteness, framed by the Japanese idea of moe, acted as a shared emotional trigger that fired instant warmth across borders. What fans made of the character, though, bent to each culture's own frames, rituals, and fan habits. Brands chasing global reach get a two-part lesson: the first emotional spark may be universal, while the community built around it must be grown locally.
pmc-13617421:
Andrew Kurtzman and five colleagues study fracture risk in dogs treated with palliative radiation for appendicular osteosarcoma, a common bone cancer of large breeds. Radiation can weaken bone, and low-dose-rate delivery spares late-responding tissues, raising the question of whether it changes fracture rates or tumor control. The retrospective study compared dogs irradiated by cobalt units at low dose rates with dogs treated on linear accelerators at standard rates.

About one in five dogs suffered a pathologic fracture, and the two dose-rate groups did not differ in fracture rate or in survival, which ran to roughly eight months in both. Body weight and tumor location did not predict fracture, and no dog under twenty kilograms fractured. Surprisingly, pre-treatment X-ray appearance did not forecast fracture either. Added chemotherapy did lengthen survival, and results from cobalt-era studies can be compared with modern reports.
pmc-13617621:
Miao Miao and Zhaoxi Wang survey a 2026 research direction with a double payoff. At stake is succinic acid, a versatile industrial building block used in plastics, medicines, and food additives, made from carbon dioxide instead of fossil fuels or fermentation. Their review organizes the field around a single chain, in which electricity-driven steps first convert carbon dioxide into intermediate chemicals and heat-driven catalysis then upgrades those intermediates to the final acid.

Gas intermediates such as ethylene, carbon monoxide, and hydrogen, liquid ones such as acetic acid, and alcohol routes each get assessed for feasibility, conditions, and bottlenecks. The four-carbon route through maleic anhydride looks most feasible in the near term, while gas-liquid oxidative carbonylation offers the strongest potential for integrated plants. The authors offer the framework as guidance for building succinic acid production that is both scalable and carbon-cutting.
pmc-13617821:
Ye, Zheng, and Ye examine in 2026 whether adverse childhood experiences, the harmful events of childhood such as abuse or household dysfunction, speed up aging decades later in China. They use a national survey of middle-aged and older adults.

The analysis covered 8,327 participants aged 45 and older in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. Biological age was estimated from 2011 biomarkers, and childhood experiences were reported in a 2014 life history survey. Each additional type of childhood adversity raised the odds of accelerated aging by about five percent in the adjusted models they fitted for this cohort. People reporting four or more types had clearly higher odds still, and the risk rose steadily with the count, a dose-response pattern. The link looked similar across demographic, lifestyle, and disease subgroups.
pmc-13618521:
Bajramshahe Shkodra and eleven colleagues build a graphene transistor sensor that measures cortisol, the primary stress hormone, directly in human saliva within minutes. Standard hormone testing needs centralized laboratories and slow protocols, which blocks real-time or bedside use. Their chip uses electrolyte-gated graphene field-effect transistors, coated with linker molecules that anchor antibody fragments designed to grab cortisol specifically.

The sensor responded across a wide dynamic range spanning the concentrations found in human saliva, from one hundred femtomolar up to one micromolar. On the same real samples, its readings correlated strongly with the standard laboratory ELISA test run in parallel. Detection is label-free and fast, about ten minutes, which the authors call a major step for miniaturized biosensing. They see the platform extending to other biomarkers and eventually to portable units for real-time stress monitoring outside the laboratory.
pmc-13618921:
Allameddine Allameddine and Andrea Piccin propose Donor Blood Management, a framework to protect the value of donated blood all the way from the donor's arm to the patient's vein. Patient Blood Management transformed how hospitals use blood, yet nothing like it guards the donor side, where value leaks away through collection and processing losses, inventory waste, expiry, handling errors, and misuse. The authors define donor value broadly: the gift itself plus the donor's time and trust.

Their framework rests on four pillars: optimizing collection and processing, optimizing inventory, ensuring fitting utilization, and haemovigilance with continuous improvement. Accountability is shared among blood services, hospitals, clinicians, and regulators. They also propose a stewardship metric, the Donor-to-Recipient Value Yield, the share of donated blood that ends up transfused well. It is meant to read linked donor-to-recipient data for quality gains, adding to rather than replacing existing tracking systems.
pmc-13620221:
Raphaëlle Abensur and seven colleagues used sixty camera traps to watch fruit-eating animals at nutmeg trees in three French Guiana forests with different disturbance histories. One site is protected mature forest, one was logged in the past, and one sits near a road with ongoing hunting and logging. Cameras covered both the canopy and the forest floor.

Species counts barely budged across sites, with about twenty species in the canopy and fifteen below. Visiting rates told another story: ground visits fell steeply as disturbance rose, while canopy visits climbed. The busiest disturbed canopy belonged largely to kinkajous and small tamarin monkeys. Down below, hunted and slow-breeding species such as white-lipped peccaries and trumpeter birds nearly vanished from the most disturbed site. The authors say head counts alone would miss this hollowing out, and they credit protected forest with keeping the full community working.
pmc-13620421:
Sacha E Gandhi and three colleagues report new movement symptoms in a man with a PTEN gene variant, a condition known for overgrowth and tumor risk. His story began at thirty-three with an action tremor in one arm plus mild abnormal posturing. Both he and his daughter had large heads, and her scans showed white matter changes like his.

Through his forties the tremor spread and resting tremor appeared, yet clear parkinsonism stayed absent for years. By forty-nine he showed slowness, a masked face, and a shuffling walk with lost arm swing. A dopamine transporter scan showed reduced signal on both sides of the brain. Gene testing found no other parkinsonism gene and confirmed the PTEN change. Levodopa treatment brought clear gains in tremor, slowness, and gait. The authors propose PTEN may help drive this form of parkinsonism, widening the syndrome's known nerve features.
pmc-13621521:
Richard L Lieber, David J Reinkensmeyer, Joel W Burdick, and Arun Jayaraman memorialize V. Reggie Edgerton, the physiologist who recast the spinal cord as a learning organ. Edgerton died in March 2026 at eighty-five. Trained as an exercise scientist, he built his career on the idea that spinal networks below an injury can process sensation and relearn movement, much like a small brain.

The tribute traces his locomotor training work, from manually moving the limbs of spinal-injured rats toward the robotic rat stepper of the late nineteen-nineties. Later came human gait-training robots and an exoskeleton case that restored some voluntary control in chronic paralysis. It also covers his push into neuromodulation, pairing electrical stimulation with training as a therapy. The authors credit his persistence with opening a new era of rehabilitation engineering that still shapes devices in clinics and labs today.
pmc-13621621:
Xiaoyan Huang and Qian Zhu report, in 2026, the first documented case of internal abdominal bleeding caused by tissue left behind after a medical abortion. A thirty-three-year-old woman arrived with sudden heavy vaginal bleeding and mild abdominal pain thirty-three days after ending a first-trimester pregnancy with the standard two-drug regimen. Ultrasound showed a mass inside her uterus plus a significant pool of blood in her abdomen.

Surgeons performed emergency scraping of the uterus, and tissue examination confirmed retained products of conception with degenerated pregnancy villi. The authors propose that blood escaped backward through a fallopian tube from the retained tissue, a route clinicians rarely consider. Blood in the abdomen in women of childbearing age usually points to a burst cyst or a tubal pregnancy. Their message: after abortion care, retained tissue belongs on that differential list, since the disguise invites dangerous misdiagnosis.
pmc-13623521:
Zhu and colleagues launch in 2026 AIDrugDesigner, a free web server that puts deep learning molecule design within reach of researchers who cannot code or maintain model software. Designing molecules with preset properties is central to drug discovery and notoriously slow by hand.

The server has two modules. The generation module creates candidate molecules four ways: aimed at a chosen target, guided by a pharmacophore pattern, conditioned on desired properties, or by designing the linker between two fragments. The optimization module then polishes molecules a user supplies, improving drug-likeness, the fat-water balance measure called LogP, and ease of synthesis. Tests across several design tasks showed the platform's versatility. By wrapping many generative strategies in one interface, the authors aim to lower the technical barrier to AI-assisted drug design.
pmc-13624021:
Ratchada Kitsommart and colleagues run a randomised trial in Bangkok, Thailand, testing whether a glucose solution given by mouth can treat low blood sugar in newborns who show no symptoms. At-risk babies born late-preterm or at term often dip in blood sugar after birth; the standard fix, intravenous glucose, separates mother and baby and needs a drip line.

Four hundred babies whose blood sugar stayed low after a first feed received either the glucose solution on the cheek lining or a placebo, followed by feeding, in a double-blind design. Fewer babies in the glucose group needed intravenous treatment, but the gap was small enough to be chance. Blood sugar climbed higher after treatment in the glucose group, no baby overshot into high sugar. Older newborns and those born small or large responded less. The authors say the solution's clinical role needs more study.
pmc-13624321:
Xianfeng Ye and colleagues describe a three-bacterium team from cucumber root soil that protects the plant against Fusarium wilt, a fungal disease. The partners, strains of Achromobacter, Bacillus, and Flavobacterium, feed each other: the Flavobacterium member cannot make one amino acid it needs and depends on the others, a dependency organising the alliance.

Inside the partnership, the other two strains handle most carbon and nitrogen processing while the dependent partner quiets those same functions. Together they build layered biofilms, structured films on the root surface, far better than any strain alone, and that architecture lets two of the partners slip inside the root and live there. Once resident, the Flavobacterium switches on the plant's system-wide defences, priming it against fungal attack. The authors present cross-feeding dependency, usually seen as a weakness, as an engineering principle for building protective microbe teams for farming.
pmc-13624421:
Lirong Liang and co-authors trace how a common anesthesia drug can leave lasting marks on the young brain. Baby mice breathed sevoflurane for two hours a day over three days early in life. As adults, those mice showed damage in the hippocampus, a brain area tied to memory and social recognition, and they performed worse on memory tests.

The damage centered on perineuronal nets, mesh-like coatings that wrap certain nerve cells and limit their change. Sevoflurane lifted a chemical brake on a gene that makes MMP9, an enzyme that chewed up those nets. Restoring a net-building protein or blocking MMP9 protected the nets, steadied cell connections, and reversed the memory problems, pointing to a way to guard infants under anesthesia.
pmc-13624821:
